title: Research
text:
These applied research studies tackle concrete machine-learning problems, from identity-preserving fine-tuning and controlled image generation to scalable clustering of large malware corpora. Each study (except clustering) follows an end-to-end workflow spanning problem formulation, experimental design, model adaptation, hyperparameter optimization, quantitative evaluation, and error analysis.
The work applies foundation models such as FLUX.1-dev using parameter-efficient fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and controlled generation with ControlNet. Experiments are evaluated against explicit metrics, including face similarity and image-text similarity. Findings are grounded in systematic experiments and reproducible evaluation, with documented trade-offs, limitations, and failure modes.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
Question: A Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) trained on a person’s images (persona-LoRA) controls the persona’s identity fidelity in images generated by a base model like FLUX.1-dev, while a ControlNet guided by a control image controls their spatial structure. Applied together, do the two conflict, what does each trade, and which conditioning strengths are optimal?
Design:

Conditioning: FLUX.1-dev with a persona-LoRA and a ControlNet conditioned on the template. Five configurations vary, the guidance scale (gs), the LoRA scale (ls) and the canny, depth and pose scales (cs, ds, ps), plus the seed; the three ControlNet scales are the control modes and their total the conditioning sum.
Scoring: Identity fidelity is scored by a face-similarity service against held-out reference photographs, 0–100 (face_sim); template adherence compares the image with the template on edges (canny_f1), depth (depth_corr) and pose (pose_sim).
Search: Two branches, one per ControlNet implementation, the Union-Pro ControlNet and the FLUX.1 Control LoRA (control-LoRA), in stages, each a set of configuration grids (sweeps) scored and refined before the next; twenty-one sweeps, 2,716 images, nine personas and 21 templates in all. Every score is compared with measured floors, ceilings and seed noise.

Findings: All but the last group are about the Union-Pro ControlNet.
Guidance and LoRA scales:

Guidance changes both axes in the same direction, frozen at 6: Identity increases and template adherence is preserved or increases until 6, and most of the step-to-7 gains do not clear the seed noise (Section 6.1).
No strong evidence for a LoRA scale other than the trained 1.0, frozen there: Increasing it decreases identity and edge fidelity together, and every change inside the refinements is inside its seed noise (Section 6.1).

Conditioning mode: canny alone:

The scale induces the trade-off; the optimal grid is cs ≈ 0.40: Increasing it decreases identity and increases template adherence in every stage; at 0.40 identity is still usable and the structure scores stop increasing beyond seed noise (Section 6.1, Section 6.9).
A higher scale increases seed noise on identity and suppresses it on depth and pose: At cs 0.60 only four of ten seeds retain the usable 80 face_sim (Section 6.2).
One value is not suitable for every persona-LoRA: The same step increases structure for all six but decreases identity unevenly, from none to a large loss, so a set of values selected on the measured scores carries forward (Section 6.3).

Conditioning mode: canny with depth:

The optimal grid is the frozen quadrant, which persists across personas and templates and cannot be restricted to one cell: With both scales at 0.25 or 0.30 (frozen quadrant), the per-sum mean identity stays usable at every conditioning sum and every persona-LoRA and template retains the trade-off’s direction; further restriction to one cell alone fails the structure floors on about half of fifteen templates (Section 6.5).
The frozen quadrant ends one step before an identity cliff, at or below the floor of the model card’s recommended range: Inside the quadrant identity decreases moderately and past it collapses (identity cliff), by an amount that varies across persona-LoRAs and cannot be predicted from their identity before it. The quadrant with gs 6 and ls 1.0 (frozen configuration) retains identity for four of six persona-LoRAs; two decrease inside it (Section 6.9).
The template sets the absolute depth and pose scores; on any mode depth_corr is the weakest discriminator: In the frozen quadrant templates are further apart on pose_sim than the conditioning sum changes it; depth_corr’s small floor-to-ceiling span makes it a tie breaker only (Section 6.10).

Conditioning mode: canny, depth and pose:

The optimal grid is the conditioning sum band 0.80–0.85: The pose scale is at 0.5–0.6 and the other two at most 0.25 each; identity stays usable on all six templates while three are under a structure floor (Section 6.6).

The control-LoRA against Union-Pro:

Guidance changes neither axis; on Union-Pro it increased both (Section 6.8).
The canny trade-off recurs, past a threshold and with diminishing return, and the mean identity does not collapse at high canny scale, though single images do (Section 6.8).
At the same identity it retains more structure, with the steeper trade-off lines on the structure scores, but persona, template set and implementation change together between the branches, so the difference is not attributed to the implementation (Section 6.8.2).

Limits:

Single-seed findings hold as direction, not size: Four depend on one seed or on differences inside the seed noise: the guidance and LoRA-scale freezes, the fifteen-template cell check and the identity cliff, whose per-persona cells are single-seed. The rest is replicated across seeds and clear of its seed noise (Section 7).
Cross-persona identity gaps are partly the face model’s: The reference sets differ in source and quality across personas, so per-persona claims depend on within-persona contrasts, not on statements about the people photographed.
Cross-branch comparisons are shape comparisons only: The second branch conditions through a control-LoRA rather than a ControlNet, so its canny scale values do not compare with Union-Pro’s.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
3.1 Personas
The study uses nine persona-LoRAs, pf1–pf8 and pm1 (persona-female, persona-male). Personas pf1–pf8 are trained on well-known people, two of them on the same person, for research only: no generated image is published or used in an advertisement, the people are not identified, and no consent for commercial use of their identity is sought or implied; an advertisement would need it under right-of-publicity law.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
3.2 ControlNets
Two ControlNet implementations are used. The Union-Pro ControlNet [4] is a single model carrying seven control modes, of which this study uses canny, depth and pose. The Black Forest Labs control-LoRA [5] is a LoRA rather than a separate network: it is loaded alongside the persona-LoRA in one pipeline, and it ships in canny and depth variants, of which only the canny one, FLUX.1-Canny-dev-lora, is used here.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
3.3 Templates
The 21 templates are creative ad templates for fashion, product and lifestyle, each showing a male or female model posing with a product, coded tf1–tf15 and tm1–tm6 (template-female, template-male) by the subject’s gender. Each has a paired prompt describing its scene and product and naming the subject’s gender, so persona and template are matched: female personas with female templates, the male persona with male templates.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
3.4 Reference data
Identity fidelity is assessed against a reference set: six reference photographs per persona, none used in training, every one with a clearly visible face across a range of events and lighting.

Candidates were collected from openly licensed and press sources, machine-clustered for identity, frontality-filtered, cropped to 1024×1024 at 2.2× the detected face box, and reviewed by manual inspection.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
3.5 Prompt set
Each paired prompt is followed by a photorealism suffix. Some of the examples are:

female facing front, posing while holding credit card in the left hand, a photorealistic photo, 8k, hi res
female posing with coffee mug in the left hand, a photorealistic photo, 8k, hi res
male facing front, posing sideways while eating ice cream from a small cup with a spoon in the left hand, a photorealistic photo, 8k, hi res, plain background

A persona-LoRA needs its trigger word at generation only if its training used one. Five personas do (pf1, pf2, pf3, pf5 and pm1), and the generator supplies it by substituting the trigger word for the word female or male in the template prompt.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
3.6 Scoring

3.6.1 Identity fidelity scoring

face_sim is scored by AWS Rekognition, a commercial face-similarity service.
Each image of a persona is scored against its six reference photographs in one call with the match threshold set to 0, so every reference photograph returns a similarity [16]. The reported face_sim value is their mean.

\text{face\_sim}_m = \frac{1}{6} \sum_{j \in S_P} s(m, j)
\tag{1}
where s(m, j) is the similarity returned for image m and reference photograph j, and S_P is the reference set of the image’s persona P.
An image whose face the detector cannot find returns no match and is scored 0. 14 of the 2,716 scored rows had this issue.



3.6.2 Template adherence scoring

Edge fidelity: Measured by canny_f1, an F1 score. Edge maps are extracted from template and generation [17] and matched with a small dilation tolerance.
Depth-layout agreement: Measured by depth_corr. Monocular depth is estimated from both images by Depth Anything V2 [18] and compared by Pearson r, which is invariant to the scale and shift a monocular estimate is only defined up to.
Pose similarity: Measured by pose_sim. Body keypoints are detected in both images by YOLO11n-pose [19] and scored by an object keypoint similarity in the Common Objects in Context (COCO) form with COCO’s per-joint sigmas [20], at half the COCO tolerance and with the person’s box area as the scale.
An image in which the pose detector finds no person, or fewer than four joints in common with the template, has no pose_sim and is left out of every pose_sim mean; 5 of the 2,716 scored rows are such.

The three are cycle-consistency measurements: they re-extract from the output the controls the ControlNet consumed [2] and ask how much of the template’s structure persisted. This is the standard controllability measure of the ControlNet literature: ControlNet reports mean intersection over union (mIoU) between re-extracted and input segmentation maps, and Uni-ControlNet compares re-extracted edges, depth and pose to the input condition [2], [3].

3.7.2 Seed noise and the inside-the-noise rule
The seed-noise terms are defined in Table 1 above.
A difference \Delta between two single-seed means at c_0 and c_1 has sd \sqrt{\text{sd}_{\text{mean}}(c_0)^2 + \text{sd}_{\text{mean}}(c_1)^2}, \sqrt{2}\ \text{sd}_{\text{mean}} when the two are equal; it is inside the noise when it is under two sds of that:

\lvert\Delta\rvert < 2\sqrt{\text{sd}_{\text{mean}}(c_0)^2 + \text{sd}_{\text{mean}}(c_1)^2}
\tag{2}

Which trained identity the persona-LoRA carries.

The creative ad template the ControlNet conditions on.
Values: One template, tf4, is used through U4 so the scale sweeps are comparable; U5 opens to six and then the full female set, and U6 introduces the male set.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
5.3 Seed
Not a configuration but the noise the configurations are measured against.
Values: Seven sweeps vary the seed, at three resolutions: widely spaced in U2.a, consecutive in U2.b, a few elsewhere; the other fourteen generate one seed per cell. Of the single-seed sweeps, the two that decide cells are repeated on more seeds: U4’s quadrant in U5.a and U6.g’s band cells in U6.h.

Multi-seed sweeps: U2.a, U2.b, U3, U5.a, U6.h, C1.a and C1.b
Single-seed sweeps: U1.a to U1.e, U4, U5.b and U6.a to U6.g

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
5.4 Guidance scale (gs)
FLUX.1-dev is guidance-distilled: the guidance scale is an input the model was trained to take in place of the classifier-free guidance weight, and no unconditional pass runs at inference [22]. Higher values follow the prompt more strongly, as they would under classifier-free guidance.
Values: U1’s two coarse grids interleave rather than repeat, from near-unguided to strong guidance across the model’s shipped default [22], and its refinements tighten on the top of that range; C1.a, on the control-LoRA, runs past every Union-Pro value, as the control-LoRAs’ providers recommend higher guidance.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
5.5 LoRA scale (ls)
The LoRA scale controls the persona-LoRA’s contribution at generation time.
Values: The trained scale is 1.0; the coarse grids bracket it and the refinements tighten around it.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
5.6 Canny scale (cs)
The canny scale is the primary ControlNet scale and the search’s main axis.
Values: Varied in nearly every sweep, it is walked down from the coarse grids to the quadrant with the step shrinking twentyfold: coarse-to-fine spacing places cells where the response changes, not where it is flat [23]. U2.b retains the wide grid while seeds vary, U4 re-centres it downward once depth carries part of the conditioning, and U6 walks it down again with pose added.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
5.7 Depth scale (ds)
The depth scale sets the strength of the second control mode.
Values: No sweep before U4 conditions on depth. U4’s grid brackets the hypothesis that two control modes each need roughly half the single-mode scale: canny alone reaches its high structure scores near cs 0.6 in U2.b, so the joint grid centres both scales near 0.3; U5 retains that quadrant, and U6 sweeps depth again alongside canny and pose.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
5.8 Pose scale (ps)
The pose scale sets how strongly the template’s pose skeleton conditions generation; it is the one configuration only the last Union stage, U6, conditions on.
Values: Swept inside U6 only, jointly with cs and ds.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
5.10 Stopping rules and evidence tiers
Two rules bound the search:

Structure floors: A cell whose canny_f1, depth_corr or pose_sim mean is under the floor (Section 11.3.2) has not retained the template, whatever its identity.
The usable line: A cell whose face_sim mean is under the usable 80 has not retained the persona, whatever its structure.

A configuration is retained where both rules pass, and the trade-off is measured only inside that region.
Every sweep carries an evidence tier under its plan row:

Single-seed: One seed per cell, every change measured against the seed noise borrowed from the nearest multi-seed sweep.
Replicated: Several seeds per cell.

Neither tier is confirmatory in the sense of a hypothesis fixed before the data: an adaptive search is exploratory throughout [24], [25]. The Summary’s Limits name the single-seed findings.

The coarse step loses identity before it gains structure, so the usable region is under cs 0.5:

Changing cs 0.3 → 0.5, face_sim decreases 81.8 → 21.6 while canny_f1 and depth_corr change by a few hundredths and pose_sim increases 0.26 → 0.42.
Changing cs 0.5 → 0.7, each of the structure scores increases, canny_f1 the most, 0.25 → 0.52, with identity already lost.
The step is too wide to locate the region, which U1.c refines around cs 0.4.





6.1.2 U1 decision

Guidance scale — both axes change in the same direction; frozen at 6: In every sweep increasing gs increased face_sim and increased or preserved canny_f1, pose_sim never decreasing beyond a few hundredths, so the higher value is taken wherever its gain clears the seed noise. 7 was the top of the range tried between U1.a and U1.e, but most of its gains did not clear the seed noise, so 6 was frozen as its gain did clear.
LoRA scale — every change inside its seed noise but one; frozen at 1.0: In the coarse grids, ls < 1.0 gives slightly higher face_sim and canny_f1 and ls > 1.0 slightly lower, a decrease in both as ls increases that is inside the seed noise at every step, only U1.b’s whole-range canny_f1 decrease clear of the seed noise, while the refinements around 1.0 change nothing, so there is no clear evidence for any value other than 1.0.
Canny scale — identity decreases as the structure increases; cs ≈ 0.4 is the optimal grid for canny alone and is carried forward: In every sweep increasing cs decreased face_sim while increasing canny_f1, in the coarse grids each of the structure scores increased, which indicates a trade-off. Past cs 0.40 identity decreases in every sweep, and across the last refinements, 0.39–0.47, the structure scores no longer increase clear of the seed noise; no positive return interval excludes zero, so 0.40 is carried forward on that pattern.

U2 next measures how much of U1’s canny evidence is seed noise before cs ≈ 0.40 is carried forward.

Figure 7: Each point is the mean over the 10 seeds generated at that canny scale, 50 images in the sweep. The band is two standard deviations either side of the mean, clipped to the range the score can take, so its width is the seed spread at that value. The gains in the structure scores persist under seed stress; the identity value does not: Across cs 0.40 → 0.60 each of the structure scores’ change is well clear of its seed noise; face_sim’s decrease is marginally clear.
Identity’s seed noise grows as depth’s and pose’s shrinks; canny’s does neither: Negligible at cs 0.40 and 0.45, face_sim’s seed noise then widens to tens of points, while canny_f1’s ends about where it started and depth_corr’s and pose_sim’s shrink to about a third of their width; every seed is usable at 0.40 and 0.45, four of ten at 0.60.

6.2.3 U2 decision
Two consequences follow from the seed noise above cs 0.45:

every claim that depends on a single seed needs stress-testing on several, so where a later decision depends on canny values in that region the sweep generates several seeds;
the low end of the canny range is preferred for a second reason: identity is not merely lower at high cs, it becomes more volatile.

6.4.1 Canny scale and depth scale: persona mean






Figure 10: Each point is the mean of the images at its value, 54 in the sweep, so a canny point averages the three depth scales and a depth point the three canny scales. Shading: one sd_mean either side of the mean, sd_seed borrowed from U5.a.

6.4.2 Canny scale and depth scale: per persona






Figure 11: One line per persona, 3 images per point, 54 in the sweep. Shading: one sd_mean either side of the mean, sd_seed borrowed from U5.a.




face_sim, both control modes decrease identity, half the persona-LoRAs clear of the seed noise: Increasing cs 0.25 → 0.35 decreases face_sim by 0 to 56 points, and increasing ds 0.25 → 0.35 by 7 to 44 points; three of the six changes are clear of the borrowed seed noise on either mode.
canny_f1, both modes increase edge agreement alike for every persona-LoRA: Increasing cs 0.25 → 0.35 increases canny_f1 by 0.16 to 0.24, every change clear of the borrowed seed noise. Increasing ds 0.25 → 0.35 increases canny_f1 by 0.12 to 0.21, four of the six changes clear of the borrowed seed noise.
depth_corr, depth agreement converges across persona-LoRAs on both modes: Increasing cs 0.25 → 0.35 increases depth_corr for every persona-LoRA by less than the borrowed seed noise, and the spread across persona-LoRAs halves, 0.12 → 0.06. Increasing ds 0.25 → 0.35 does the same, the spread contracting 0.12 → 0.07. Depth agreement converges across persona-LoRAs where identity diverges.
pose_sim, only the canny scale increases pose adherence for every persona-LoRA, within the seed noise: Increasing cs 0.25 → 0.35 increases pose_sim by 0.11 to 0.22 for all six. Increasing ds 0.25 → 0.35 changes pose_sim by 0.00 to 0.21, one persona-LoRA constant; every change is inside the borrowed seed noise on either mode, so the distinction is a single-seed observation.



6.4.3 Joint view






Figure 12: Six personas at seed 1; cell labels are the means. Lightness carries the value within each panel, so the panels compare shapes rather than heights. The outlined quadrant is the frozen configuration.




The identity loss and the structure improvement track the scale sum, not the individual scales:

As we follow the left-bottom to right-top diagonal the conditioning sum increases from 0.5 → 0.6 → 0.7, which results in face_sim decreasing 97 → 47 and the structure scores increasing 0.35 → 0.71, 0.71 → 0.96 and 0.33 → 0.66. The off-diagonal cells are between their diagonal neighbours on every score; the one exception is (0.25, 0.3), below both neighbours on face_sim. The cells summing to 0.60 have almost identical face_sim and structure scores.
If we focus on the cells where face_sim is in the usable region and exclude the (0.35, 0.25) and (0.25, 0.35) cells and retain (0.3, 0.3), which gives almost identical results as they share the same conditioning sum, we get a “frozen quadrant”, i.e. the four cells with cs and ds at 0.25 or 0.30. This quadrant looks like a good candidate to restrict to.




6.4.4 The structure scores against face_sim, as the conditioning sum increases






Figure 13: Each point is one conditioning sum, the mean over its cells, six personas at one seed.




The conditioning sum trades identity for structure, and the trade steepens past 0.60: Across conditioning sums 0.50 → 0.70 face_sim halves while each of the structure scores increases, canny_f1 and pose_sim doubling.



6.4.5 U4 decision
The two scales were frozen at cs, ds ∈ {0.25, 0.30}, the optimal grid for canny with depth, on two measurements: the conditioning sum, not either scale, drives both axes; and the sums retaining face_sim > 80 run 0.50 → 0.60, past which the identity loss per step doubles, the four low-corner cells of that range being the frozen quadrant.

6.5.1.1 Conditioning sum: per persona






Figure 14: One line per persona, 30 to 60 images per point, 720 in the sweep; the middle sum is two cells of the quadrant, the ends one each. 3 images without a detectable face are scored 0. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals over seed groups.




The quadrant persists: the per-sum mean identity stays usable for every persona-LoRA, except pf6 at 0.6 conditioning sum: Increasing the conditioning sum 0.50 → 0.60 decreases face_sim and increases the structure scores for every persona-LoRA, so there is a trade-off for each. The structure scores change consistently, however identity is where the impact differs: pf3 and pf2 decrease by a few face_sim points, inside their seed noise, against more than twenty for pf6, which makes its identity unusable at conditioning sum 0.6.



6.5.1.2 Conditioning sum: per template






Figure 15: One line per template, 30 to 60 images per point, 720 in the sweep; the middle sum is two cells of the quadrant, the ends one each. 3 images without a detectable face are scored 0. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals over seed groups.




The quadrant persists: the per-sum mean identity stays usable for every template, except tf9 and tf13 at 0.6 conditioning sum: Increasing the conditioning sum 0.50 → 0.60 decreases face_sim and increases the structure scores for every template, tf5, tf6 and tf8 inside their seed noise on face_sim, so there is a trade-off for each. Canny and depth scores change consistently, however identity and pose are where the impact differs.



6.5.1.3 The structure scores against face_sim, as the conditioning sum increases






Figure 16: Each point is one conditioning sum, the mean over its cells, 720 images.




The quadrant persists through the wider generation, so does the trade-off but the return halves on the second step: The per-sum mean identity stays usable at every conditioning sum. Across conditioning sums 0.50 → 0.60 face_sim decreases and the structure scores increase at both steps, the second step returning about half the structure per identity point of the first.




6.5.2 U5 decision
U5.a stress tested the frozen quadrant on five seeds, six personas and six templates. The quadrant persisted: the per-sum mean identity stays usable at every conditioning sum, and every persona-LoRA and every template retains the direction the search selected on, pf2, pf3 and the tf5, tf6 and tf8 templates on face_sim inside their seed noise.
U5.b attempted to restrict the quadrant to one cell, cs 0.25 and ds 0.30. Stress tested on fifteen templates, the cell is under a structure floor on about half of them and under all three on four.
Thus further restriction of the frozen quadrant is not supported, and it stays the frozen set, the optimal grid for canny with depth. The warning the stage adds: the template changes the absolute structure scores, canny_f1 excepted, and the persona-LoRA the absolute face_sim, more than any configuration left to vary.
The frozen quadrant is at or below the floor of the range the Union-Pro model card recommends, 0.3–0.8 [4]: it spans 0.25 to 0.30 on each scale and tops out at the model card’s recommended minimum.

6.6.3 U6 decision
The three-mode grid with its conditioning sum band persists on all six templates on identity and on all three seeds on direction, though tm3, tm4 and tm5 are under a structure floor, so it is the optimal grid for canny, depth and pose together.

text:
6.7 The optimal grids: per conditioning mode
The Union branch ends with three optimal grids, one per control-mode set, each checked against the template and the seed, to be selected by the modes in use.

Canny alone (U1–U3): The canny scale at about 0.40.
Canny and depth (U4–U5): The frozen quadrant, cs and ds each at 0.25 or 0.30.
Canny, depth and pose (U6): The band 0.80 ≤ ps + cs + ds ≤ 0.85, over cs and ds each in {0.05, 0.15, 0.25} and ps in {0.5, 0.55, 0.6}.

Figure 22: Each point is the mean of the images at its value, 630 in the sweep. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals over seed groups.




The cs curve is a threshold, then a saturating increase: Changing the canny scale 0.31 → 0.91, face_sim stays constant through 0.61 and then decreases, the per-cs mean staying > 86 while single images collapse from cs 0.71. canny_f1 and depth_corr gain three quarters of their whole-range increase past 0.61, in steps that shrink by about half each time. pose_sim is the one that does not saturate: under its floor through 0.61, then increasing steeply and still increasing at 0.91.

Figure 24: Each point is one canny scale on the control-LoRA, averaged over the 630 images in the sweep. The scale is in the control-LoRA’s own units and does not compare with the Union stages’.




The return diminishes past the threshold: Below the threshold face_sim does not change, so there is no return to quote; past it each canny step returns less structure per identity point than the step before, the last about a quarter of the first.

This pipeline clears the structure floors from cs 0.71, where the Union branch’s canny-only sweeps work at 0.40–0.50.

What the next sweep changed: C1.a’s face_sim is flat below its threshold, so C1.b removes that half of the range and resamples the upper half at twice the density, freezes guidance at the centre of C1.a’s range, and changes the material: seven female persona-LoRAs on five female templates against C1.a’s one male persona on six male templates.




6.8.2 The comparison






Figure 25: The number beside each point is its canny scale. Union-Pro runs cs 0.3 to 0.8 and the control-LoRA cs 0.3 to 0.9, sharing six values; at every one the control-LoRA retains more face_sim, so the same scale value is not the same conditioning. The branches differ in persona and template set as well as implementation, so only the shape is comparable.




The control-LoRA’s lines are the more vertical set:

A steeper line means the structure scores increase over a smaller range of identity, and the control-LoRA’s are steeper on the structure scores, eight to ten times, no interval overlapping the other branch’s; the study cannot attribute that to the implementation, since persona, template set and implementation change together between the branches.

At the same face_sim the control-LoRA gives better structure: At the three canny scales where its identity is inside Union-Pro’s range it is higher on canny_f1 and depth_corr at every one, and higher on pose_sim at the two stronger scales and the weakest.

6.9.1 The identity cliff






Figure 26: Each point is the mean of the U4 cells at that conditioning sum (one cell at sum 0.50, two at 0.55, three at 0.60, two at 0.65, one at 0.70). The number on each step is the change from the point before. The shaded step 0.60 to 0.65 is the start of the cliff. The structure scores increase with the sum; face_sim decreases inside the quadrant and collapses past it.




Up to conditioning sum 0.60 identity loses moderately while template adherence gains steadily: Across the two steps inside the quadrant face_sim decreases on U4 and on U5.a while each of the structure scores increases at each step: the U4 steps differ from U5.a’s in size, the direction does not: on U4 every in-quadrant step, on U5.a each.
Past conditioning sum 0.60 the change is drastic: Across conditioning sum 0.60 → 0.65 face_sim decreases nearly twice the largest in-quadrant step and further across 0.65 → 0.70; canny_f1’s gain of a step doubles with it, while depth_corr’s and pose_sim’s do not grow beyond the noise.



6.9.2 The identity cliff: per persona

Every persona-LoRA decreases at the cliff but the size varies:

Every persona-LoRA loses face_sim across the cliff step at the same conditioning sum, pf1 and pf6 and the other four, by amounts spanning an order of magnitude.
The loss cannot be related to the start: at sum 0.60 pf1 and pf2 are a few face_sim points apart, yet one loses most of its identity on the cliff step and the other almost none.

The frozen quadrant retains identity for four of the six personas:

Across the quadrant pf1, pf2, pf3 and pf4 stay high.
pf5 and pf6 decrease across the first step alone, 0.50 → 0.55, and stay down at 0.60, so pf6’s cliff lies inside the quadrant, one step before the others’; the six are within about ten face_sim points at sum 0.50.
The quadrant is one strength for all six, selected on their mean; the two that retain identity least at 0.50 are the two it fails.

The persona-LoRA means span 25 face_sim points: Over the study the mean face_sim runs from pf8, the lowest, to pm1, the highest; pf6, pf7 and pf8 are the three lowest.

6.10.3 depth_corr is the weakest discriminator

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.1 Single-seed grid cells
Generation is stochastic per seed, so a cell-level comparison needs several seeds averaged, not one sample each [26]. Four findings were not re-run on several seeds, and they are the threat:

The guidance and LoRA-scale freezes: Both depend on the same end-to-end direction across many independent series, never on a cell.
The position of the cliff: No multi-seed sweep reaches past the quadrant, so where identity collapses depends on U4’s single-seed cells; the quadrant itself, one step inside, is the multi-seed part.
The fifteen-template cell check: That the quadrant cannot be restricted to (cs 0.25, ds 0.30) depends on U5.b, one seed on each of its 105 images (Section 6.5).

The borrowing of sd_seed itself depends on two assumptions the study does not test: that a single-seed sweep’s seed is exchangeable with the seeds of the sweep that lends sd_seed, and that the seed noise at the lender’s nearest measured value transfers to the borrower’s own value.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
section: 7.2 Selection bias: the scores that select the frozen configuration also report it
text:
7.2 Selection bias: the scores that select the frozen configuration also report it
The cell that comes out top of a noisy search is partly the one whose noise decreased on the high side [27], so a selected configuration’s value is trustworthy only when it is scored again on images that took no part in the choice. The state of each decision:

The frozen quadrant is re-scored: Selected on U4’s single-seed cells and re-scored by U5.a on fresh seeds and templates. On the fresh seeds the quadrant’s order by conditioning sum persists and the selection luck at the top is small, so the top cell’s U4 value is an upper bound and the two sum-0.55 cells are not separable.
The U6 band is re-scored on seeds: It was selected on U6.g’s single-seed cells, and U6.h retains those cells and adds two fresh seeds. On the fresh seeds alone the band’s face_sim mean is 97.3, against 98.4 on the seed it was selected on.
The guidance and LoRA-scale freezes are not re-scored: The scores quoted for gs 6 and ls 1.0 are the single-seed U1 grids’ own, so the bias there is unmeasured and those values are upper bounds.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.3 The usable line
The usable face_sim of 80 is the scorer’s default match threshold, not a value the study derived [28], so every decision that names it was recomputed with the usable line at 70, 75, 85 and 90. Every decision remains valid for a usable line ≤ 80; for a usable line > 80 the frozen quadrant starts losing cells, because its own face_sim means exceed the line by a few points.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.4 Images with no detectable face
Fourteen of the 2,716 rows have no detectable face, score 0 on face_sim and stay in every mean. Removing them instead changes no decision.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.5 Multiple comparisons
Across the sweeps the report quotes returns and treats an interval that excludes zero as evidence of a trade; 20 of the 27 intervals do (one of them negative), and 19 still do after Holm’s correction [29]; the one the correction removes is the negative one. No decision depends on one interval, nor on the single-seed change claims, which are judged one at a time against two sds of a difference without correction, so about one in twenty of those marked clear could be noise.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.6 Face-model demographic differentials
Every face_sim value inherits the face model’s behaviour across demographics, and the documented differentials are large, up to two orders of magnitude in false-match rates across groups [30], [31]. The three lowest-scoring persona-LoRAs are the two East-Asian people, face_sim was not characterised per demographic here, and the reference sets differ in source, so cross-persona face_sim gaps may partly reflect the face model: per-persona claims lean on within-persona contrasts.
Whether face_sim separates personas on generated images was checked on the 457 images of U3, U4, U5.a, U5.b and C1.b that were also scored against a second persona’s reference set, as the share whose own set scores higher (Equation 3):

\text{share} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^{M} \mathbf{1}\left[\text{own}_m > \text{second}_m\right]
\tag{3}
where \text{own}_m and \text{second}_m are the two face_sim values of image m, M = 457, and \mathbf{1}[\cdot] is 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise.
The own set scores higher on nearly every image, and on all but a few once the pf6-against-pf8 ties are set aside (the two share one reference set); arcface_sim gives the same share, and against all nine reference sets the own set scores highest on nearly every image it scores.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.7 Sequential coverage
A staged search only generates where earlier stages pointed; regions scored out early were never revisited at later fidelity.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.8 No persona-LoRA-free control
No sweep generates without a persona-LoRA, so the ControlNet’s structure transfer is never measured free of persona-LoRA interference; the U1 LoRA-scale series are the only probe of it, and they bound the direction, not the size.
Two more are of the same kind: no sweep generates with the persona-LoRA and no ControlNet, so the structure the template alone would have retained is unmeasured, and no other identity method than a trained LoRA was run, so the trade-off is measured for persona-LoRAs only.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
7.9 Incommensurable stages
The two branches condition by different mechanisms, so their cs values are different quantities sharing a name and are never compared. What is compared is shape: the control-LoRA’s canny-only curves are steeper, and Section 6.8.2 does not attribute that to the implementation, because persona gender and template gender change together, so U6, C1.a and C1.b each differ from the lineage in at least two respects. The sets change the slope too: within U5.a the return varies fourfold across templates and sixfold across personas, so a cross-branch ratio of eight to ten is within what a change of sets produces.

On canny_f1 at the top of the range every gs 2 series is below every gs 4 and gs 6 series, while depth_corr and pose_sim reach the same value whatever the guidance.

tf1, tf2, tf10 and tf11 are under all three floors, failing on every control mode at once; the rest of the low end fails on one or two.




9.2.1.2 tf11 dissected further

9.2.1.2.1 Persona






Figure 45: Each point is one persona-LoRA at tf11, one image each at cs 0.25 and ds 0.30. The grey dashed line is the mean over the 7, the red one the floor: what a generation made from a different template scores.




tf11 fails on each of the structure scores, not on identity:

All seven persona-LoRAs are usable on identity except pf8, a point or two under the usable 80.
All seven are under every structure floor, canny_f1 at about two thirds of its floor, depth_corr under half and pose_sim near zero.




9.2.1.2.2 Cycle consistency for 3 personas






Figure 46: Generated at cs 0.25 and ds 0.30, the cell U5.b holds fixed. Left: the maps re-extracted from the tf11 template. Right: the same maps from the three generations on it with its lowest canny_f1, depth_corr and pose_sim, one per control mode; a red frame marks the lowest score in its row; the bottom row carries the template pose skeleton dashed. Over its seven persona-LoRAs tf11 averages canny_f1 0.18, depth_corr 0.21 and pose_sim 0.008. tf11 fails on all three control modes.




pf7, lowest canny_f1: its edges share nothing with the template’s: A portrait on a plain wall, identity usable, the bottle low at the chest where the template holds it up beside the head. The template’s lines are an arm, a bottle held away from the body and a hard background edge; the generation’s are a face on an empty wall, so almost none coincide.
pf8, lowest depth_corr: flat where the template has relief: A portrait leaning on one hand with a large tube across the chest, identity under the usable 80. canny_f1 comes near its floor, since the tube and hand supply edges where the template has an arm and a bottle; depth fails because the tube lies at the face’s distance, where the template separates figure, held-out bottle and flat backdrop, so the relief maps coincide nowhere.
pf5, lowest pose_sim: a pose mismatch, not a missing pose skeleton: A portrait turned to the side with no product, identity usable. canny_f1 and depth_corr come nearer their floors; the extractor finds a person in both, but the template’s is a whole upper body with an arm up and the generation’s a head and shoulders, so no keypoint pair meets.

The U5 decision is in Section 6.5.

10.1.1.1 Canny scale






Figure 57: Each point is the mean of the images at its value, 525 in the sweep. 2 images without a detectable face are scored 0. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals over seed groups.




The canny trade-off recurs at this implementation’s own scales, and the mean identity does not collapse: Changing the canny scale 0.70 → 0.90, each of the structure scores increases while face_sim decreases moderately to the usable line and then recovers slightly, a fraction of what the Union branch’s canny-only ladder loses across its own range.
The increase saturates, as in C1.a past its threshold: Every canny scale here is past C1.a’s threshold, and the structure steps shrink from first to last, at every step on canny_f1 and from the second on depth_corr and pose_sim.



10.1.1.2 Canny scale: per persona






Figure 58: One line per persona, 15 images per point, 525 in the sweep. 2 images without a detectable face are scored 0. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals over seed groups.




The persona-LoRA decides identity and affects structure little: Changing the canny scale 0.70 → 0.90, face_sim decreases on six of the seven persona-LoRAs while all seven increase on the structure scores. At the top they are spread over a third of the face_sim scale and within two hundredths of each other on canny_f1.



10.1.1.3 Canny scale: per template






Figure 59: One line per template, 21 images per point, 525 in the sweep. 2 images without a detectable face are scored 0. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals over seed groups.




The template decides how much structure is reachable: Changing the canny scale 0.70 → 0.90, face_sim decreases on four of the five templates while all five increase on the structure scores. At the top the templates are five times further apart on pose_sim than the persona-LoRAs are.



10.1.1.4 The structure scores against face_sim, as the canny scale increases






Figure 60: Each point is one canny scale on the control-LoRA, averaged over the 525 images in the sweep. Arrow labels, on the first step only, are the slope the text quotes on canny_f1 and pose_sim. The scale is in the control-LoRA’s own units and does not compare with the Union stages’.




Only the first step has a measurable trade: Across cs 0.70 → 0.75 the identity change returns 0.013 canny_f1/face_sim and 0.024 pose_sim/face_sim. The next two steps’ face_sim changes quote no return; across 0.85 → 0.90 face_sim increases while canny_f1 and depth_corr continue increasing and pose_sim changes, so that step trades nothing.

Purpose: The span the other anchors are compared against.
Data used:

Sweeps: all twenty-one.
Images: all 2,716 generated images.
Scores: all four scores.
Scored against: face_sim – own reference set, structure scores – own template.

face_sim is 0 for the 14 images whose face the detector cannot find, and pose_sim is empty for the 5 images with no pose.
Computation method: Each score is ranked over all 2,716 study images, the empty pose_sim values left out, and the 5th and 95th percentiles are computed by linear interpolation between neighbouring ranks:

h = (N - 1)\, p

where N is the number of scores and p is 0.05 or 0.95; then, with the scores sorted as x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(N)} and \lfloor h \rfloor the integer part of h,

x_p = x_{(\lfloor h \rfloor + 1)} + \left(h - \lfloor h \rfloor\right)\left(x_{(\lfloor h \rfloor + 2)} - x_{(\lfloor h \rfloor + 1)}\right)
\tag{4}
Place of use: The blue band of Figure 1.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
11.2 Seed noise






Figure 61: Solid line: the pooled sd, the root mean square over seed groups of the sd across seeds inside one group (one persona, one template, one value of every scale); shaded: the 10th to 90th percentile of groups. A single-seed number borrows the sd_seed nearest to it.




11.2.1 sd_seed: estimated multi-seed noise of a score at one conditioning value

Purpose: The benchmark every later difference is measured against.
Data used:

Sweeps: all multi-seed sweeps.
Images: every image of these sweeps.
Configurations: persona, template, seed, gs, ls, cs, ds and ps.
Scores: all four scores.
Scored against: face_sim – own reference set, structure scores – own template.

Computation method: The images are grouped by persona, template and the value of every scale into the sets of images that differ only by seed, the seed groups. Inside each seed group, the sd of a score across its seeds:

\bar{x}_g = \frac{1}{n_g} \sum_{i=1}^{n_g} x_{g,i}


s_g = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_g - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_g} \left(x_{g,i} - \bar{x}_g\right)^2}

where x_{g,i} is the score of the image seed group g produced at its i-th seed, n_g is the number of seeds in the group and \bar{x}_g their mean. Then, at each conditioning value, the root-mean-square of that sd over the seed groups that share the value, the pooled sd:

\text{sd}_{\text{seed}}(c) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{G_c} \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}_c} s_g^2}
\tag{5}
where \mathcal{G}_c is the set of seed groups whose configuration has the conditioning value c and G_c their number (Figure 61): one number per sweep, score and conditioning value.
Place of use: The seed charts of U2.a and U2.b show two sd_seed either side of the mean; single-seed charts shade one sd_mean, and every single-seed change is compared against sd_mean.



11.2.2 sd_mean: the seed noise a single-seed sweep’s mean score at one conditioning value is measured against

Purpose: A single-seed sweep has no sd_seed of its own, so it borrows one to judge its differences against.
Data used:

Sweeps: all single-seed sweeps.
Images: every image of these sweeps.
Configurations: persona, template, seed, gs, ls, cs, ds and ps.
Scores: all four scores.
Scored against: face_sim – own reference set, structure scores – own template.
Key: the conditioning value c each per-value mean is computed at, cs, cs + ds or cs + ds + ps as per x-axis used in the trade-off charts.

Imported sd_seed: Each score’s sd_seed (Equation 5) at c^{*}, the lender’s measured value closest to the borrower’s c:

U1.a to U1.e: from U2, the pooled rows of U2.a and U2.b, which generated the same seed group at seeds that overlap at one, seed 6, so the cs 0.40 row pools 20 distinct seeds.
U4 and U5.b: from U5.a.
U6.a to U6.g: from U6.h.

Computation method: The imported sd_seed, divided by the square root of the number of images the single-seed mean averages, the sd of that mean:

\text{sd}_{\text{mean}}(c) = \frac{\text{sd}_{\text{seed}}(c^{*})}{\sqrt{n}}
\tag{6}
where c is the borrower’s conditioning value, c^{*} the lender’s measured value closest to it and n the number of images in the mean at c.
Place of use: Shaded one sd_mean either side of each mean on every single-seed sweep’s charts, and the inside-the-noise rule (Equation 2) is applied wherever the report quotes a single-seed difference.



11.2.3 ci_mean: the 95% bootstrapped interval of a mean score at one conditioning value

Purpose: To show the variation of a score mean computed over several seeds.
Data used:

Sweeps: all twenty-one, drawn on the multi-seed sweeps’ charts.
Images: every image of these sweeps with the conditioning value c.
Configurations: persona, template, seed, gs, ls, cs, ds and ps.
Scores: one of the four scores.
Scored against: face_sim – own reference set, structure scores – own template.
Key: the value c of the factor the chart’s x axis varies, a conditioning value or gs, ls, persona, template or seed.

Computation method: A bootstrap 95% interval from resampling the seed groups with their images retained together [32]. Let G_c be the number of seed groups whose configuration has the conditioning value c. Take b = 1, \dots, B resamples of G_c of those groups with replacement, g^{*}_{b,1}, \dots, g^{*}_{b,G_c}, and compute the mean over their images:

m_b(c) = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{G_c} \sum_{i \in g^{*}_{b,k}} x_i}{\sum_{k=1}^{G_c} n_{g^{*}_{b,k}}}

where x_i is the score of image i and n_{g} the number of images in group g. The interval is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the B resampled means:

\left[\, P_{2.5}(m_1(c), \dots, m_B(c)),\ P_{97.5}(m_1(c), \dots, m_B(c)) \,\right]
\tag{7}
with B = 2000 and P_q the q-th percentile, one interval per value. On a sweep with one seed per group, n_g = 1, this is the ordinary bootstrap over images.
Place of use: The per-value charts of multi-seed sweeps draw it as bars around each mean.



11.2.4 ci_return: the 95% interval of the return, the slope on a trade-off chart

Purpose: To say whether a trade between two conditioning values is resolved: a return whose interval spans zero is not.
Data used:

Sweeps: computed for U1.c, U2.b, U3, U4, U5.a, U6.a to U6.h, C1.a and C1.b; quoted where the face_sim change is resolved, in U1.c, U4, U5.a, C1.a and C1.b.
Images: every image of these sweeps.
Configurations: persona, template, seed, gs, ls, cs, ds and ps.
Scores: all four scores.
Scored against: face_sim – own reference set, structure scores – own template.
Key: the conditioning values c_0 and c_1 the return runs between, cs, cs + ds or cs + ds + ps as per x-axis used in the trade-off charts.

Computation method: A return is the slope of a structure score against face_sim on a trade-off chart, between two conditioning values c_0 and c_1, with its sign selected so that a structure score gained as face_sim is lost is positive:

r = \frac{a}{b}, \quad a = -\left(\bar{y}(c_1) - \bar{y}(c_0)\right), \quad b = \bar{f}(c_1) - \bar{f}(c_0)
\tag{8}
where \bar{y}(c) is the mean structure score and \bar{f}(c) the mean face_sim at c. The images are grouped into blocks by persona, template and every scale the axis does not set; the blocks are resampled with their images at both values retained together, B = 4000 times [32], and a and b recomputed on each resample. A single-seed sweep has no seed groups, so each per-value mean is resampled from a normal distribution centred on it with sd its sd_mean, B = 4000 times. The resamples give variances s_a^2, s_b^2 and covariance s_{ab}, and the interval is Fieller’s [33] for a ratio of two means:

g = \frac{z^2 s_b^2}{b^2}


\frac{1}{1 - g} \left[\, r - \frac{g\, s_{ab}}{s_b^2} \pm \frac{z}{|b|}
\sqrt{s_a^2 - 2 r\, s_{ab} + r^2 s_b^2 - g \left(s_a^2 - \frac{s_{ab}^2}{s_b^2}\right)} \,\right]
\tag{9}
with z = 1.96. When g \geq 1, that is when b is within z standard errors of zero, the interval is unbounded. A return is quoted only where the interval of its denominator b, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its resampled values, excludes zero.
Place of use: A return is quoted in the text only where its interval excludes zero.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
11.3 Ceilings and floors

11.3.1 Identity

11.3.1.1 Floor

Purpose: The score an impostor reaches: the bottom of the measurable range, where a different person’s reference photograph can score.
Data used:

Images: the 54 reference photographs, six per persona, 48 of them distinct since pf6 and pf8 share one reference set.
Scores: face_sim.
Scored against: each of the eight other personas’ reference sets, pf6 and pf8 excluded from each other, since they share one reference set.

Computation method: The impostor comparison of biometric evaluation [28]. The impostor score of a reference photograph k against an impostor persona Q is the mean face_sim computed using Q’s reference set S_Q with reference photographs j \in S_Q:

\text{imp}_{k,Q} = \frac{1}{6} \sum_{j \in S_Q} s(k, j)
\tag{10}
The floor is the 90th percentile of \text{imp}_{k,Q} over the 420 pairs.
Place of use: The usable 80 is > the floor; the floor lane of Figure 1 and the face_sim row of Table 2.
Result: Mean 2.9, 90th percentile 4.1, the floor, highest 52.2.



11.3.1.2 Ceiling

Purpose: The score a genuine reference photograph reaches: the top of the measurable range, which no generated image can be expected to exceed.
Data used:

Images: the 54 reference photographs, six per persona, 48 of them distinct since pf6 and pf8 share one reference set.
Scores: face_sim.
Scored against: own reference set with the match to itself removed.

Computation method: The genuine comparison of biometric evaluation [28]. For a persona P, its reference set S_P and a reference photograph k \in S_P, the genuine score of k is its mean face_sim against the other five:

\text{gen}_k = \frac{1}{5} \sum_{j \in S_P,\ j \ne k} s(k, j)
\tag{11}
The ceiling is the mean of \text{gen}_k.
Place of use: The ceiling marker of Figure 1 and the face_sim row of Table 2; the usable 80 is 19 points short of it. With the floor (Equation 10) it bounds the no-error interval, above every impostor pair and below every genuine reference photograph, on which the usable-line check (Section 7) depends.
Result: Mean 99.3, the ceiling, lowest 87.9; the no-error interval is 52.2 to 87.9.




11.3.2 Structure

11.3.2.1 Floors

Purpose: The first stopping rule: a score under its floor is in the range where an unrelated image can get a similar score, so it has not adhered to the template (Section 5.10).
Data used:

Templates: the 21 templates.
Scores: the 3 structure scores.
Scored against: eight randomly sampled images generated using some other template.

Computation method: For a template T and one of eight randomly sampled generations for it u, the floor of a score is the 90th percentile over such 168 pairs:

\text{floor} = P_{90}\left\{\text{score}(T, u)\right\}
\tag{12}
where P_{90} is the percentile by the same linear interpolation as the working ranges (Equation 4).
Place of use: The stopping rule; the U5.b charts draw the floor as a red line and the U6 sweeps test each score against it; Table 2 and Figure 1 carry the values.
Result: The floors are canny_f1 0.277, depth_corr 0.554 and pose_sim 0.156; depth_corr’s is the highest because unrelated generations already correlate, 0.34 on average, most ads sharing a centred-subject layout, which is why it is the weakest discriminator (Section 6.10.3).



11.3.2.2 Ceilings

Purpose: A validity check that structure scoring, the edge, depth and pose extraction and the comparison, adds no noise of its own: a template against itself must score 1.0. Not an achievable target: the achievable ceiling, what the pipeline reaches with the ControlNet and no persona-LoRA, is the control the study lacks (Section 7.8).
Data used:

Templates: the 21 templates.
Scores: the 3 structure scores.
Scored against: the template itself.

Computation method: The template against itself by the same scoring pass:

\text{ceiling} = \text{score}(T, T)
\tag{13}
for each template T.
Place of use: The ceiling marker of Figure 1 and the pose_sim span in Section 6.10.
Result: A score of exactly 1.0 for all three on every template.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
11.4 Resolvable difference

Purpose: To size the smallest effect a score can resolve at a given seed count.
Data used:

Sweeps: all multi-seed sweeps.
Configurations: the conditioning value, 29 in all.
sd_seed: for four scores at each value.

Computation method: The minimum detectable effect between two cell means at 80% power and a two-sided 5% alpha [34], [35]:

\Delta_{\min} = \left(z_{0.975} + z_{0.80}\right)\ \tilde{\sigma}\ \sqrt{\frac{2}{n}} = 2.80\ \tilde{\sigma}\ \sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}
\tag{14}
where z_q is the q-th quantile of the standard normal distribution, n the number of seeds per cell, and \tilde{\sigma} the pooled sd_seed over the 29 conditioning values, the root mean square, the same pooling rule as sd_seed itself (Equation 5):

\tilde{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{29} \sum_{c} \text{sd}_{\text{seed}}(c)^2}

Place of use: Section 6.10, where the ten seeds a 0.2 pose_sim effect needs come from it.

title: FLUX Persona-in-Template Ad Generation
text:
11.5 Variance shares

Purpose: To rank which factor changes each score.
Data used:

Sweeps: all twenty-one, then U5.a and U3 on their own.
Images: all 2,716 generated images.
Configurations: branch, persona, template, seed, gs, ls, cs, ds and ps.
Scores: all four scores.
Scored against: face_sim – own reference set, structure scores – own template.

Computation method: The increase in R² a factor adds to a one-hot least-squares model of the other factors, the semi-partial R² [36]. For a least-squares fit of one score s on a set of factors, fitted separately for each of the four scores,

R^2_s = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}_s}{\text{SST}_s}

where \text{SSE}_s is the sum of squared residuals of the fit and \text{SST}_s the sum of squared deviations of the score from its mean; the share of factor f in score s is

\text{share}_{f,s} = R^2_{s,\ \text{all factors}} - R^2_{s,\ \text{all factors except } f}
\tag{15}
Place of use: The U5.a finding (Section 6.5) and the variance subsection of Section 6.10.

title: Continuous-Time Generative Models
text:
This series develops the mathematical foundations of modern generative AI through first-principles derivations, drawing on stochastic calculus and stochastic processes. Topics include diffusion models, score-based stochastic differential equations (SDEs), flow matching, optimal transport, Langevin sampling, and the design space of diffusion models.
The focus is on deriving training objectives, understanding the underlying probabilistic dynamics, and analyzing sampling algorithms, including accelerated generation through ordinary differential equation (ODE) solvers, distillation, and consistency models. The emphasis is on mathematical reasoning that explains why these methods work, not just how they are implemented.

Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid






No matching items

I used to work in quantitative finance, but when generative AI began reshaping whole industries I grew curious enough to investigate how the new models worked. The deeper I went, the more I kept meeting old friends wearing new names. The “forward process” in a diffusion paper was an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process used for modeling interest rates. The same paper’s “reverse process”, which generates the image, can be derived by Girsanov’s theorem [1], which gives the same \mathbb{P}\to\mathbb{Q} change of measure that sits underneath every option price. The vocabularies had diverged; the mathematics had not. What was new was the application, not the machinery: a familiar toolkit aimed at a new field.
Digging into why the two lined up so neatly, I found that none of it began in either field. It started with Robert Brown in 1827, watching particles released from pollen grains jitter under a microscope and publishing the account the next year [2]. Einstein explained the jitter in 1905 [3]; Norbert Wiener made it rigorous in the 1920s as the Wiener process [4]. Kiyosi Itô then built stochastic calculus in the 1940s [5]: a chain rule for random paths (Itô’s lemma) and integration against Brownian motion. Its analytic twins, the Fokker-Planck equation [6], [7] for how a density evolves and the Feynman-Kac formula [8] linking such partial differential equations (PDEs) to expectations, complete the framework. Both finance and generative AI are downstream of physicists and mathematicians who were thinking about neither.
Finance borrowed it early. Louis Bachelier modeled stock prices as Brownian motion in 1900 [9], five years before Einstein’s paper, though it sat ignored for decades. Real adoption came in 1973, when Black, Scholes [10], and Merton [11] priced options by modeling the stock as geometric Brownian motion and applying Itô’s lemma to a hedged portfolio; the resulting PDE solves, via Feynman-Kac, to an expected discounted payoff. From there it spread: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process [12] became the Vasicek model [13] of mean-reverting rates, and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation the backbone of optimal portfolio choice [14]. A quant lives inside SDEs and PDE-expectation duality daily, rarely calling them by their physics names.
Diffusion models are borrowing it now. A generator defines a forward process that turns data into noise, then learns to run it backward. Song and colleagues’ 2021 framework [15] wrote this as an SDE; Anderson’s 1982 result [16] on reverse-time diffusions shows the generative process is that SDE run backward, driven by the score, the gradient of the log density. The most common forward choice, the Variance-Preserving SDE, is a time-dependent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; the marginal distribution evolves by Fokker-Planck. A quant reading this is not learning new mathematics, but recognizing familiar territory.
That is why the crossing is easy both ways. The core skill is identical: fluency with stochastic processes and Itô calculus, the instinct to move between an SDE and its PDE, and a feel for how probability flows under drift plus diffusion. A quant who knows why a martingale has no drift and how to discretize an SDE for Monte Carlo already owns the hard part of diffusion; an AI researcher who has tuned samplers and reasoned about score matching has practiced the continuous-time skills at the heart of quantitative finance. The new material on each side is real but learnable, sitting atop a shared core.
So here is my case to both rooms. The barrier is lexical, not conceptual: “risk-neutral drift” and “reverse-time drift” are two names for one operation, reshaping the drift by a change of measure, so each field keeps rediscovering what the other knows. Ideas already migrate both ways, but only the hard way, through specialists who stay in one field and learn the other’s dialect to do the work. Bühler, Teichmann and colleagues pulled the neural network, a tool born in AI, into derivatives hedging [17]; Wang, Zariphopoulou and Zhou carried stochastic optimal control, central to quantitative finance, into the AI problem of reinforcement learning [18]. That it works at all is the point: it works because the mathematics is already shared. It could happen far more readily, and by design. The wall between you is thinner than it looks, and some of the best ideas you could borrow are already sitting on the other side.
Now that you have the full context, dive in. Each post is math-first and derives its results in full, building on the posts before it. They are listed below in reading order, starting with post 1, each with a summary of what it covers.






Aug 10, 2026 Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models


The math that prices a stock option is the math that helps generate images: Wall Street to AI labs, same machinery, different century.



stochastic calculus

Brownian motion

Black-Scholes

diffusion models

normalizing flows

This post lays the mathematical foundation for the entire series. It begins with Brownian motion and the key rule (dW)^2=dt, uses them to derive Itô’s lemma from first principles, and solves geometric Brownian motion and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with it. The same result then derives the Black-Scholes equation through hedging and the no-arbitrage condition.
After that the post introduces generative models, explains variational autoencoders, normalizing flows, and energy-based models, and presents diffusion models, their two lineages and Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM).
It then formulates DDPM’s forward process as a Variance-Preserving SDE and returns to Itô’s lemma twice, deriving its perturbation kernel and the Fokker-Planck equation. A closing comparison sets the three derivations side by side, so quantitative finance and generative AI meet through the same mathematics.







Sep 10, 2026 The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion


How two methods, each inspired by a branch of statistical physics, became the foundations of modern image generation.



diffusion models

variational autoencoders

ELBO

DDPM

energy-based models

score matching

denoising score matching

Tweedie's formula

Langevin dynamics

NCSN




This post focuses entirely on generative AI, tracing the two main lineages of diffusion modeling. It begins with the variational route, from latent-variable models to variational autoencoders (VAEs), the evidence lower bound (ELBO), variational inference, and hierarchical VAEs. It then shows how DDPM can be understood as a hierarchical VAE with a fixed encoder, trained with the same variational bound, which reduces to a noise-prediction loss, and sampled through ancestral sampling.
The second half develops the score-based route from first principles. Energy-based models leave a normalizing constant that cannot be computed, and the score does not depend on it. Explicit and implicit score matching with Langevin sampling work in principle but meet four pitfalls on real data. Denoising score matching resolves them and cuts the cost per example from O(d) to O(1). Vincent’s theorem shows it has the same minimizer as score matching on the perturbed data, and Tweedie’s formula ties that minimizer to the posterior mean.
A single noise level still forces a dilemma. Song and Ermon’s score matching with Langevin dynamics resolves it by perturbing the data at a finite sequence of noise levels, training one noise-conditional score network across them, and sampling with annealed Langevin dynamics. The post closes by weighing what the reformulation from densities to scores gained and what it cost, leaving the unification of the two lineages to post 3.







Oct 16, 2026 SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching


How the stochastic calculus of Itô, Fokker and Planck generalizes diffusion models to a single continuous-time framework.



stochastic calculus

linear SDEs

Fokker-Planck equation

Girsanov's theorem

diffusion models

VP-SDE

VE-SDE

reverse-time SDE

probability-flow ODE

score matching

denoising score matching

predictor-corrector sampling




This post brings the two lineages together in continuous time, showing that both are instances of one family of linear SDEs. It presents the Variance-Exploding (VE) and Variance-Preserving (VP) SDEs as its two variance regimes, one with no drift and growing variance, the other with mean-reverting drift and bounded variance.
Anderson’s theorem then provides the reverse-time SDE, whose one unknown term is the score and whose solution reproduces the forward process in reverse. The post derives this result twice, through the Fokker-Planck equation and through Bayes’ rule, whose reweighting is Girsanov’s change of measure, and checks it in closed form for Gaussian data. It then introduces the probability-flow ODE, whose deterministic solution has the same marginals as the solutions of the forward and reverse-time SDEs, and which returns each sample when solved forward and back.
It shows how denoising score matching learns the score and, with DDPM’s weighting, reduces to DDPM’s noise-prediction loss, while with the likelihood weighting it is, in continuous time, the part of the ELBO that sums over the denoising steps. It then solves the reverse-time SDE with three samplers. Reverse diffusion sampling and post 2’s ancestral sampling are two discretizations of the same equation, and predictor-corrector sampling adds post 2’s Langevin steps as corrections.







Oct 22, 2026 Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid


How the 18th-century mathematics of Euler made generative models faster to sample and simpler to train.



fluid mechanics

continuity equation

optimal transport

diffusion models

normalizing flows

flow models

flow matching

conditional flow matching

probability-flow ODE




This post asks whether the velocity field that carries noise toward data can be learned directly, by regression, without learning the score first. Diffusion models also need hundreds or thousands of network evaluations per sample, their trajectories curve and change speed, the forward SDE fixes the path of distributions between data and noise, and generation starts from Gaussian noise. The post begins with normalizing flows, which give exact likelihoods but need tractable Jacobian determinants and often deep stacks of maps. Flow models replace the maps with an ODE, drawing their mathematics from Euler’s description of fluid motion, and sample by solving it numerically, with exact likelihoods, but their maximum-likelihood training solves the ODE at each training step and leaves the path between noise and data unspecified.
Flow matching specifies a path of intermediate distributions and learns its velocity field by regression, without solving the ODE, which gives another view of post 3’s probability-flow ODE, re-derived here from the continuity equation. The continuity equation does not determine that velocity field uniquely, and the marginal velocity field, the particular one that flow matching regresses onto, is intractable, so it offers no direct regression target. Lipman et al. build the path from conditional paths, one per data point, whose velocity fields are known in closed form. Averaging them, weighted by the posterior probability of each data point given the current sample, gives a velocity field that transports the marginal distributions along the path, and the conditional and marginal objectives have the same gradient.
Gaussian conditional paths make the construction concrete. The perturbation kernels of the VP and VE SDEs, with time reversed, are instances, so diffusion is approximately a special case. The simplest of them moves each noise sample along a straight line to a data point at constant speed, with their difference as its velocity. The post ends with the limitations these paths keep: curved marginal trajectories, independent pairing of noise and data, and a Gaussian source.
