title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
This series — Continuous-Time Generative Models
Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) and score matching with Langevin dynamics appear to be two different models, but they share one goal, which is to reverse a noising process. Each perturbs the data at a finite sequence of noise levels and learns to remove the noise one level at a time. They differ in how the noise grows from level to level, in what the network is trained to output and in how samples are generated. This post shows that all three differences are choices within one framework.
Post #2 developed the two routes to denoising diffusion. The variational route, built on an ELBO loss, led to a denoising network trained by a noise-prediction loss, and to ancestral sampling. The score-based route began with plain score matching and ended with denoising score matching over a finite sequence of noise levels, since no single level serves both fidelity and signal, and sampled with annealed Langevin dynamics.
This post picks up from there. Song et al. [1] unified the two lineages by letting the noise level become a continuum indexed by time and the forward process a stochastic differential equation (SDE), and the two predecessors became two instances of one general form, the Variance-Preserving and Variance-Exploding SDEs.
In both, the drift is linear in the state and the diffusion coefficient depends on time alone, so Itô’s lemma derives one Gaussian perturbation kernel for the whole family, with a closed-form mean and variance. The noise schedule of the Variance-Preserving SDE, such as DDPM’s linear schedule [2] or the cosine schedule [3], sets how fast that variance grows. Song et al.’s sub-VP SDE is a third instance, whose variance never exceeds the Variance-Preserving one.
Side by side, the three SDEs fall into two variance regimes. The Variance-Exploding SDE has no drift and a growing variance, while the Variance-Preserving and sub-VP SDEs have a mean-reverting drift and a bounded variance.
The forward SDE turns data into noise. Generation needs the opposite direction, from noise back to an image, so the question is how to run the SDE backward. Anderson’s 1982 theorem [4] answers it. Under regularity conditions, the solution of the forward SDE, run backward in time, solves another SDE, the reverse-time SDE. Besides the forward coefficients, it needs one more quantity, the score \nabla_x \log p_t.
The post derives the theorem twice, once through the equivalence between the marginals of an SDE’s solution and the Fokker-Planck equation, and once through Bayes’ rule, whose reweighting is the change of measure of Girsanov’s theorem [5], the one behind risk-neutral pricing. For Gaussian data it then checks the result in closed form.
The continuous view also yields an equation the discrete view could not express, the probability-flow ordinary differential equation (ODE). It is the member without noise of a family of SDEs whose solutions share the forward marginals, the reverse-time SDE among them. Its solution is deterministic, so generation becomes solving an ODE, and solving it forward from a sample and back returns that sample.
The score is learned by denoising score matching [6], a regression on the known score of the perturbation kernel, weighted over time. With DDPM’s weighting it reduces to DDPM’s noise-prediction loss [2], so the variational and score-based routes train with the same loss. With Song et al.’s likelihood weighting it is, in continuous time, the part of the ELBO that sums over the denoising steps, all of the bound but its prior and reconstruction terms.
The regression needs the kernel’s score in closed form, which the linear SDEs above provide. For an SDE with a nonlinear drift the kernel is in general unknown, and sliced score matching [7], which needs no target score, replaces denoising score matching.
Generation solves the reverse-time SDE with the learned score. Reverse diffusion sampling is its Euler-Maruyama discretization, post #2’s ancestral sampler is a second discretization of the same equation, and the predictor-corrector sampler adds Langevin correction steps. A final application of Tweedie’s formula [8] removes the noise that the last sampling step injects. Every sampler uses the model only through its score, so once the score is learned any sampler can be used, thus training and sampling are decoupled.
The post ends with why the unification matters. More than any single model, Song et al.’s main contribution is a common framework: the forward SDE, the score-based reverse-time SDE, and the deterministic probability-flow ODE. A generative model written in this framework inherits a century of mathematics on diffusion processes, from the Fokker-Planck equation to Itô calculus and Girsanov’s theorem.
The noise schedule becomes a design choice rather than the defining feature of a model, and the methods that followed, Karras et al.’s EDM [9], flow matching [10] and consistency models [11], are built on the same framework.
Post #1 built the forward process, post #2 reversed it by two methods, and this post unifies the two methods as one forward SDE and its reverse-time SDE.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
Roadmap

Part 1: Replaces the finite sequence of noise levels with a continuum, which makes the forward process an SDE whose linear form and Gaussian perturbation kernel cover the Variance-Preserving, Variance-Exploding and sub-VP SDEs alike.
Part 2: Runs that SDE backward with Anderson’s theorem, derived through the equivalence between the marginals of an SDE’s solution and the Fokker-Planck equation, and through Bayes’ rule, whose reweighting is Girsanov’s change of measure, then checks it in closed form for Gaussian data.
Part 3: Derives the probability-flow ODE, the member without noise of the family of SDEs in Part 2 that share the marginals of the forward SDE’s solution. Its deterministic solution has the same marginals as the solutions of both SDEs and can be solved forward, from data to noise, or backward, from noise to data.
Part 4: Estimates the reverse-time SDE’s one unknown term, the score, by denoising score matching, shows that it and DDPM’s variational bound lead to the same noise-prediction loss, and shows that, in continuous time, the bound’s sum over the denoising steps is denoising score matching with the likelihood weighting.
Part 5: Discretizes the reverse-time SDE using three samplers: reverse diffusion sampling, post #2’s ancestral sampler as a second discretization of the same equation, and the predictor-corrector sampler, which adds Langevin correction steps.
Part 6: Asserts that the framework, more than any single model, is Song et al.’s main contribution and the foundation of the methods that followed, then shows why the choice of noise schedule matters in practice, and previews post #4.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
1.1 The linear SDE
For the forward SDE Eq. 1, the perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) is the distribution of the state x_t at time t given a fixed initial condition x_0, a density p_{0t}(\cdot \mid x_0): \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty) for each x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in (0, T].
Linearity is what makes the perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) Gaussian, with a closed-form mean and variance. This section derives the kernel of Eq. 2 once, for arbitrary f_{\mathrm{lin}} and g, so the two canonical SDEs of Song et al. [1] are distinguished entirely by their choice of f_{\mathrm{lin}} and g.

1.1.1 The perturbation kernel
For each f_{\mathrm{lin}} and g, the perturbation kernel of Eq. 2 is

\boxed{p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_t;\; m(t)\, x_0,\; \Sigma(t)\, I\big)}
\tag{3}
with the mean coefficient m: [0, T] \to (0, \infty)

\boxed{m(t) = \exp\!\Big(\int_0^t f_{\mathrm{lin}}(s)\, ds\Big)}
\tag{4}
and the per-component variance \Sigma: [0, T] \to [0, \infty)

\boxed{\Sigma(t) = m(t)^2 \int_0^t \frac{g(s)^2}{m(s)^2}\, ds}
\tag{5}


1.1.2 Deriving the perturbation kernel using Itô’s lemma
The kernel follows from solving Eq. 2 explicitly, with the stochastic counterpart of the integrating factor that solves a linear ODE. Itô’s lemma of post #1, applied to a transformed state, removes the drift. The driftless SDE then integrates directly to an Itô integral, whose distribution gives the kernel of the transformed state, and the reverse transform returns the kernel of x_t.
The state is a d-vector, but the SDE acts on each coordinate separately. We write x^k_t and W^k_t for the k-th components of x_t and W_t, k = 1, \ldots, d. A symbol with the superscript k is a scalar, and the same symbol without it is the d-vector.

1.1.2.1 Removing the drift with Itô’s lemma
The SDE:
The state x_t follows Eq. 2,

dx_t = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, x_t\, dt + g(t)\, dW_t

Because f_{\mathrm{lin}} and g are scalars, the SDE decouples into d scalar SDEs, one per component, each driven by its own component of W_t. Taking the k-th component,

dx^k_t = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, x^k_t\, dt + g(t)\, dW^k_t

where W^k_t is a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion. Until the components are stacked again, every quantity below is a scalar.
Itô’s lemma:
Let h: \mathbb{R} \times [0, T] \to \mathbb{R} be twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t. For the transform h(x^k_t, t) of a scalar process dx^k_t = f\, dt + g\, dW^k_t, with drift coefficient f and diffusion coefficient g,

dh = \left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} + f\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}\right) dt + g\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\, dW^k_t
\tag{6}
where the partial derivatives of h(x, t) are taken in its scalar argument x and evaluated at x = x^k_t.
Integrating factor:
A linear ODE is solved by multiplying it by an integrating factor, a function that turns it into a total derivative. Its analogue for a linear SDE applies Itô’s lemma to the transform y^k_t = h(x^k_t, t), with

h(x, t) = e^{-F(t)}\, x, \qquad F(t) = \int_0^t f_{\mathrm{lin}}(s)\, ds
\tag{7}
so that F: [0, T] \to \mathbb{R} has \frac{dF}{dt} = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) and F(0) = 0. The factor e^{-F(t)} is the same for each component.
Coefficients (from Eq. 2):
The drift of the k-th component is f = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, x^k_t and its diffusion coefficient is g(t).
Partials (from the transform Eq. 7):
With \frac{dF}{dt} = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t), by the chain rule,

\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = -f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, e^{-F(t)}\, x, \qquad \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} = e^{-F(t)}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} = 0

Substituting f = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, x^k_t and the three partials, evaluated at x = x^k_t, into Itô’s lemma Eq. 6,

dy^k_t = \Big(-f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, e^{-F(t)}\, x^k_t + f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, x^k_t\, e^{-F(t)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2 \cdot 0\Big)\, dt + g(t)\, e^{-F(t)}\, dW^k_t

Cancelling the explicit-time term against the drift term,

dy^k_t = g(t)\, e^{-F(t)}\, dW^k_t

Stacking the d components, the vector y_t = e^{-F(t)}\, x_t satisfies

dy_t = g(t)\, e^{-F(t)}\, dW_t

so y_t is driftless.


1.1.2.2 Integrating the driftless SDE
The right side of the driftless SDE involves only time and the Brownian motion, so it integrates directly. Integrating both sides from 0 to t,

\int_0^t dy_s = \int_0^t g(s)\, e^{-F(s)}\, dW_s

Evaluating the left side by the fundamental theorem of calculus,

y_t - y_0 = \int_0^t g(s)\, e^{-F(s)}\, dW_s

Substituting y_0 = e^{-F(0)}\, x_0 = x_0, since F(0) = 0,

y_t - x_0 = \int_0^t g(s)\, e^{-F(s)}\, dW_s

Moving x_0 across,

y_t = x_0 + \int_0^t g(s)\, e^{-F(s)}\, dW_s



1.1.2.3 Properties of the solution distribution
The Itô integral has a deterministic integrand g(s)\, e^{-F(s)}, and a deterministic integrand makes the integral Gaussian. For a deterministic \varphi and a one-dimensional Brownian motion, P1:Eq. 7 gives the distribution of such an integral,

\int_0^t \varphi(s)\, dW^k_s \sim \mathcal{N}\Big(0,\; \int_0^t \varphi(s)^2\, ds\Big)

With \varphi = g\, e^{-F}, the k-th component of the integral is Gaussian, with mean 0 and variance \int_0^t g(s)^2\, e^{-2F(s)}\, ds. The d components are driven by independent components of W_t, so they are independent, and the integral is a Gaussian vector with covariance \big(\int_0^t g(s)^2\, e^{-2F(s)}\, ds\big) I.
Conditioning on x_0, which is independent of the Brownian motion and hence of the integral, the offset x_0 is a deterministic constant. Adding it to the Gaussian integral is an affine transformation, and an affine function of a Gaussian is Gaussian, hence

y_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\Big(x_0,\; \Big(\int_0^t g(s)^2\, e^{-2F(s)}\, ds\Big) I\Big)

Applying the reverse transform of Eq. 7, x_t = e^{F(t)}\, y_t, which multiplies the mean by e^{F(t)} and the covariance by e^{2F(t)},

p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\Big(x_t;\; e^{F(t)}\, x_0,\; e^{2F(t)} \Big(\int_0^t g(s)^2\, e^{-2F(s)}\, ds\Big) I\Big)
\tag{8}
Now we compute the two moments of this kernel without F.
The mean:
The mean of the kernel Eq. 8 is the initial state multiplied by the deterministic factor e^{F(t)},

\mathbb{E}[x_t \mid x_0] = e^{F(t)}\, x_0

Substituting back F(t) = \int_0^t f_{\mathrm{lin}}(s)\, ds from Eq. 7,

\mathbb{E}[x_t \mid x_0] = \exp\!\Big(\int_0^t f_{\mathrm{lin}}(s)\, ds\Big)\, x_0

Naming the exponential factor m(t),

\mathbb{E}[x_t \mid x_0] = m(t)\, x_0

where

\boxed{m(t) = \exp\!\Big(\int_0^t f_{\mathrm{lin}}(s)\, ds\Big)}

which is Eq. 4.
The variance:
The per-component variance of the kernel Eq. 8 is

\Sigma(t) = e^{2F(t)} \int_0^t g(s)^2\, e^{-2F(s)}\, ds

Substituting e^{F} = m,

\boxed{\Sigma(t) = m(t)^2 \int_0^t \frac{g(s)^2}{m(s)^2}\, ds}

which is Eq. 5.
The kernel:
Substituting m(t) and \Sigma(t) into the perturbation kernel,

\boxed{p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_t;\; m(t)\, x_0,\; \Sigma(t)\, I\big)}

which is Eq. 3. \square
Every linear SDE therefore has a Gaussian perturbation kernel, centered at m(t)\, x_0 and with the same variance \Sigma(t) in every coordinate. Both moments are integrals of f_{\mathrm{lin}} and g alone, so the two coefficients fix the kernel completely. The next three sections make three choices of them, and each kernel follows by evaluating the two integrals.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
1.2 VP-SDE: DDPM forward process
The DDPM forward process of Ho et al. [2] was built in post #1, and its continuum limit is the Variance-Preserving (VP) SDE of Song et al. [1]. The first choice recovers it.
With a noise schedule \beta: [0, T] \to (0, \infty), which sets the rate at which noise is injected, the VP-SDE is

\boxed{dx_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\; dW_t}
\tag{9}

1.2.1 Deriving the VP-SDE
The VP-SDE is the continuum limit of DDPM’s noising chain, which P1:§7.5 derives step by step. Partition [0, T] into the N steps of even width \Delta t = T/N, with t_i = i\,\Delta t. Each step of the chain shrinks the state and adds independent Gaussian noise,

x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\; x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\; \epsilon_i

where \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the independent noise injected at step i and \beta_i = \beta(t_i)\, \Delta t is the discrete noise schedule. Taylor-expanding the square root for small \Delta t, writing \sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i as the Brownian increment \Delta W_i and letting \Delta t \to 0 turns the chain into Eq. 9.


1.2.2 Solving the VP-SDE
Comparing Eq. 9 with Eq. 2 identifies the coefficients,

f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) = -\tfrac12\beta(t), \qquad g(t) = \sqrt{\beta(t)}

Both moments are simplest in terms of the cumulative product \bar\alpha: [0, T] \to (0, 1] of post #1,

\bar\alpha(t) = \exp\!\Big(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\Big)
\tag{10}
The mean:
Substituting f_{\mathrm{lin}} = -\tfrac12\beta into Eq. 4,

m(t) = \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12 \int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\Big)

Rewriting by the definition of \bar\alpha, Eq. 10,

m(t) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}

The variance:
Substituting m^2 = \bar\alpha and g^2 = \beta into Eq. 5,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \int_0^t \frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}\, ds

Differentiating \bar\alpha, Eq. 10, by the chain rule gives \bar\alpha'(s) = -\beta(s)\, \bar\alpha(s). Substituting \beta(s) = -\bar\alpha'(s)/\bar\alpha(s),

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \int_0^t \frac{-\bar\alpha'(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)^2}\, ds

Recognizing the integrand as \frac{d}{ds}\Big[\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)}\Big],

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \int_0^t \frac{d}{ds}\Big[\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)}\Big]\, ds

Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \Big(\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(t)} - \frac{1}{\bar\alpha(0)}\Big)

Evaluating, with \bar\alpha(0) = 1,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \Big(\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(t)} - 1\Big)

Multiplying out,

\Sigma(t) = 1 - \bar\alpha(t)

The kernel:
Collecting the two moments,

\boxed{m(t) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}, \qquad \Sigma(t) = 1 - \bar\alpha(t)}
\tag{11}
Substituting these into Eq. 3, the perturbation kernel is

\boxed{p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_t;\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\; (1 - \bar\alpha(t))\, I\big)}
\tag{12}
which is the kernel derived for DDPM with the same integrating factor in P1:§7.6. \square
The name of the SDE captures how the two coefficients interact. The drift contracts the data while the diffusion adds noise. For standardized data, with identity covariance, the two effects cancel, and the marginal variance stays I for each t (P1:§8.1.1). As the accumulated noise grows, \bar\alpha(t) \to 0, and every initial condition is carried to the standard normal prior \mathcal{N}(0, I) (P1:§7.6.3.4).
Comparing the perturbation kernel with an SDE simulation:
Here we check the closed-form VP perturbation kernel, Eq. 12, against a direct simulation of the VP-SDE, Eq. 9. The simulation discretizes it with the Euler-Maruyama scheme [12] and a small step \Delta t,

x_{t+\Delta t} = x_t - \tfrac12 \beta(t)\, x_t\, \Delta t + \sqrt{\beta(t)\, \Delta t}\; z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)

The error of the scheme shrinks with the step at a known rate, for smooth coefficients. Writing \hat x_T for its value after T/\Delta t steps, the scheme has weak order 1, which means that for a smooth function \varphi the error \lvert \mathbb{E}[\varphi(\hat x_T)] - \mathbb{E}[\varphi(x_T)] \rvert of an expectation is at most a constant times \Delta t. Its strong order, the rate of the mean pathwise error \mathbb{E}\lVert \hat x_T - x_T \rVert, is \tfrac12 in general and 1 when, as here, the diffusion coefficient does not depend on the state [13]. The check below compares distributions, so the weak order is the one that applies.
All paths have the same initial condition x_0, and their histograms at three times are compared with the kernel at those times in Figure 1 below.








Figure 1: A check of the VP perturbation kernel. Histograms of x_t from 20,000 Euler-Maruyama paths of the VP-SDE, all with the initial condition x_0 = 1.5, at three times, against the closed-form kernel \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\, 1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) (curves). The kernel samples x_t at any t in one step, without simulating the path.





At each time the histograms match the kernel. As t grows, \bar\alpha(t) falls and the peak moves toward zero and widens. The simulation needs 50, 150 and 400 Euler-Maruyama steps to reach these times, while the kernel gives the distribution directly.
Simulating the VP forward process:
Here we follow a two-mode data distribution through the VP-SDE into the standard normal prior, as Figure 2 shows below.








Figure 2: Sample paths of the forward VP-SDE for a two-mode data distribution. Each path has as its initial condition a data sample on one of the modes at t = 0, and it is carried by the contracting drift and growing noise into the standard normal prior at t = T. The shading is the marginal distribution p_t: two ridges that merge into a single Gaussian band. The right panel is a histogram of x_T over many paths, with the terminal marginal p_T (solid curve), close to \mathcal{N}(0,1). Time flows left to right.





The drift shifts both modes toward zero while the noise widens them. The two ridges stay apart early, merge into one band once the modes overlap, and by t = T the histogram of x_T matches \mathcal{N}(0, 1). These data are not standardized, so their variance is not preserved; it falls toward 1, the variance of the prior.


1.2.3 The linear and cosine schedules
The VP-SDE leaves the noise schedule \beta(t) free, and through Eq. 11 the schedule decides how fast \bar\alpha(t) falls from 1 toward 0. DDPM used a linear schedule, \beta_i rising from 10^{-4} to 0.02 over 1000 steps [2]. Nichol and Dhariwal found that it drives \bar\alpha close to zero well before the last step, so the final stretch of the forward process is nearly pure noise and contributes little. Their cosine schedule changes \bar\alpha slowly near both ends instead [3],

\bar\alpha(t) = \frac{\cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{t/T + s}{1 + s} \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{2}\big)}{\cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{s}{1 + s} \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{2}\big)}

with a small offset s.
Comparing the two schedules:
Here we plot \bar\alpha against t = i/N for the linear schedule and for the cosine schedule with s = 0.008, as Figure 3 shows below.








Figure 3: The cumulative product \bar\alpha under DDPM’s linear schedule, \beta_i from 10^{-4} to 0.02 over N = 1000 steps, and the cosine schedule of Nichol and Dhariwal with s = 0.008, against t = i/N. The linear schedule drives \bar\alpha below 0.03 by t = 0.6, so the last stretch of the forward process is nearly pure noise; the cosine schedule changes \bar\alpha slowly near both ends.





By t = 0.6 the linear schedule has driven \bar\alpha below 0.03, while the cosine schedule keeps it near 0.34.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
1.3 VE-SDE: SMLD noise perturbation
The noise perturbation of score matching with Langevin dynamics (SMLD), the method of Song and Ermon [14] that trains a noise-conditional score network (NCSN), was built in post #2. Its continuum limit is the Variance-Exploding (VE) SDE, which has no drift and a growing noise level. The second choice recovers it.
With an increasing noise function \sigma: [0, T] \to (0, \infty), the VE-SDE is

\boxed{dx_t = \sqrt{\frac{d\,[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}}\; dW_t}
\tag{13}

1.3.1 Deriving the VE-SDE
SMLD’s noise levels:
SMLD perturbs the data at L noise levels \sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > \cdots > \sigma_L, a geometric sequence in which each level is a fixed multiple of the next (P2:§5). At level k the perturbed sample is x_0 + \sigma_k\, \epsilon with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), so each level has its own perturbation kernel \mathcal{N}(x_0, \sigma_k^2 I). The index follows annealed Langevin dynamics, which starts at the largest level \sigma_1 and descends to \sigma_L.
From the geometric sequence to the schedule:
The forward process traverses the levels in increasing order of noise, from \sigma_L = \sigma_{\min} to \sigma_1 = \sigma_{\max}. We take the partition of [0, T] from §1.2, with N = L - 1 steps of even width \Delta t = T/N,

0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_N = T, \qquad t_i = i\, \Delta t

and assign the levels to its N + 1 = L grid points in that order, \sigma(t_i) = \sigma_{L-i}. The sequence is geometric, so each step up multiplies the level by a fixed ratio r. After i steps up from \sigma_{\min},

\sigma(t_i) = \sigma_{\min}\, r^i

The N steps reach \sigma_{\max} = \sigma_{\min}\, r^N, so r = (\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min})^{1/N}. Substituting it,

\sigma(t_i) = \sigma_{\min} \Big(\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}\Big)^{i/N}

Substituting i/N = t_i/T, from t_i = i\, \Delta t and \Delta t = T/N,

\sigma(t_i) = \sigma_{\min} \Big(\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}\Big)^{t_i/T}

The right side depends on the partition only through the grid point t_i. Taking the continuum limit N \to \infty with t = t_i fixed, so that the step size \Delta t = T/N \to 0, gives the continuous geometric schedule of Song et al. [1],

\sigma(t) = \sigma_{\min} \Big(\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}\Big)^{t/T}

The L levels are this schedule at the L grid points. Song et al. choose \sigma_{\max} near the largest distance between training points, far above the data’s scale [1].
From the noising chain to the SDE:
SMLD applies the noise of each level to the data sample in one step, x_0 + \sigma(t_i)\, \epsilon. An SDE instead requires the noise to accumulate over many small steps, as in DDPM’s forward process. Each step of the partition therefore adds an independent Gaussian increment of variance v_i. Since the variances of independent Gaussians add, raising the noise level from \sigma(t_{i-1}) to \sigma(t_i) at step i requires

\sigma^2(t_i) = \sigma^2(t_{i-1}) + v_i

Solving for the step variance,

v_i = \sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})

which is positive because \sigma increases.
Applying this at each step of the partition gives SMLD’s noising chain, a sequence of small Gaussian noise additions, one per step [1],

x_i = x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})}\; \epsilon_i

where \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the independent noise injected at step i. Started from the data x_0 at the grid point t_0, the chain gives x_i the variance \sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_0) about x_0, which is SMLD’s variance \sigma^2(t_i) less the offset \sigma^2(t_0) = \sigma_{\min}^2.
For small \Delta t, Taylor-expanding the variance increment gives \sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1}) \approx \frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}\, \Delta t, with the continuous time t in place of the grid point t_i. Substituting the expansion into the previous line,

x_i \approx x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}\, \Delta t}\; \epsilon_i

Subtracting x_{i-1},

x_i - x_{i-1} \approx \sqrt{\frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}\, \Delta t}\; \epsilon_i

Factoring the noise term as \sqrt{d[\sigma^2(t)]/dt}\,\big(\sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i\big),

x_i - x_{i-1} \approx \sqrt{\frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}}\; \big(\sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i\big)

The factor \sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i, with \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), is a Brownian increment \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t\, I) over [t_{i-1}, t_i],

x_i - x_{i-1} \approx \sqrt{\frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}}\; \Delta W_i

This difference equation is the Euler-Maruyama scheme of the SDE below, and such schemes converge to the SDE’s solution as \Delta t \to 0 under the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions of §A.1, with coefficients continuous in t as the geometric schedule’s are [12]. Taking that limit gives the VE-SDE,

\boxed{dx_t = \sqrt{\frac{d\,[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}}\; dW_t}

which is Eq. 13. \square


1.3.2 Solving the VE-SDE
Comparing Eq. 13 with Eq. 2 identifies the coefficients,

f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) = 0, \qquad g(t)^2 = \tfrac{d}{dt}\sigma^2(t)

The mean:
Substituting f_{\mathrm{lin}} = 0 into Eq. 4,

m(t) = 1

The variance:
Substituting m = 1 and g^2 = \tfrac{d}{ds}\sigma^2 into Eq. 5,

\Sigma(t) = \int_0^t \frac{d}{ds}\big[\sigma^2(s)\big]\, ds

Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus,

\Sigma(t) = \sigma^2(t) - \sigma^2(0)

The kernel:
Substituting m(t) = 1 and \Sigma(t) into Eq. 3, the perturbation kernel is

\boxed{p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_t;\; x_0,\; [\sigma^2(t) - \sigma^2(0)]\, I\big)}
\tag{14}
This is the VE perturbation kernel. At the grid times it matches SMLD’s noising chain, whose independent increments have variances that add and telescope to \sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_0). \square
With m(t) = 1 the data is never contracted, so the kernel stays centered at x_0 while its variance grows with the noise level. Unlike the VP kernel, it approaches no fixed distribution, so the noise level itself must outgrow the data scale, as the endpoints below make precise.
The two endpoints:
Each endpoint has one consequence. Since \sigma_{\min} \ll 1, \sigma(0) is negligible against the working noise levels, and the kernel is approximated by \mathcal{N}(x_t;\, x_0,\, \sigma^2(t)\, I), an idealization used from here on. Since \sigma_{\max} \gg 1, the variance explodes, which is what the name captures. Setting t = T,

x_T \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(x_0, \sigma_{\max}^2 I)

Averaging over x_0 leaves p_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\max}^2 I) because \sigma_{\max} swamps the data scale, the typical size of one coordinate of x_0. This is the x_0-free prior that serves as the sampler’s initial condition.
Simulating the VE forward process:
Here we follow the same two-mode data through the VE-SDE, as Figure 4 shows below.








Figure 4: Sample paths of the forward VE-SDE for the two-mode data distribution, with \sigma_{\min} = 0.01 and \sigma_{\max} = 10, smaller than the \sigma_{\max} = 50 used elsewhere in this post, so that the modes stay visible. With no drift, the paths are not shifted toward zero. They stay near their modes while \sigma(t) is small, then spread as it grows. At t = T the two modes are lost in a Gaussian of standard deviation close to \sigma_{\max} (right panel, a histogram over many paths with the marginal p_T). The VP paths above, by contrast, stay at unit scale.





With no drift, each mode stays centered where it started while the noise widens it. The geometric schedule keeps the noise small for most of the interval, so the paths barely spread at first and then spread rapidly near the end, where the two ridges merge. The variance grows to about \sigma_{\max}^2, while the VP variance of Figure 2 fell to 1.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
1.4 The sub-VP SDE
The third choice has no discrete predecessor. It is Song et al.’s own construction, the sub-VP SDE [1], whose variance stays below the VP variance.
It keeps the VP drift and scales the VP g(t)^2 = \beta(t) by the factor 1 - \bar\alpha(t)^2. The factor is 0 at t = 0 and approaches 1 as \bar\alpha(t) \to 0. With \bar\alpha the cumulative product Eq. 10 of the VP-SDE,

\boxed{dx_t = -\tfrac12 \beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)\big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)^2\big)}\; dW_t}
\tag{15}
Song et al. write the factor as 1 - e^{-2\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds}, which is 1 - \bar\alpha(t)^2.

1.4.1 Solving the sub-VP SDE
Comparing Eq. 15 with Eq. 2 identifies the coefficients,

f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) = -\tfrac12 \beta(t), \qquad g(t)^2 = \beta(t)\big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)^2\big)

The mean:
The drift is identical to VP, so the mean is the VP mean, m(t) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}.
The variance:
Substituting m^2 = \bar\alpha and g^2 = \beta(1-\bar\alpha^2) into Eq. 5,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \int_0^t \frac{\beta(s)\big(1 - \bar\alpha(s)^2\big)}{\bar\alpha(s)}\, ds

Splitting the fraction,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \int_0^t \Big(\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)} - \beta(s)\, \bar\alpha(s)\Big)\, ds

Substituting \beta(s) = -\bar\alpha'(s)/\bar\alpha(s), as in the VP variance,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \int_0^t \Big(-\frac{\bar\alpha'(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)^2} + \bar\alpha'(s)\Big)\, ds

Recognizing the integrand as \frac{d}{ds}\Big[\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)} + \bar\alpha(s)\Big],

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \int_0^t \frac{d}{ds}\Big[\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)} + \bar\alpha(s)\Big]\, ds

Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \Big(\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(t)} + \bar\alpha(t) - \frac{1}{\bar\alpha(0)} - \bar\alpha(0)\Big)

Evaluating, with \bar\alpha(0) = 1,

\Sigma(t) = \bar\alpha(t) \Big(\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(t)} + \bar\alpha(t) - 2\Big)

Multiplying out,

\Sigma(t) = 1 + \bar\alpha(t)^2 - 2\, \bar\alpha(t)

Factoring,

\Sigma(t) = \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big)^2

The kernel:
Substituting m(t) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} and \Sigma(t) into Eq. 3, the perturbation kernel is

\boxed{p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_t;\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\; (1 - \bar\alpha(t))^2\, I\big)}
\tag{16}
This is the sub-VP perturbation kernel. \square
Sub-VP shares the VP mean, and its variance is the VP variance squared. For \bar\alpha(t) \in (0, 1), (1 - \bar\alpha)^2 < 1 - \bar\alpha, so the sub-VP variance lies strictly below the VP variance at each intermediate time. The two meet at both ends: at 0 when t = 0, and at 1 as \bar\alpha \to 0. Sub-VP therefore has the same initial condition, the data, and reaches the same prior \mathcal{N}(0, I) with less noise in between.
This is the bound the name captures. In Song et al.’s experiments on CIFAR-10, a dataset of 32 \times 32 colour images, it gives higher likelihoods than VP for each model compared [1]. The likelihood here is the density the trained model assigns to held-out test images, computed exactly through the instantaneous change of variables (P4:§3.4), which P5:§4.2 applies to diffusion models.
On CIFAR-10 sub-VP reached 2.99 bits per dimension [1], the negative base-2 log-likelihood of a test image divided by its number of pixel values, so lower is better. The integer pixel values were first dequantized, by adding uniform noise, so that the data has a density.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
section: 1.5 Side by side: three SDEs, two variance regimes
text:
1.5 Side by side: three SDEs, two variance regimes
Table 1 sets the three forward SDEs side by side, each column obtained from Eq. 4 and Eq. 5 by substitution. They fall into two variance regimes, which give the SDEs their names. VP and sub-VP keep the kernel variance bounded, and it reaches 1. VE lets it grow without an intrinsic bound, to \sigma_{\max}^2 at t = T. The drift is what produces the regime. Differentiating Eq. 5 by the product rule,

\Sigma'(t) = 2\, m(t)\, m'(t) \int_0^t \frac{g(s)^2}{m(s)^2}\, ds + g(t)^2

Substituting m' = f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, m from Eq. 4, the first term becomes 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, \Sigma,

\Sigma'(t) = 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, \Sigma(t) + g(t)^2

The diffusion adds variance at rate g^2, and a negative drift removes it at a rate proportional to \Sigma itself. For VP, f_{\mathrm{lin}} = -\tfrac12\beta and g^2 = \beta, so

\Sigma' = \beta(t)\,(1 - \Sigma)

and the variance relaxes to 1 whatever the schedule. VP’s drift is the one that makes the removal balance the injection at \Sigma = 1. VE has no drift, so \Sigma' = g^2 \ge 0 and nothing offsets the added noise. Sub-VP has VP’s drift and the diffusion g^2 = \beta(1 - \bar\alpha^2), so

\Sigma' = \beta(t)\,\big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)^2 - \Sigma\big)

Its variance (1 - \bar\alpha)^2 stays below the level 1 - \bar\alpha^2, which approaches 1 as \bar\alpha \to 0.
The mean row follows from the drift alone, and the variance and prior rows from the drift and diffusion together. The schedule row collects §1.2.3 and §1.3. The input-scale row and the two CIFAR-10 rows are discussed after Figure 5 below.



Table 1: Coefficients, schedules and perturbation-kernel moments of the VP, VE and sub-VP SDEs, the terminal marginal of each forward process, and the best CIFAR-10 results Song et al. report for each [1]. The likelihood row is in bits per dimension and the sample-quality row in Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [15], the Fréchet distance between Gaussians fitted to the features a pretrained Inception network extracts from generated and from real images; lower is better for both, and bold marks the best value in each. The two rows come from different checkpoints and samplers in Song et al.’s Tables 2 and 3.

Comparing the three perturbation kernels:
Here we plot the mean coefficient and the variance of the perturbation kernel over time for the VP, sub-VP and VE SDEs, as Figure 5 shows below.








Figure 5: The perturbation kernel over time for the VP, sub-VP and VE processes. Left: the mean coefficient m(t). VP and sub-VP share \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}, which falls to 0, while VE keeps m = 1. Right: the kernel variance (log scale). VP rises to 1, the variance of its \mathcal{N}(0, I) limit. Sub-VP (dashed) stays below VP at each intermediate time and reaches 1 at the end. VE grows to \sigma_{\max}^2 \gg 1 (the exploding regime, unbounded in the \sigma_{\max}\to\infty design limit).





VP and sub-VP shrink the mean coefficient to 0, while VE keeps it at 1. The VP variance saturates at 1. The sub-VP variance starts orders of magnitude below it and joins it at the end. The VE variance grows by several orders of magnitude, to \sigma_{\max}^2.
The two regimes also affect training. The VP variance stays bounded for each t, so the network sees inputs of comparable scale at each noise level. VE has no such bound, and its \sigma_{\max} lies far above the data scale, so the scale of its inputs grows by orders of magnitude across t. In return, VE gave Song et al. their best sample quality, while VP and sub-VP gave higher likelihoods, as the last two rows of Table 1 show [1].

1.5.1 The moment equations from Itô’s lemma
The variance equation above came from differentiating the solution Eq. 5. Both moments also satisfy ODEs that follow from the SDE itself, by Itô’s lemma and expectations, without solving it. The derivation below allows an additive term in the drift, because §2.4 applies the same equations to a reverse-time SDE whose drift has one.
Set-up:
Let x_t be one component of the solution of an SDE with an affine drift and a state-independent diffusion coefficient,

dx_t = \big(a(t)\, x_t + b(t)\big)\, dt + g(t)\, dW_t

with continuous coefficients a, b, g: [0, T] \to \mathbb{R} and an initial condition x_0 that is independent of W_t and has a finite second moment. The solution then has a finite second moment, bounded on [0, T] (§A.1). We write M(t) = \mathbb{E}[x_t] and V(t) = \operatorname{Var}[x_t] for its mean and variance, with M, V: [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}.
The mean:
Writing the SDE in its integral form,

x_t = x_0 + \int_0^t \big(a(s)\, x_s + b(s)\big)\, ds + \int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s

Taking expectations, where the Itô integral with the deterministic integrand g has mean zero (P1:Eq. 7) and the bounded second moment lets the expectation pass inside the time integral,

M(t) = M(0) + \int_0^t \big(a(s)\, M(s) + b(s)\big)\, ds

Differentiating in t by the fundamental theorem of calculus,

\boxed{M'(t) = a(t)\, M(t) + b(t)}
\tag{17}
The variance:
The variance is the mean of h(x_t, t) for the transform h(x, t) = \big(x - M(t)\big)^2, which is twice continuously differentiable in x and, since Eq. 17 makes M continuously differentiable, once in t. Its partials are

\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = -2\big(x - M(t)\big)\, M'(t), \qquad \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} = 2\big(x - M(t)\big), \qquad \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} = 2

Substituting them, the drift a\, x_t + b and the diffusion coefficient g into Itô’s lemma Eq. 6, with M, M', a, b and g evaluated at t,

d\big(x_t - M\big)^2 = \Big(-2\big(x_t - M\big) M' + 2\big(a\, x_t + b\big)\big(x_t - M\big) + g^2\Big)\, dt + 2g\, \big(x_t - M\big)\, dW_t

Writing a\, x_t + b = a\, (x_t - M) + (a M + b) in the second term,

d\big(x_t - M\big)^2 = \Big(-2\big(x_t - M\big) M' + 2a\, \big(x_t - M\big)^2 + 2\big(a M + b\big)\big(x_t - M\big) + g^2\Big)\, dt + 2g\, \big(x_t - M\big)\, dW_t

Writing it in integral form,

\begin{aligned}
\big(x_t - M(t)\big)^2 = {} & \big(x_0 - M(0)\big)^2 + \int_0^t \Big(-2\big(x_s - M\big) M' + 2a\, \big(x_s - M\big)^2 \\[4pt]
& + 2\big(a M + b\big)\big(x_s - M\big) + g^2\Big)\, ds \\[4pt]
& + \int_0^t 2g\, \big(x_s - M\big)\, dW_s
\end{aligned}

Taking expectations, where the Itô integral has mean zero because its integrand 2g\,(x_s - M(s)) is adapted and square-integrable [16], \big(x_0 - M(0)\big)^2 has the mean V(0), and the bounded second moment lets the expectation pass inside the time integral,

V(t) = V(0) + \int_0^t \mathbb{E}\Big[-2\big(x_s - M\big) M' + 2a\, \big(x_s - M\big)^2 + 2\big(a M + b\big)\big(x_s - M\big) + g^2\Big]\, ds

Evaluating the expectation term by term, with \mathbb{E}[x_s - M(s)] = 0 and \mathbb{E}\big[(x_s - M(s))^2\big] = V(s),

V(t) = V(0) + \int_0^t \big(2a(s)\, V(s) + g(s)^2\big)\, ds

Differentiating in t by the fundamental theorem of calculus,

\boxed{V'(t) = 2a(t)\, V(t) + g(t)^2}
\tag{18}
The perturbation kernel:
For the forward SDE Eq. 2 started from a fixed x_0, the coefficients are a = f_{\mathrm{lin}} and b = 0, and by Eq. 3 the moments of a component are M(t) = m(t)\, x_0 and V(t) = \Sigma(t). Substituting them into Eq. 17,

m'(t)\, x_0 = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, m(t)\, x_0

Taking x_0 = 1, since the identity holds for each x_0,

\boxed{m'(t) = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, m(t)}

whose solution with m(0) = 1 is Eq. 4. Substituting a = f_{\mathrm{lin}} and V = \Sigma into Eq. 18,

\boxed{\Sigma'(t) = 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, \Sigma(t) + g(t)^2}

the variance equation obtained above by differentiating Eq. 5, now derived from the SDE without its solution. With \Sigma(0) = 0, its solution is Eq. 5.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
2.1 Marginal path ⟺ Fokker-Planck equation
This section states the equivalence between the marginals of an SDE’s solution and the Fokker-Planck equation. §A.4 derives the Fokker-Planck equation for a general SDE, whose diffusion is a d \times d matrix G(x, t) that may depend on the state.
Definitions:

A probability path is a family of probability densities \rho_t: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), one for each time t \in (0, T], with \rho_t(x) continuously differentiable in t and twice continuously differentiable in x, together with an initial distribution \rho_0, which need not have a density, such that \int \psi\, \rho_t\, dx \to \mathbb{E}_{\rho_0}[\psi] as t \to 0 for each bounded continuous \psi.
The marginal path of a process is the probability path formed by its marginal densities for t > 0, with its distribution at t = 0 as the initial distribution.
A test function is a function \varphi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} that is infinitely differentiable and zero outside a bounded set.
A function of x decays at infinity when it and its first two derivatives tend to zero as \lVert x \rVert \to \infty fast enough to leave no boundary terms when it is integrated by parts against a bounded function with bounded derivatives. This must hold also after the function is multiplied by one that grows at most linearly in x, such as a Lipschitz drift.
A probability path is dominated when, on each interval [a, b] with 0 < a \le b \le T, the functions (1 + \lVert x \rVert)\, \rho_t(x) and \lvert \partial_t \rho_t(x) \rvert, for t \in [a, b], are bounded by one integrable function of x.

Assumptions:

The SDE dx_t = f(x_t, t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW_t has the initial condition x_0 \sim \rho_0, with \rho_0 of finite second moment, and its drift f and diffusion coefficient g satisfy the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions of §A.1 and are continuous in t, so it has a unique solution x_t.
The drift f is infinitely differentiable in x, with bounded derivatives.
The diffusion coefficient g(t) does not depend on x.
The probability path \rho_t decays at infinity for each t > 0 and is dominated.

Theorem:
Under these assumptions,

\boxed{\begin{aligned}
&x_t \sim \rho_t \ \forall t \in (0, T] \\[4pt]
\Longleftrightarrow\quad &\partial_t \rho_t(x) = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f(x, t)\, \rho_t(x)\big) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \Delta_x \rho_t(x) \ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ t \in (0, T]
\end{aligned}}
\tag{20}
The left side of Eq. 20 says that \rho_t is the marginal path of x_t, and the right side is the Fokker-Planck equation. The theorem therefore states that the Fokker-Planck equation is a necessary and sufficient condition for a probability path to be the marginal path of x_t.

Necessity (\Rightarrow): The marginal path of x_t satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation.
Sufficiency (\Leftarrow): A probability path that satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation is the marginal path of x_t, the solution of the SDE with the initial condition x_0 \sim \rho_0.

For data in a bounded set, the linear forward SDE Eq. 2 with the initial condition x_0 \sim p_0 is one case. Its drift is affine, and its marginal path p_t, a Gaussian convolution of p_0, decays at infinity and is dominated. So by the necessity part p_t satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation.

2.1.1 Proof of necessity (⇒)
Post #1 proves necessity in P1:§8.3, where the Fokker-Planck equation is P1:Eq. 45. \square


2.1.2 Proof of sufficiency (⇐)
The proof is outlined here and given in full below. It fixes a time s \in (0, T] and a test function \varphi, and shows in four steps that \int \varphi\, \rho_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}[\varphi(x_s)].

The function u(x, t) = \mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(x_s) \mid x_t = x\big], for t \in [0, s], carries the test function back in time, with u(x, s) = \varphi(x).
The solution x_t is a Markov process, so its future given its present state does not depend on its past. With Itô’s lemma, this makes u satisfy the backward Kolmogorov equation 
\partial_t u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u = 0

When \rho_t satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation, integrating by parts turns \frac{d}{dt}\int u\, \rho_t\, dx into the integral of the left side of the backward Kolmogorov equation against \rho_t, which is zero. So \int u\, \rho_t\, dx is constant on (0, s].
Comparing its value at t = s with its limit as t \to 0, where x_0 \sim \rho_0, gives \int \varphi\, \rho_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}[\varphi(x_s)] for each test function, so \rho_s is the density of x_s.







NoteProof: sufficiency of the Fokker-Planck equation





Let \rho_t satisfy the Fokker-Planck equation.
Step 1 — a function that carries the test function back in time:
Fixing s \in (0, T] and a test function \varphi, we define u: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, s] \to \mathbb{R} by

u(x, t) = \mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(x_s) \mid x_t = x\big]

the expected value of \varphi(x_s) for the solution of the SDE started from x at time t. At t = s, x_s = x, so u(x, s) = \varphi(x). Under assumptions 1 and 2, u is twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t, u and its derivatives in x are bounded, and \partial_t u grows at most linearly in x [16].
Step 2 — u satisfies the backward Kolmogorov equation:
We fix x, a time t < s, and a step \delta > 0 with t + \delta \le s. By the Markov property of the solution [16], conditioning \varphi(x_s) first on x_{t+\delta} and then on x_t,

u(x, t) = \mathbb{E}\big[u(x_{t+\delta}, t + \delta) \mid x_t = x\big]

Itô’s lemma applies to a function h: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, T] \to \mathbb{R} that is twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t. For the SDE of assumption 1, whose diffusion is g(t)\, I, it is P1:Eq. 50,

dh(x_t, t) = \Big(\partial_t h + f\cdot\nabla_x h + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x h\Big)\, dt + g\, \nabla_x h\cdot dW_t

Applying it to u and integrating from t to t + \delta with x_t = x,

u(x_{t+\delta}, t + \delta) - u(x, t) = \int_t^{t+\delta} \big(\partial_r u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u\big)(x_r, r)\, dr + \int_t^{t+\delta} g\, \nabla_x u(x_r, r)\cdot dW_r

Taking expectations given x_t = x, which removes the Itô integral, since an Itô integral of a bounded integrand has mean zero (P1:§A.4),

\mathbb{E}\big[u(x_{t+\delta}, t + \delta) \mid x_t = x\big] - u(x, t) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_t^{t+\delta} \big(\partial_r u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u\big)(x_r, r)\, dr \;\Big|\; x_t = x\Big]

Substituting the identity u(x, t) = \mathbb{E}\big[u(x_{t+\delta}, t + \delta) \mid x_t = x\big] from the start of this step, the left side is zero,

0 = \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_t^{t+\delta} \big(\partial_r u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u\big)(x_r, r)\, dr \;\Big|\; x_t = x\Big]

Dividing by \delta,

0 = \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{\delta}\int_t^{t+\delta} \big(\partial_r u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u\big)(x_r, r)\, dr \;\Big|\; x_t = x\Big]

Letting \delta \to 0, which dominated convergence allows because the integrand is continuous, x_r \to x as r \to t, and the integrand grows at most linearly in x_r (Step 1 and assumption 1) while \mathbb{E}\big[\sup_r \lVert x_r \rVert^2\big] < \infty (§A.1),

0 = \big(\partial_t u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u\big)(x, t)

This holds for each x and each t < s. Together with u(x, s) = \varphi(x) from Step 1, u satisfies the backward Kolmogorov equation

\partial_t u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u = 0, \qquad u(x, s) = \varphi(x)

Step 3 — the integral of u against \rho_t is constant in time:
Differentiating \int u\, \rho_t\, dx in t under the integral, for t \in (0, s), which the domination of assumption 4 permits because u is bounded and \partial_t u = -\big(f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u\big) grows at most linearly in x,

\frac{d}{dt}\int u\, \rho_t\, dx = \int \partial_t u\, \rho_t\, dx + \int u\, \partial_t \rho_t\, dx

Substituting the Fokker-Planck equation for \partial_t \rho_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\int u\, \rho_t\, dx = \int \partial_t u\, \rho_t\, dx + \int u\, \Big[-\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, \rho_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x \rho_t\Big]\, dx

Integrating by parts, once in the drift term and twice in the diffusion term, with no boundary terms because \rho_t decays at infinity (assumption 4), f grows at most linearly (assumption 1) and u is bounded with bounded derivatives (Step 1),

\frac{d}{dt}\int u\, \rho_t\, dx = \int \Big(\partial_t u + f\cdot\nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x u\Big)\, \rho_t\, dx

Substituting the backward Kolmogorov equation of Step 2,

\frac{d}{dt}\int u\, \rho_t\, dx = 0

This holds for each t \in (0, s), and \int u\, \rho_t\, dx is continuous on (0, s] by the same domination, so it is constant on (0, s].
Step 4 — \int \varphi\, \rho_s\, dx equals \mathbb{E}[\varphi(x_s)]:
By Step 3, \int u\, \rho_t\, dx takes the same value at each t \in (0, s]. Using u(x, s) = \varphi(x) at t = s,

\int \varphi\, \rho_s\, dx = \int u(x, t)\, \rho_t(x)\, dx \quad \forall t \in (0, s]

Letting t \to 0, where u(\cdot, t) \to u(\cdot, 0) uniformly on bounded sets because \partial_t u grows at most linearly in x, u is bounded, and \rho_t converges to the distribution \rho_0 of x_0 (assumption 1 and the definition of a probability path),

\int \varphi\, \rho_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}\big[u(x_0, 0)\big]

By the definition of u at t = 0,

\int \varphi\, \rho_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(x_s) \mid x_0\big]\Big]

By the tower property of conditional expectation, \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z]\big] = \mathbb{E}[Y] for an integrable Y and each random variable Z,

\int \varphi\, \rho_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(x_s)\big]

A density that gives each test function its expected value under x_s is the density of x_s, so x_s \sim \rho_s. As s \in (0, T] was arbitrary, x_t \sim \rho_t for each t \in (0, T]. \square

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
section: 2.2 Deriving the reverse-time SDE using the Fokker-Planck equation
text:
2.2 Deriving the reverse-time SDE using the Fokker-Planck equation
The reverse-time SDE is an SDE whose solution, run backward in time from \bar x_T \sim p_T, has the forward marginal p_t for each t; §2.2.1 shows that such SDEs form a family and which member is the time reversal.
The derivation constructs it in three steps. Step 1 rewrites the Fokker-Planck equation that p_t satisfies so that, once time is reversed, it is the Fokker-Planck equation of an SDE. Step 2 checks that this SDE meets the assumptions of the equivalence in Eq. 20. Step 3 applies its sufficiency part, which makes the forward marginals, in reverse time order, the marginal path of that SDE’s solution, and writes the SDE in the forward time. §A.4 repeats the derivation for the general SDE.
The log-derivative identity:
This derivation uses one identity, and so does each member of the family of §2.2.1, the probability-flow ODE among them. For a positive density p, the chain rule for the logarithm gives

\nabla_x \log p = \frac{\nabla_x p}{p}

Multiplying both sides by p,

p\, \nabla_x \log p = \nabla_x p

Taking the divergence of both sides,

\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p\, \nabla_x \log p\big) = \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\nabla_x p

Writing the divergence of the gradient as the Laplacian,

\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p\, \nabla_x \log p\big) = \Delta_x p
\tag{21}
So the Laplacian in the diffusion term is the divergence of the vector field p\, \nabla_x \log p, the density times the score. This is what turns the forward diffusion term into part of the reverse drift.
Step 1 — the reversed marginals satisfy a Fokker-Planck equation:
Starting from the Fokker-Planck equation, which the marginal path p_t satisfies by the necessity part of Eq. 20,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

Writing the diffusion term as g^2\, \Delta_x p_t - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + g^2\, \Delta_x p_t - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

Substituting the log-derivative identity from Eq. 21 for the first \Delta_x p_t,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(g^2\, p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big) - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

Combining the first two terms into one divergence,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\big(f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big)\, p_t\Big] - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

The last term has the opposite sign to a diffusion term, so on its own it would concentrate the density instead of spreading it. Reversing time flips its sign.
Let \tau = T - t, so \tau runs from 0 to T as t runs from T to 0, and let the reversed marginals \bar p_\tau = p_{T-\tau}, a density \bar p_\tau: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty) for each \tau, be the forward marginals in reverse time order. In what follows, f and g are evaluated at t = T - \tau. Reversing time, with \partial_t p_t = -\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau and p_t = p_{T-\tau} = \bar p_\tau,

-\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\big(f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big] - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x \bar p_\tau

Multiplying both sides by -1,

\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\big(f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big] + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x \bar p_\tau

Writing the sign inside the divergence,

\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[-\big(f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big] + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x \bar p_\tau

This is the Fokker-Planck equation, in the time \tau, of the SDE

dy_\tau = -\Big[f(y_\tau, T - \tau) - g(T - \tau)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_{T-\tau}(y_\tau)\Big]\, d\tau + g(T - \tau)\, d\bar W_\tau
\tag{22}
with \bar W_\tau a standard Brownian motion in \tau. So \bar p_\tau satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation built from the coefficients of Eq. 22. Whether it is the marginal path of that SDE’s solution is what Steps 2 and 3 determine.
Step 2 — the assumptions of the equivalence hold:
The equivalence Eq. 20 has four assumptions, and each holds for Eq. 22 in the time \tau, with \bar p_\tau as the probability path. Assumptions 1 and 2 ask the drift of Eq. 22 to be Lipschitz and smooth with bounded derivatives. That drift contains the score \nabla_x \log p_t, so the two assumptions hold once the derivatives of \log p_t are bounded, which needs one property of the data.
The bound on the derivatives of \log p_t: If p_0 is supported in a solid sphere of radius R centered at the origin, each derivative of \log p_t of order two or more is bounded, uniformly for t \ge t_{\min}. We write \nabla_x^k for the k-th derivative in x, an array with k indices, so that \nabla_x^2 is the Hessian, and \lVert \cdot \rVert for the largest absolute value of its entries. Then

\boxed{\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ t \in [t_{\min}, T]} \big\lVert \nabla_x^k \log p_t(x) \big\rVert < \infty \quad \forall k \ge 2}
\tag{23}
The cumulant generating function of a random vector Z \in \mathbb{R}^d is \lambda \mapsto \log \mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda \cdot Z}\big], \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^d. Its k-th derivative at \lambda = 0 is the k-th cumulant \operatorname{cum}_k[Z], an array with k indices. The first cumulant is the mean of Z and the second its covariance.
The proof has three steps.

\log p_t is a quadratic in x plus a function K evaluated at m(t)\, x / \Sigma(t), and the derivatives of K at that point are the cumulants of x_0 given x_t = x.
Differentiating k \ge 2 times turns the K term into (m(t)/\Sigma(t))^k times the k-th cumulant of x_0 given x_t = x, and the quadratic adds -I/\Sigma(t) when k = 2.
Given x_t, x_0 stays in the solid sphere, so its cumulants are bounded, and so are these derivatives.







NoteProof: the bound on the derivatives of the log marginal





Step 1 — \log p_t through a cumulant generating function:
We fix t > 0 and write m = m(t) and \Sigma = \Sigma(t). Each marginal is the perturbation kernel Eq. 3 averaged over the data,

p_t(x) = \int \mathcal{N}\big(x;\; m\, x_0,\; \Sigma\, I\big)\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0

Writing out the Gaussian density,

p_t(x) = (2\pi\Sigma)^{-d/2} \int e^{-\lVert x - m\, x_0 \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0

Expanding the square, \lVert x - m\, x_0 \rVert^2 = \lVert x \rVert^2 - 2m\, x \cdot x_0 + m^2 \lVert x_0 \rVert^2,

p_t(x) = (2\pi\Sigma)^{-d/2} \int e^{-\lVert x \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, e^{(m/\Sigma)\, x \cdot x_0}\, e^{-m^2 \lVert x_0 \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0

Factoring e^{-\lVert x \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}, which does not depend on x_0, out of the integral,

p_t(x) = (2\pi\Sigma)^{-d/2}\, e^{-\lVert x \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)} \int e^{(m/\Sigma)\, x \cdot x_0}\, e^{-m^2 \lVert x_0 \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0

Applying the logarithm to both sides,

\log p_t(x) = -\tfrac{d}{2} \log(2\pi\Sigma) - \frac{\lVert x \rVert^2}{2\Sigma} + \log \int e^{(m/\Sigma)\, x \cdot x_0}\, e^{-m^2 \lVert x_0 \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0

Writing the last term as K(m x / \Sigma), with K: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} defined by K(\eta) = \log \int e^{\eta \cdot x_0}\, e^{-m^2 \lVert x_0 \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0,

\log p_t(x) = -\tfrac{d}{2} \log(2\pi\Sigma) - \frac{\lVert x \rVert^2}{2\Sigma} + K\big(m x / \Sigma\big)

The derivatives of K are cumulants. For each \eta, let q_\eta be the density

q_\eta(x_0) \propto e^{\eta \cdot x_0}\, e^{-m^2 \lVert x_0 \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, p_0(x_0)

Then

K(\eta + \lambda) - K(\eta) = \log \mathbb{E}_{q_\eta}\big[e^{\lambda \cdot x_0}\big]

is the cumulant generating function of q_\eta, so \nabla_\eta^k K(\eta) is the k-th cumulant of q_\eta.
At \eta = m x / \Sigma, q_\eta is the density of x_0 given x_t = x. By Bayes’ rule that density is proportional to p_{0t}(x \mid x_0)\, p_0(x_0), and the factors of the kernel that do not involve x_0 cancel in the normalization. So

\nabla_\eta^k K(\eta)\big|_{\eta = m x/\Sigma} = \operatorname{cum}_k\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big]

which for k = 2 is \operatorname{Cov}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big].
Step 2 — the derivatives of \log p_t are cumulants:
Differentiating twice in x, where the chain rule gives each derivative of K(m x / \Sigma) a factor m / \Sigma,

\nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x) = -\frac{I}{\Sigma} + \Big(\frac{m}{\Sigma}\Big)^2 \nabla_\eta^2 K(\eta)\big|_{\eta = m x/\Sigma}

Substituting the covariance for \nabla_\eta^2 K,

\nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x) = -\frac{I}{\Sigma} + \Big(\frac{m}{\Sigma}\Big)^2 \operatorname{Cov}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big]

Differentiating k \ge 3 times instead, where the quadratic term no longer contributes,

\nabla_x^k \log p_t(x) = \Big(\frac{m}{\Sigma}\Big)^k \nabla_\eta^k K(\eta)\big|_{\eta = m x/\Sigma}

Substituting the k-th cumulant for \nabla_\eta^k K,

\nabla_x^k \log p_t(x) = \Big(\frac{m}{\Sigma}\Big)^k \operatorname{cum}_k\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big]

Step 3 — the cumulants are bounded:
The density of x_0 given x_t is supported in the same solid sphere as p_0, so its moments of order k are at most R^k in absolute value, and its k-th cumulant is a polynomial in its moments of order at most k. So each \operatorname{cum}_k\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big] is bounded in x and t.
On [t_{\min}, T], \Sigma(t) is bounded below by a positive constant, since it is continuous and positive for t > 0, and m(t) is bounded. By the two identities of Step 2, each derivative of \log p_t of order k \ge 2 is then bounded for x \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in [t_{\min}, T], which is Eq. 23. \square



Assumption 1 — Lipschitz coefficients and initial condition: The drift f is affine in x, so it is Lipschitz. By Eq. 23 with k = 2, the Hessian of \log p_t is bounded, so the score \nabla_x \log p_t is Lipschitz in x too, uniformly for t \ge t_{\min}. So the drift of Eq. 22 is Lipschitz, and hence of at most linear growth, for each \tau < T, which is each t > 0, and it and g are continuous in time. The SDE has the initial condition y_0 \sim \bar p_0, which is p_T, of finite second moment.
Assumption 2 — smooth drift: Each derivative of the score is a derivative of \log p_t of order two or more, so by Eq. 23 it is bounded for each t > 0. The drift f is affine, so the drift of Eq. 22 is infinitely differentiable with bounded derivatives.
Assumption 3 — state-independent diffusion: The diffusion coefficient g(T - \tau) does not depend on y.
Assumption 4 — decay at infinity: On each horizon [0, \tau'] with \tau' < T, which is each t > 0, the reversed marginal \bar p_\tau = p_{T-\tau} is a Gaussian convolution of data with bounded support. So it is smooth, a probability path with the initial distribution \bar p_0 = p_T, it decays at infinity, and it is dominated, because its Gaussian tails, and those of \partial_\tau \bar p_\tau, are uniform in \tau \le \tau'.
Step 3 — the sufficiency part applies:
By Step 1, \bar p_\tau satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation of Eq. 22, and by Step 2 the assumptions of Eq. 20 hold. Its sufficiency part therefore makes \bar p_\tau the marginal path of y_\tau, the solution of Eq. 22 with the initial condition y_0 \sim \bar p_0. So y_\tau \sim \bar p_\tau for each \tau < T.
Since \bar p_\tau = p_{T-\tau}, this is y_\tau \sim p_{T-\tau}, from the initial condition y_0 \sim p_T.
Writing the time arguments of Eq. 22 in the forward time t = T - \tau,

dy_\tau = -\big[f(y_\tau, t) - g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y_\tau)\big]\, d\tau + g(t)\, d\bar W_\tau

Writing the state in the forward time, as the reverse-time process \bar x_t = y_{T-t}, the solution y_\tau indexed by the forward time, with the bar of a time-reversed object,

dy_\tau = -\big[f(\bar x_t, t) - g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(\bar x_t)\big]\, d\tau + g(t)\, d\bar W_\tau

Writing the time increment in the forward time, d\tau = -dt, under which the increment dy_\tau = y_{\tau + d\tau} - y_\tau is \bar x_{t + dt} - \bar x_t = d\bar x_t, an increment over a negative time step dt,

d\bar x_t = \big[f(\bar x_t, t) - g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(\bar x_t)\big]\, dt + g(t)\, d\bar W_\tau

Writing the Brownian motion in the forward time, \bar W_t for \bar W_\tau at \tau = T - t,

\boxed{d\bar x_t = \Big[\, f(\bar x_t, t) - g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(\bar x_t) \,\Big] dt + g(t)\, d\bar W_t}

which is Eq. 19. Since y_\tau \sim p_{T-\tau}, its solution \bar x_t = y_{T-t} has \bar x_t \sim p_t for each t > 0, so it is a new process that shares the marginals of the forward SDE’s solution. \square

2.2.1 The choice of the reverse diffusion coefficient
Step 1 converted twice the diffusion term into part of the drift and kept -\tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t, which the reversal of time turned into the diffusion term of Eq. 22. A different split gives a different SDE with the same marginals. For a diffusion coefficient h: [0, T] \to [0, \infty), writing the diffusion term as

\frac{1}{2}\big(g^2 + h^2\big)\, \Delta_x p_t - \frac{1}{2} h^2\, \Delta_x p_t

and repeating Steps 1 to 3 gives the SDE

d\bar x_t = \Big[f(\bar x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\big(g(t)^2 + h(t)^2\big)\, \nabla_x \log p_t(\bar x_t)\Big]\, dt + h(t)\, d\bar W_t

whose solution, run backward from \bar x_T \sim p_T, has the marginals p_t for each choice of h. So the marginals alone do not determine the reverse diffusion. The choice h = 0 removes the noise and gives the probability-flow ODE of Part 3.
The choice h = g gives the reverse-time SDE, the time reversal of the forward process. The quadratic variation of a path, the limit of its summed squared increments over ever finer partitions, is computed from that path alone and does not change when the path runs backward. So the forward paths run backward keep the quadratic variation g^2\, dt of the forward SDE, and only h = g matches it.
Anderson’s theorem [4] proves that with h = g the reversed process reproduces the joint distribution of the forward process, not only its marginals, and §2.3 derives the same drift from the transition over one short time step. With h = g, half of the g^2 in the drift comes from the forward diffusion term and half from the diffusion term of the reversed process.


2.2.2 Tweedie’s formula and its second-order form
The proof of Eq. 23 gives more than a bound. Its Step 1 writes the density of x_0 given x_t = x as q_\eta at \eta = m x / \Sigma, with q_\eta(x_0) \propto e^{\eta \cdot x_0}\, e^{-m^2 \lVert x_0 \rVert^2 / (2\Sigma)}\, p_0(x_0). Densities of the form e^{\eta \cdot x_0} times a fixed base density, normalized, make up an exponential family with the natural parameter \eta \in \mathbb{R}^d. The logarithm of the normalizing integral, here K(\eta), is the log-normalizer of the family.
By Step 1, the derivatives of the log-normalizer are the cumulants of x_0 under q_\eta, and Step 2 relates them to the derivatives of \log p_t. Efron derives the first two as formulas for the posterior mean and variance under Gaussian noise [8]. The same derivation holds for each linear SDE, and it needs no bounded support, because the Gaussian factor of q_\eta makes each of its moments finite for each p_0, so K is infinitely differentiable, with its derivatives taken under the integral. With m = m(t) and \Sigma = \Sigma(t) as in that proof, its Step 1 gives

\log p_t(x) = -\tfrac{d}{2} \log(2\pi\Sigma) - \frac{\lVert x \rVert^2}{2\Sigma} + K\big(m x / \Sigma\big)

The posterior mean:
Differentiating once in x, where the chain rule gives \nabla_x K(m x / \Sigma) the factor m / \Sigma,

\nabla_x \log p_t(x) = -\frac{x}{\Sigma} + \frac{m}{\Sigma}\, \nabla_\eta K(\eta)\big|_{\eta = m x/\Sigma}

Substituting the first cumulant, the posterior mean, for \nabla_\eta K,

\nabla_x \log p_t(x) = -\frac{x}{\Sigma} + \frac{m}{\Sigma}\, \mathbb{E}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big]

Multiplying both sides by \Sigma / m,

\frac{\Sigma}{m}\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x) = -\frac{x}{m} + \mathbb{E}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big]

Adding x / m to both sides,

\boxed{\mathbb{E}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big] = \frac{x + \Sigma(t)\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x)}{m(t)}}
\tag{24}
which is Tweedie’s formula, P2:Eq. 47, for the perturbation kernel Eq. 3.
The posterior covariance:
Differentiating a second time, Step 2 of the proof obtains

\nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x) = -\frac{I}{\Sigma} + \Big(\frac{m}{\Sigma}\Big)^2 \operatorname{Cov}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big]

Multiplying both sides by (\Sigma / m)^2,

\Big(\frac{\Sigma}{m}\Big)^2 \nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x) = -\frac{\Sigma}{m^2}\, I + \operatorname{Cov}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big]

Adding (\Sigma / m^2)\, I to both sides,

\operatorname{Cov}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big] = \frac{\Sigma}{m^2}\, I + \Big(\frac{\Sigma}{m}\Big)^2 \nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x)

Factoring out \Sigma / m^2,

\boxed{\operatorname{Cov}\big[x_0 \mid x_t = x\big] = \frac{\Sigma(t)}{m(t)^2}\, \Big(I + \Sigma(t)\, \nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x)\Big)}
\tag{25}
With m = 1, as for the VE-SDE, the two formulas are Efron’s posterior mean x + \Sigma\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x) and posterior covariance \Sigma\, I + \Sigma^2\, \nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x) for a state observed through Gaussian noise of variance \Sigma [8]. Differentiating k \ge 3 times continues the pattern: by Step 2, the k-th derivative of \log p_t is (m/\Sigma)^k times the k-th posterior cumulant.
A covariance is positive semidefinite, so Eq. 25 also bounds the curvature of \log p_t from below, \nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x) \succeq -I/\Sigma(t) in the order of positive semidefinite matrices. The log-density of p_t is never more concave than that of the kernel Eq. 3. Along a unit vector u it reaches that curvature, u^\top \nabla_x^2 \log p_t(x)\, u = -1/\Sigma(t), exactly when the posterior of x_0 given x_t = x has zero variance along u. It reaches it along every direction at once only when p_0 is a point mass.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
section: 2.3 Deriving the reverse-time SDE using Bayes’ rule
text:
2.3 Deriving the reverse-time SDE using Bayes’ rule
A second route derives the same drift over one short time step. There, Bayes’ rule turns the forward transition into the reverse one. Letting the step shrink to zero then gives the SDE.
The forward transition:
Over a small step \Delta t, the Euler-Maruyama scheme [12] advances the forward SDE Eq. 1 by

x_{t+\Delta t} = x_t + f(x_t, t)\, \Delta t + g(t)\sqrt{\Delta t}\; \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)

Given x_t, the only random term is Gaussian, so x_{t+\Delta t} is Gaussian with mean x_t + f(x_t, t)\, \Delta t and covariance g(t)^2\, \Delta t\, I,

p(x_{t+\Delta t} \mid x_t) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_{t+\Delta t};\; x_t + f(x_t,t)\,\Delta t,\; g(t)^2\, \Delta t\, I\big)
\tag{26}
This agrees with the SDE to first order in \Delta t, the accuracy kept throughout.
The reverse transition by Bayes’ rule:
Bayes’ rule turns the forward transition into the reverse one, with the marginals as prior and evidence,

p(x_t \mid x_{t+\Delta t}) = \frac{p(x_{t+\Delta t}\mid x_t)\; p_t(x_t)}{p_{t+\Delta t}(x_{t+\Delta t})}

Writing y for the given later state x_{t+\Delta t},

p(x_t \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid x_t)\; p_t(x_t)}{p_{t+\Delta t}(y)}
\tag{27}
Its logarithm:
The evidence p_{t+\Delta t}(y) does not depend on x_t, so its log is a constant here. Taking logs,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = \log p(y \mid x_t) + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

The normalizing factor of the Gaussian Eq. 26 depends on t and \Delta t alone, so it joins the constant too. Substituting the log of the Gaussian,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert y - x_t - f(x_t, t)\,\Delta t \rVert^2}{2 g(t)^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

Over one step, y - x_t = f(x_t, t)\,\Delta t + g(t)\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\epsilon is of the size of the noise, so the difference u = x_t - y is O(\sqrt{\Delta t}). Writing g for g(t) and the norm in u, with y - x_t = -u,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert u + f(x_t, t)\,\Delta t \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

Expanding the square, with each term over 2 g^2 \Delta t,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{2\Delta t\, f(x_t, t)\cdot u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{\Delta t^2\, \lVert f(x_t, t) \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

The drift is evaluated at the unknown x_t. Expanding it about the known y, f(x_t, t) = f(y, t) + J u + O(\lVert u \rVert^2), with J \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} the Jacobian of f(\cdot, t) at y, and writing f for f(y, t),

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{2\Delta t\, (f + J u)\cdot u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{\Delta t^2\, \lVert f + J u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \cdots + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

Multiplying out,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{2\Delta t\, f\cdot u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{2\Delta t\, u^\top J u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{\Delta t^2\, \lVert f \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{2\Delta t^2\, f\cdot J u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{\Delta t^2\, \lVert J u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \cdots + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

The reverse transition is needed to first order in \Delta t, like the forward one, so its mean is needed to O(\Delta t) and its variance to leading order. In a Gaussian exponent -\lVert u \rVert^2/(2 g^2 \Delta t), an added linear term b\cdot u shifts the mean by g^2 \Delta t\, b, and an added quadratic term changes the precision 1/(g^2 \Delta t). With u = O(\sqrt{\Delta t}), the six terms behave as follows.

The first term, 
\frac{\lVert u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t}
 is O(1). It is the leading quadratic, which sets the variance g^2 \Delta t. It stays.
The second term, 
\frac{2\Delta t\, f\cdot u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} = \frac{f\cdot u}{g^2}
 is linear in u with an O(1) coefficient. It shifts the mean by -f\,\Delta t, a first-order effect, so it stays.
The third term, 
\frac{2\Delta t\, u^\top J u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} = \frac{u^\top J u}{g^2}
 is quadratic in u with an O(1) coefficient. It changes the precision 1/(g^2\Delta t) by a relative O(\Delta t), so it changes the variance and the mean only at O(\Delta t^2). It goes.
The fourth term, 
\frac{\Delta t^2\, \lVert f \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t}
 does not depend on x_t. It joins the constant.
The fifth term, 
\frac{2\Delta t^2\, f\cdot J u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} = \frac{\Delta t\, f\cdot J u}{g^2}
 is linear in u with an O(\Delta t) coefficient. It shifts the mean by g^2 \Delta t \cdot O(\Delta t) = O(\Delta t^2). It goes.
The sixth term, 
\frac{\Delta t^2\, \lVert J u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t}
 is quadratic in u with an O(\Delta t) coefficient, smaller than term 3. It goes.

The terms in \cdots come from the O(\lVert u \rVert^2) remainder of the drift. They are cubic in u or smaller, and they shift the mean only at O(\Delta t^2), so they go too. Keeping terms 1 and 2 and absorbing term 4 into the constant,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert u \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} - \frac{2\Delta t\, f\cdot u}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

Completing the square in u, with the leftover \Delta t\, \lVert f \rVert^2/(2g^2) absorbed into the constant,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert u + f\,\Delta t \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

Writing x_t - y back for u,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert x_t - (y - f\,\Delta t) \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(x_t) + \text{const}

Expanding \log p_t(x_t) to second order about y,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert x_t - (y - f\,\Delta t) \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(y) + \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\cdot(x_t - y) + \tfrac{1}{2}(x_t - y)^\top \nabla_x^2 \log p_t(y)\,(x_t - y) + O\big(\lVert x_t - y\rVert^3\big) + \text{const}

The Hessian term is quadratic in x_t - y with an O(1) coefficient, like term 3 above, so it changes the transition only at O(\Delta t^2). The remainder is cubic in x_t - y, and it shifts the mean only at O(\Delta t^2), like the remainder of the drift above. Both statements need \log p_t to have bounded derivatives up to third order near y. That holds at each t > 0 when the data have bounded support, by Eq. 23 with k = 2 and k = 3. Dropping both,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert x_t - (y - f\,\Delta t) \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \log p_t(y) + \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\cdot(x_t - y) + \text{const}

The term \log p_t(y) depends on y alone. Absorbing it into the constant,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert x_t - (y - f\,\Delta t) \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\cdot(x_t - y) + \text{const}

Completing the square:
Factoring 1/(2g^2\Delta t) out of the two terms that depend on x_t,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert x_t - (y - f\,\Delta t) \rVert^2 - 2 g^2 \Delta t\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\cdot(x_t - y)}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \text{const}

The numerator has the form

\lVert x_t - a \rVert^2 - 2\, b\cdot(x_t - y)

with a = y - f\,\Delta t and b = g^2 \Delta t\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y). Completing the square turns it into

\lVert x_t - (a + b) \rVert^2 - \lVert b \rVert^2 - 2\, b\cdot(a - y)

The last two terms do not depend on x_t, so they join the constant. Substituting the completed square,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert x_t - \big(y - f\,\Delta t + g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\, \Delta t\big) \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \text{const}

Writing \mu = y - f\,\Delta t + g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\, \Delta t for the center,

\log p(x_t \mid y) = -\frac{\lVert x_t - \mu \rVert^2}{2 g^2 \Delta t} + \text{const}

The reverse step:
This is the log-density of a Gaussian in x_t, with mean \mu and covariance g^2 \Delta t\, I. A sample from it is

x_t = \mu + g\sqrt{\Delta t}\; z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)

Substituting \mu,

x_t = y - f\,\Delta t + g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\, \Delta t + g\sqrt{\Delta t}\; z

Writing x_{t+\Delta t} back for y,

x_t = x_{t+\Delta t} - f\,\Delta t + g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_{t+\Delta t})\, \Delta t + g\sqrt{\Delta t}\; z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
\tag{28}
The continuous-time limit:
Subtracting x_{t+\Delta t},

x_t - x_{t+\Delta t} = -\big[f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_{t+\Delta t})\big]\, \Delta t + g\sqrt{\Delta t}\; z

The step runs backward, from t + \Delta t to t, so its time increment is -\Delta t. Writing the drift term with it,

x_t - x_{t+\Delta t} = \big[f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_{t+\Delta t})\big]\, (-\Delta t) + g\sqrt{\Delta t}\; z

The factor \sqrt{\Delta t}\, z has the distribution of a Brownian increment over the step. Writing it as \Delta\bar W, the increment of a Brownian motion \bar W run backward in time,

x_t - x_{t+\Delta t} = \big[f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_{t+\Delta t})\big]\, (-\Delta t) + g\, \Delta\bar W

This difference equation is the Euler-Maruyama scheme of the SDE below, taken over the negative time step -\Delta t. As \Delta t \to 0, these reverse transitions define the reverse-time process \bar x_t, the forward solution run backward. Then x_t - x_{t+\Delta t} becomes its increment d\bar x_t, -\Delta t becomes the negative increment dt, and \Delta\bar W becomes d\bar W_t. Taking the limit, which the time-reversal theory justifies (§2.3.2),

\boxed{d\bar x_t = \Big[\, f(\bar x_t, t) - g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(\bar x_t) \,\Big] dt + g(t)\, d\bar W_t}

which is Eq. 19. \square

2.3.1 The reweighting in the two-mode example
Computing the reverse kernel:
Here we compute the reverse kernel for one later state y in the two-mode example, as Figure 7 shows below.








Figure 7: The short-time reverse kernel for the two-mode example at t = 0.15, with a step \Delta t = 0.01 and y = x_{t+\Delta t} = 0.4. The forward step run backward with no correction is a Gaussian centered at y - f\,\Delta t (dashed). Bayes’ rule reweights it by the marginal p_t (shaded, rescaled), which rises toward the mode at the right, and the product is the reverse kernel (solid), shifted toward higher density. Its center agrees with the first-order mean \mu = y - f\,\Delta t + g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y)\, \Delta t (dotted line).





The dashed curve is the forward step run backward, centered at y - f\,\Delta t. Bayes’ rule reweights it by the marginal p_t, which rises toward the mode on the right. The product is the reverse kernel. It is shifted toward higher density, and its center agrees with the first-order mean \mu.


2.3.2 From the Bayes factor to Girsanov’s theorem
The score entered through the Bayes factor p_t(x_t)/p_{t+\Delta t}(y) of Eq. 27. As a function of x_t, p(y \mid x_t) is the forward step run backward with no correction. Its mean is y - f\,\Delta t and its covariance g^2 \Delta t\, I. The Bayes factor converts it into the reverse transition. It is a likelihood ratio, the factor by which one density is multiplied to give another.
Multiplied along a path, these factors give, up to the normalizing factor \exp\big(-\int_{t_{\min}}^T \nabla_x\!\cdot\! f\, dt\big), a constant for the affine drifts of this post, the likelihood ratio between the distributions of the two processes over whole paths, the Radon-Nikodym derivative of §A.3. Girsanov’s theorem writes that derivative as a stochastic exponential, the exponential of an Itô integral corrected so that its expectation is one. Girsanov’s drift-change formula Eq. 47 gives the shift directly.
