The theorem of §A.3 runs in increasing time, so it applies to the reversed process in the time \tau, where the drift to install is \psi = g\, \nabla_x \log p_{T-\tau}. Written in the forward time t, where dt < 0, the same change has \psi = -g\, \nabla_x \log p_t and shifts the drift by g\psi = -g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t, and g is untouched.
A change of measure cannot alter quadratic variation. That is why the forward and reverse processes share the same diffusion coefficient. The time reversal itself is not a change of measure. The time-reversal theory [17] shows that the short-time kernel above has Anderson’s reverse-time diffusion [4] as its continuous-time limit.


2.3.3 The risk-neutral parallel
This is the operation a quantitative analyst performs in pricing (§A.3). There, the stock follows post #1’s geometric Brownian motion with drift rate \mu and volatility \sigma, and this \mu is not the reverse mean above. Reweighting by a Radon-Nikodym derivative shifts the drift rate from \mu to the risk-free interest rate r and leaves \sigma untouched.
Here, reweighting by the marginal-density ratio shifts the forward drift f to the reverse drift f - g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t and leaves g untouched. In both, a change of measure reshapes the drift and never the diffusion. The quantity g\, \nabla_x \log p_t plays the role that the market price of risk (\mu - r)/\sigma, the stock’s excess drift per unit of volatility, plays in finance.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
section: 2.4 Gaussian data: the reverse-time SDE in closed form
text:
2.4 Gaussian data: the reverse-time SDE in closed form
Both derivations rest on general theorems. When the data distribution is Gaussian, each marginal is Gaussian and the score is linear, so the solution of the reverse-time SDE can be computed directly and its marginals compared with p_t, using the moment equations of §1.5.1. Lai et al. compute the reverse-time SDE itself for Gaussian data from one discretization step and Bayes’ rule [18]. Here the reverse-time SDE is taken as given, and its solution is computed.
Set-up:
The forward SDE is linear, Eq. 2. Each coordinate of its solution evolves separately, as in §1.1, so we work in one dimension, with the data distribution p_0 = \mathcal{N}(c_0, s_0^2), c_0 \in \mathbb{R} and s_0 > 0. For data \mathcal{N}(c_0, s_0^2 I) in \mathbb{R}^d, the results below hold for each component.
The marginals:
By Eq. 3, x_t = m(t)\, x_0 + \sqrt{\Sigma(t)}\, \epsilon, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) independent of x_0. A sum of independent Gaussians is Gaussian, with the means added and the variances added, so

\boxed{p_t = \mathcal{N}\big(c(t),\, v(t)\big), \qquad c(t) = m(t)\, c_0, \qquad v(t) = m(t)^2 s_0^2 + \Sigma(t)}
\tag{29}
with c, v: [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}. Since s_0 > 0 and m > 0, v(t) > 0 for each t \in [0, T], including t = 0.
The score:
Differentiating the log-density of Eq. 29,

\nabla_x \log p_t(x) = -\frac{x - c(t)}{v(t)}

The score is linear in x, with a coefficient that stays bounded down to t = 0, so this example needs no cutoff t_{\min}, unlike data concentrated on a low-dimensional set.
The reverse-time SDE:
Substituting the score and f(y, t) = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, y into Eq. 22, the reverse-time SDE in the time \tau = T - t,

dy_\tau = -\Big[f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, y_\tau + g(t)^2\, \frac{y_\tau - c(t)}{v(t)}\Big]\, d\tau + g(t)\, d\bar W_\tau

with t = T - \tau and the initial condition y_0 \sim p_T = \mathcal{N}\big(c(T), v(T)\big). Its drift is affine in y_\tau, of the form of §1.5.1 in the time \tau, with the continuous coefficients

a(\tau) = -f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) - \frac{g(t)^2}{v(t)}, \qquad b(\tau) = \frac{g(t)^2\, c(t)}{v(t)}

and the diffusion coefficient g(T - \tau), which does not depend on y_\tau. An SDE of this kind keeps a Gaussian initial condition Gaussian, so y_\tau is Gaussian for each \tau, and its mean M(\tau) and variance V(\tau) determine its distribution.






NoteProof: the solution is Gaussian





With A(\tau) = \int_0^\tau a(r)\, dr, the integrating factor of §1.1 applies with a in place of f_{\mathrm{lin}}. The function h(y, \tau) = e^{-A(\tau)}\, y has the partials

\frac{\partial h}{\partial \tau} = -a\, e^{-A}\, y, \qquad \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} = e^{-A}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial y^2} = 0

Applying Itô’s lemma Eq. 6 to h with these partials,

d\big(e^{-A} y_\tau\big) = \Big(-a\, e^{-A}\, y_\tau + \big(a\, y_\tau + b\big)\, e^{-A}\Big)\, d\tau + g\, e^{-A}\, d\bar W_\tau

Cancelling the terms in y_\tau,

d\big(e^{-A} y_\tau\big) = e^{-A}\, b\, d\tau + e^{-A}\, g\, d\bar W_\tau

Integrating from 0 to \tau, with A(0) = 0,

e^{-A(\tau)}\, y_\tau = y_0 + \int_0^\tau e^{-A(r)}\, b(r)\, dr + \int_0^\tau e^{-A(r)}\, g(T - r)\, d\bar W_r

The middle term is deterministic. The Itô integral has a deterministic integrand, so it is Gaussian (P1:Eq. 7) and independent of y_0. A Gaussian plus a constant plus an independent Gaussian is Gaussian, and multiplying by e^{A(\tau)} keeps it Gaussian. \square



By Eq. 17 and Eq. 18, the moments satisfy M' = a M + b and V' = 2a V + g^2, with M(0) = c(T) and V(0) = v(T). Each is a linear ODE with continuous coefficients, which has exactly one solution for each initial value, by Grönwall’s inequality [19]. It is therefore enough to check that the forward moments taken in reverse time order, c(T - \tau) and v(T - \tau), solve the two equations, since they have the same initial values.
The mean equation:
Differentiating c(T - \tau) in \tau by the chain rule,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, c(T - \tau) = -c'(t)

Substituting c' = m'\, c_0, the derivative of c in Eq. 29,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, c(T - \tau) = -m'(t)\, c_0

Substituting m' = f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, m from §1.5.1,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, c(T - \tau) = -f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, m(t)\, c_0

Writing m(t)\, c_0 = c(t),

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, c(T - \tau) = -f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, c(t)

Adding and subtracting g(t)^2\, c(t) / v(t),

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, c(T - \tau) = -f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, c(t) - \frac{g(t)^2\, c(t)}{v(t)} + \frac{g(t)^2\, c(t)}{v(t)}

Factoring c(t) out of the first two terms,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, c(T - \tau) = \Big(-f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) - \frac{g(t)^2}{v(t)}\Big)\, c(t) + \frac{g(t)^2\, c(t)}{v(t)}

Writing the coefficients as a(\tau) and b(\tau), with t = T - \tau,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, c(T - \tau) = a(\tau)\, c(T - \tau) + b(\tau)

so M(\tau) = c(T - \tau).
The variance equation:
Differentiating v(T - \tau) in \tau by the chain rule,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = -v'(t)

Substituting v' = 2 m\, m'\, s_0^2 + \Sigma', the derivative of v in Eq. 29,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = -2 m(t)\, m'(t)\, s_0^2 - \Sigma'(t)

Substituting m' = f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, m and \Sigma' = 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, \Sigma + g^2 from §1.5.1,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = -2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, m(t)^2 s_0^2 - 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, \Sigma(t) - g(t)^2

Factoring -2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) out of the first two terms,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = -2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, \big(m(t)^2 s_0^2 + \Sigma(t)\big) - g(t)^2

Writing m(t)^2 s_0^2 + \Sigma(t) = v(t),

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = -2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, v(t) - g(t)^2

Writing -g(t)^2 = -2g(t)^2 + g(t)^2,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = -2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, v(t) - 2 g(t)^2 + g(t)^2

Writing 2 g(t)^2 = 2\, \big(g(t)^2 / v(t)\big)\, v(t),

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = -2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, v(t) - 2\, \frac{g(t)^2}{v(t)}\, v(t) + g(t)^2

Factoring 2 v(t) out of the first two terms,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = 2\Big(-f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t) - \frac{g(t)^2}{v(t)}\Big)\, v(t) + g(t)^2

Writing the coefficient as a(\tau), with t = T - \tau,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\, v(T - \tau) = 2a(\tau)\, v(T - \tau) + g(T - \tau)^2

so V(\tau) = v(T - \tau).
The marginals of the solution:
So y_\tau \sim \mathcal{N}\big(c(T - \tau), v(T - \tau)\big) = p_{T-\tau} for each \tau, and the reverse-time process \bar x_t = y_{T-t} has \bar x_t \sim p_t for each t \in [0, T], with \bar x_0 \sim p_0. This is the equality of marginals that the derivation through the Fokker-Planck equation proves in general, reached here from the moment equations alone. \square
The variance equations show how the score term undoes the noising. Forward, the variance evolves as v' = 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, v + g^2. In reverse time the score term of the drift contributes -2g^2 to 2a V, and the diffusion adds back +g^2, so the net -g^2 cancels the growth g^2 that the forward diffusion added.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
section: 3.1 Deriving the probability-flow ODE using the Fokker-Planck equation
text:
3.1 Deriving the probability-flow ODE using the Fokker-Planck equation
Step 1 — the reversed marginals satisfy the Fokker-Planck equation of an ODE:
Starting from the Fokker-Planck equation, which the marginal path p_t satisfies by the necessity part of Eq. 20,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

Substituting the log-derivative identity Eq. 21 for \Delta_x p_t,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\Big)

Combining into one divergence,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\Big(f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t\Big)\, p_t\Big]

Reversing time with \tau = T - t and the reversed marginals \bar p_\tau = p_{T-\tau} of §2.2, with \partial_t p_t = -\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau and f and g evaluated at t = T - \tau,

-\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\Big(f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\Big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big]

Multiplying both sides by -1,

\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\Big(f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\Big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big]

Writing the sign inside the divergence,

\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[-\Big(f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\Big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big]

This is the Fokker-Planck equation, in the time \tau and with zero diffusion, of the ODE

\frac{dy_\tau}{d\tau} = -\Big[f(y_\tau, T - \tau) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(T - \tau)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_{T-\tau}(y_\tau)\Big]

the SDE with this drift and the diffusion coefficient 0.
Step 2 — the assumptions of the equivalence hold:
The four assumptions of Eq. 20 hold as in Step 2 of §2.2, with the same initial condition y_0 \sim p_T. The drift contains the score with the coefficient \tfrac{1}{2} g^2 in place of g^2, so Eq. 23 makes it Lipschitz and infinitely differentiable with bounded derivatives for each \tau < T. The diffusion coefficient 0 does not depend on y, and the reversed marginal \bar p_\tau decays at infinity and is dominated on each [0, \tau'] with \tau' < T, as there.
Step 3 — the sufficiency part applies:
By Step 1, \bar p_\tau satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation of the ODE of Step 1, and by Step 2 the assumptions of Eq. 20 hold. Its sufficiency part, with zero diffusion, therefore makes \bar p_\tau the marginal path of y_\tau, the solution of that ODE with the initial condition y_0 \sim p_T, so y_\tau \sim p_{T-\tau} for each \tau < T.
Writing the time arguments in the forward time t = T - \tau,

\frac{dy_\tau}{d\tau} = -\Big[f(y_\tau, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(y_\tau)\Big]

Writing the state in the forward time, as x_t = y_{T-t},

\frac{dy_\tau}{d\tau} = -\Big[f(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)\Big]

Writing the derivative in the forward time, d/d\tau = -d/dt,

-\frac{dx_t}{dt} = -\Big[f(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)\Big]

Multiplying both sides by -1,

\boxed{\frac{dx_t}{dt} = f(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)}

which is Eq. 30. Since y_\tau \sim p_{T-\tau}, its solution x_t = y_{T-t}, solved backward from the initial condition x_T \sim p_T, has x_t \sim p_t for each t > 0. \square
Solving the ODE forward gives the same marginals. The drift f is affine, and for data with bounded support Eq. 23 makes the score Lipschitz in x away from t = 0, so the drift of the ODE is Lipschitz there. Exactly one trajectory, the solution from a single initial state, then passes through each state at each time t > 0. The backward solution has x_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} at each t_0 > 0, so the solution started forward from the initial condition x_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} follows the same trajectories and has the marginals p_t for each t \ge t_0.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
3.2 Comparison with the reverse-time SDE
The reverse-time SDE comes from a different split of the same Fokker-Planck equation. The probability-flow ODE converts the whole diffusion term into part of the drift and keeps no diffusion, while §2.2 converts twice the diffusion term and keeps a diffusion term of the opposite sign, which becomes a diffusion once time is reversed.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
3.3 Probability-flow trajectories
Simulating the probability-flow ODE:
Generating with the probability-flow ODE is an ODE solve, so each initial condition x_T leads to a single x_0. Here we solve it for the two-mode example of Figure 6, with the same initial conditions, as Figure 8 shows below.








Figure 8: Trajectories of the probability-flow ODE for the same two-mode setup, driven by the exact score and with the same initial conditions x_T as the reverse-time SDE paths above. Each path is smooth and deterministic, so each x_T leads to a single x_0. The right panel is a histogram of x_0 over many paths, with the data distribution p_0 (solid curve): the solutions of the ODE and of the reverse-time SDE have the same marginals. The time axis is reversed, t = T at the left and t = 0 at the right, so generation runs left to right.





Each path is smooth and deterministic, unlike the reverse-time SDE paths of Figure 6, yet the endpoints have the same distribution, the data distribution p_0.

3.3.1 Solving forward from data and back
Exactly one trajectory passes through each state at each time t > 0, as the paragraph after the derivation in §3.1 shows. The same holds at t = 0 when the score is Lipschitz in x down to t = 0, as in the two-mode example, whose modes have a positive variance; for other data the round trip starts at the cutoff t_{\min} of Part 2 instead.
With a unique trajectory through each state, solving the probability-flow ODE forward from x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d to time T, and then backward from the state it reaches, returns x_0. The map that the forward solve defines, from the state at t = 0 to the state at T, is invertible, with the backward solve as its inverse. It is deterministic, and with the exact score it depends only on p_0 and the forward SDE, which has no trainable parameters [1].
With a trained model, s_\theta replaces the score, and the map assigns each image a point of the prior’s space. Song, Meng and Ermon reconstructed images this way, with very low error, using their deterministic DDIM sampler [21], which post #8 relates to the probability-flow ODE. Song et al. edit images by modifying that point, interpolating between two such points or rescaling its norm, and then solving back [1].
A numerical solver makes the round trip inexact. Each step here is a step of the Euler-Maruyama scheme with zero diffusion. A backward step from the state at t_{i+1} evaluates the drift of the ODE at t_{i+1}, while the forward step that produced that state evaluated it at t_i. So each pair of steps returns to its starting state only up to \Delta t times the change of the drift over the step, an error of order \Delta t^2, and the T/\Delta t pairs add up to a round-trip error of order \Delta t.
Solving forward and back:
Here we solve the ODE forward from samples of the two-mode data distribution and back from the states they reach, with the exact score, and measure the round-trip error against the number of steps, as Figure 9 shows below.








Figure 9: Solving the probability-flow ODE forward from data and back, for the two-mode setup with the exact score. Left: forward solutions (solid) from seven samples of the data distribution at t = 0 to t = T, and the backward solutions from their end points (dashed gray), which retrace them. Time runs left to right here, from data to noise. Right: the mean distance between a sample and its value after the round trip, over 4000 samples, against the number of steps N in each direction (log scales), with a reference line proportional to 1/N.





The backward solutions retrace the forward ones, and the forward solutions carry the two modes into one band at t = T, where the states follow p_T, close to \mathcal{N}(0, 1). The mean round-trip error halves each time the number of steps doubles, from 0.0093 with 100 steps in each direction to 0.0023 with 400, the first-order rate of the scheme.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
section: 4.1 The minimizer of the weighted DSM objective
text:
4.1 The minimizer of the weighted DSM objective
The weighted DSM objective Eq. 31 regresses on the score of the kernel, which is known, while the reverse-time SDE needs the score of the marginal, which is not. This section shows that the regression nevertheless learns the marginal score.
At each time t, Eq. 31 contains the DSM objective at time t,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0)\rVert^{2}\big]

and Eq. 31 is its average over t with the weight 2\lambda(t), \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_t\big\{2\lambda(t)\, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta)\big\}.
Theorem:
For each t \in (0, T], the DSM objective at time t, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}, is minimized over s_\theta(\cdot, t) by the marginal score, s_\theta(\cdot, t) = \nabla_x \log p_t. So a model flexible enough to represent the score for each t minimizes Eq. 31 with the marginal score for each t \in (0, T].
Proof:
Post #2 defined the DSM objective for one noise level \sigma, P2:Eq. 44,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})-\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\rVert^{2}\big]

Its joint p_\sigma(x, \tilde x) = \hat p(x)\, p_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x) pairs the empirical distribution \hat p of the training set with the perturbation kernel p_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x). For a fixed time t, four substitutions turn it into an objective for the forward SDE at that time.

The data distribution p_0 replaces the empirical \hat p, the population form of the objective.
The perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) of the forward SDE replaces p_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x), with x_0 for x and x_t for \tilde x.
The joint p_t(x_0, x_t) = p_0(x_0)\, p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0), the joint distribution of the forward process at times 0 and t, replaces p_\sigma(x, \tilde x) = \hat p(x)\, p_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x), the product of the two replacements above.
The model has the time as a second argument, s_\theta(x_t, t).

The result is \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}, the DSM objective at time t defined above.
The objective that regresses on the marginal score directly is the explicit score matching (ESM) objective at time t,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_t}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t)\rVert^{2}\big]

Post #2 proved that the two differ only by a constant, P2:Eq. 45. Its proof used three facts about the setup, and each holds here.
Fact 1 — the joint density: The joint density is the base distribution times the kernel. Here it is the joint p_t(x_0, x_t).
Fact 2 — the perturbed density: The perturbed density is the integral of the joint over the base variable. Here it is the marginal, p_t(x_t) = \int p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0)\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0.
Fact 3 — the gradient under the integral: The gradient in x_t may be taken under that integral. In post #2 the integral was a finite sum, so this needed no argument. Here it needs a bound on the gradient of the integrand that is integrable in x_0 and the same for each x_t.
Writing out the kernel Eq. 3 with y = x_t - m(t)\, x_0,

p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \big(2\pi\Sigma(t)\big)^{-d/2}\, e^{-\lVert y \rVert^2/(2\Sigma(t))}

Differentiating in x_t, with \nabla_{x_t} y = I,

\nabla_{x_t} p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = -\frac{y}{\Sigma(t)}\, \big(2\pi\Sigma(t)\big)^{-d/2}\, e^{-\lVert y \rVert^2/(2\Sigma(t))}

Taking the norm of both sides,

\big\lVert \nabla_{x_t} p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert = \frac{\lVert y \rVert\, e^{-\lVert y \rVert^2/(2\Sigma(t))}}{\Sigma(t)}\, \big(2\pi\Sigma(t)\big)^{-d/2}

Bounding \lVert y \rVert\, e^{-\lVert y \rVert^2/(2\Sigma(t))} by its maximum \sqrt{\Sigma(t)}\, e^{-1/2}, attained at \lVert y \rVert = \sqrt{\Sigma(t)},

\big\lVert \nabla_{x_t} p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert \le \frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{\Sigma(t)}}\, \big(2\pi\Sigma(t)\big)^{-d/2}

Multiplying both sides by p_0(x_0),

\big\lVert p_0(x_0)\, \nabla_{x_t} p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert \le \frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{\Sigma(t)}}\, \big(2\pi\Sigma(t)\big)^{-d/2}\, p_0(x_0)

The right side does not depend on x_t, and its integral over x_0 is e^{-1/2}\, \Sigma(t)^{-1/2}\, \big(2\pi\Sigma(t)\big)^{-d/2}, finite for t > 0. An integrable bound of this kind, the same for each x_t, is a dominating function, and it permits differentiation under the integral sign.
Post #2’s theorem therefore holds at each t,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_t}}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta) + C_t, \qquad \frac{\partial C_t}{\partial \theta} = 0

The explicit objective is non-negative, and it is zero when s_\theta(\cdot, t) = \nabla_x \log p_t, so the marginal score is its minimizer. The two objectives differ by a constant, so the DSM objective at time t has the same minimizer. Eq. 31 weights these objectives by 2\lambda(t), positive for t > 0, and averages them over t. For a model flexible enough to represent the score for each t, minimizing the average minimizes each of them, so the minimizer of Eq. 31 is the marginal score for each t \in (0, T]. \square

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
section: 4.2 The noise-prediction loss shared by the ELBO and DSM
text:
4.2 The noise-prediction loss shared by the ELBO and DSM
Post #2 trained the two lineages with different objectives. The variational route bounded the log-likelihood by the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and, by dropping its time-dependent weights, reached DDPM’s simple objective, a noise-prediction loss. The score-based route trained by DSM, which post #2 also rewrote as a noise-prediction loss, at a different perturbation of the data. Whether the two routes lead to one loss was left open.
They do. On DDPM’s own perturbation, the weighted DSM objective Eq. 31 with the weighting \lambda(t) = 1 - \bar\alpha(t) is DDPM’s simple objective, once the network’s output is parameterized as a noise prediction. The two lineages therefore train on the same loss and differ only in the weighting \lambda(t) and in how the network’s output is parameterized. The ELBO’s sum over the denoising steps, with its weights kept, corresponds in the continuous-time limit to another choice of \lambda, Song et al.’s likelihood weighting \lambda(t) = g(t)^2 [22], which is \beta(t) for the VP SDE, as §4.2.4 derives. P6:§3.3 develops the likelihood bound that this weighting gives.
Showing that the weighting \lambda(t) = 1 - \bar\alpha(t) gives the simple objective requires two steps. DDPM’s simple objective averages over N discrete steps, while Eq. 31 averages over continuous time, so the first subsection below converts the simple objective to continuous time, and the second derives the result from Eq. 31.

4.2.1 Converting DDPM’s simple objective to continuous time
DDPM’s simple objective, P2:Eq. 32, is

L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{i,\, x_0,\, \epsilon}\big[\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\, \epsilon,\ i\big)\rVert^2\big]

In it, i is sampled uniformly from \{1, \ldots, N\}, x_0 \sim p_0 and \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), and \epsilon_\theta(\cdot, i): \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d is the denoising network’s prediction of the noise \epsilon at step i. The steps lie on the partition of [0, T] of §1.2, with the step width \Delta t = T/N, the grid times t_i = i\, \Delta t and the discrete noise schedule \beta_i = \beta(t_i)\, \Delta t.
Indexing every quantity by the grid time t_i instead of the step i, with t_i as the network’s second input and the cumulative product written as \bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i) = \bar\alpha_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i} \big(1 - \beta(t_j)\, \Delta t\big), a product over the grid times up to t_i,

L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t_i,\, x_0,\, \epsilon}\big[\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i)}\, \epsilon,\ t_i\big)\rVert^2\big]

with t_i sampled uniformly from the grid \{t_1, \ldots, t_N\}.
Writing the uniform average over the grid times as a sum,

L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\, \epsilon}\big[\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i)}\, \epsilon,\ t_i\big)\rVert^2\big]

Writing 1/N as \Delta t / T,

L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\, \epsilon}\big[\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i)}\, \epsilon,\ t_i\big)\rVert^2\big]\, \Delta t

Letting N \to \infty, where the discrete cumulative product converges to the continuous one, \bar\alpha^{(N)}(t_i) \to \bar\alpha(t_i) with \bar\alpha(t) = \exp\big(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\big) (P1:Eq. 40), uniformly over the grid because, for a bounded \beta of bounded variation such as the linear schedule, the two exponents differ by O(\Delta t) at each t_i. For a network continuous in its inputs and of at most linear growth, with p_0 of finite second moment, the sum then differs by a vanishing amount from a Riemann sum of an integrand continuous in t, which converges to an integral,

\lim_{N \to \infty} L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{T} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\, \epsilon}\big[\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon,\ t\big)\rVert^2\big]\, dt

Writing \tfrac{1}{T}\int_{t_{\min}}^T \cdots\, dt as the expectation over t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, T], and writing L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) also for this limit, the continuous-time simple objective,

\boxed{L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon}\left[\,\left\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon,\ t\right)\right\|^2\,\right]}
\tag{32}
On the grid, DDPM’s smallest step time, t_1 = T/N, keeps t above 0, as Part 2 requires.


4.2.2 Deriving the continuous-time simple objective from the weighted DSM objective
Theorem:
For the VP-SDE, DSM and the ELBO route give the same noise-prediction loss. With the score-based model parameterized as s_\theta(x_t, t) = -\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)/\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)} and the weighting \lambda(t) = 1 - \bar\alpha(t), the weighted DSM objective Eq. 31 equals DDPM’s continuous-time simple objective Eq. 32.
Proof:
Starting from Eq. 31,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\,\Big\{ \lambda(t)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0} \big[\, \| s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \|^2 \,\big] \Big\}

Substituting the log-density of the VP perturbation kernel Eq. 12,

\log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = -\lVert x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0\rVert^2 / \big(2\,(1 - \bar\alpha(t))\big) + \text{const}

into the previous line,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\,\Big\{ \lambda(t)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0} \Big[\, \Big\| s_\theta(x_t, t) + \nabla_{x_t}\frac{\lVert x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0\rVert^2}{2\,(1 - \bar\alpha(t))} \Big\|^2 \,\Big] \Big\}

Differentiating with the gradient \nabla_{x_t}\lVert x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0\rVert^2 = 2\big(x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0\big),

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\,\Big\{ \lambda(t)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0} \Big[\, \Big\| s_\theta(x_t, t) + \frac{x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0}{1 - \bar\alpha(t)} \Big\|^2 \,\Big] \Big\}

Sampling x_t through the reparameterization of Eq. 12, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),

x_t \;=\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon
\tag{33}
the residual x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 becomes \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon, and

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\,\Big\{ \lambda(t)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\, \epsilon} \Big[\, \Big\| s_\theta(x_t, t) + \frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}} \Big\|^2 \,\Big] \Big\}

Parameterizing the score-based model as s_\theta(x_t, t) = -\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)/\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}, so that the network outputs a noise prediction rescaled into a score estimate,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\,\Big\{ \lambda(t)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\, \epsilon} \Big[\, \Big\| -\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}} + \frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}} \Big\|^2 \,\Big] \Big\}

Factoring 1/\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)} out of the norm, where it is squared,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\,\Big\{ \frac{\lambda(t)}{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\, \epsilon} \big[\, \|\epsilon \,-\, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\|^2 \,\big] \Big\}

Choosing the DDPM weighting \lambda(t) = 1 - \bar\alpha(t), which cancels the denominator,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\,\Big\{ \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\, \epsilon} \big[\, \|\epsilon \,-\, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\|^2 \,\big] \Big\}

Writing x_t in the form of Eq. 33,

\boxed{L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{t,\, x_0,\, \epsilon}\!\left[\,\big\|\, \epsilon \,-\, \epsilon_\theta\!\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 \,+\, \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon,\;\, t\big)\,\big\|^2\,\right]}

which is Eq. 32. \square
So the ELBO route of post #2 and DSM lead to the same noise-prediction loss. The weighting \lambda(t) = 1 - \bar\alpha(t) corresponds to DDPM’s unweighted form, which Ho et al. preferred empirically for image generation and which drops the time-dependent weights the ELBO itself prescribes [2].


4.2.3 Other linear SDEs and the weighting rule
The steps of the proof above go through for each linear SDE. With a general kernel \mathcal{N}\big(m(t)\, x_0,\, \Sigma(t)\, I\big) (Eq. 3), m(t) takes the place of \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} and \Sigma(t) that of 1 - \bar\alpha(t), so the parameterization, the weighting and the sampling become

s_\theta = -\frac{\epsilon_\theta}{\sqrt{\Sigma(t)}} \qquad \lambda(t) = \Sigma(t) \qquad x_t = m(t)\, x_0 + \sqrt{\Sigma(t)}\, \epsilon

The VE and sub-VP SDEs of §1.3 and §1.4 therefore give the same noise-prediction loss, with their own m(t) and \Sigma(t).
The weighting \lambda(t) = \Sigma(t) is the rule Song et al. recommend [1],

\lambda(t) \propto \frac{1}{\mathbb{E}\lVert \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \rVert^2}

The conditional score is -\epsilon/\sqrt{\Sigma(t)}, whose expected squared norm is \mathbb{E}\lVert\epsilon\rVert^2/\Sigma(t) = d/\Sigma(t), so the rule gives \lambda(t) \propto \Sigma(t). With it, \lambda(t) times the expected squared norm of the regression target is \Sigma(t) \cdot d/\Sigma(t) = d for each t, so each time contributes to Eq. 31 on the same scale.


4.2.4 The ELBO in continuous time
The simple objective drops the weights that the ELBO puts on its terms. The ELBO with its weights kept also has a continuous-time limit, which Kingma et al. derived for each Gaussian forward process [23].
This section derives it for the linear SDEs of Part 1 and shows that it is the weighted DSM objective with Song et al.’s likelihood weighting \lambda(t) = g(t)^2 [22]. It needs three Gaussian quantities of the forward SDE, in the order the ELBO uses them: the distribution of a later state given an earlier one, the true reverse posterior, and the KL divergence of one reverse step.
The forward transition:
For 0 \le s < t \le T, the forward transition from s to t is the distribution p(x_t \mid x_s) of the state at time t given the state at time s, and the perturbation kernel is its case s = 0. Over one step of width \Delta t, the Euler-Maruyama transition Eq. 26 approximates it to first order. From here on, p(\cdot \mid \cdot) denotes the exact transition.
Integrating the driftless SDE of §1.1 from s to t instead of from 0,

y_t - y_s = \int_s^t g(r)\, e^{-F(r)}\, dW_r

Substituting y = e^{-F} x and e^{-F} = 1/m, by Eq. 7 and Eq. 4,

\frac{x_t}{m(t)} - \frac{x_s}{m(s)} = \int_s^t \frac{g(r)}{m(r)}\, dW_r

Multiplying both sides by m(t),

x_t - \frac{m(t)}{m(s)}\, x_s = m(t) \int_s^t \frac{g(r)}{m(r)}\, dW_r

Moving the x_s term across,

x_t = \frac{m(t)}{m(s)}\, x_s + m(t) \int_s^t \frac{g(r)}{m(r)}\, dW_r

The Itô integral involves only the Brownian increments after s, so it is independent of x_s. It is Gaussian with mean zero in each component (P1:Eq. 7), so x_t given x_s is Gaussian, with the mean \big(m(t)/m(s)\big)\, x_s and, in each component, the variance

\operatorname{Var}(x_t \mid x_s) = m(t)^2 \int_s^t \frac{g(r)^2}{m(r)^2}\, dr

Splitting \int_s^t = \int_0^t - \int_0^s,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t \mid x_s) = m(t)^2 \int_0^t \frac{g(r)^2}{m(r)^2}\, dr - m(t)^2 \int_0^s \frac{g(r)^2}{m(r)^2}\, dr

Substituting Eq. 5 at t and at s,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t \mid x_s) = \Sigma(t) - \frac{m(t)^2}{m(s)^2}\, \Sigma(s)

So

\boxed{\begin{aligned}
p(x_t \mid x_s) &= \mathcal{N}\big(x_t;\; m_{t|s}\, x_s,\; \Sigma_{t|s}\, I\big) \\[4pt]
m_{t|s} &= \frac{m(t)}{m(s)}, \qquad \Sigma_{t|s} = \Sigma(t) - m_{t|s}^2\, \Sigma(s)
\end{aligned}}
\tag{34}
For the VP-SDE, m_{t|s}^2 = \bar\alpha(t)/\bar\alpha(s) and \Sigma_{t|s} = 1 - \bar\alpha(t)/\bar\alpha(s), the continuous-time counterparts of DDPM’s \alpha_i and \beta_i.
The true reverse posterior:
Given x_0, the states x_s and x_t are jointly Gaussian. In each component, x_s has the variance \Sigma(s) and x_t the variance \Sigma(t), and since x_t is m_{t|s}\, x_s plus noise independent of x_s and x_0, their covariance is m_{t|s}\, \Sigma(s). For a jointly Gaussian pair (a, b),

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[a \mid b] &= \mathbb{E}a + \operatorname{Cov}(a, b)\operatorname{Var}(b)^{-1}(b - \mathbb{E}b) \\[4pt]
\operatorname{Var}(a \mid b) &= \operatorname{Var}(a) - \operatorname{Cov}(a, b)\operatorname{Var}(b)^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(b, a)
\end{aligned}

They hold because a - \operatorname{Cov}(a, b)\operatorname{Var}(b)^{-1} b is uncorrelated with b, and for a jointly Gaussian pair uncorrelated means independent.
The mean: Substituting the moments into the first formula,

\mathbb{E}[x_s \mid x_t, x_0] = m(s)\, x_0 + \frac{m_{t|s}\, \Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\, \big(x_t - m(t)\, x_0\big)

Collecting the x_0 terms, with m(t) = m_{t|s}\, m(s),

\mathbb{E}[x_s \mid x_t, x_0] = \frac{m_{t|s}\, \Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_t + m(s)\Big(1 - \frac{m_{t|s}^2\, \Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\Big)\, x_0

Writing 1 - m_{t|s}^2\, \Sigma(s)/\Sigma(t) = \Sigma_{t|s}/\Sigma(t), by Eq. 34,

\mathbb{E}[x_s \mid x_t, x_0] = \frac{m_{t|s}\, \Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_t + \frac{m(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_0

The variance: Substituting the moments into the second formula,

\operatorname{Var}(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) = \Sigma(s) - \frac{m_{t|s}^2\, \Sigma(s)^2}{\Sigma(t)}

Factoring out \Sigma(s)/\Sigma(t),

\operatorname{Var}(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) = \frac{\Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\, \big(\Sigma(t) - m_{t|s}^2\, \Sigma(s)\big)

Writing the bracket as \Sigma_{t|s},

\operatorname{Var}(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) = \frac{\Sigma(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{\Sigma(t)}

Collecting the two moments,

\boxed{\begin{aligned}
q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) &= \mathcal{N}\big(x_s;\; \tilde\mu_{s|t}(x_t, x_0),\; \tilde\Sigma_{s|t}\, I\big) \\[4pt]
\tilde\mu_{s|t}(x_t, x_0) &= \frac{m_{t|s}\, \Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_t + \frac{m(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_0, \qquad \tilde\Sigma_{s|t} = \frac{\Sigma(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{\Sigma(t)}
\end{aligned}}
\tag{35}
the continuous-time counterpart of post #2’s true reverse posterior, P2:Eq. 24.
One step of the ELBO:
The ELBO’s main terms, the L_{i-1} of P2:Eq. 22, each compare the true reverse posterior with a learned reverse step. Following Kingma et al. [23], the learned reverse step from t to s is the true reverse posterior with x_0 replaced by a data prediction \hat x_\theta(\cdot, t): \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, the parameterization post #2 calls predicting x_0,

q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_s;\; \tilde\mu_{s|t}\big(x_t, \hat x_\theta(x_t, t)\big),\; \tilde\Sigma_{s|t}\, I\big)

The two Gaussians share the covariance \tilde\Sigma_{s|t}\, I, so their KL divergence is the squared distance between the means divided by 2\tilde\Sigma_{s|t}, P2:Eq. 26, whose constant C is zero when the two variances agree,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{1}{2\tilde\Sigma_{s|t}}\, \big\lVert \tilde\mu_{s|t}(x_t, x_0) - \tilde\mu_{s|t}\big(x_t, \hat x_\theta(x_t, t)\big) \big\rVert^2

Substituting the mean of Eq. 35,

\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{1}{2\tilde\Sigma_{s|t}}\, \Big\lVert\, & \frac{m_{t|s}\, \Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_t + \frac{m(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_0 \\[4pt]
& - \frac{m_{t|s}\, \Sigma(s)}{\Sigma(t)}\, x_t - \frac{m(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{\Sigma(t)}\, \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \Big\rVert^2
\end{aligned}

Cancelling the x_t terms,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{1}{2\tilde\Sigma_{s|t}}\, \Big\lVert \frac{m(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{\Sigma(t)}\, \big(x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t)\big) \Big\rVert^2

Taking the scalar out of the norm, where it is squared,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{m(s)^2\, \Sigma_{t|s}^2}{2\, \Sigma(t)^2\, \tilde\Sigma_{s|t}}\, \big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2

Substituting \tilde\Sigma_{s|t} = \Sigma(s)\, \Sigma_{t|s}/\Sigma(t),

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{m(s)^2\, \Sigma_{t|s}}{2\, \Sigma(s)\, \Sigma(t)}\, \big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2

Writing m(s)^2\, \Sigma_{t|s} = m(s)^2\, \Sigma(t) - m(t)^2\, \Sigma(s), by Eq. 34 and m(t) = m_{t|s}\, m(s),

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{m(s)^2\, \Sigma(t) - m(t)^2\, \Sigma(s)}{2\, \Sigma(s)\, \Sigma(t)}\, \big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2

Splitting the fraction,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{m(s)^2}{\Sigma(s)} - \frac{m(t)^2}{\Sigma(t)}\Big)\, \big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2

The ratio m(t)^2/\Sigma(t) of the squared mean coefficient to the kernel variance is the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), \mathrm{SNR}: (0, T] \to (0, \infty), \mathrm{SNR}(t) = m(t)^2/\Sigma(t). Writing the two ratios with it,

\boxed{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(x_s \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, q_\theta(x_s \mid x_t)\big) = \frac{1}{2}\big(\mathrm{SNR}(s) - \mathrm{SNR}(t)\big)\, \big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2}
\tag{36}
which is Kingma et al.’s form of one step of the ELBO [23].
The continuous-time limit:
On a grid t_{\min} = t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_N = T, whose first time is the cutoff t_{\min} of Part 2, the terms L_{i-1} of P2:Eq. 22 are the expected KL divergences of the steps from t_i to t_{i-1}. Summing Eq. 36 with s = t_{i-1} and t = t_i,

\sum_{i=2}^{N} L_{i-1} = \sum_{i=2}^{N} \frac{1}{2}\big(\mathrm{SNR}(t_{i-1}) - \mathrm{SNR}(t_i)\big)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_{t_i} \mid x_0}\big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_{t_i}, t_i) \big\rVert^2

Writing each difference by the mean value theorem, \mathrm{SNR}(t_{i-1}) - \mathrm{SNR}(t_i) = -\mathrm{SNR}'(\xi_i)\, (t_i - t_{i-1}) for some \xi_i \in (t_{i-1}, t_i),

\sum_{i=2}^{N} L_{i-1} = \sum_{i=2}^{N} \frac{1}{2}\big(-\mathrm{SNR}'(\xi_i)\big)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_{t_i} \mid x_0}\big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_{t_i}, t_i) \big\rVert^2\, (t_i - t_{i-1})

Letting the largest step go to zero with t_1 = t_{\min} held fixed, the sum converges to an integral over [t_{\min}, T]. Its two factors are continuous on [t_{\min}, T] under the conditions of §4.2.1, hence uniformly continuous there, so evaluating them at the different points \xi_i and t_i of each step does not change the limit. Writing L_\infty(\theta) for the limit, the continuous-time diffusion term of the ELBO,

\boxed{L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'(t)\big)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big\lVert x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2\, dt}
\tag{37}
which is Kingma et al.’s continuous-time loss [23], with its largest SNR at t_{\min}.
The likelihood weighting:
The score of the perturbation kernel Eq. 3 is

\nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = -\frac{x_t - m(t)\, x_0}{\Sigma(t)}

Solving it for x_0 gives the first term inside the norm below. Substituting that expression for x_0, and leaving the arguments of m and \Sigma implicit,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'\big)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\Big\lVert \frac{x_t + \Sigma\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0)}{m} - \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) \Big\rVert^2\, dt

Parameterizing the data prediction by Tweedie’s formula Eq. 24, \hat x_\theta(x_t, t) = \big(x_t + \Sigma\, s_\theta(x_t, t)\big)/m,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'\big)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\Big\lVert \frac{x_t + \Sigma\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0)}{m} - \frac{x_t + \Sigma\, s_\theta(x_t, t)}{m} \Big\rVert^2\, dt

Cancelling x_t/m,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'\big)\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\Big\lVert \frac{\Sigma}{m}\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) - \frac{\Sigma}{m}\, s_\theta(x_t, t) \Big\rVert^2\, dt

Taking \Sigma/m out of the norm, where it is squared,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'\big)\, \frac{\Sigma^2}{m^2}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big\lVert \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) - s_\theta(x_t, t) \big\rVert^2\, dt

Writing the model term first, since the norm of a difference does not depend on its order,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'\big)\, \frac{\Sigma^2}{m^2}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert^2\, dt

Substituting -\mathrm{SNR}' = \big(m^2\, \Sigma' - 2 m\, m'\, \Sigma\big)/\Sigma^2, the derivative of \mathrm{SNR} = m^2/\Sigma by the quotient rule,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \frac{m^2\, \Sigma' - 2 m\, m'\, \Sigma}{\Sigma^2}\, \frac{\Sigma^2}{m^2}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert^2\, dt

Substituting m' = f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, m and \Sigma' = 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, \Sigma + g^2 from §1.5.1,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \frac{m^2\, \big(2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, \Sigma + g^2\big) - 2 f_{\mathrm{lin}}\, m^2\, \Sigma}{\Sigma^2}\, \frac{\Sigma^2}{m^2}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert^2\, dt

Cancelling the f_{\mathrm{lin}} terms,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T \frac{m^2\, g^2}{\Sigma^2}\, \frac{\Sigma^2}{m^2}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert^2\, dt

Cancelling m^2/\Sigma^2 against \Sigma^2/m^2,

L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^T g(t)^2\, \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_t \mid x_0}\big\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) \big\rVert^2\, dt

Writing \int_{t_{\min}}^T \cdots\, dt as T - t_{\min} times the expectation over t \sim \mathcal{U}[t_{\min}, T], the time range of Eq. 31 with the cutoff of Part 2 made explicit, the integral becomes Eq. 31 with \lambda = g^2,

\boxed{L_\infty(\theta) = \frac{T - t_{\min}}{2}\, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_t}}\big(\theta; g^2\big)}
\tag{38}
which is the weighted DSM objective with the likelihood weighting. \square
The diffusion term of the ELBO, in continuous time, is therefore the weighted DSM objective with \lambda = g^2 on [t_{\min}, T], which is \beta(t) for the VP-SDE. The other two terms of the ELBO, the prior term L_N and the reconstruction term L_0, do not involve the steps in between.

4.2.4.1 More steps lower the diffusion term
For the best data prediction, the limit Eq. 37 is the smallest diffusion term of the family, not only a convenient one. Kingma et al. show that, with the SNR function fixed, doubling the number of steps lowers the diffusion term, so the continuous-time limit lies below each discrete one [23]. Their argument assumes that the network denoises a less noisy state better. For the best data prediction that assumption is a theorem, which this subsection proves.
Each term of the sum above Eq. 37, and the integrand of Eq. 37 itself, is smallest when the data prediction at time t is the posterior mean \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t], because the posterior mean minimizes the expected squared error over all functions of the conditioning variable (P2:§4.10). With \mathbb{E} the expectation over x_0 \sim p_0 and the forward noise, the expected error of that prediction is the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) of denoising at time t, \mathrm{MMSE}: [t_{\min}, T] \to [0, \infty),

\mathrm{MMSE}(t) = \mathbb{E}\big\lVert x_0 - \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t] \big\rVert^2

Step 1 — the MMSE grows with t:
For t_{\min} \le t' < t \le T, Eq. 34 writes x_t = m_{t|t'}\, x_{t'} + \sqrt{\Sigma_{t|t'}}\, \epsilon' with \epsilon' \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) independent of (x_0, x_{t'}), since the Itô integral in its derivation uses only the Brownian increments after t'. The posterior mean \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t] is therefore a function \Phi of (x_{t'}, \epsilon'). Substituting \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t] = \Phi(x_{t'}, \epsilon') into the definition of \mathrm{MMSE}(t),

\mathrm{MMSE}(t) = \mathbb{E}\big\lVert x_0 - \Phi(x_{t'}, \epsilon') \big\rVert^2

Bounding below by the best function of (x_{t'}, \epsilon'), which is the posterior mean given both,

\mathrm{MMSE}(t) \ge \mathbb{E}\big\lVert x_0 - \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_{t'}, \epsilon'] \big\rVert^2

Dropping \epsilon' from the condition, since it is independent of (x_0, x_{t'}),

\mathrm{MMSE}(t) \ge \mathbb{E}\big\lVert x_0 - \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_{t'}] \big\rVert^2

Recognizing the right side,

\mathrm{MMSE}(t) \ge \mathrm{MMSE}(t')

Step 2 — the discrete term lies above the continuous one:
The coefficient of each step is nonnegative. By the identity before Eq. 36, \mathrm{SNR}(s) - \mathrm{SNR}(t) = m(s)^2\, \Sigma_{t|s} / \big(\Sigma(s)\, \Sigma(t)\big), and \Sigma_{t|s} \ge 0. So SNR is nonincreasing and -\mathrm{SNR}' \ge 0. With the best data prediction in each term, the sum of the diffusion terms is

\sum_{i=2}^{N} L_{i-1} = \sum_{i=2}^{N} \frac{1}{2}\big(\mathrm{SNR}(t_{i-1}) - \mathrm{SNR}(t_i)\big)\, \mathrm{MMSE}(t_i)

Writing each SNR difference as the integral of -\mathrm{SNR}' over its step,

\sum_{i=2}^{N} L_{i-1} = \sum_{i=2}^{N} \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'(r)\big)\, dr\; \mathrm{MMSE}(t_i)

Writing the constant \mathrm{MMSE}(t_i) inside each integral,

\sum_{i=2}^{N} L_{i-1} = \sum_{i=2}^{N} \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'(r)\big)\, \mathrm{MMSE}(t_i)\, dr

Bounding \mathrm{MMSE}(t_i) below by \mathrm{MMSE}(r) for each r in the step, by Step 1, which the factor -\mathrm{SNR}'(r) \ge 0 preserves,

\sum_{i=2}^{N} L_{i-1} \ge \sum_{i=2}^{N} \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'(r)\big)\, \mathrm{MMSE}(r)\, dr

Joining the steps into one integral over [t_{\min}, T],

\boxed{\sum_{i=2}^{N} L_{i-1} \ge \frac{1}{2} \int_{t_{\min}}^{T} \big(-\mathrm{SNR}'(r)\big)\, \mathrm{MMSE}(r)\, dr}

The right side is Eq. 37 with the best data prediction in place of \hat x_\theta. \square
The discrete sum is an upper Riemann sum of the integral of \mathrm{MMSE} over the SNR, since each step evaluates the nondecreasing \mathrm{MMSE} at its right end. The same comparison shows that refining a grid never raises the sum. Inserting a time c between t_{i-1} and t_i changes the step’s term by

\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\mathrm{SNR}(t_{i-1}) - \mathrm{SNR}(c)\big)\big(\mathrm{MMSE}(c) - \mathrm{MMSE}(t_i)\big) \le 0

which is Kingma et al.’s form of the result.
For a trained network, the error need not grow with t as the MMSE does, and Kingma et al. state the result for a network that denoises well enough. Their CIFAR-10 experiments show it holding. Models trained and evaluated with 10, 100 and 1000 steps reach 4.31, 2.84 and 2.67 bits per dimension, and the model trained in continuous time reaches 2.65 [23]. That is their reason for training with the continuous-time bound.


4.2.4.2 Comparing with DDPM’s weighting
DDPM’s simple objective replaces g^2 by \lambda = \Sigma(t), which is 1 - \bar\alpha(t) for the VP-SDE and gives less weight to small t. Ho et al. chose it so that the network spends less effort on the easy task of removing very small amounts of noise [2]. P6:§3.3 shows that the weighting g^2 also turns the training objective into a bound on the KL divergence between the data and the model.


4.2.4.3 The cutoff cannot be removed
The integral in Eq. 37 starts at t_{\min}, and it diverges as t_{\min} \to 0 even for the best model. The Gaussian data of §2.4 show it. There, by §4.1, the best s_\theta is the marginal score -(x - c)/v. Writing x_0 = c_0 + s_0 z and x_t = m\, x_0 + \sqrt{\Sigma}\, \epsilon, with z and \epsilon independent standard normal variables, the marginal score at x_t minus the kernel’s score -\epsilon/\sqrt{\Sigma} is \epsilon\, \big(1/\sqrt{\Sigma} - \sqrt{\Sigma}/v\big) - m s_0 z / v. Its mean is zero, so at the best model the integrand of the g^2-weighted integral above Eq. 38 is g^2 times its variance, which is the sum of the variances of its two independent terms,

\operatorname{Var} = \Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\Sigma}} - \frac{\sqrt{\Sigma}}{v}\Big)^2 + \frac{m^2 s_0^2}{v^2}

Writing the bracket as (v - \Sigma)/(\sqrt{\Sigma}\, v) and substituting v - \Sigma = m^2 s_0^2 from Eq. 29,

\operatorname{Var} = \frac{m^4 s_0^4}{\Sigma\, v^2} + \frac{m^2 s_0^2}{v^2}

Adding the fractions, with m^2 s_0^2 + \Sigma = v,

\operatorname{Var} = \frac{m^2 s_0^2}{\Sigma\, v}

Near t = 0, m \to 1 and v \to s_0^2, so the integrand g^2 \operatorname{Var} is close to g^2/\Sigma. For the VP-SDE, \Sigma(t) \approx \beta(0)\, t and g^2 \approx \beta(0) near t = 0, so the integrand is close to 1/t, whose integral over [t_{\min}, T] grows without bound as t_{\min} \to 0. The bound in continuous time therefore needs a first time with a finite SNR, as Kingma et al.’s does [23].

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
5.1 Reverse diffusion sampling
Writing Eq. 28 on the grid, with the score-based model in place of the true score and with f, g and the score evaluated at the step’s start time t_i rather than at t_{i-1}, a change of higher order in \Delta t per step that keeps the score away from t = 0,

\boxed{x_{i-1} = x_i - \big[\,f(x_i, t_i) - g(t_i)^2\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)\,\big]\Delta t \;+\; g(t_i)\sqrt{\Delta t}\; z}
\tag{39}
with a fresh z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) at each step. The loop this defines is the whole sampler.
Algorithm 4 — Reverse diffusion sampling [1]:
1: x_N \sim p(x_N)
2: for i = N, \ldots, 1 do
    3: z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
    4: x_{i-1} = x_i - \big[f(x_i, t_i) - g(t_i)^2\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)\big]\Delta t + g(t_i)\sqrt{\Delta t}\; z
5: end for
6: return x_0
The prior p(x_N) on line 1 approximates the terminal marginal p_T of the forward process: \mathcal{N}(0, I) for the VP and sub-VP SDEs, and \mathcal{N}\big(0, \sigma_{\max}^2 I\big) for the VE-SDE. Nothing else enters. The drift and diffusion are the modeler’s own choice of forward process, and the network supplies the one quantity the forward pass discarded.
The Variance-Preserving instance:
We write \beta_i = \beta(t_i)\,\Delta t for the noise added over one step.
Substituting f = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x and g = \sqrt{\beta(t)} into Eq. 39,

\boxed{x_{i-1} = \Big(1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_i\Big) x_i \;+\; \beta_i\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i) \;+\; \sqrt{\beta_i}\; z}
\tag{40}
Song et al. write the leading coefficient as 2 - \sqrt{1-\beta_i}, which agrees with 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_i to first order in \beta_i and mirrors the \sqrt{1-\beta_i} appearing in the forward discretization. That matched pairing is their reverse diffusion sampler [1].
The Variance-Exploding instance:
Here f = 0 and g^2 = \tfrac{d}{dt}\sigma^2(t), so g(t_i)^2\, \Delta t \approx \sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1}), the noise variance added over one step and the counterpart of \beta_i. Substituting into Eq. 39,

x_{i-1} = x_i + \big(\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})\big)\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i) + \sqrt{\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})}\; z

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
5.2 Ancestral sampling
Post #2’s ancestral sampler is the VP instance of Eq. 39, discretized differently. It was derived from the variational reverse Markov chain, with no SDE anywhere in its construction. It uses \alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i and \bar\alpha_i = \prod_{j \le i}\alpha_j.
Algorithm 5 — Ancestral sampling [2]:
1: x_N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
2: for i = N, \ldots, 1 do
    3: z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) if i > 1, else z = 0
    4: \mu_\theta \leftarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_i}}\Big(x_i - \frac{\beta_i}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}}\, \epsilon_\theta(x_i, i)\Big)
    5: x_{i-1} \leftarrow \mu_\theta + \sigma_i\, z
6: end for
7: return x_0
The deterministic part is the reverse drift in noise-prediction form, and the \sigma_i z term is the retained diffusion, with \sigma_i^2 = \beta_i or the posterior variance of post #2,

\tilde\beta_i = \frac{1-\bar\alpha_{i-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\beta_i

Both appear in [2].
Starting from lines 4 and 5 of Algorithm 5,

x_{i-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_i}}\Big(x_i - \frac{\beta_i}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}}\, \epsilon_\theta(x_i, i)\Big) + \sigma_i\, z

Substituting \epsilon_\theta = -\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\, s_\theta, the relation of §4.2,

x_{i-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_i}}\big(x_i + \beta_i\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)\big) + \sigma_i\, z

Writing \alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i,

x_{i-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_i}}\big(x_i + \beta_i\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)\big) + \sigma_i\, z

Taking \sigma_i^2 = \beta_i,

x_{i-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_i}}\big(x_i + \beta_i\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)\big) + \sqrt{\beta_i}\; z

Expanding (1-\beta_i)^{-1/2} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_i + O(\beta_i^2),

x_{i-1} = \Big(1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_i\Big)\big(x_i + \beta_i\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)\big) + \sqrt{\beta_i}\; z + O(\beta_i^2)

Multiplying out, with the resulting \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_i^2\, s_\theta absorbed into the remainder,

x_{i-1} = \Big(1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_i\Big) x_i + \beta_i\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i) + \sqrt{\beta_i}\; z + O(\beta_i^2)

which is Eq. 40 to first order in \beta_i. \square
The two samplers therefore solve one equation by two numerical schemes [1]. Post #2 reached its update by bounding a likelihood, and this Part reached its own by discretizing a time reversal. The agreement shown for the training objective in §4.2 extends to the generative procedure itself.
Ancestral sampling for SMLD:
The same construction applies to the VE side [1]. We start from the noising chain of §1.3 and set \sigma(t_0) = 0, Song et al.’s simplification and the idealization \sigma_{\min} \to 0 of that section, so that x_i \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\big(x_0, \sigma^2(t_i)\, I\big). This is the kernel Eq. 3 with m = 1 and \Sigma(t) = \sigma^2(t). Substituting these, s = t_{i-1} and t = t_i into Eq. 35, with m_{t|s} = 1 and \Sigma_{t|s} = \sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1}), the true reverse posterior is

q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i, x_0) = \mathcal{N}\Big(x_{i-1};\; \frac{\sigma^2(t_{i-1})}{\sigma^2(t_i)}\, x_i + \frac{\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})}{\sigma^2(t_i)}\, x_0,\; \frac{\sigma^2(t_{i-1})\,(\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1}))}{\sigma^2(t_i)}\, I\Big)

The learned reverse step replaces the unknown x_0 by its posterior mean given x_i. For this kernel, Tweedie’s formula Eq. 24, with m = 1 and \Sigma = \sigma^2(t_i), states

\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_i] = x_i + \sigma^2(t_i)\, \nabla_x \log p_{t_i}(x_i)

It is estimated by x_i + \sigma^2(t_i)\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i).
Substituting this estimate for x_0 in the posterior mean,

\mu_\theta(x_i) = \frac{\sigma^2(t_{i-1})}{\sigma^2(t_i)}\, x_i + \frac{\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})}{\sigma^2(t_i)}\, \big(x_i + \sigma^2(t_i)\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)\big)

Expanding the product,

\mu_\theta(x_i) = \frac{\sigma^2(t_{i-1})}{\sigma^2(t_i)}\, x_i + \frac{\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})}{\sigma^2(t_i)}\, x_i + \big(\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})\big)\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)

Combining the two x_i terms,

\mu_\theta(x_i) = x_i + \big(\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})\big)\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i)

Sampling with the posterior variance, the ancestral step is

x_{i-1} = x_i + \big(\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1})\big)\, s_\theta(x_i, t_i) + \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2(t_{i-1})\,(\sigma^2(t_i) - \sigma^2(t_{i-1}))}{\sigma^2(t_i)}}\; z

It has the drift of the VE instance of Eq. 39 and an injected variance smaller by the factor \sigma^2(t_{i-1})/\sigma^2(t_i), which tends to 1 as the grid is refined. Song et al. reach the same step by matching a term of the ELBO, as DDPM does.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
5.3 Predictor-corrector sampling
Algorithm 4 is a predictor, a scheme that advances the state one step down the time grid. Each pass is one Euler-Maruyama step, and two errors accumulate with no mechanism for removing them. The step is finite, so the discretization is inexact, and s_\theta is only an estimate, so the drift is inexact as well.
But the network returns the score at every time, not only along the path the sampler follows. The score at a fixed t is what the Langevin Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler of P2:§3.3.2 needs to sample p_t. Interleaving M Langevin steps at the current time after each step of Algorithm 4, each of the form

x_{i-1} \;\leftarrow\; x_{i-1} + \varepsilon\, s_\theta(x_{i-1}, t_{i-1}) + \sqrt{2\varepsilon}\; z

drives the state back toward p_{t_{i-1}} before the next step. These Langevin steps are the corrector, which corrects the state at a fixed time instead of advancing it.
The step size is fixed by a target ratio r between the score term and the injected noise [1],

r = \lVert \varepsilon\, s_\theta \rVert / \lVert \sqrt{2\varepsilon}\, z \rVert

which inverts to

\varepsilon = 2\big(r\, \lVert z \rVert / \lVert s_\theta \rVert\big)^2

Algorithm 6 — Predictor-corrector sampling [1]:
1: x_N \sim p(x_N)
2: for i = N, \ldots, 1 do
    3: x_{i-1} \leftarrow one step of Algorithm 4 from x_i
    4: for j = 1, \ldots, M do
        5: z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
        6: x_{i-1} \leftarrow x_{i-1} + \varepsilon\, s_\theta(x_{i-1}, t_{i-1}) + \sqrt{2\varepsilon}\; z
    7: end for
8: end for
9: return x_0
Adding corrector steps:
The two-mode example keeps t_0 = 0 on this grid, because its exact score, with modes of standard deviation 0.3, is Lipschitz there. Here we compare, on the two-mode example of Figure 2 with the exact score, the predictor alone on a coarse grid of N = 10 steps, the same grid with M = 3 corrector steps per level, and the predictor alone with N = 40 steps, as Figure 10 shows below.








Figure 10: Samples from the two-mode example with the exact score, against the data distribution p_0 (solid curve). Left: the predictor alone on a coarse grid of N = 10 steps. Middle: the same grid with M = 3 Langevin corrector steps per level. Right: the predictor alone with N = 40 steps, the same number of score evaluations as the middle panel. Each title gives the total-variation distance to p_0, half the integral of the absolute difference between the histogram density and p_0.





Three corrector steps per level bring the samples much closer to p_0, at the cost of three extra score evaluations per step. In this example a predictor-only run with the same 40 evaluations does better still, since the score is exact and the only error is the discretization. With a learned score on CIFAR-10, Song et al. found one corrector step per predictor step typically better than doubling the predictor steps [1].
This arrangement names the samplers already met. Using the predictor alone is Algorithm 4. Using the corrector alone, applied along a decreasing sequence of noise levels, is the annealed Langevin dynamics of P2:§5. Using both is the predictor-corrector sampler, and post #2’s sampler over a finite sequence of noise levels is the corrector half of a scheme whose other half only became available once the reverse-time SDE was written down.
The predictor contains Langevin dynamics as well. The reverse-time SDE is the member h = g of the family of §2.2.1, and its drift differs from that of the probability-flow ODE, the member h = 0, by \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t. That drift, with the noise g\, d\bar W_t, is Langevin dynamics for p_t at the rate \tfrac{1}{2} g^2 per unit of reverse time, which leaves p_t unchanged. The corrector therefore repeats, at a fixed noise level, an operation that the predictor performs while the noise level decreases.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
5.4 Denoising the final sample
The final step of Algorithms 4 and 6 still injects noise, so the sample they return carries a little of it. A single application of Tweedie’s formula Eq. 24 removes it. Applied at the last noisy state x_1, with s_\theta(x_1, t_1) in place of the score, it replaces the final step by the posterior mean \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_1], which is reported instead. Post #2’s ancestral sampler applies the same correction in its own idiom: line 3 of Algorithm 5 sets z = 0 on the final step, returning the mean rather than a perturbed value.
Denoising the last step:
Here we compare the last step of reverse diffusion sampling with and without this correction, on a grid of N = 25 steps with the exact score, for data on five discrete levels like pixel intensities, as Figure 11 shows below.








Figure 11: The last step of reverse diffusion sampling on a grid of N = 25 steps, with the exact score, for data on five levels. Left: Algorithm 4 as written, whose final step injects noise, so the samples scatter around each level. Right: the final step replaced by Tweedie’s posterior mean at x_1, which puts the samples on the levels (dotted lines).





As written, Algorithm 4 injects noise in its final step, so the samples scatter around each level. With the final step replaced by Tweedie’s posterior mean at x_1, the samples lie on the levels.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
5.5 Decoupling training from sampling
Training and sampling are decoupled, a separation the SDE framework [1] makes explicit: what to learn is fixed and how to sample is free. Whatever forward SDE we pick, VP, VE or sub-VP, the only learned object is the time-indexed score \nabla_x \log p_t, trained once by the weighted DSM objective Eq. 31. Generation can then use any numerical solver of the reverse-time SDE (Eq. 19) or the probability-flow ODE (Eq. 30), and Algorithms 4 to 6 are three such solvers.
For the probability-flow ODE, substituting the score-based model for the score in Eq. 30 leaves an ODE with no unknown terms,

\frac{dx_t}{dt} = f(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, s_\theta(x_t, t)

and solving it backward from an initial state drawn from the prior p(x_N) of Algorithm 4 generates samples with any ODE solver. Song et al. use an adaptive solver of Dormand and Prince [24], which chooses its own step sizes. With a larger error tolerance it reduces the number of score evaluations by over 90% without a visible loss of sample quality [1].
The equality of marginals in Parts 2 and 3 holds for the exact score. With s_\theta in its place, the reverse-time SDE and the probability-flow ODE in general generate different distributions, and each differs from p_0 by an amount that depends on the error of s_\theta. P6:§3.2 bounds that difference for the reverse-time SDE.
The three forward SDEs are not different models trained differently. They are three choices of the forward coefficients f, g, feeding the same score-learning scheme and the same family of samplers. This decoupling is also why sampler quality has improved independently of the model. Better solvers, of higher order or with fewer steps, replace earlier ones without retraining.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
6.1 What comes next
Post #4 develops the probability-flow ODE further. As a continuous normalizing flow, a normalizing flow (P1:§5.2) whose invertible map is obtained by solving an ODE [27], it gives exact likelihoods through the instantaneous change of variables, and flow matching trains such a flow directly.

title: SDE-Based Generative Models: The Unification of the Variational Bound and Score Matching
text:
Appendix

A.1 Existence and uniqueness of strong solutions
Post #1 wrote down SDEs (P1:§2.1) and solved specific ones in closed form. This appendix states the conditions under which a solution exists and is unique, which guarantees that the objects manipulated in the body are well defined. Consider

dX_t = f(X_t, t)\, dt + g(X_t, t)\, dW_t, \qquad X_0 = \xi

on [0, T]. The state is X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d, W_t is an m-dimensional Brownian motion, f : \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^d and g : \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^{d \times m} are measurable, and the initial value \xi is independent of W with \mathbb{E}\,|\xi|^2 < \infty. Here f is the drift and g the diffusion coefficient, the letters of this post’s forward SDE. Post #1 writes them \mu and \sigma. Throughout, |\cdot| is the Euclidean norm of a vector and the Frobenius norm of a matrix, the square root of the sum of its squared entries.
Conditions: Suppose the coefficients satisfy, for some constant K and all x, y \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in [0, T]:

Global Lipschitz:

|f(x,t) - f(y,t)| + |g(x,t) - g(y,t)| \le K\, |x - y|
\tag{41}
Linear growth:

|f(x,t)| + |g(x,t)| \le K\,(1 + |x|)
\tag{42}

Theorem (existence and uniqueness): Under the conditions Eq. 41 and Eq. 42 there is an adapted, continuous strong solution X_t on [0, T], unique in that any two such solutions X and Y satisfy \mathbb{P}\big(X_t = Y_t\ \forall t \in [0, T]\big) = 1, with

\mathbb{E}\big[\sup_{t \le T} |X_t|^2\big] < \infty

Proof sketch (Picard iteration):
Starting from X^{(0)}_t \equiv \xi, the iteration is

X^{(n+1)}_t = \xi + \int_0^t f\big(X^{(n)}_s, s\big)\, ds + \int_0^t g\big(X^{(n)}_s, s\big)\, dW_s

The stochastic term is bounded by Doob’s maximal inequality, \mathbb{E}\big[\sup_{s \le t} |M_s|^2\big] \le 4\, \mathbb{E}\,|M_t|^2 for a square-integrable martingale M, followed by the Itô isometry, P1:Eq. 47, summed over components,

\mathbb{E}\,\Big|\int_0^t H_s\, dW_s\Big|^2 = \mathbb{E}\int_0^t |H_s|^2\, ds

and the drift term by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. With the Lipschitz condition Eq. 41, the two bounds give

\mathbb{E}\!\sup_{s \le t} \big|X^{(n+1)}_s - X^{(n)}_s\big|^2 \;\le\; C \int_0^t \mathbb{E}\!\sup_{r \le s} \big|X^{(n)}_r - X^{(n-1)}_r\big|^2\, ds

with C depending only on K and T. By induction, successive differences are bounded by a constant times (Ct)^n / n!, so the iterates are Cauchy in L^2 and converge to a solution. Linear growth, Eq. 42, keeps every iterate in L^2, so no solution blows up in finite time. A Grönwall argument [19] applied to the difference of two solutions forces uniqueness. Full details are in [16], [28]. \square
The series’ SDEs all qualify. Every forward process in this series is affine in the state, with coefficients that are bounded and measurable in t on [0, T]:

Geometric Brownian motion (GBM) (f = \mu x, g = \sigma x) and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) (f = \kappa(\bar\mu - x), g = \sigma), the processes of post #1.
VP-SDE (f = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x, g = \sqrt{\beta(t)}), VE-SDE (f = 0, g = \sqrt{d\sigma^2/dt}) and sub-VP SDE (f = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x, g = \sqrt{\beta(t)\big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)^2\big)}), the processes of this post.

An affine map with bounded coefficients is Lipschitz with linear growth, so each has a unique strong solution. Affinity is far more than the theorem requires, and it is also what makes their kernels closed-form: Gaussian when the diffusion coefficient is state-independent (§1.1 for this post’s SDEs, P1:§2.4.2 for OU), lognormal for GBM (P1:§2.4.1).
The conditions start to matter only outside the affine family. The reverse-time SDE Eq. 19 with a learned score is the case in point. Its drift is affine in x only if the score is, so its well-posedness rests on the Lipschitz continuity of the network. The true score it approximates is Lipschitz only away from t = 0 (the conditions stated at the start of Part 2), which is one reason samplers stop short of t = 0.


A.2 Gaussian perturbation kernels require an affine drift
The previous appendix noted that an affine drift makes the kernels of the series’ SDEs Gaussian, and §1.1 derives the Gaussian kernel of the linear SDE Eq. 2. This appendix proves the converse in one dimension: if the perturbation kernel is Gaussian for each initial condition, the drift is affine in the state. So the requirement of Gaussian kernels forces the affine form, and the series’ linear SDEs are its case c = 0. The form is not a convenience.
Consider the forward SDE Eq. 1 in one dimension,

dx_t = f(x_t, t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW_t, \qquad x_t \in \mathbb{R}

with g(t) > 0 and f continuously differentiable in x.
Theorem (Gaussian kernels force an affine drift): Suppose that for each initial condition x_0 and each t \in (0, T] the perturbation kernel is Gaussian,

p_{0t}(x \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(x;\; \nu(t),\; \Sigma(t)\big)

with mean \nu: (0, T] \to \mathbb{R} and variance \Sigma: (0, T] \to (0, \infty) that depend on x_0 and are differentiable in t, and that at each t the kernel depends on the initial condition. Then the drift is affine in x, with coefficients f_{\mathrm{lin}}, c: (0, T] \to \mathbb{R},

\boxed{f(x, t) = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, x + c(t)}
\tag{43}
The last hypothesis excludes only a process that forgets its starting point for each t > 0, whose kernel would carry no information about the data.
Proof:
We fix t \in (0, T] and a starting point x_0, and write p for p_{0t}(x \mid x_0) and u = x - \nu(t), so that

\log p = -\frac{u^2}{2\Sigma} - \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\Sigma)

and let primes denote \frac{d}{dt}.
For t > 0, p is the density of x_t for the process started at the point x_0, so it satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation, P1:Eq. 45, here in one dimension with drift f and diffusion coefficient g(t),

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big[f\, p\big] + \tfrac12\, g^2\, \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2}

Expanding the drift term by the product rule,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, p - f\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial x} + \tfrac12\, g^2\, \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2}

Dividing by p > 0,

\frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} - f\, \frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} + \tfrac12\, g^2\, \frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2}

Substituting the identity

\frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial x} = -\frac{u}{\Sigma}

into the previous line,

\frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\, \frac{u}{\Sigma} + \tfrac12\, g^2\, \frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2}

Substituting the identity

\frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial^2 \log p}{\partial x^2} + \Big(\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial x}\Big)^2 = -\frac{1}{\Sigma} + \frac{u^2}{\Sigma^2}

into the previous line,

\frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\, \frac{u}{\Sigma} + \tfrac12\, g^2 \Big(\frac{u^2}{\Sigma^2} - \frac{1}{\Sigma}\Big)

Substituting the identity

\frac{1}{p}\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial t} = \frac{\nu'\, u}{\Sigma} + \frac{\Sigma'\, u^2}{2\Sigma^2} - \frac{\Sigma'}{2\Sigma}

which uses \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = -\nu', into the previous line,

\frac{\nu'\, u}{\Sigma} + \frac{\Sigma'\, u^2}{2\Sigma^2} - \frac{\Sigma'}{2\Sigma} = -\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\, \frac{u}{\Sigma} + \tfrac12\, g^2 \Big(\frac{u^2}{\Sigma^2} - \frac{1}{\Sigma}\Big)

Moving the terms in f to the left and every other term to the right,

-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\, \frac{u}{\Sigma} = \frac{\nu'\, u}{\Sigma} + \frac{\Sigma'\, u^2}{2\Sigma^2} - \frac{\Sigma'}{2\Sigma} - \tfrac12\, g^2 \Big(\frac{u^2}{\Sigma^2} - \frac{1}{\Sigma}\Big)

Grouping by powers of u,

-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\, \frac{u}{\Sigma} = \frac{\nu'}{\Sigma}\, u + \frac{\Sigma' - g^2}{2\Sigma^2}\, u^2 - \frac{\Sigma' - g^2}{2\Sigma}

The right side is a polynomial in x of degree at most two, with coefficients that depend on t and x_0. Writing it as a function Q: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} of x and restoring u = x - \nu,

-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, t) + f(x, t)\, \frac{x - \nu}{\Sigma} = Q(x)
\tag{44}
Now take two starting points whose kernels at time t differ, with means \nu_1, \nu_2, variances \Sigma_1, \Sigma_2 and right sides Q_1, Q_2. Writing the identity Eq. 44 for each,

\begin{aligned}
-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\, \frac{x - \nu_1}{\Sigma_1} &= Q_1(x) \\[4pt]
-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\, \frac{x - \nu_2}{\Sigma_2} &= Q_2(x)
\end{aligned}

Subtracting the second from the first, the term \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} cancels because the drift is the same function for both initial conditions,

f(x, t)\, \Big(\frac{x - \nu_1}{\Sigma_1} - \frac{x - \nu_2}{\Sigma_2}\Big) = Q_1(x) - Q_2(x)
\tag{45}
We write \ell: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} for the bracket as a function of x. It is affine in x,

\ell(x) = \Big(\frac{1}{\Sigma_1} - \frac{1}{\Sigma_2}\Big)\, x - \Big(\frac{\nu_1}{\Sigma_1} - \frac{\nu_2}{\Sigma_2}\Big)

and it vanishes identically only if \Sigma_1 = \Sigma_2 and \nu_1 = \nu_2, which the choice of initial conditions excludes. Two cases remain.
Unequal variances:
If \Sigma_1 \neq \Sigma_2, \ell has a single root x^*. Evaluating the difference Eq. 45 at x^* gives Q_1(x^*) - Q_2(x^*) = f(x^*, t)\, \ell(x^*) = 0, so \ell divides the polynomial Q_1 - Q_2, with a quotient L of degree at most one. Dividing by \ell for x \neq x^*,

f(x, t) = L(x)

and continuity of f in x extends this to x^*. So f is affine in x.
Equal variances:
If \Sigma_1 = \Sigma_2 = \Sigma, then \nu_1 \neq \nu_2 and \ell(x) = (\nu_2 - \nu_1)/\Sigma is a nonzero constant. Dividing Eq. 45 by it,

f(x, t) = \frac{\Sigma\, \big(Q_1(x) - Q_2(x)\big)}{\nu_2 - \nu_1}

which is a polynomial of degree at most two, f = c_0 + c_1 x + c_2 x^2. In the identity Eq. 44 for the first initial condition, -\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} has degree at most one and f\, (x - \nu_1)/\Sigma contributes the single cubic term c_2 x^3/\Sigma, while Q_1 has degree at most two. Matching the coefficients of x^3 gives c_2 = 0, so f is affine in x.
In both cases, for each t,

\boxed{f(x, t) = f_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)\, x + c(t)}

which is Eq. 43, the statement of the theorem. \square
The converse and the series’ choice: An affine drift gives a Gaussian kernel. The integrating-factor solution of §1.1 carries over with c(t) present: the transform leaves the deterministic drift e^{-F(t)}\, c(t), which adds e^{F(t)} \int_0^t e^{-F(s)}\, c(s)\, ds to the mean and leaves the variance unchanged. In one dimension, then, a Gaussian kernel for each initial condition and an affine drift are equivalent. The series’ forward processes have c = 0, which gives the linear SDE Eq. 2.
Simulating a non-affine drift:
Here we simulate the SDE dx_t = -x_t^3\, dt + dW_t, whose drift is not affine, and compare two of its kernels with Gaussians of the same mean and variance, as Figure 12 shows below.








Figure 12: Kernels of the SDE dx_t = -x_t^3\, dt + dW_t, whose drift is not affine, from 50,000 Euler-Maruyama paths, against Gaussians with the same mean and variance (curves). Left: initial condition x_0 = 0, at t = 1, flatter than a Gaussian at the top. Right: initial condition x_0 = 2, at t = 0.2, slightly skewed. Neither is Gaussian, consistent with the theorem.





From x_0 = 0, the kernel at t = 1 is flatter than a Gaussian at the top, and from x_0 = 2, the kernel at t = 0.2 is skewed. Neither is Gaussian, consistent with the theorem.
Scope: The proof is one-dimensional. It also covers a drift in \mathbb{R}^d that acts on each coordinate separately, f_j(x, t) = f_j(x_j, t), with the isotropic diffusion g(t)\, I of this post. Each coordinate then solves a scalar SDE of the form above, driven by its own Brownian component. Its kernel is a marginal of the Gaussian kernel, hence Gaussian, so the theorem applies to each coordinate in turn.
For a drift that couples the coordinates, subtracting the two identities leaves f \cdot \ell(x) with a vector \ell(x). That is one scalar equation for a vector f, so it does not isolate f, and this proof does not apply.


A.3 Girsanov’s theorem: changing the drift by changing the measure
Itô’s lemma transforms a function of a process. Girsanov’s theorem [5] does something orthogonal: it transforms the measure under which the process is viewed. The effect is to change the drift while leaving the diffusion untouched. In finance this is the change from the real-world measure \mathbb{P} to the risk-neutral measure \mathbb{Q}, which P1:§A.2 invoked when pricing. In this post it accounts for the drift correction that separates the reverse-time SDE from the forward SDE run backward without correction (§2.3).
It is developed here in full, with four classical inputs cited rather than proved, namely Novikov’s criterion, the local-martingale property of driftless Itô processes, the optional sampling theorem and Lévy’s characterization of Brownian motion. Same machinery, two settings.
The idea: Reweighting each path by a positive factor Z_t makes paths that happen to drift in a chosen direction more (or less) likely, which is indistinguishable from having added a drift to the dynamics. Reweighting cannot change how irregular the paths are. Quadratic variation is a pathwise property (P1:§A.4), so (dW)^2 = dt is unchanged by a change of measure. Hence the rule: a change of measure can add or remove drift, never volatility.
Set-up:
We work on [0, T] with a d-dimensional \mathbb{P}-Brownian motion W_t and its filtration \mathcal{F}_t, the information generated by the Brownian path up to time t.
