P1:§A.5 defines filtrations, adapted processes and martingales. We fix an adapted process \psi_t \in \mathbb{R}^d, the drift to be installed, satisfying Novikov’s condition

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\big[\exp(\tfrac{1}{2}\int_0^T \lVert\psi_s\rVert^2\, ds)\big] < \infty

which Step 1 cites to make the density defined next a true martingale. We define the stochastic exponential

\boxed{\,Z_t \;=\; \exp\!\Big(\int_0^t \psi_s^\top dW_s \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2}\int_0^t \lVert\psi_s\rVert^2\, ds\Big)\,}
\tag{46}
and a new measure \mathbb{Q} on \mathcal{F}_T by d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P} = Z_T, the Radon-Nikodym derivative of \mathbb{Q} with respect to \mathbb{P}. It is the factor by which \mathbb{Q} reweights each path, so that, for each event A \in \mathcal{F}_T,

\mathbb{Q}(A) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[Z_T \mathbf{1}_A]

More generally, for each integrable random variable Y determined by the path up to T,

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[Z_T\, Y]

Theorem (Girsanov): Under \mathbb{Q}, the process

\tilde W_t \;=\; W_t \;-\; \int_0^t \psi_s\, ds

is a d-dimensional standard Brownian motion. Equivalently dW_t = d\tilde W_t + \psi_t\, dt: the same noise, viewed under \mathbb{Q}, carries an extra drift \psi_t\, dt. For d = 1 this is the scalar form the finance interpretation below uses.
Reweighting Brownian paths:
Here we reweight the endpoints of Brownian paths by Z_T for d = 1 and a constant \psi, as Figure 13 shows below.








Figure 13: A change of measure in action for d = 1. Endpoints W_T of 100,000 Brownian paths with T = 1 under \mathbb{P} (grey), and the same endpoints reweighted by Z_T = \exp(\psi W_T - \tfrac{1}{2}\psi^2 T) with \psi = 1 (teal), against \mathcal{N}(\psi T, T) (curve). Reweighting shifts the mean by \psi T and leaves the spread unchanged, which is the drift shift of the theorem.





Reweighting shifts the mean of W_T by \psi T and leaves its spread unchanged, which is the drift shift of the theorem.
The proof uses two results of post #1. The first is the cross rule for the independent components of W_t, P1:Eq. 48,

dW^i_t\, dW^j_t = \delta_{ij}\, dt

The second is Itô’s lemma, P1:Eq. 49, for a scalar process driven by W_t, dX_t = a_t\, dt + b_t^\top dW_t with a_t \in \mathbb{R} and b_t \in \mathbb{R}^d,

dh = \Big(\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} + a_t\, \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} + \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert b_t\rVert^2\, \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}\Big)\, dt + \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\, b_t^\top dW_t

Step 1 — Z_t is a positive \mathbb{P}-martingale with Z_0 = 1:
We write Z_t = e^{X_t} with X_t = \int_0^t \psi_s^\top dW_s - \tfrac{1}{2}\int_0^t \lVert\psi_s\rVert^2\, ds, so that

dX_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\psi_t\rVert^2\, dt + \psi_t^\top dW_t

and apply the lemma to Z_t = h(X_t) with h(x) = e^{x}.
Coefficients (from dX_t):
a_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\psi_t\rVert^2 and b_t = \psi_t, so \lVert b_t \rVert^2 = \lVert\psi_t\rVert^2.
Partials (from h = e^{x}):

\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} = e^{x}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} = e^{x}

Substituting the coefficients and the three partials into the lemma,

dZ_t = \Big(0 - \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\psi_t\rVert^2\, e^{X_t} + \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\psi_t\rVert^2\, e^{X_t}\Big)\, dt + e^{X_t}\, \psi_t^\top dW_t

Cancelling the two dt terms,

dZ_t = e^{X_t}\, \psi_t^\top dW_t

Substituting e^{X_t} = Z_t,

dZ_t = Z_t\, \psi_t^\top dW_t

So Z_t has no drift and is a positive local \mathbb{P}-martingale. A local martingale is a process that becomes a martingale when stopped at each time of some sequence of random times increasing to T, each decided by the path up to that time, and such a sequence is a localizing sequence. A driftless Itô process is a local martingale [28] but need not be a true one. Novikov’s condition makes Z_t a true martingale [28], with \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[Z_t] = Z_0 = 1. Hence \mathbb{Q} is a probability measure equivalent to \mathbb{P}: since Z_T > 0, the two assign positive probability to the same events.
Step 2 — \tilde W_t is a d-dimensional \mathbb{Q}-Brownian motion:
By Lévy’s characterization in d dimensions [28], it is enough that each component \tilde W^i_t is a continuous \mathbb{Q}-local martingale and that [\tilde W^i, \tilde W^j]_t = \delta_{ij}\, t.
Continuity is inherited from W. Quadratic variation is pathwise, so the change of measure leaves it unchanged, and subtracting \int_0^t \psi^i_s\, ds does not change the products of increments, since dt\, dW^j_t = 0 and (dt)^2 = 0. By the cross rule,

[\tilde W^i, \tilde W^j]_t = [W^i, W^j]_t = \delta_{ij}\, t

For the local-martingale property, we use the change-of-measure rule: M_t is a \mathbb{Q}-martingale iff M_t Z_t is a \mathbb{P}-martingale. We fix s \le t and an event A \in \mathcal{F}_s.
By the definition of \mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[Z_T\, Y] with Y = M_t \mathbf{1}_A,

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[M_t \mathbf{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[M_t Z_T \mathbf{1}_A]

By the tower property and the martingale property of Z,

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[M_t \mathbf{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[M_t Z_t \mathbf{1}_A]

So the equalities that make M a \mathbb{Q}-martingale,

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[M_t \mathbf{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[M_s \mathbf{1}_A]

are the equalities that make M Z a \mathbb{P}-martingale,

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[M_t Z_t \mathbf{1}_A] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[M_s Z_s \mathbf{1}_A]

The rule extends to local martingales. Let MZ be a \mathbb{P}-local martingale with a localizing sequence \tau_n (Step 1), so that each M_{\tau_n \wedge t} Z_{\tau_n \wedge t} is a \mathbb{P}-martingale. Then M_{\tau_n \wedge t} Z_t is a \mathbb{P}-martingale too. For s \le t and A \in \mathcal{F}_s, on \{\tau_n \le s\} the factor M_{\tau_n \wedge t} is known at time s and Z is a martingale. On \{\tau_n > s\}, where A \cap \{\tau_n > s\} lies in \mathcal{F}_{\tau_n \wedge t}, optional sampling [28] gives

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[M_{\tau_n \wedge t} Z_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{\tau_n \wedge t}] = M_{\tau_n \wedge t} Z_{\tau_n \wedge t}

By the rule, each stopped M_{\tau_n \wedge t} is a \mathbb{Q}-martingale, so M is a \mathbb{Q}-local martingale.
Taking M_t = \tilde W^i_t, the Itô product rule, derived in P1:§A.3, gives

d(\tilde W^i_t Z_t) = \tilde W^i_t\, dZ_t + Z_t\, d\tilde W^i_t + d\tilde W^i_t\, dZ_t

Substituting dZ_t = Z_t \sum_j \psi^j_t\, dW^j_t and d\tilde W^i_t = dW^i_t - \psi^i_t\, dt,

d(\tilde W^i_t Z_t) = \tilde W^i_t Z_t \sum_j \psi^j_t\, dW^j_t + Z_t\big(dW^i_t - \psi^i_t\, dt\big) + \big(dW^i_t - \psi^i_t\, dt\big)\, Z_t \sum_j \psi^j_t\, dW^j_t

Using dW^i_t\, dW^j_t = \delta_{ij}\, dt and dt\, dW^j_t = 0,

d(\tilde W^i_t Z_t) = \tilde W^i_t Z_t \sum_j \psi^j_t\, dW^j_t + Z_t\, dW^i_t - Z_t \psi^i_t\, dt + Z_t \psi^i_t\, dt

The \pm Z_t \psi^i_t\, dt terms cancel,

d(\tilde W^i_t Z_t) = Z_t \Big(\tilde W^i_t \sum_j \psi^j_t\, dW^j_t + dW^i_t\Big)

The result is driftless, so \tilde W^i Z is a \mathbb{P}-local martingale, and by the rule \tilde W^i is a \mathbb{Q}-local martingale. With [\tilde W^i, \tilde W^j]_t = \delta_{ij}\, t, Lévy’s characterization gives that \tilde W_t is a d-dimensional standard Brownian motion under \mathbb{Q}. \square
The corollary the series uses (reshaping an SDE’s drift):
Suppose under \mathbb{P} a process solves dX_t = f(X_t, t)\, dt + g(X_t, t)\, dW_t (P1:§2.1), with g a d \times d matrix (the scalar g(t) times I in this post’s forward SDE). Substituting dW_t = d\tilde W_t + \psi_t\, dt,

\boxed{\,dX_t \;=\; \big[\, f(X_t, t) + g(X_t, t)\, \psi_t \,\big]\, dt \;+\; g(X_t, t)\, d\tilde W_t \quad (\text{under } \mathbb{Q})\,}
\tag{47}
The drift shifts by g\psi, and the diffusion coefficient g is invariant. To install a desired new drift \tilde f, with g invertible, choose

\psi_t \;=\; g(X_t, t)^{-1}\big(\tilde f(X_t, t) - f(X_t, t)\big)

and the change of measure delivers dX_t = \tilde f\, dt + g\, d\tilde W_t. This “pick \psi to retarget the drift” step is the content of risk-neutral pricing, and of the drift correction in the reverse-time SDE (§2.3).
The finance interpretation (risk-neutral pricing, d = 1): In P1:§A.2 the stock obeys dS = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW under \mathbb{P}, with r the risk-free interest rate. Pricing requires the discounted stock e^{-rt} S_t, the stock price in units of a money-market account that grows as e^{rt}, to be a martingale, i.e. drift r instead of \mu. By Eq. 47 that means \sigma S\,\psi = (r - \mu) S, so

\psi \;=\; \frac{r - \mu}{\sigma} \;=\; -\,(\text{market price of risk})

a constant Girsanov shift. Under the resulting measure \mathbb{Q} the log-return is normal with mean \big(r - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)T, so the stock itself grows at mean rate r (the computation of P1:§2.4.1 with \mu \to r). And N(d_2) is the risk-neutral exercise probability, N(d_2) = \mathbb{Q}(S_T > K), the interpretation named in P1:§A.2.
N(d_1) is also a probability, but under a different measure. A numéraire is the asset in whose units prices are quoted. \mathbb{Q} quotes them in the money-market account, and the stock-numéraire measure \mathbb{Q}^S quotes them in the stock. A second Girsanov change, to \mathbb{Q}^S, gives N(d_1) = \mathbb{Q}^S(S_T > K), which is also the option’s delta, the sensitivity \partial V/\partial S of its value V to the stock price. That change is Eq. 47 applied once more with \psi = \sigma, so d\mathbb{Q}^S/d\mathbb{Q} = S_T/(S_0 e^{rT}).
Back-reference: The Bayes’-rule derivation of this post (§2.3) relates to the same theorem (§2.3.2). In the reversed time \tau, with \psi = g\, \nabla_x \log p_{T-\tau}, Eq. 47 accounts for the whole difference between the forward SDE run backward and the reverse-time SDE. In the forward time it is a shift of -g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t in the drift, with \psi = -g\, \nabla_x \log p_t and the diffusion g(t) untouched. The time reversal itself is not a change of measure; supplying it is the content of the time-reversal theory [17]. For complete proofs of Girsanov’s theorem and Lévy’s characterization see [16], [28].


A.4 The framework for general SDEs
The body of this post restricts the diffusion to a scalar function of time times the identity, g(t)\, I. Song et al. state the framework for the general SDE [1]

dX_t = f(X_t, t)\, dt + G(X_t, t)\, dW_t

with a diffusion matrix G: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} that may depend on the state. This appendix derives its Fokker-Planck equation, reverse-time SDE and probability-flow ODE, and the training objective that replaces DSM when the kernel has no closed form. We write D = G G^\top: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} for the diffusion tensor, \partial_i for \partial / \partial x_i, and \nabla_x \cdot D for the row-wise divergence, (\nabla_x \cdot D)_i = \sum_j \partial_j D_{ij}.
The Fokker-Planck equation:
The weak-form derivation of P1:Eq. 45, in P1:§8.3, carries over, and only the diffusion term changes. Itô’s lemma for a state in \mathbb{R}^d, P1:Eq. 49, restated with drift f and diffusion matrix G, gives for a smooth test function \varphi(x) with compact support

d\varphi(X_t) = \Big(f \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr}\!\big(D\, \nabla_x^2 \varphi\big)\Big)\, dt + \nabla_x \varphi \cdot G\, dW_t

Taking expectations, which removes the Itô integral, and writing them as integrals against p_t, as in Step 2 there,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t}\, dx = \int \Big(f \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} D_{ij}\, \partial_i \partial_j \varphi\Big)\, p_t\, dx

Integrating the drift term by parts once and each diffusion term twice, as in Step 3 there, so that every derivative falls on f\, p_t and D_{ij}\, p_t,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t}\, dx = \int \varphi\, \Big(-\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big)\Big)\, dx

Since this holds for each test function, the integrands agree,

\boxed{\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big)}
\tag{48}
For D = g(t)^2 I it is the Fokker-Planck equation, the right side of Eq. 20.
The diffusion term as a divergence:
Both the reverse-time SDE and the probability-flow ODE rest on writing the diffusion term as a divergence, as the log-derivative identity from Eq. 21 does for D = I. Expanding the inner derivative by the product rule,

\sum_j \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big) = p_t\, (\nabla_x \cdot D)_i + \sum_j D_{ij}\, \partial_j p_t

Substituting \partial_j p_t = p_t\, \partial_j \log p_t,

\sum_j \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big) = p_t\, \big[(\nabla_x \cdot D)_i + (D\, \nabla_x \log p_t)_i\big]

Taking \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_i \partial_i of both sides,

\tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big) = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \nabla_x \cdot \Big[p_t\, \big(\nabla_x \cdot D + D\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big)\Big]
\tag{49}
The reverse-time SDE:
The construction of §2.2 carries over. Starting from Eq. 48,

\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big)

Writing the diffusion term as twice itself minus itself,

\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big) - \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big)

Substituting twice the divergence form Eq. 49 for the middle term,

\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \nabla_x \cdot \Big[p_t\, \big(\nabla_x \cdot D + D\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big)\Big] - \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big)

Combining the first two terms into one divergence,

\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot \Big[\big(f - \nabla_x \cdot D - D\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big)\, p_t\Big] - \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, p_t\big)

Reversing time as in §2.2, with \bar p_\tau = p_{T-\tau}, \partial_t p_t = -\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau, and the coefficients evaluated at t = T - \tau,

-\frac{\partial \bar p_\tau}{\partial \tau} = -\nabla_x \cdot \Big[\big(f - \nabla_x \cdot D - D\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big] - \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, \bar p_\tau\big)

Multiplying both sides by -1,

\frac{\partial \bar p_\tau}{\partial \tau} = \nabla_x \cdot \Big[\big(f - \nabla_x \cdot D - D\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big] + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, \bar p_\tau\big)

Writing the sign inside the divergence,

\frac{\partial \bar p_\tau}{\partial \tau} = -\nabla_x \cdot \Big[-\big(f - \nabla_x \cdot D - D\, \nabla_x \log \bar p_\tau\big)\, \bar p_\tau\Big] + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j\big(D_{ij}\, \bar p_\tau\big)

This is the Fokker-Planck equation Eq. 48, in the time \tau, of the SDE with the drift

-\big(f - \nabla_x \cdot D - D\, \nabla_x \log p_{T-\tau}\big)

and the diffusion matrix G(y_\tau, T - \tau). The sufficiency proof of §2.1.2 carries over to a diffusion matrix that depends on the state, for coefficients that are smooth with bounded derivatives [16]. The operator of the backward Kolmogorov equation changes from the first form below to the second,

f \cdot \nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x u \;\longrightarrow\; f \cdot \nabla_x u + \tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr}\!\big(D\, \nabla_x^2 u\big)

Assume that the coefficients of that SDE are smooth and Lipschitz with bounded derivatives, and that \bar p_\tau, together with D\, \bar p_\tau, decays at infinity and is dominated. The body verifies these for its linear SDEs, and the general case needs them as hypotheses of this argument; Haussmann and Pardoux prove the reversal under weaker conditions [17]. Then \bar p_\tau is the marginal path of the solution of that SDE with the initial condition y_0 \sim \bar p_0, which is p_T. Writing it in the original time as in §2.2, with \bar x_t = y_{T-t},

\boxed{d\bar x_t = \Big[f(\bar x_t, t) - \nabla_x \cdot D(\bar x_t, t) - D(\bar x_t, t)\, \nabla_x \log p_t(\bar x_t)\Big]\, dt + G(\bar x_t, t)\, d\bar W_t}
\tag{50}
The probability-flow ODE:
Substituting the divergence form Eq. 49 of the diffusion term into Eq. 48,

\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \nabla_x \cdot \Big[p_t\, \big(\nabla_x \cdot D + D\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big)\Big]

Combining into one divergence,

\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot \Big[\Big(f - \tfrac{1}{2}\, \nabla_x \cdot D - \tfrac{1}{2}\, D\, \nabla_x \log p_t\Big)\, p_t\Big]

This is the Fokker-Planck equation, with zero diffusion, of the ODE with this drift. Assume that the drift is continuous in t and infinitely differentiable in x with bounded derivatives away from t = 0, and that p_t decays at infinity and is dominated, the same kind of hypotheses as in §2.2. Reversing time as for the reverse-time SDE above, the sufficiency part of Eq. 20 with zero diffusion then makes p_t the marginal path of the solution of that ODE solved backward from the initial condition x_T \sim p_T,

\boxed{\frac{dx_t}{dt} = f(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, \nabla_x \cdot D(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, D(x_t, t)\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)}
\tag{51}
For G = g(t)\, I, \nabla_x \cdot D = 0 and D = g^2 I, so Eq. 50 and Eq. 51 reduce to Eq. 19 and Eq. 30.
Training without a closed-form kernel:
When f is not affine, the perturbation kernel is in general not Gaussian, as §A.2 proves, with a state-independent diffusion g(t), in one dimension and for a drift acting on each coordinate separately, and it has no closed form, so the regression target \nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) of DSM is unavailable. Song et al. [1] then sample x_t by simulating the forward SDE with data samples as initial conditions and train with sliced score matching (SSM) [7], which needs no target score. Its starting point is the implicit score matching (ISM) objective [29], P2:Eq. 36,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\Big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(x)\rVert^2 + \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)\Big]
\tag{52}
whose trace costs d backward passes (P2:Table 1). Hutchinson’s estimator [30] replaces the trace by a random projection: for v with \mathbb{E}[v v^\top] = I and each matrix A, \mathbb{E}_v[v^\top A v] = \mathbb{E}_v[\operatorname{tr}(A\, v v^\top)] = \operatorname{tr}(A). Applied for each t with the weight \lambda(t), it gives the weighted SSM objective

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSM}_{p_t}}(\theta; \lambda) = \mathbb{E}_t\Big\{\lambda(t)\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\, \mathbb{E}_v\Big[\lVert s_\theta(x_t, t)\rVert^2 + 2\, v^\top \nabla_x s_\theta(x_t, t)\, v\Big]\Big\}}
\tag{53}
Each term needs one Jacobian-vector product, the product \nabla_x s_\theta\, v that automatic differentiation computes in one pass without forming the Jacobian, instead of d backward passes. Its expectation over v is \mathbb{E}_t\big\{2\lambda(t)\, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_t}}(\theta)\big\}, where \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_t}} is Eq. 52 with p_t in place of p_0, so its minimizer is the marginal score, as for ISM.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
This series — Continuous-Time Generative Models
The first time I saw the forward process of a diffusion model written as an SDE by Song et al. [1], what struck me was not the idea but the notation. Change a few words, "noise schedule" for "volatility", and it was an equation I had solved many times before. The process is presented as something new, a device for training image generators that adds a little Gaussian noise step after step until the data dissolves into pure noise. But the equation underneath was one I had spent years with in a different domain. I had seen that drift-plus-noise structure before; I had taken that same N \to \infty limit before; I had used that same lemma to reduce a state-dependent SDE to one I could solve.
That lemma is Itô’s. In quantitative finance it underlies the Black-Scholes equation: feed it a stochastic stock price, hedge away the randomness, and a deterministic PDE for the option’s fair value remains. In a diffusion model it performs two operations that look unrelated. Applied one way it turns the noised state into a Gaussian that can be sampled in a single step; applied another it yields a PDE for how that noise spreads. Same lemma, two fields, half a century apart.
What connects them is a single rule of stochastic calculus, (dW)^2 = dt, the one fact for which ordinary calculus has no term. Pricing derivatives, I had taken its consequences for granted. In image generation, the very same correction term reappears at the heart of the diffusion machinery.
This post lays the mathematical foundation for the series. It develops Brownian motion and that rule from first principles, derives Itô’s lemma from them, and solves geometric Brownian motion and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with it. The lemma then derives the Black-Scholes equation through hedging and the no-arbitrage condition.
Between the finance and the diffusion halves, the post sets out what a generative model is. It learns from data through a model family, a divergence that measures how far the model is from the data, and an optimization procedure that minimizes it, and it then answers queries such as sampling and density estimation. Variational autoencoders, normalizing flows and energy-based models illustrate the framework. Diffusion models follow, with their two lineages and DDPM.
The post then writes DDPM’s forward process as a Variance-Preserving SDE and returns to Itô’s lemma twice, to derive its closed-form perturbation kernel and the Fokker-Planck equation for the density of the noised state. A closing comparison sets the three derivations (Black-Scholes, the perturbation kernel and the Fokker-Planck equation) side by side. One identity, (dW)^2 = dt, carried to two ends of a bridge that quantitative finance and generative AI did not know they shared.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
Roadmap
This post is structured in ten parts:

Part 1: Develops Brownian motion, the foundational random process underlying all the SDEs in this series.
Part 2: Introduces SDEs and Itô’s lemma, the calculus that turns Brownian inputs into derived processes.
Part 3: Derives the Black-Scholes equation using Itô’s lemma, the canonical application from quantitative finance.
Part 4: Defines a generative model, how it learns from data through a model family, a divergence and an optimization procedure, and the inference queries it answers.
Part 5: Works through three model families, variational autoencoders, normalizing flows and energy-based models, from training to inference.
Part 6: Introduces diffusion models: their two lineages and Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.
Part 7: Uses Itô’s lemma to derive the perturbation kernel of DDPM’s forward process [2], written as an SDE [1].
Part 8: Applies Itô’s lemma a second time to derive the Fokker-Planck equation for the density of the noised state.
Part 9: Draws the three derivations together (Black-Scholes, the perturbation kernel and the Fokker-Planck equation), comparing the effect of the Itô correction on each.
Part 10: Discusses why this unification matters, for ML practitioners and for quants.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
1.1 The physics
In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown watched particles released from pollen grains jitter randomly in water [3]. In 1905 Einstein explained it [4]: invisible water molecules bombard the particle, and the accumulation of countless random collisions produces a random, continuous path (Figure 1).







Figure 1: A particle released from a pollen grain, suspended in water and displaced along a ceaseless, irregular path by countless molecular collisions. Brownian motion idealizes this physical process. Each collision is independent of the last, and the particle reflects off the walls of its container. The animation cycles through several independent runs: each restart is a fresh, unrepeatable path.




The mathematics describing such a path, and, crucially, describing how the probability of finding the particle at each location spreads over time, comes in two complementary forms: an equation for the random trajectory of one particle (the Langevin equation [5]), and an equation for the evolving probability cloud of where it might be (the Fokker-Planck equation). These two views (one trajectory, one distribution) are the same physics seen two ways (Figure 2).








Figure 2: The two complementary descriptions of the same diffusing particle. Left (trajectory view): individual random paths X_t of a particle buffeted by noise (each irregular, continuous and unrepeatable), the object the Langevin equation describes. Right (density view): the probability cloud p(x,t) of where the particle might be (dark and concentrated at first, then spreading and fading as probability is conserved), the object the Fokker-Planck equation describes. The identical \pm\sqrt{t} envelope (dashed) traces the typical spread of the paths (the ±1-standard-deviation cone) on the left and the widening of the cloud on the right: one physics, two views.





That duality recurs through this entire blog series. In Part 2 of this first post it reappears as the two ways of applying Itô’s lemma: Pattern A follows the trajectory, Pattern B tracks the density (§2.3).

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
1.2 Definition
Brownian motion is the mathematical idealization of that path (Figure 1). It is the continuum limit of a random walk, as the steps shrink toward zero and grow infinitely frequent (§A.1). Integrating against it, transforming it and building SDEs on it need more than this informal description, so the properties below specify the object precisely.
It is the foundational random process of continuous-time stochastic calculus, the noise source of every SDE in this series, from the stock-price models of Parts 2–3 to the diffusion-model forward process of Part 7, and its defining surprise is a path that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere.
Formally, a standard Brownian motion (or Wiener process) is a stochastic process W_t on [0, \infty) satisfying:

W_0 = 0
For 0 \le s < t, the increment W_t - W_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, t - s)
Increments over non-overlapping intervals are independent
The sample paths t \mapsto W_t are continuous (almost surely)









Figure 3: Five independent sample paths of standard Brownian motion on [0, 1], each starting at W_0 = 0, the noise source underlying every SDE in this post. Every path is continuous yet irregular at each scale. Because the variance is t, the spread grows with time: the marginal W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, t) widens (broader Gaussians, in rose), and the standard-deviation cone \pm\sqrt{t} opens accordingly.





The properties imply a non-obvious fact: although W_t is continuous, its sample paths are not differentiable (Figure 3). The route to it, and the ground of every later rule of Itô calculus, is the quadratic variation of W. What it delivers is that no continuously differentiable path survives; the stronger statement, that the paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable, is a theorem of Paley, Wiener and Zygmund [6], quoted in the geometric interpretation below.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 1.4 Smooth functions have zero quadratic variation
text:
1.4 Smooth functions have zero quadratic variation
Before turning to W, we compute [g]_t for a smooth function as a baseline. It will vanish, and tracking why is what later determines what makes Brownian motion different. Each increment of a C^1 function is of order \Delta t_i, so its square is of order (\Delta t_i)^2, one power of the mesh too small to survive the sum.
If g \in C^1 with |g'| \le M on [0, t] (where M = \max_{s \in [0, t]} |g'(s)|), then for some \tau_i \in (t_i, t_{i+1}) the mean-value theorem applied on each subinterval gives

g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i) \;=\; g'(\tau_i)\,(t_{i+1} - t_i)

Squaring,

\big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;=\; \big(g'(\tau_i)\big)^2 (\Delta t_i)^2

Using |g'| \le M,

\big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2 (\Delta t_i)^2

Summing across the partition,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2 \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, \Delta t_i since \Delta t_i \le \|\Pi\|,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2\, \|\Pi\| \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Delta t_i

Telescoping \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Delta t_i = t,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

So the partition sum is squeezed to zero. Smooth functions have [g]_t = 0.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 1.5 Brownian motion has quadratic variation t
text:
1.5 Brownian motion has quadratic variation t
The smooth case was deterministic; this one is not. In §1.4 the mean-value theorem fixed each increment at a definite value, so the partition sum was an ordinary number we could squeeze to zero. For Brownian motion there is no mean-value theorem (W is nowhere differentiable), and the increments \Delta W_i = W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i} are random, which makes the sum S = \sum_i (\Delta W_i)^2 itself a random variable.
Thus, a pointwise squeeze is unavailable and “[W]_t” must be read as a probabilistic limit. So we show S concentrates on a single deterministic value in L^2 (i.e. in mean square: \mathbb{E}[(S - t)^2] \to 0), in four steps:

Computing its mean (linearity of expectation, telescoping to t)
Computing its variance (Gaussian fourth moments, plus independent increments so variances add)
Shrinking the mesh to send the variance to 0 via the same inequality \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\,t as before, the difference being that it now eliminates a variance, not the sum itself
Concluding that mean t with vanishing variance forces S \to t

For W_t, each increment satisfies \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t_i), the common starting point for all four steps.
Step 1 — the mean:
By linearity of expectation,

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \mathbb{E}\!\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big]

Substituting \mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_i)^2] = \Delta t_i (each \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t_i) is mean-zero, so its second moment equals its variance \Delta t_i),

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Delta t_i

Telescoping \sum_i \Delta t_i = t,

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; t

Step 2 — the variance:
The increments are independent, so variances add across the sum,

\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \operatorname{Var}\!\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big)

Substituting the value

\operatorname{Var}\!\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big) = 2(\Delta t_i)^2

into the previous line, since

\operatorname{Var}(X^2) = \mathbb{E}[X^4] - \big(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\big)^2 = 3\sigma^4 - \sigma^4

for X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) (with \mathbb{E}[X^4] = 3\sigma^4: write X = \sigma Z, and one Gaussian integration by parts gives \mathbb{E}[Z^4] = 3),

\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; 2\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta t_i)^2

Step 3 — shrink the mesh:
Applying the mesh inequality \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t,

\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;\le\; 2\,\|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\|\to 0}\; 0

Step 4 — conclude:
The partition sum has mean t and variance vanishing to zero, so it converges in L^2 to the deterministic limit:

\boxed{\,[W]_t \;=\; t\,}
\tag{2}
The quadratic variation of Brownian motion on [0, t] is exactly t, not zero, a structural property of W, not an artifact of any specific partition. \square

1.5.1 Where smoothness made the difference
Both derivations look structurally similar (square the increment, sum across the partition, apply the mesh inequality), yet the smooth sum collapses to 0 while the Brownian sum converges to t. Table 1 sets the two side by side, step by step.
For the smooth function, the mean-value theorem and squaring allowed us to take M^2 out as a factor. As the expression was degree 2 in \Delta t_i, one factor of \Delta t_i was absorbed by the mesh inequality and the other telescoped to t; once the limit \|\Pi\| \to 0 was applied, we found that [g]_t = 0.
For Brownian motion, W isn’t differentiable, so we cannot apply the mean-value theorem and take M^2 out as a factor. Instead, the increments \Delta W_i being random made the sum S = \sum_i (\Delta W_i)^2 itself a random variable, which forced us to take the mean-variance route. The variance vanished, eliminated by the mesh inequality as the smooth sum was, because it carries (\Delta t_i)^2. The mean did not, because \mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_i)^2] = \Delta t_i leaves it degree 1 in \Delta t_i, and a degree-1 sum telescopes to t instead of vanishing. That single power difference explains the result:



Table 1: Where the smooth and Brownian quadratic-variation derivations diverge, and why one vanishes while the other doesn’t.

The smooth case has an extra \Delta t_i per term that the mesh inequality absorbs; one factor becomes \|\Pi\|, the other telescopes to t, net bound M^2\,\|\Pi\|\,t \to 0. The Brownian case has only one factor of \Delta t_i per term, so the sum telescopes to t directly, with no extra \Delta t_i left for the mesh inequality to absorb. Differentiability buys that one extra power of \Delta t_i, and that one extra power is what makes the sum vanish.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 1.6 Geometric interpretation of why [W]_t = t makes Brownian motion non-differentiable
text:
1.6 Geometric interpretation of why [W]_t = t makes Brownian motion non-differentiable
The quadratic-variation results of the previous sections have a vivid geometric reading. A function’s local smoothness is what a magnifying glass reveals: zoom far enough into a differentiable curve and it appears to be a straight line, its tangent, whereas zoom into a Brownian path and it stays as irregular as ever. The two subsections below make this contrast precise, and it is the same contrast that decides whether a squared increment survives in the limit.

1.6.1 Smooth functions
A differentiable function has a well-defined slope at each point. Geometrically that means it is locally linear: over a small step \Delta t its increment is f'(t)\,\Delta t = O(\Delta t), proportional to the step. Zoom in on even a high-curvature region, and the curve bends less and less, approaching its tangent line (Figure 4). For f twice differentiable, the departure from the tangent over a window of width \Delta t is the curvature term \tfrac{1}{2} f''\,(\Delta t)^2 = O(\Delta t^2); it shrinks faster than the window, so the squared increment is negligible next to \Delta t, which is why a smooth path has zero quadratic variation.








Figure 4: Left: a parabola with its horizontal tangent at the minimum (dashed), the dotted box marking the minimum region. Right: that boxed region magnified, at the same axis scale. The curve is far shallower and lies close to the tangent, with only a slight residual bend.





The magnified curve is shallower but not perfectly straight. A slight bend remains at finite zoom, and zooming further would reduce it further still, approaching a straight line in the limit. Because the bend shrinks this way, the squared increment is negligible: (\Delta f)^2 = O(\Delta t^2) \to 0 relative to \Delta t. This is the geometric face of the zero quadratic variation derived in §1.4. Brownian motion, we will now see, refuses to straighten.


1.6.2 Brownian motion
The quadratic-variation result [W]_t = t (Eq. 2) is the algebraic statement that a Brownian increment scales as \Delta W \sim \sqrt{\Delta t}. That square-root scaling has an immediate geometric consequence: the slope of a chord over a step is \Delta W / \Delta t \sim 1/\sqrt{\Delta t} \to \infty as \Delta t \to 0, so the difference quotient blows up rather than converging to a finite slope, and the path is not continuously differentiable. In fact a classical theorem of Paley, Wiener and Zygmund [6] establishes the stronger property that Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable; the scaling here is the intuition behind that result, not a proof of it. Figure 5 makes this visible through statistical self-similarity [7]: zooming into any sub-interval and rescaling by the same \sqrt{\Delta t} law reproduces a path just as irregular as the original, so there is no scale at which the path ever straightens out.








Figure 5: Left: a Brownian sample path on [0, 1], with a small sub-interval [a, b] boxed. Right: that boxed sub-interval, rescaled by \times 20 in time and \times\sqrt{20} in value. The zoom is just as irregular as the whole path, with no smoother, straighter segment revealed.





The same \sqrt{\Delta t} scaling is what makes a squared increment matter. A smooth curve flattens toward its tangent under magnification, so its increment is O(\Delta t) and its square O(\Delta t^2), negligible. The Brownian path never flattens: its increment is O(\sqrt{\Delta t}), so its square is O(\Delta t), the same order as dt itself. That is the content of [W]_t = t, and it is why a squared Brownian increment cannot be discarded, the fact we turn into a precise calculus rule in the next section.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
1.7 The (dW)^2 = dt rule
What Eq. 2 says at the level of infinitesimals is that (\Delta W)^2 behaves, in sum, like \Delta t. This is the meaning of the working rule

\boxed{(dW)^2 = dt}
\tag{3}
It is not a literal pointwise equality of random variables, but a calculus rule for what sums of (\Delta W)^2 terms converge to inside an integral.

1.7.1 What the rule means inside an integral
The precise content of Eq. 3 is an integral statement. For each bounded, Riemann-integrable deterministic function f on [0, t] (continuous suffices),

\boxed{\int_0^t f(s)\,(dW_s)^2 \;:=\; \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2 \;=\; \int_0^t f(s)\, ds}
\tag{4}
with convergence in L^2, the same calculation that gave [W]_t = t, now carrying the weight f.
Mean:
By linearity of expectation,

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big]

Substituting \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big] = \Delta t_i,

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0 (a Riemann sum),

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; \int_0^t f(s)\, ds

Variance:
By independence the variances add,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; \sum_i \operatorname{Var}\big(f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\big)

Taking each deterministic factor out squared,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, \operatorname{Var}\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big)

Substituting the value

\operatorname{Var}\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big) = 2(\Delta t_i)^2

into the previous line,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; 2 \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding f(t_i)^2 \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2 \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t by the mesh,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

A random variable whose mean converges to \int_0^t f(s)\, ds and whose variance vanishes converges in L^2 to that limit, since

\mathbb{E}\big[(S - \int_0^t f\, ds)^2\big] = \operatorname{Var}(S) + \big(\mathbb{E}[S] - \int_0^t f\, ds\big)^2

and both terms vanish. So the sum converges to \int_0^t f(s)\, ds, which is the value Eq. 4 asserts. \square
Setting f \equiv 1 specializes it to the plain quadratic variation Eq. 2. So whenever (dW)^2 appears inside a stochastic integral with a deterministic weight, we may substitute dt for it, and the two integrals agree in the limit. Itô’s lemma will apply the rule with a random weight that depends only on the path up to that time. The same mean-and-variance argument goes through conditionally on that past, since the increment \Delta W_i is independent of it.


1.7.2 Companion rules
Two further rules,

\boxed{(dt)^2 = 0}
\tag{5}

\boxed{dt\,dW = 0}
\tag{6}
follow by the same partition-sum reasoning, established next.

1.7.2.1 The (dt)^2 rule is deterministic
This rule carries no randomness, so a single deterministic bound suffices, but the weight f may change sign, so the bound must control the sum in absolute value. By the triangle inequality,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \sum_i |f(t_i)|\,(\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding the weight by |f(t_i)| \le \sup_{[0,t]}|f|,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big) \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t by the mesh,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

The bound is deterministic (no randomness enters), and it squeezes the partition sum to zero in absolute value as the mesh refines, so the sum itself converges to zero, giving the integral form

\int_0^t f(s)\,(ds)^2 = 0

whose equivalent differential form is (dt)^2 = 0, Eq. 5.


1.7.2.2 The dt\,dW rule is an L^2 statement
The partition sum \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i has mean zero, since each \Delta W_i is mean-zero. For its variance, the increments are independent across non-overlapping intervals, so variances add,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i \operatorname{Var}\big(f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\big)

Taking each deterministic factor out squared,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^2\, \operatorname{Var}(\Delta W_i)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}(\Delta W_i) = \Delta t_i,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^3

Bounding f(t_i)^2 \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2 \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^3

Bounding two of the three factors of each (\Delta t_i)^3 by the mesh, (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2 \sum_i \Delta t_i

Telescoping \sum_i \Delta t_i = t,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

The partition sum thus has mean zero and a variance vanishing to zero as the mesh refines. A sequence with mean zero whose variance tends to zero converges to zero in L^2, so the partition sum converges in L^2 to zero, giving the integral form

\int_0^t f(s)\, ds\, dW_s = 0

whose equivalent differential form is dt\,dW = 0, Eq. 6.
So only (dW)^2 survives at first order in dt, and what survives, by Eq. 4, is dt.
For several independent Brownian motions, §A.8.1 shows that the products of increments of two different components vanish as well, dW^i\, dW^j = 0 for i \neq j.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 1.8 The Itô integral: a Gaussian under L^2
text:
1.8 The Itô integral: a Gaussian under L^2
The same partition-sum construction determines one more object used throughout: the Itô integral of a deterministic function against Brownian motion,

\int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s := \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_i g(t_i)\, \Delta W_i

which is the left-endpoint limit of partition sums, as in Eq. 4 but now linear in \Delta W_i instead of (\Delta W_i)^2. Defining it rigorously for general random integrands is carried out in §A.4 [7]; the deterministic case is all the closed-form solutions of this post need, and there the Wiener increment structure alone fixes the full distribution. The Fokker-Planck derivation of Part 8 uses one property of the random case, its zero mean, and cites it from that appendix.
For deterministic g,

\boxed{\int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\;\; \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds\right)}
\tag{7}
Why:
Approximate the integral by a partition sum \sum_i g(t_i)\, \Delta W_i, with independent increments \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t_i). A finite linear combination of independent Gaussians is Gaussian, so each partition sum is Gaussian; its mean vanishes term by term, and by independence its variance is a Riemann sum, which converges since g is continuous,

\sum_i g(t_i)^2\, \Delta t_i \to \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds

As \|\Pi\| \to 0 the sums converge in L^2 to the integral, because each partition sum is the integral of a step function, and those integrals form a Cauchy sequence in L^2 as the mesh refines, the construction carried out in §A.4. Because L^2 convergence carries the mean and variance to the limit, the limit has mean 0 and variance \int_0^t g^2\, ds; and a mean-square limit of Gaussians is itself Gaussian (the Gaussian family is closed under L^2 limits, proved in §A.6), so the integral is Gaussian. The variance identity is the Itô isometry; the zero mean follows from the martingale property of the Itô integral.
Martingale property: (made precise in §A.5) A martingale is a process with no systematic trend. Given everything observed up to the present, its expected future value equals its present value. The Itô integral M_t = \int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s is one, and since it starts at M_0 = 0, taking expectations gives \mathbb{E}[M_t] = 0 for each t. On average it neither rises nor falls. This is the zero-mean half of Eq. 7.
Itô isometry: An isometry is a map that preserves size. The map g \mapsto \int_0^t g\, dW_s sends a function to a random variable while preserving the L^2 norm,

\mathbb{E}\big[\big(\int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s\big)^2\big] = \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds

that is, the mean-square size of the integral equals the ordinary size of the integrand. This is the variance half of Eq. 7.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
2.1 Stochastic differential equations
Brownian motion is pure, undirected noise, mean-zero increments whose variance accumulates at unit rate (Eq. 2). Real systems rarely behave so simply: a stock price exhibits a trend, a temperature relaxes toward ambient, a population grows, each carrying its own deterministic tendency while still being buffeted by randomness, often responding to that noise with an intensity that depends on the current state. To describe such a process we specify not its value but its instantaneous change, a deterministic change over dt plus a scaled increment of W_t, and let those infinitesimal updates accumulate into a path.
A (one-dimensional) Itô stochastic differential equation (SDE) has the form

\boxed{dX_t = \mu(X_t, t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t, t)\, dW_t}
\tag{8}
where \mu is the drift coefficient and \sigma is the diffusion coefficient. The notation dX_t, dt, dW_t is shorthand for the integral equation

\boxed{X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \mu(X_s, s)\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s, s)\, dW_s}
\tag{9}
where the second integral is the Itô integral of §1.8. There the integrand is deterministic; here \sigma(X_s, s) is generally state-dependent and therefore random, but the same heuristic form is all that is needed here.
The integral equation is the definition of the SDE, not a consequence of it. For an ordinary differential equation (ODE) dx/dt = \mu(x, t) with \mu continuous, the integral form follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus, because the solution x is continuously differentiable. Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable (Part 1), so dW_t/dt does not exist and the SDE has no derivative to integrate.
The drift term governs the deterministic evolution of X_t; the diffusion term governs the size of random fluctuations. Conditions under which such an SDE has a unique solution, global Lipschitz and linear growth on \mu and \sigma, are stated, with a proof sketch, in P3:§A.1; every process in this post satisfies them, and post #3 states the conditions its learned reverse-time drift must meet.
The next two subsections introduce two concrete instances of this form, geometric Brownian motion (GBM) and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, each obtained by choosing the drift and diffusion coefficients \mu(x,t) and \sigma(x,t). We solve both later with Itô’s lemma (GBM in §2.4.1, the OU process in §2.4.2), and both recur downstream: the former as the Black-Scholes stock model in Part 3, the latter as the template for the DDPM forward process in Part 7.

2.1.1 Geometric Brownian motion
In the Black-Scholes framework, S_t denotes the price of a stock at time t, and is modeled by the SDE

\boxed{dS_t \;=\; \mu\, S_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t}
\tag{10}
with scalar constants \mu, \sigma. This is Eq. 8 with drift coefficient \mu(x, t) = \mu\, x and diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) = \sigma\, x, both linear in x. (The symbols \mu, \sigma are reused here as scalar constants, distinct from the coefficient functions \mu(x,t), \sigma(x,t) of Eq. 8; the reuse is standard finance notation.)
The parameters have precise finance meanings:

Drift (\mu): The instantaneous expected rate of return per unit time, \mathbb{E}[dS_t/S_t] = \mu\, dt. \mu = 0.15 means a 15\% per-year expected return (with t measured in years); the continuously-compounded growth rate is the smaller \mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 (the Itô correction, derived below).
Volatility (\sigma): The standard deviation of the return per unit time. \sigma = 0.20 means 20\% per-year volatility.









Figure 6: Sample paths of geometric Brownian motion with \mu = 0.15, \sigma = 0.35, S_0 = 1 over one year (a larger \sigma than the 0.20 example in the text, chosen so the skew below is visible). The dashed line is the deterministic expected value \mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{\mu t}. Paths trend upward in expectation but remain strictly positive throughout. The right panel is the marginal distribution of the endpoint S_1 (histogram of many paths, analytic density in rose): it is lognormal, right-skewed with a long upper tail and bounded below by zero, the property guaranteed by the model and derived in §2.4.1.





Sample paths trend upward in expectation while remaining strictly positive (Figure 6). We solve this SDE for the full distribution of S_t, applying Itô’s lemma to \log S_t, in §2.4.1, where the price is shown to be lognormally distributed.


2.1.2 Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
The OU process [8] is the canonical mean-reverting SDE. With state X_t \in \mathbb{R}, long-run mean \bar\mu, mean-reversion rate \kappa > 0, and constant volatility \sigma > 0,

\boxed{dX_t \;=\; \kappa\,(\bar\mu - X_t)\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t}
\tag{11}
This is Eq. 8 with drift coefficient \kappa(\bar\mu - x) (linear in x, restoring toward \bar\mu) and constant diffusion \sigma (independent of x).
The parameters:

Long-run mean (\bar\mu): The value toward which the drift drives the process.
Mean-reversion rate (\kappa): Units 1/\text{time}; a larger \kappa drives the process back faster. The expected excursion decays as e^{-\kappa t} (Eq. 17, derived in §2.4.2), so its “half-life”, the time to halve, is \ln 2 / \kappa.
Volatility (\sigma): The constant volatility of the noise, units \text{state}/\sqrt{\text{time}}.

The mean-reversion intuition: If X_t > \bar\mu, the drift \kappa(\bar\mu - X_t) < 0 drives X_t back down. If X_t < \bar\mu, the drift drives it back up. The noise term \sigma\, dW_t keeps the process jittering around \bar\mu rather than converging to it (Figure 7).








Figure 7: Sample paths of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with long-run mean \bar\mu = 0, mean-reversion rate \kappa = 1, and volatility \sigma = 0.5, started from several different points. Whatever the start, the drift drives every path into the same stationary band \bar\mu \pm \sqrt{\sigma^2/(2\kappa)} (shaded) around \bar\mu (dashed). The right panel is a histogram of one long run: the paths converge to the stationary distribution \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2/2\kappa) (solid curve), independent of where they began.





Stationary distribution: Unlike GBM, whose spread grows without bound (its log-return variance is \sigma^2 t, derived in §2.4.1), OU has a finite-variance equilibrium. As t \to \infty,

\boxed{X_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{dist}}\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\bar\mu,\;\, \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\right)}
\tag{12}
The equilibrium variance \sigma^2/(2\kappa) arises from the balance between noise injection (\sigma) and restoring force (\kappa): more noise widens the spread, stronger reversion tightens it. The full derivation, solving the SDE by an integrating factor and letting t \to \infty, is in §2.4.2 after Itô’s lemma is introduced.
Where OU appears:

In finance:

In interest-rate modeling, the Vasicek model [9] treats the instantaneous risk-free rate as an OU process.
In statistical-arbitrage, cointegrated price spreads, the difference between two related instruments, are modeled as mean-reverting OU processes.

In generative AI:

OU is the simplest non-trivial Langevin-style SDE: it samples its Gaussian equilibrium \mathcal{N}(\bar\mu,\, \sigma^2/(2\kappa)) by mean reversion plus noise, and the same drift-plus-noise template lets Langevin dynamics sample any target distribution with a differentiable log-density (post #6).
The reverse, generative process of DDPM is that template generalized: a learned, time-dependent score \nabla_x \log p_t replaces OU’s fixed linear drift, turning pure noise back into data (post #3).

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
2.2 Itô’s lemma
The SDEs of §2.1 describe how a state X_t evolves; the question of interest is how functions of that state evolve. Given dX_t = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t, what SDE governs a transformed quantity Y_t = f(X_t, t), a log-price, an option value, a rescaled noised state? For a smooth, deterministic X the ordinary chain rule would answer at once, but it fails here: the (dW)^2 = dt rule of Eq. 3 means a second-order term that classical calculus discards instead survives at order dt. Itô’s lemma resolves this. It is the ordinary chain rule plus exactly one correction term.
Let X_t satisfy the SDE dX_t = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW_t, and let f(x, t) be a function that is twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t. Then according to Itô’s lemma the process Y_t = f(X_t, t) satisfies [10]

\boxed{df = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt + \sigma \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW}
\tag{13}
The term \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt is the Itô correction. It is what distinguishes Itô calculus from ordinary calculus.

2.2.1 Derivation
Taylor-expand [11] f(X_{t+dt}, t+dt) to second order in x and first order in t, which is all the smoothness f is assumed to possess; the omitted higher terms are of order dt \cdot dX and (dt)^2, which the companion rules Eq. 6 and Eq. 5 annihilate. The remainder of the second-order expansion is o\big((dX)^2\big), and (dX)^2 is itself of order dt, so the remainder contributes nothing at order dt:

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dX \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, (dX)^2

Substituting dX = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, (\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW)^2

Expanding the square,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\,\bigl(\mu^2 (dt)^2 + 2\mu\sigma\, dt\, dW + \sigma^2 (dW)^2\bigr)

Reducing the squared increment via the companion rules (dt)^2 = 0, dt\,dW = 0, (dW)^2 = dt,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt

Distributing \partial f / \partial x across the bracket,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt

Grouping by dt and dW gives,

\boxed{df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW}

which is Eq. 13. \square
§A.8 derives the lemma for a vector state driven by several independent Brownian motions.


2.2.2 Comparison to the chain rule
Suppose we naively applied the ordinary chain rule to a stochastic X with dX = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW (substitute dX, stop at first order, as we do in the ordinary case). We’d write

df \;\stackrel{?}{=}\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

That is what ordinary calculus would give. In Itô calculus it is the wrong answer. Itô’s lemma is character-for-character the same, except for one extra term in the dt coefficient:

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \underbrace{\boxed{\tfrac{1}{2}\,\sigma^2\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}}}_{\text{Itô correction, the square term}}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

The boxed second-order term is the only structural difference between the two equations. Every other character matches the naive chain rule. It is the surviving term from the (dW)^2 = dt rule of Eq. 3, that partition-sum identity, promoted to a calculus correction.


2.2.3 The deterministic limit (\sigma \to 0)
A correct stochastic chain rule must reduce to the ordinary one when the noise is switched off. That is the sanity check.
With \sigma = 0, the SDE loses its diffusion term,

dX_t = \mu\, dt

so X is now a smooth (differentiable) path with derivative \dot X = dX_t / dt = \mu.
For a smooth path, Y_t = f(X_t, t) changes for two reasons: f depends on t directly, and it depends on t through X_t. The ordinary multivariable chain rule sums the two contributions, namely the explicit rate \partial f / \partial t and the rate transmitted through X moving at speed \dot X, which is \dot X\, \partial f / \partial x:

\frac{dY}{dt} \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \dot X\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}

Substituting \dot X = \mu,

\frac{dY}{dt} \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}

Multiplying by dt,

dY \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt

Now set \sigma = 0 in Itô’s lemma. Starting from the full result,

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

Setting \sigma = 0 (the second-order term \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \partial^2 f / \partial x^2 and the \sigma\, \partial f / \partial x\, dW term both vanish),

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt

The two agree exactly: with no noise, Itô’s lemma is the ordinary chain rule. The second-order term is what the (dW)^2 = dt rule adds once \sigma \neq 0.
Thus, Itô’s lemma = ordinary chain rule + (dW)^2 = dt correction.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
2.3 Application patterns of Itô’s lemma
Two patterns will recur. In one, we follow the path a particle takes once it starts moving; in the other, we track the probability-density cloud, estimating how likely the particle is to be at a given place and time after its journey begins. Specifically, Pattern A rides along a single trajectory: it transforms one SDE into another, tracking some function of the moving state. Pattern B steps back to ask, at each time and place, how likely the state is to be there: it turns the SDE into a partial differential equation (PDE) for the probability density. Same lemma, same SDE. One follows the path, the other predicts the distribution. These are the two views of one diffusion introduced in §1.1, now made into two ways of applying the lemma.
Pattern A: Given an SDE for X_t, derive an SDE for a transformed quantity f(X_t, t). It recurs in Parts 2, 3 and 7:

§2.4.1: f(S) = \log S applied to the GBM stock price gives its closed-form lognormal distribution.
§2.4.2: The integrating-factor transform f(Z, t) = e^{\kappa t} Z applied to the long-run-mean-centered OU process gives its closed-form Gaussian distribution.
§3.3 – §3.7: f = V(S, t) applied to the GBM stock price yields the Black-Scholes PDE.
§7.6: A similar integrating-factor transform f(x, t) = x / \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} applied to the DDPM VP-SDE turns it into a driftless process, giving its closed-form Gaussian distribution, the perturbation kernel.

Pattern B: Given an SDE for X_t, derive a PDE for its probability density p(x, t), the Fokker-Planck equation. It appears once:

§8: Applying Itô to a test function and taking expectations turns the VP-SDE into the Fokker-Planck equation for its marginal distribution p(x, t), giving the PDE that governs how the DDPM forward process spreads the data density into noise over time.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 2.4 Itô’s lemma solves GBM and the OU process
text:
2.4 Itô’s lemma solves GBM and the OU process
Itô’s lemma is most convincing in action. We turn it on the two example SDEs from §2.1, GBM and the OU process, and in each case a single application collapses a state-dependent SDE into one we can integrate in closed form.

2.4.1 Solving GBM
We solve GBM for the full distribution of the price S_t by applying Itô’s lemma to the transform f(S) = \log S, a function of S alone, with no explicit time dependence. (\log S requires S_t > 0, so the step is valid while the price stays positive; the resulting solution Eq. 14 is an exponential, strictly positive for each t, and applying Itô’s lemma to it recovers Eq. 10, so it solves the SDE with no assumption on the sign. Uniqueness of the solution under the conditions of §2.1 makes it the solution, which discharges the assumption.)

2.4.1.1 Use Itô to obtain the reduced SDE
The SDE:
The price S_t follows the GBM SDE Eq. 10,

dS_t \;=\; \mu\, S_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma:
To avoid clashing with the GBM constants \mu, \sigma, write the generic lemma with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b; that is, for a transform f(S_t, t) of a process dS_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t, the lemma Eq. 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial S}\, dW

To apply it to f = \log S we need two elements: the coefficients a, b, identified from the GBM equation, and the partials of f, computed from f = \log S. We collect each, then substitute.
Coefficients (from the GBM equation):
a = \mu\, S_t and b = \sigma\, S_t.
Partials (from f = \log S):

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial S} \;=\; \frac{1}{S}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2} \;=\; -\frac{1}{S^2}

Substituting a = \mu\, S, b = \sigma\, S, and the three partials into the lemma,

d(\log S_t) \;=\; \left(0 \;+\; (\mu\, S) \cdot \frac{1}{S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, (\sigma\, S)^2 \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{S^2}\right)\right) dt \;+\; (\sigma\, S) \cdot \frac{1}{S}\, dW_t

Simplifying,

d(\log S_t) \;=\; \left(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) dt + \sigma\, dW_t

a constant-drift, constant-diffusion SDE: both coefficients are independent of S_t.


2.4.1.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration
Integrating this reduced SDE over [0, t],

\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;=\; \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t dW_s

Since W_0 = 0, the Itô integral is \int_0^t dW_s = W_t,

\boxed{\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;=\; \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t \;+\; \sigma\, W_t}
\tag{14}


2.4.1.3 Properties of the solution distribution
Since W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t), the log-return is an affine function of a Gaussian, hence Gaussian:

\boxed{\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\Big(\, \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t,\;\; \sigma^2\, t \,\Big)}
\tag{15}
Taking expectations of S_t = S_0\, e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t + \sigma W_t}, with the deterministic factor factored out,

\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t}\, \mathbb{E}[e^{\sigma W_t}]

Substituting the Gaussian moment \mathbb{E}[e^{\sigma W_t}] = e^{\sigma^2 t/2}, which follows by completing the square in the \mathcal{N}(0, t) density,

\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{\mu t}

The level grows at the full rate \mu even as the typical log-return grows at \mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2.
So log-returns have mean (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t and variance \sigma^2 t, variance linear in time (characteristic of Brownian motion), so the standard deviation grows like \sigma\sqrt{t}. Equivalently, the price S_t itself is lognormally distributed: its logarithm is Gaussian, which forces S_t > 0 always (essential, because stock prices can’t go negative).
The -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 term is the Itô correction in action (Figure 8). Naive chain-rule reasoning would give

d(\log S) = dS/S = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW

which misses the -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, dt contribution that the (dW)^2 = dt rule supplies. The mean of the log-return is therefore not \mu\, t but (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t; the gap is sometimes referred to in finance as the volatility drag.








Figure 8: The Itô correction, numerically. A single geometric Brownian motion path (\mu = 0.10, \sigma = 0.40) is generated by Euler-Maruyama on dS = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW (the log-formula is not assumed) and then logged. The naive chain rule would predict \log(S_t/S_0) = \mu t + \sigma W_t, but the simulated log-return instead tracks (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t + \sigma W_t. Both are driven by the same noise W_t, so they vary together yet separate at the steady rate \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2: the shaded wedge is the -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t correction the naive rule omits.








2.4.2 Solving the OU process
The OU process Eq. 11 is the mean-reverting counterpart, and the same lemma determines its long-run distribution. We solve it in closed form and recover the stationary distribution Eq. 12.

2.4.2.1 Use Itô to obtain the reduced SDE
The SDE:
The OU process Eq. 11 is

dX_t \;=\; \kappa\,(\bar\mu - X_t)\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t

Centering on its long-run mean, Z_t = X_t - \bar\mu, so that the SDE becomes

dZ_t \;=\; -\kappa\, Z_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma:
For a transform f(Z_t, t) of a process with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b, that is, dZ_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t, the lemma Eq. 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial Z^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z}\, dW

Integrating factor:
The standard technique for a linear SDE is to apply Itô’s lemma to the transform Y_t = f(Z_t, t) with f(Z, t) = e^{\kappa t} Z, chosen so the explicit-time term cancels the drift.
Coefficients (from the centered SDE):
a = -\kappa\, Z_t and b = \sigma.
Partials (from f = e^{\kappa t} Z):

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; \kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z} \;=\; e^{\kappa t}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial Z^2} \;=\; 0

Substituting a = -\kappa\, Z, b = \sigma, and the three partials into the lemma,

d\!\left(e^{\kappa t} Z_t\right) \;=\; \Big(\kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z \;+\; (-\kappa\, Z)\, e^{\kappa t} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 \cdot 0\Big) dt \;+\; \sigma\, e^{\kappa t}\, dW_t

Simplifying (the explicit-time term \kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z and the drift term -\kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z cancel),

d\!\left(e^{\kappa t} Z_t\right) \;=\; \sigma\, e^{\kappa t}\, dW_t



2.4.2.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration
Integrating from 0 to t,

\int_0^t d\!\left(e^{\kappa s} Z_s\right) \;=\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\kappa s}\, dW_s

Evaluating the left side with the identity

\int_0^t d\!\left(e^{\kappa s} Z_s\right) = e^{\kappa t} Z_t - Z_0

gives

e^{\kappa t} Z_t \;=\; Z_0 \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\kappa s}\, dW_s

As Z_0 = X_0 - \bar\mu,

e^{\kappa t} Z_t \;=\; (X_0 - \bar\mu) \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\kappa s}\, dW_s

Dividing by e^{\kappa t},

Z_t \;=\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\kappa t} \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{-\kappa(t - s)}\, dW_s

Substituting Z_t = X_t - \bar\mu,

\boxed{X_t \;=\; \bar\mu \;+\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\kappa t} \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{-\kappa(t - s)}\, dW_s}
\tag{16}


2.4.2.3 Properties of the solution distribution
Given X_0, the offset \bar\mu + (X_0 - \bar\mu)e^{-\kappa t} is a deterministic constant, and the Itô integral is Gaussian by Eq. 7; adding the constant leaves X_t an affine function of that Gaussian, and an affine function of a Gaussian is Gaussian.
Mean:
The Itô integral has zero mean by Eq. 7, so

\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X_t] \;=\; \bar\mu \;+\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\kappa t}}
\tag{17}
Variance:
By Eq. 7 with g(s) = \sigma\, e^{-\kappa(t - s)},

\operatorname{Var}[X_t] \;=\; \sigma^2 \int_0^t e^{-2\kappa(t - s)}\, ds

Evaluating the integral,

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}[X_t] \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\big(1 - e^{-2\kappa t}\big)}
\tag{18}
Stationary distribution:
As t \to \infty the decaying exponentials vanish, e^{-\kappa t} \to 0 in the mean and e^{-2\kappa t} \to 0 in the variance, so \mathbb{E}[X_t] \to \bar\mu and \operatorname{Var}[X_t] \to \sigma^2/(2\kappa). Since X_t is Gaussian for each t, its distribution converges to

\boxed{\mathcal{N}\!\left(\bar\mu,\;\, \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\right)}

which is Eq. 12. \square

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.1 What is an option?
An option is a contract whose value depends on, is derived from, the price of an underlying stock S_t. The contract grants its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an agreed quantity of the stock at a pre-agreed price per share (strike, K) at a specified maturity (T). The two basic types are:

Call option: Confers its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy an agreed quantity of the stock at the strike price K at maturity T.
Put option: Confers its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell an agreed quantity of the stock at the strike price K at maturity T.

American options can be exercised at any time up to maturity T while European options can be exercised only at the maturity T. This post restricts attention to European options; American options require additional theory beyond the present scope.
Payoff at expiry: At t = T, the option’s value depends only on S_T. A rational holder exercises the option only when doing so is profitable, giving the piecewise-linear payoff functions:
The call payoff is

\boxed{V_{\text{call}}(S_T) = \max(S_T - K,\, 0)}
\tag{20}
The holder exercises if S_T > K, gaining S_T - K; otherwise the option expires worthless.
The put payoff is

\boxed{V_{\text{put}}(S_T) = \max(K - S_T,\, 0)}
\tag{21}
The holder exercises if S_T < K, gaining K - S_T; otherwise the option expires worthless.
The kinked “hockey-stick” shape (Figure 9) is the structural signature of an option: identically zero on the unfavourable side of the strike, linear on the favourable side.








Figure 9: Payoff at expiry t = T for European call (left) and put (right) options with strike K = 100. The call holder exercises only if S_T > K, receiving S_T - K; the put holder exercises only if S_T < K, receiving K - S_T. The kinked ‘hockey-stick’ shape, flat on the unfavourable side of the strike, linear on the favourable side, is the structural signature of an option.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.2 Key finance terms

Risk-free rate: The interest rate an investor can expect to earn on an investment that carries zero risk. In practice, usually the interest paid on a 10-year highly rated government Treasury note.
Risky asset: An instrument whose future price is uncertain, evolving stochastically. In other words, the diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) in its dynamics will not be 0. For example, a stock.
Risk-free asset: An instrument whose return is known in advance, carrying no price uncertainty. In other words, the diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) in its dynamics will be 0. For example, a bank account; a unit of cash held in it grows deterministically at the risk-free rate.
Long / short positions: Holding +q units of an instrument is being long q; owing q units (selling now, buying back later) is being short q (a negative position, -q). A long position profits when the price rises; a short position profits when it falls.
Portfolio: A collection of financial investments such as stocks, bonds, and options. If a portfolio has i = 1, \dots, n instruments and the quantity and price of the ith instrument are q_i and P_i respectively, the portfolio value \Pi_t (the symbol is standard in finance, and unrelated to the partition \Pi of Part 1) is 
\Pi_t = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\, P_i

Delta: The sensitivity of an instrument’s value to a one-unit change in the stock price, the partial derivative of that value with respect to S.
Portfolio delta: The sensitivity of the portfolio value to a one-unit change in the stock price, \partial \Pi / \partial S. Distributing the partial derivative through the sum, 
\frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial S} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\, \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial S}

Delta-neutral: A portfolio with zero portfolio delta, \partial \Pi / \partial S = 0. The quantities q_i are chosen so the deltas of the instruments held cancel, leaving no delta exposure, so the portfolio is immune to a change in the stock price to first order.
Self-financing strategy: A trading approach where a portfolio’s value changes only due to gains or losses from its assets, with no external cash inflows or withdrawals.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.3 The option-value process
Given the terminal payoff of Eq. 20 as the boundary condition, pricing the option requires finding the SDE its value obeys, and Itô’s lemma provides it, applied to V(S, t) under the same GBM stock dynamics we used for \log S in §2.4.1.
Let V(S, t) denote the per-share value of a European call option on S with strike K and maturity T. (Real option contracts typically represent multiple shares; the pricing is done per share throughout this derivation and scales linearly with quantity.) Assume V is twice continuously differentiable in S and once in t for t < T, the hypothesis of Eq. 13; the closed-form solution of §3.7.1 confirms it for the call, the payoff’s kink at S = K smoothing out instantly for t < T. Applying Itô’s lemma to V under the GBM dynamics of Eq. 10 (constant drift \mu, constant volatility \sigma),

dV = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \mu S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt + \sigma S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t
\tag{22}
The challenge that Black-Scholes addresses is the prior question: given today’s price S_t and the stock-price dynamics, what is the fair value V(S_t, t) of the option before expiry, for t < T? Itô’s lemma combined with a delta-neutral, risk-free portfolio of the stock and the option produces a PDE for V whose boundary condition is the terminal call payoff V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Eq. 20).

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.4 Black-Scholes assumptions
The Black-Scholes derivation [12], [13] rests on a specific set of idealizing assumptions about the market and the assets traded in it. Collecting them upfront makes both the construction and its limitations transparent.

3.4.1 Market structure
The market consists of two instruments:

A risk-free asset, a bank account or zero-coupon bond.
A risky asset, a single stock with price S_t.



3.4.2 Assumptions on the assets

Risk-free asset dynamics: The risk-free asset B_t earns a continuously-compounded rate r that does not vary with time, 
dB_t = r\, B_t\, dt
 Being risk-free, its diffusion term is 0 (there is no dW_t), so its value grows deterministically as B_t = B_0\, e^{rt}.
Stock dynamics: The stock price follows the GBM dynamics of Eq. 10, with constant drift \mu and constant volatility \sigma, 
dS_t = \mu\, S_t\, dt + \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t
 Here the diffusion term is not 0: the \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t term is the source of the stock’s uncertainty, and is what makes it risky.
No dividends: The stock pays no dividends over [t, T].



3.4.3 Assumptions on the market

No arbitrage: No strategy delivers a risk-free profit in excess of r. In particular, any two portfolios with identical payoffs in every future scenario must have identical prices today.
Frictionless trading: Transactions are executed instantaneously with no fees, no bid–ask spread, no taxes, and no market impact. Continuous-time trading is permitted.
Unlimited borrowing and lending at r: Cash may be borrowed or lent in any real-valued amount at the risk-free rate.
Unrestricted stock positions: Any real-valued quantity of the stock may be held, including short positions (negative quantities), with no borrowing cost or quantity constraint.

The assumptions above are idealizations. Real markets violate every one of them to some degree. Their utility is conceptual: under these conditions, the derivative-pricing problem reduces to a well-posed PDE with a known closed-form solution.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.5 Black-Scholes pricing strategy
Given a European option with terminal payoff V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Eq. 20) and the option-value SDE Eq. 22, the remaining argument unfolds in three steps:

Form a hedged portfolio: Construct a portfolio by holding +1 unit of the call option and -\Delta_t units of the stock, where \Delta_t = \partial V / \partial S is the option’s delta (§3.2), giving 
\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t
 The dW_t contributions from dV and from \Delta_t\, dS_t cancel exactly, rendering the portfolio instantaneously risk-free. (§3.6)
Invoke no-arbitrage: A risk-free portfolio must earn the risk-free rate: d\Pi_t = r\, \Pi_t\, dt. Equating this with the deterministic dynamics from Step 1 yields a PDE for V(S, t), the Black-Scholes PDE. (§3.7)
