Solve the PDE: Solving the PDE using the boundary condition V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Eq. 20) gives the Black-Scholes pricing formula for a European call.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.6 The hedging portfolio
We want to hold the option together with something else so that the combined position is delta-neutral, its value insensitive to small moves in the stock price. Of the other instruments in the market, the risk-free asset has zero delta and cannot offset S-exposure, so the stock is the only candidate: hold the option long and a quantity q_t of the stock, with q_t to be determined:

\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) + q_t\, S_t

Its portfolio delta is the sensitivity of \Pi_t to the stock price, computed from this definition (treating q_t as constant in S at the instant t):

\frac{\partial \Pi_t}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + q_t
\tag{23}
Delta-neutrality requires \partial \Pi_t/\partial S = 0, which forces q_t = -\partial V/\partial S = -\Delta_t. Thus, the delta-neutral and risk-free portfolio is

\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t S_t
\tag{24}
Over an infinitesimal interval, the portfolio changes by

d\Pi_t = dV - \Delta_t\, dS_t

Writing it this way drops the -S_t\, d\Delta_t - d\Delta_t\, dS_t terms that the Itô product rule adds for a time-varying \Delta_t. This is not an approximation: the hedge is run as a self-financing strategy, so the cash released or absorbed by rebalancing the stock position is exactly offset by a cash account and nets to zero in d\Pi_t over [t, t+dt]. The accounting is in §A.3.
Step 1 — substitute the option change:
Substituting Eq. 22 (Itô’s lemma applied to V) for dV,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t \;-\; \Delta_t\, dS_t

Step 2 — substitute the stock change:
Substituting Eq. 10, dS_t = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW_t,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t \;-\; \Delta_t\, \mu S\, dt \;-\; \Delta_t\, \sigma S\, dW_t

Step 3 — collect like differentials:
Grouping the dt terms and the dW_t terms,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;-\; \Delta_t\, \mu S \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \left(\sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;-\; \Delta_t\, \sigma S\right) dW_t

Step 4 — factor the paired terms:
Factoring \mu S out of the drift pair and \sigma S out of the dW_t pair,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - \Delta_t\right) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - \Delta_t\right) dW_t

The same factor \big(\partial V/\partial S - \Delta_t\big) now multiplies both the \mu-dependent drift and the entire dW_t exposure.
Step 5 — substitute the hedge:
Substituting \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S (the position q_t = -\Delta_t chosen above), both parentheses vanish at once,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt
\tag{25}
Vanishing of the first parentheses means that the expected return of the stock (\mu) has disappeared from the hedged portfolio’s dynamics, meaning the option’s fair value doesn’t depend on it. This implies that two investors who disagree about the stock’s expected return still agree on the option’s price (provided they agree on the volatility \sigma and the risk-free rate r).
Similarly, vanishing of the second parentheses means that d\Pi_t has become independent of dW_t randomness entirely. So the same position choice q_t = -\Delta_t creates a portfolio that is delta-neutral and dW_t-free.
This is the crux of the construction. In Eq. 22 the term \sigma S\, \partial V / \partial S\, dW_t made dV random; Eq. 25 has no dW_t term at all. A position whose return depended on the random fluctuations of S_t is rendered instantaneously risk-free, and the exposure was hedged away by adding a short stock position to our portfolio.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.7 The Black-Scholes equation
Because the hedged portfolio \Pi_t has no random component over [t, t+dt], we invoke the no-arbitrage condition and assert that it must earn the risk-free rate r; otherwise there would be a risk-free arbitrage. Thus:

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \Pi_t\, dt
\tag{26}
Substituting the portfolio definition \Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t from Eq. 24,

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \big[\, V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t \,\big]\, dt

Using \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S,

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \left[\, V \;-\; S_t\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \,\right] dt

Equating the drift above with the drift from Eq. 25,

\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = r V - r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}

Rearranging gives,

\boxed{\,\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = r V\,}

which is Eq. 19. \square
It is worth pausing on what we have arrived at. This is the Black-Scholes equation, published by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes in 1973 [12] and, in the same year, set on a more general footing by Robert Merton [13]. It was the first time anyone had shown that a derivative could be priced by replication, that the option’s risk could be hedged away entirely, leaving a fair value fixed by no-arbitrage alone, independent of any investor’s risk appetite or view on the stock’s expected return. Its impact was immediate and enduring: it gave traders a closed-form price and a hedge ratio they could act on, and the derivatives markets that grew on top of it became among the largest in the world. In 1997 the work was recognized with the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, awarded to Scholes and Merton [14]; Black, who had died in 1995, could not share it, as the prize is not awarded posthumously, though the committee named his role explicitly.
For our purposes the equation is a landmark of a different kind: its second-order term \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2\,\partial_S^2 V, the one that distinguishes it from a deterministic pricing equation, traces back to the single rule (dW)^2 = dt, the same rule we are about to carry into diffusion models.

3.7.1 Solution to the Black-Scholes equation
With the boundary condition V(S, T) = \max(S - K, 0) (Eq. 20) for a European call, this PDE has the famous closed-form solution

\boxed{V(S, t) = S\, N(d_1) - K e^{-r(T-t)} N(d_2)}
\tag{27}
where N(\cdot) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF) and

d_1 = \frac{\log(S/K) + (r + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)(T-t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}, \quad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T-t}

Solving the PDE (via change of variables to the heat equation) is a textbook exercise [15]; a step-by-step sketch is in §A.2. The derivation we care about is everything up to the PDE.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.8 What the derivation establishes
The derivation has a clear logical structure:

We started with an SDE for S_t (the stock price).
We considered a function of that SDE: V(S, t) (the option value).
Itô’s lemma yielded the SDE for V.
The dW term in dV was hedgeable. We could remove the random component with a \Delta-position in the stock.
The hedged portfolio’s drift must match the risk-free rate, yielding a PDE for V.

The Itô correction term, \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \partial_S^2 V, survives the hedging and becomes the second-order term in the PDE. Geometrically, it is the contribution of the option value’s curvature in S (the second derivative \partial_S^2 V, known in finance as the option’s gamma), weighted by the variance rate \sigma^2 S^2.
This structural fact is central: the second-order term in the Black-Scholes PDE comes directly from (dW)^2 = dt. The same pattern appears in Part 8.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.1 Learning








Figure 10: Learning: choose a family \mathcal{M}=\{p_\theta\} and fit it to the data distribution p_0 by minimizing a divergence D(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta).





To approximate p_0 parametrically, three elements are required (Figure 10) [16], [17]:

Model family (\mathcal{M}): The candidate distributions p_\theta that learning searches over.
Divergence (D): A function D(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) that quantifies the discrepancy between the data and the model.
Optimization procedure: A method that minimizes the divergence over \theta.


4.1.1 Model family
A model family \mathcal{M} = \{p_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\} is a collection of probability density functions parameterized by a set of parameters \theta, where each choice of \theta in \Theta, the set of admissible parameters, defines a specific probability distribution within the family. It represents the set of candidate distributions that can be used to approximate the unknown data distribution p_0, so it fixes which distributions learning can reach.
The parameters determine the characteristics of each distribution, such as its location, scale, or shape, depending on the chosen model. For example, a Gaussian model family can be defined by its mean and variance, with different parameter values producing different Gaussian distributions. The objective is to identify the parameter values \theta that yield the distribution p_\theta that best approximates p_0, according to a chosen divergence.
Choosing a family therefore means choosing how a distribution is represented and how its parameters \theta determine it. The choice weighs several questions, and different families answer them differently:

Expressiveness: Is the family rich enough to approximate complex distributions, such as those of images?
Ease of representation: Can its members be built from standard network architectures, without structural constraints on the network?
Ease of learning: Can the training loss be computed from the data and minimized stably and efficiently?
Ease of density estimation: Is the density p_\theta(x), or a bound on it, easy to evaluate in closed form, as training by maximum likelihood needs?
Ease of sampling: Does a sample x \sim p_\theta require few network evaluations, as generation needs?
Sample quality: Are the samples realistic and as diverse as the data?

In practice \theta represents the weights of a neural network that estimates the density or another quantity that determines the model.
Part 5 develops three examples of the families used in this series: a variational autoencoder (VAE), which represents the density through an unobserved latent variable; a normalizing flow, which represents it through an invertible change of variables from a simple density; and an energy-based model (EBM), which represents it through an energy that scores each input.


4.1.2 Divergence
A divergence is a function of two distributions satisfying D(p \,\|\, q) \ge 0, with equality if and only if p = q. Generative learning is then the optimization problem

\boxed{\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta}\, D(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta)}
\tag{28}
If p_0 \in \mathcal{M}, the minimum value is zero and p_{\theta^*} = p_0. Otherwise p_{\theta^*} is the member of \mathcal{M} closest to p_0 as measured by D, not p_0 itself, as Figure 11 shows below.








Figure 11: The two outcomes of generative learning, Eq. 28, drawn schematically in the space of distributions, after Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [16]. Left: The data distribution p_0 lies in the model family \mathcal{M}, so the minimizer p_{\theta^*} is p_0 itself and the minimum divergence is zero. Right: p_0 lies outside \mathcal{M}, so p_{\theta^*} is the member of \mathcal{M} closest to p_0 as measured by D, and the minimum divergence is positive.





Divergences differ in what they compare.
Kullback-Leibler divergence: This divergence, abbreviated KL [18], compares two densities through the logarithm of their ratio,

\boxed{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\, dx}
\tag{29}
It is infinite when p puts probability where q has none, so minimizing D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) forces p_\theta to put probability wherever p_0 does. Minimizing it over \theta amounts to maximizing the model’s expected log-density under p_0, as the derivation below shows.
Substituting p_0 and p_\theta into Eq. 29,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} p_0(x) \log \frac{p_0(x)}{p_\theta(x)}\, dx

Writing the integral against p_0 as an expectation,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\log \frac{p_0(x)}{p_\theta(x)}\right]

Splitting the logarithm of the ratio,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\log p_0(x) - \log p_\theta(x)\big]

When \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big|\log p_0(x)\big| and \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big|\log p_\theta(x)\big| are finite, by linearity of expectation,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\log p_0(x)\big] - \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\log p_\theta(x)\big]

The first term does not depend on \theta. Writing it as a constant,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\log p_\theta(x)\big] + \text{const}

Taking the minimizer over \theta of both sides, where the constant does not change where the minimum lies,

\arg\min_{\theta}\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) = \arg\min_{\theta}\, \big(-\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\log p_\theta(x)\big]\big)

Since minimizing a negated quantity is maximizing it,

\arg\min_{\theta}\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) = \arg\max_{\theta}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\log p_\theta(x)\big]

The expectation on the right is taken under the unknown p_0, and the dataset \mathcal{D} supplies its estimate. The likelihood of \theta is the joint density of the observed samples under the model. By independence it factorizes,

p_\theta\big(x^{(1)}, \ldots, x^{(n)}\big) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_\theta\big(x^{(i)}\big)

The maximum-likelihood estimate maximizes it. Since the logarithm is increasing, the logarithm of the product is the sum of the logarithms, and 1/n is a positive constant, it equally maximizes the average log-likelihood,

\boxed{\hat\theta = \arg\max_{\theta}\, \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p_\theta\big(x^{(i)}\big)}
\tag{30}
Under the second of those conditions, the law of large numbers [19], in Kolmogorov’s strong form [20], makes this average converge to \mathbb{E}_{p_0}[\log p_\theta(x)] as n \to \infty. Maximum likelihood is therefore the finite-sample form of KL minimization, and the negative average log-likelihood is the loss associated with the KL divergence.
Fisher divergence: It compares two densities through the gradients of their log-densities [21],

\boxed{D_F(p, q) = \frac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_p\big\lVert \nabla_x \log p(x) - \nabla_x \log q(x) \big\rVert^2}
\tag{31}
The gradient of the logarithm removes a normalizing constant, so the Fisher divergence can be evaluated for a model known only up to that constant, which is why score matching minimizes it (P2:§3.3.1).
2-Wasserstein distance: It compares two distributions [22] by the least cost of rearranging one into the other [23], with the cost \lVert x - y \rVert^2 of carrying probability from x to y,

\boxed{W_2^2(p, q) = \inf_{\gamma}\ \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim \gamma} \lVert X - Y \rVert^2}
\tag{32}
where the infimum runs over the couplings \gamma of p and q [24], the joint distributions of pairs (X, Y) with X \sim p and Y \sim q. Unlike the KL divergence, which is infinite for two distributions on disjoint sets, it grows with how far apart the two distributions lie. P5:§3.1 develops these distances.

4.1.2.1 From divergence to loss
The problem of Eq. 28 cannot be solved as stated, since p_0 is unknown and the divergence cannot be evaluated. Training instead minimizes a loss, a function of \theta computable from \mathcal{D} that equals a divergence up to a constant independent of \theta, or bounds it from above. Minimizing the loss then minimizes the divergence, or an upper bound on it. The core losses of this series:

Negative log-likelihood: It equals the KL divergence between the data and the model, up to a constant, as derived above. Normalizing flows train on it directly, since their likelihood is exact (P4:§2 and P4:§3.5).
Negative evidence lower bound: It is an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood, used when the likelihood itself is intractable, as for VAEs (P2:§1.2.3) and DDPM (P2:§2.3).
Score-matching loss: It equals the Fisher divergence between the data and the model, up to a constant (P2:§3.3.1).
Denoising score matching objective: It equals the score-matching loss for data with Gaussian noise added, up to a constant independent of \theta, and it can be computed without the score of the data (P2:§4.8).
Flow matching and conditional flow matching objectives: Flow matching regresses a network onto the velocity field that carries noise to data, which is intractable. Conditional flow matching regresses it onto conditional velocities instead, with the same minimizer (P4:§5.2.2).




4.1.3 Optimization procedure
Neural networks minimize a loss through an iterative optimization process in which their parameters, known as weights and biases and collectively denoted by \theta, are adjusted to reduce the error in their predictions. During training, the network processes input data to produce outputs, and the loss assigns a numerical value to the discrepancy between these outputs and the desired behavior.
A common optimization method is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [25], which uses backpropagation to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter. Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the network’s layers, determining how each parameter affects the loss [26], [27]. At each iteration, the network estimates the loss using a small random subset of the training data \mathcal{D}, called a minibatch, and updates its parameters according to

\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \nabla_\theta \hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)

where \hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta) is the minibatch loss estimate and \eta > 0 is the learning rate. Repeating this update over many iterations gradually reduces the loss, allowing the network to learn patterns in the data, as illustrated in Figure 12.








Figure 12: One iteration of training a neural network. A minibatch of data passes forward through the network, whose weights and biases make up \theta, and the minibatch loss estimate \hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta) scores its outputs. Backpropagation then computes the gradient \nabla_\theta \hat{\mathcal{L}} of the loss estimate with respect to every parameter, and gradient descent updates \theta against it with learning rate \eta. The loop repeats over many iterations.





Two choices then determine the process: the network that represents p_\theta, and the optimizer that takes the steps.

4.1.3.1 Network architecture
A neural network is a composition of differentiable layers, each defined by its input and weights. The following core architectures, ordered from simplest to largest, are used in the papers covered in this series:

Multilayer perceptron [27]: The original VAE [28], the denoising autoencoder of Vincent [29], the coupling networks of NICE [30] and the planar flows of Rezende and Mohamed [31], and the two-dimensional experiments of flow matching [32], rectified flow [33] and stochastic interpolants [34].
Convolutional networks [35] and residual networks [36]: The coupling networks of RealNVP [37] and Glow [38], the dynamics of neural ODEs [39] and the backbones of the U-Nets below, and the multi-scale convolutions [40] of Sohl-Dickstein et al. [41].
Invertible networks: The coupling layers of NICE [30], RealNVP [37] and Glow [38], planar flows [31] and invertible residual networks [42], [43], and the continuous normalizing flows of neural ODEs [39], FFJORD [44] and RNODE [45].
U-Net [46]: DDPM [2], and noise-conditional score networks [47] in a RefineNet variant [48].
Transformer [49]: The self-attention blocks of DDPM’s U-Net [2] and the diffusion transformer below.
Vision transformer [50]: The patch-based design of the diffusion transformer below.
Diffusion transformer [51]: Stable Diffusion 3, in its multimodal diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) variant [52].



4.1.3.2 Optimizers
The papers covered in this series refine the basic step of SGD with a few optimizers:

Momentum: It adds a fraction of the previous step to the current one, which smooths the step direction [53].
Adaptive step sizes: Adagrad [54] and RMSProp [55] give each weight its own step size, dividing by the square root of an accumulated sum or a running average of its squared gradients. The original VAE trains with Adagrad [28], Rezende and Mohamed [31] with RMSProp, and Sohl-Dickstein et al. [41] with RMSProp on CIFAR-10, a dataset of 60,000 color images of 32 \times 32 pixels in ten classes.
Adam: It combines momentum with adaptive step sizes, keeping running averages of each coordinate’s gradient and squared gradient and dividing the first by the square root of the second [56]. It is the usual choice, from DDPM [2] and noise-conditional score networks [47] to RealNVP [37], Glow [38], FFJORD [44], flow matching [32] and rectified flow [33].
AdamW: It applies weight decay, which shrinks every weight toward zero at each step [57], directly to the weights rather than through Adam’s rescaled gradient [58]. Stable Diffusion 3 [52] uses it, and so do the image-translation experiments of rectified flow [33].

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.2 Inference
Once trained, a generative model answers three inference queries [16], [17]:

Density estimation: Given x, return its density p_\theta(x). Some families return it exactly; others give only a lower bound on the model’s log-density.
Sampling: Generation is the task of sampling from the data distribution, i.e. producing new objects x_{\text{new}} \sim p_\theta. A sampler is an algorithm whose output is a random vector distributed according to p_\theta. The density and the sampler are distinct descriptions of the same distribution.
Representation learning: Map x to a feature vector that is useful downstream, typically through an encoder network.

Not every model family supports all three efficiently; the trade-offs drive the diversity of generative approaches.
Conditional generation: Everything above extends to generating under a condition c, such as a caption or a class label. The target becomes the conditional distribution p_0(x \mid c), the dataset consists of pairs (x^{(i)}, c^{(i)}), and one model p_\theta(x \mid c) serves every value of c.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
5.1 Variational autoencoders
VAEs are latent-variable models, so they model x through an unobserved latent variable z \in \mathbb{R}^{d_z} with a simple prior, usually the standard Gaussian p(z) = \mathcal{N}(z;\ 0,\ I), where I is the identity matrix, here d_z \times d_z; throughout this Part it has the dimension of the vector it accompanies.
An encoder q_\phi(z \mid x) infers z from x. It is usually the Gaussian

q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(z;\ \mu_\phi(x),\ \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_\phi(x)^2)\big)

Its mean \mu_\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d_z} and standard deviations \sigma_\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to (0, \infty)^{d_z} are estimated using a network with parameters \phi. Here \operatorname{diag}(v) is the diagonal matrix with the vector v on its diagonal, and the square is taken elementwise, so the coordinates of z are independent given x. The encoder narrows x to a lower-dimensional code z, as Figure 13 shows below.








Figure 13: Computation graph of a variational autoencoder, after Lai et al. [59], Figure 1.2, and Kingma and Welling [28]. The encoder network maps x to the mean \mu_\phi(x) and standard deviations \sigma_\phi(x) of q_\phi(z \mid x), and z is sampled from that Gaussian, as z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \epsilon, where \odot is the elementwise product, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). The decoder network maps z to \mu_\theta(z) and \sigma_\theta(z), and x' is sampled from p_\theta(x \mid z) in the same way, as x' = \mu_\theta(z) + \sigma_\theta(z) \odot \epsilon' with an independent \epsilon' \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). Generation feeds the decoder with z \sim p(z) (dashed). Boxes are variables, trapezoids are networks and ovals are sampling steps.





A stochastic decoder p_\theta(x \mid z) generates x from z. For real-valued data it is usually the Gaussian

p_\theta(x \mid z) = \mathcal{N}\big(x;\ \mu_\theta(z),\ \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_\theta(z)^2)\big)

Its mean \mu_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to \mathbb{R}^d and standard deviations \sigma_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to (0, \infty)^d are estimated using a network with parameters \theta [28]. The decoder widens z back to the data space.
The decoder outputs a distribution, not a point, so many latent z could have produced the same x. Evaluating the marginal likelihood

p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz

therefore requires integrating over every z that could have generated x, which makes it intractable.

5.1.1 Training
Training uses both the encoder and the decoder, through variational inference, in which the encoder outputs a distribution q_\phi(z \mid x) over z that approximates the posterior of z given x. With it, \log p_\theta(x) has a computable lower bound, the evidence lower bound (ELBO) [28], [60],

\boxed{\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z) + \log p(z) - \log q_\phi(z \mid x)\big]}
\tag{33}
which is at most \log p_\theta(x) (P2:§1.2.3 derives the bound). Training minimizes the negative ELBO averaged over the data,

\boxed{L_{\mathrm{VAE}}(\theta, \phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi)\big]}
\tag{34}
Training estimates the expectation in the ELBO with a sample of z, and because q_\phi depends on \phi, the gradient with respect to \phi must account for how that sample depends on \phi. The VAE writes the sample as z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \epsilon with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). This reparameterization makes z a differentiable function of \phi, so the gradient passes through the sample [28].


5.1.2 Inference
A trained VAE answers the three inference queries (density estimation, sampling and representation learning) as follows.

5.1.2.1 Density estimation
The VAE cannot return the density p_\theta(x) itself, because its marginal likelihood is intractable. Density estimation returns only a lower bound on \log p_\theta(x) [16], the ELBO of Eq. 33.


5.1.2.2 Sampling
Unlike training, generation uses only the decoder. To generate a sample, we sample z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) from the prior, feed it to the decoder to compute \mu_\theta(z) and \sigma_\theta(z), and sample x from the decoder’s Gaussian, all in one pass,

x \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\theta(z),\ \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_\theta(z)^2)\big)

That sample may be written

x = \mu_\theta(z) + \sigma_\theta(z) \odot \epsilon'

with an independent \epsilon' \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), but for x the form is optional, because no gradient passes through it. This is ancestral sampling, which samples each variable given the variables it depends on, here z \sim p(z) and then x \sim p_\theta(x \mid z) [16].


5.1.2.3 Representation learning
The encoder q_\phi(z \mid x) maps any x to a latent code z. After training, z captures the factors of variation in the data, so the encoder doubles as an unsupervised feature extractor, the VAE’s representation learning [16].

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
5.2 Normalizing flows
A simple distribution such as a Gaussian is easy to evaluate and sample, but it is not complex enough to model the distributions of images or text. An invertible transformation, often a composition of simpler ones, converts a simple distribution into a complex one and back.
A normalizing flow does so through an invertible map f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, differentiable with a differentiable inverse, which takes z to x = f_\theta(z) [61], [62]. It is like a VAE whose decoder is a deterministic, invertible map rather than a stochastic Gaussian conditional. Its inverse f_\theta^{-1} takes x back to z, as Figure 14 shows below.








Figure 14: A normalizing flow [61] in one dimension. The simple density p(z) = \mathcal{N}(z;\ 0,\ 1) (left) is carried by the invertible map f_\theta(z) = z + 2\tanh(3z) to a two-peaked density p_\theta(x) (right), computed exactly by the change-of-variables formula below. The map x = f_\theta(z) samples in one pass (top), and its inverse z = f_\theta^{-1}(x) evaluates the density in one pass (bottom). The map stretches the line most near z = 0, so the density of x is lowest there, between its two peaks.





The map and its inverse keep the dimension, so unlike in a VAE, x and z have the same size, and both variables are continuous, since the likelihood below is a density. Where f_\theta stretches the line, the density of x falls, which splits the one Gaussian peak into two. P4:§2 develops flows.
Because the map is invertible, exactly one z = f_\theta^{-1}(x) corresponds to each x. A flow therefore needs no encoder and no variational inference. With p(z) the simple density of z, the change-of-variables formula for densities gives its likelihood exactly

\boxed{p_\theta(x) = p\big(f_\theta^{-1}(x)\big)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_\theta^{-1}}{\partial x}(x) \Big\rvert}
\tag{35}
where \frac{\partial f_\theta^{-1}}{\partial x}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} is the Jacobian of f_\theta^{-1} at x, the matrix of its partial derivatives, and |\det| is the absolute value of its determinant.

5.2.1 Training
Training maximizes this likelihood directly, by maximum likelihood over the data [16], [62]. Taking the logarithm of the formula,
\log p_\theta(x) = \log p\big(f_\theta^{-1}(x)\big) + \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_\theta^{-1}}{\partial x}(x) \Big\rvert
Averaging its negative over the data gives the training objective, the negative log-likelihood

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\Big[\log p\big(f_\theta^{-1}(x)\big) + \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_\theta^{-1}}{\partial x}(x) \Big\rvert\Big]}
\tag{36}
Both terms are computed from one pass of the inverse map, and the objective is the negative log-likelihood itself, not an upper bound on it as the negative ELBO of a VAE is. The Jacobian determinant also restricts the network. For a general d \times d Jacobian it costs O(d^3) operations per data point, so flows use layers whose Jacobian is triangular, such as coupling layers [30], where the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries.


5.2.2 Inference
A trained flow answers the three inference queries (density estimation, sampling and representation learning) as follows.

5.2.2.1 Density estimation
Density estimation is exact and needs a single pass. The inverse map z = f_\theta^{-1}(x) and its Jacobian determinant give p_\theta(x) in closed form through Eq. 35. The flow therefore returns the density itself, not a bound on it as a VAE does [16]. In Figure 14 this is the bottom arrow.


5.2.2.2 Sampling
Sampling uses the forward direction and needs a single pass. We sample z \sim p(z) from the simple density and apply the map once, x = f_\theta(z). There is no second sampling step, as in a VAE’s decoder, and no iterative chain. The map is itself the sampler [16]. In Figure 14 this is the top arrow.


5.2.2.3 Representation learning
The inverse map z = f_\theta^{-1}(x) is the flow’s encoder. It maps any x to its latent code z with no separate inference network and no variational approximation [16]. The code z has the size of x, so the flow compresses nothing, and its representation is exact and deterministic rather than lower-dimensional.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
5.3 Energy-based models
EBMs [63] define the model density through an energy function E_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}, in the form of Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski [64],

p_\theta(x) = e^{-E_\theta(x)} / Z(\theta)

where the partition function

Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-E_\theta(x)}\, dx

is assumed finite but is in general intractable. The network outputs a single number, the energy, as Figure 15 shows below.








Figure 15: Computation graph of an energy-based model, after Lai et al. [59], Figure 1.2, which stops at the energy. The energy network narrows x to the scalar E_\theta(x). As in Figure 13, boxes are variables and trapezoids are networks. The density p_\theta(x) needs the division by the partition function Z(\theta) (dashed), an integral over \mathbb{R}^d that is intractable when d is large.






5.3.1 Training
Training an EBM by maximum likelihood chooses \theta so that the model assigns high density to the training data [16]. For an observed x, the log-likelihood is
\log p_\theta(x) = -E_\theta(x) - \log Z(\theta)
Averaging its negative over the data, with Z(\theta) constant in x, gives the training objective, the negative log-likelihood

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[E_\theta(x)\big] + \log Z(\theta)}
\tag{37}
Differentiating the log-likelihood in \theta,
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = -\,\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x) - \nabla_\theta \log Z(\theta)
The second term is the only place the intractable partition function enters. Applying the chain rule to the logarithm,
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = -\,\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x) - \frac{\nabla_\theta Z(\theta)}{Z(\theta)}
Substituting the definition Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)}\, d\tilde x into the numerator,
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = -\,\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x) - \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\, \nabla_\theta \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)}\, d\tilde x
Differentiation under the integral sign is permitted when there is an integrable function h: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty) such that, for \theta in a neighbourhood of each value and every \tilde x,

\lVert \nabla_\theta E_\theta(\tilde x) \rVert\, e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)} \le h(\tilde x)

which is the hypothesis of dominated convergence. Differentiating under the integral sign,
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = -\,\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x) - \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \nabla_\theta e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)}\, d\tilde x
Applying the chain rule to the exponential, \nabla_\theta e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)} = -\nabla_\theta E_\theta(\tilde x)\, e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)},
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = -\,\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x) + \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \nabla_\theta E_\theta(\tilde x)\, e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)}\, d\tilde x
Recognizing e^{-E_\theta(\tilde x)} / Z(\theta) = p_\theta(\tilde x), the integral is an expectation under the model, and the gradient of the log-likelihood has two terms,
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = -\,\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x) + \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta(\tilde x)}\big[\nabla_\theta E_\theta(\tilde x)\big]
The first term, the positive phase, lowers the energy of the observed x; the second, the negative phase, raises the energy of a sample from the model. The second term is an expectation under p_\theta, which cannot be evaluated in closed form. Replacing that expectation with its one-sample Monte Carlo estimate, a single sample \tilde x from the model,
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) \approx -\,\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x) + \nabla_\theta E_\theta(\tilde x), \qquad \tilde x \sim p_\theta
This contrasts the real data against a “negative” sample from the model. Contrastive divergence [65] reduces training cost but introduces gradient bias: instead of sampling exactly from p_\theta with a costly iterative sampler, it runs only a few steps initialized at the observed x, yielding \tilde x that is not distributed according to p_\theta.


5.3.2 Inference
A trained EBM answers the three inference queries (density estimation, sampling and representation learning) as follows.

5.3.2.1 Density estimation
Because Z(\theta) is intractable, the EBM cannot return the absolute density p_\theta(x) [16]. It can still compare two candidates exactly, because Z(\theta) cancels in the ratio,
\frac{p_\theta(x')}{p_\theta(x)} = \exp\!\big(-E_\theta(x') + E_\theta(x)\big)
Density estimation is therefore comparative, so the EBM ranks points by likelihood but does not assign each one a number.


5.3.2.2 Sampling
Sampling from p_\theta is harder still. A VAE’s decoder and a flow’s map each produce a sample in one pass, but an EBM has no such map. It is sampled instead with an iterative Markov chain Monte Carlo method. The Metropolis algorithm [66] proposes a Gaussian random step with standard deviation s > 0 in each coordinate and uses the comparison above as its acceptance test, writing x_i for the state of the chain after i steps:

Initialize x_0 randomly and set i = 0.
Propose x' = x_i + s\,\epsilon with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).
If E_\theta(x') < E_\theta(x_i), set x_{i+1} = x'.
Otherwise set x_{i+1} = x' with probability \exp\!\big(-E_\theta(x') + E_\theta(x_i)\big), and keep x_{i+1} = x_i otherwise.
Increase i by one and go to step 2.

The acceptance rule is what makes p_\theta the stationary distribution of the chain, meaning that x_i \sim p_\theta implies x_{i+1} \sim p_\theta. Steps 3 and 4 together accept x' with probability \min\{1,\ p_\theta(x') / p_\theta(x_i)\}, because the exponential in step 4 equals p_\theta(x') / p_\theta(x_i), which is greater than 1 in the case of step 3.
We write q(x' \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(x';\ x,\ s^2 I) for the density of the proposal of step 2 from a state x. It is symmetric, q(x' \mid x) = q(x \mid x'), since it depends only on \lVert x' - x \rVert. A step from x to a different point x' needs that proposal and its acceptance, so it has density
k(x' \mid x) = q(x' \mid x)\, \min\{1,\ p_\theta(x') / p_\theta(x)\}
Multiplying by p_\theta(x),
p_\theta(x)\, k(x' \mid x) = q(x' \mid x)\, \min\{p_\theta(x),\ p_\theta(x')\}
The right-hand side is unchanged when x and x' are swapped, because q and the minimum are both symmetric. Hence

p_\theta(x)\, k(x' \mid x) = p_\theta(x')\, k(x \mid x')

which means that a chain started from p_\theta steps from x to x' as often as from x' to x. This is detailed balance, and it gives stationarity. Integrating it over x, the density of arriving at x' from another point equals p_\theta(x') times the probability of leaving x'. With the remaining probability, a proposal from x' is rejected and the chain stays at x'. The density at x' after one step is therefore p_\theta(x').
The chain can still require many steps to approach p_\theta from its random start. P2:§3.1 develops EBMs, and P2:§3.2.3 shows how to avoid Z(\theta).


5.3.2.3 Representation learning
The EBM has no encoder and no latent variable, so there is no feature vector of x to extract and no representation learning [16].

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
6.1 What are diffusion models?
Diffusion models are a class of latent-variable generative models [2], whose latent variables are the noised states x_1, \ldots, x_N. A diffusion model has two components: the forward process and the reverse process. The forward process progressively adds noise to the training data until nothing but noise remains. The reverse process learns to undo that noising. Sampling starts from noise and applies the learned reverse process step by step, producing new data such as images that resemble the training data.
Two parallel approaches to diffusion models developed independently, differing primarily in the divergence they target and the loss they use for training. The variational track targets the KL divergence D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_0 \,\|\, p_\theta) and minimizes the negative ELBO. It runs from Sohl-Dickstein et al.’s nonequilibrium-thermodynamics formulation [41] to Ho et al.’s DDPM [2], where the bound is reparameterized as noise prediction. The score-based track targets the Fisher divergence, the expected squared distance between the data score and the model’s. It minimizes a score-matching loss, which averages that divergence over noise levels. It runs from Hyvärinen’s score matching [21] through Vincent’s denoising score matching [29] to Song and Ermon’s score matching with Langevin dynamics (SMLD) [47]. Song et al. unified the two into a single framework in 2021 [1]. Figure 16 places these landmarks on a common timeline.








Figure 16: The two research lineages behind diffusion models, in chronological order. Left: the variational track, from the nonequilibrium-thermodynamics formulation to DDPM. Right: the score-based track, from score matching, through its denoising form, to score matching with Langevin dynamics. The 2021 score-SDE paper unifies them, showing the Variance-Preserving and Variance-Exploding constructions to be one equation.





Table 2 maps each component of the generative-modeling framework to the endpoints of the two lineages, DDPM and SMLD, and to the score-based SDEs that unify them.
