Probability-flow ODE: A deterministic ODE whose solution has, at each time, the same marginal density as the forward SDE’s. Post #3 derives it.
Annealed Langevin dynamics: Langevin steps that follow the score at each noise level in turn, from the largest level to the smallest.
Ancestral sampling: The sampling of §5.1.2.2 applied to the learned reverse steps in sequence, i = N, \ldots, 1, the procedure of the Sampling subsection below.
Reverse diffusion: A discretization of the reverse-time SDE, taking one noisy step per time increment.
Predictor-Corrector (PC): A reverse-time-SDE step followed by score-based corrector steps at the same noise level.
Invertible probability-flow ODE latent: The ODE is deterministic and reversible, so each x_0 maps to a unique endpoint that maps back to it; that endpoint serves as a latent code, and the change-of-variables formula along the flow turns it into an exact \log p_\theta(x_0).

Each stochastic gradient step samples a fresh triple: a data point x_0 \sim p_0, a step index i (uniform over 1,\dots,N), a noise-level index \ell (uniform over 1,\dots,L) or a time t (uniform over [0,1]), and a noise vector \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I).

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
6.2 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [2] are discrete-time diffusion models with roots in nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Like other diffusion models they generate new samples through one central idea: learn to undo noise. If a model can remove a small amount of noise from a slightly noisy sample, then, starting from pure noise and applying this repeatedly, it recovers a data sample (Figure 17).








Figure 17: DDPM as a pair of Markov chains. The forward process, with transitions p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}) (top, fixed), adds Gaussian noise until x_N is pure noise. The reverse Markov chain, with learned reverse steps q_\theta(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) (bottom), denoises back to data. Training fits the reverse Markov chain to invert the forward process.






6.2.1 Forward process (noising)
A fixed, parameter-free procedure that progressively adds Gaussian noise to a data sample x_0 \sim p_0, producing a sequence x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_N in which each x_i is a noisier version of x_{i-1} and the endpoint x_N is close to pure noise, a sample from a fixed, data-independent distribution (Figure 18). How much noise enters at each step is set by a noise schedule. This forward process is not an analogy to a diffusion; it is one.








Figure 18: The forward (noising) process, illustrated on a 2-D toy dataset (two interleaving moons, standardized). Left to right, progressively more Gaussian noise is mixed into each sample; the two-moon structure dissolves until, at the final step, the points are indistinguishable from a sample from a standard Gaussian \mathcal{N}(0, I), the fixed, data-independent distribution the reverse process starts from. Colours mark the two moons, showing how all structure is erased.





The forward process yields two outputs: for training, pairs of data samples and their noised versions; for inference, pure noise.


6.2.2 Reverse process (denoising)
A learned procedure, usually implemented using neural networks, that starts from pure noise and removes noise step by step, running the forward process in reverse to produce a new sample from p_0. As shown in the table above, each learned reverse step is modeled as a Gaussian distribution whose variance is fixed beforehand, and the only entity to predict is its mean \mu_\theta. Reparameterizing converts the mean-prediction problem into a noise-prediction problem, and \epsilon_\theta is what the network learns to predict. Once the \epsilon_\theta estimate is in hand, \mu_\theta is computed deterministically. That mean, along with the pre-fixed \sigma_i, is used to sample a slightly denoised version of its input. Each reverse step is trained to invert the corresponding forward step. On a training pair the final step x_1 \to x_0 is fitted to return that training sample. At sampling time the same chain, started from a fresh noise sample, produces a new x_0, which is what generation needs.
Note that during actual training, instead of N sequential steps, i is fed to the network as an input, so a single network represents all N reverse steps and each gradient step trains one of them at random. The sequencing is encoded in the conditioning, not in a loop.


6.2.3 Sampling
The forward process is set up so that x_N has a known, simple distribution we can sample from directly, a standard Gaussian in this case. To generate new data, we sample a noise vector from this distribution and apply the reverse process to it. If the network has learned to undo a single step of the noising process, applying those steps in sequence turns noise into data.
Note that during sampling, unlike training, we take N sequential steps i = N, N-1, \ldots, 1. At each step, the current x_i and i are fed to the network, which outputs the estimated noise \epsilon_\theta for that step. Like training, that \epsilon_\theta is used to compute \mu_\theta, and this, along with the fixed \sigma_i, is used to generate a slightly denoised sample from this estimated Gaussian distribution.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 7.1 Why convert the discrete DDPM forward process into an SDE
text:
7.1 Why convert the discrete DDPM forward process into an SDE
Before getting into how the DDPM forward process becomes an SDE, and how that yields the closed-form perturbation kernel, it is worth asking why the conversion is needed at all. DDPM obtains that kernel directly, by composing Gaussians and induction on the step index. For that one result the discrete argument is shorter, and nothing below improves on it.
The continuous-time route is chosen for what it makes available beyond it. The integrating-factor transform applies to any linear SDE, so it yields the perturbation kernel for the Variance-Exploding schedule (post #3), and for each other linear-SDE noise schedule, without repeating the argument, whereas the induction depends on the particular way the Variance-Preserving steps compose.
The SDE is also the object the rest of the theory relies upon: the Fokker-Planck equation, the reverse-time SDE, and the probability-flow ODE with its numerical solvers all start from the continuous-time process, and none of them follows from the inductively obtained kernel.
And it is the same transform already applied to the OU process in Part 2, the sense in which one lemma serves both derivations.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
7.2 Definitions
As discussed in the above section, DDPM is natively discrete, so to convert it to a continuous-time process, we pick the unit interval [0, 1] and divide it into N equal intervals of size 1/N. This maps N discrete steps i = 1, 2, \ldots, N to N time steps t = 1/N, 2/N, \ldots, 1. As the final step, we let the step count N \to \infty so the per-step time shrinks to an infinitesimal dt and the sequence becomes an SDE. This is why each object below carries two labels: a discrete one indexed by the step number, and a continuous one indexed by time.

Partition (N, \Delta t, \tau_i):

N: The number of steps.
i: The step index, i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, N\}.
t: The continuous time, t \in [0, 1].
\Delta t: The step size, \Delta t = 1/N.
\tau_i: The continuous time corresponding to step i, \tau_i = i/N.

Data sample x_0: A sample from the data distribution, x_0 \sim p_0, with x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d.
State x_i / x_t:

The partially-noised version of x_0.
x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d in discrete time; x_N is the noisiest state.
x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d in continuous time; x_{t=1} is the noisiest state (written with the time explicit, since x_1 denotes the first discrete state).

Noise schedule:

Noise added at each step, fixed in advance, not learned.
\beta_i: The discrete per-step noise variance, \beta_i \in (0, 1) for i = 1, \ldots, N.
\beta(t): The continuous-time noise-variance rate, a continuous function \beta : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty). Over an interval dt the injected noise has variance \beta(t)\, dt.
\alpha_i: Defined as \alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i, the fraction of the previous state’s variance retained at step i.

Cumulative product \bar\alpha_i / \bar\alpha(t):

It is the fraction of the original data variance still present at step i in the discrete case and time t in the continuous case.
\bar\alpha_i: The discrete cumulative product \bar\alpha_i := \prod_{s=1}^{i} \alpha_s.
\bar\alpha(t): The continuous cumulative product, 
\bar\alpha(t) := \exp\!\big(-\!\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\big)


Injected noise:

\epsilon_i: The noise added at step i, \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) i.i.d., independent of x_0.
\epsilon: The standardized accumulation of the injected noise. The total noise in x_i equals \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\epsilon in distribution, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) (a different such variable for each i).

Forward transition p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}):

The conditional distribution of x_i given x_{i-1}:  p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1},\ \beta_i I\big) 
It transforms x_{i-1} into x_i by contracting the previous state by \sqrt{1 - \beta_i} and adding Gaussian noise of variance \beta_i.
Equivalently, in reparameterized form:  x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i 
The whole forward process is the chain of these transitions.

Discrete perturbation kernel p(x_i \mid x_0):

The conditional distribution of the noised state given x_0, obtained by composing the forward transitions and marginalizing out the intermediate states, Gaussian in closed form, derived by induction in §A.7:  p(x_i \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_i) I\big) 
It produces x_i from x_0 directly by scaling the data by \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i} and adding Gaussian noise of variance 1 - \bar\alpha_i.
Equivalently, in reparameterized form:  x_i = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\, \epsilon  which lets us sample x_i for each i without iterating through the intermediate steps.

Continuous perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0):

The continuous-time counterpart, likewise Gaussian in closed form, derived with Itô’s lemma in §7.6:  p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(t)) I\big) 
It produces x_t from x_0 directly by scaling the data by \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} and adding Gaussian noise of variance 1 - \bar\alpha(t).
Equivalently, in reparameterized form:  x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon  which lets us sample x_t for each t without iterating through the intermediate steps.

Marginal distribution p_t(x):

The perturbation kernel marginalized over x_0 \sim p_0, the data-averaged marginal:  p_t(x) = \int p_{0t}(x \mid x_0)\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0 
Whereas the perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) conditions on a fixed x_0, the marginal averages over it, giving the unconditional distribution of x_t.


Scope: This post analyzes the forward process only, the object Itô’s lemma acts on. The reverse process, and the score \nabla_x \log p that drives it, are the subject of post #2. What we build here, the forward process’s continuous-time form and its perturbation kernels, is what the reverse process and its training will need.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
7.3 Assumptions
The forward process rests on a few modeling choices and collecting them upfront keeps the construction, and its limitations, transparent.

Standardized data: \mathbb{E}[x_0] = 0 and \operatorname{Var}(x_0) = I (the dataset is centered and whitened to meet this).
Prior p(x_N) / p(x_{t=1}): The schedule is chosen so that the noisiest state, x_N in discrete time, x_{t=1} in continuous time, is \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I), the fixed, data-independent distribution the reverse process starts from and the endpoint the construction is engineered to reach (not to be confused with a Bayesian prior).

These are idealizations: real data is only approximately standardized, and a finite number of steps leaves x_N only approximately Gaussian.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
7.4 The plan
With the objects defined and the assumptions fixed, the analysis of the forward process unfolds in three steps, the same Itô method of Parts 1–3, put to new questions:

Write the forward process as an SDE: The discrete noising sequence that defines DDPM is the discrete-time approximation of a continuous-time SDE. (§7.5)
Transform the SDE into the perturbation kernel: As an integrating-factor transform, Itô’s lemma collapses the drift and shows x_t \mid x_0 is Gaussian, the perturbation kernel, available in closed form, whose t \to 1 limit is the prior \mathcal{N}(0, I). (§7.6)
Use the perturbation kernel for training: It lets us sample x_t for each t in a single step, which is what makes the DDPM training objective tractable. (§7.7)

Part 8 then applies the lemma a second time, to a test function, to derive the PDE governing the marginal distribution p_t(x). The two applications mirror the two roles Itô’s lemma played in Parts 2–3, transforming an SDE and deriving a PDE, now used for generation instead of option pricing.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 7.5 The forward process as an SDE
text:
7.5 The forward process as an SDE
The DDPM forward process is defined in discrete time: a Markov chain (each state depending only on its immediate predecessor, not on the earlier history) that transports a data sample toward noise through a long sequence of small Gaussian noise additions, one per step:

\boxed{x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i}
\tag{38}
where \beta_i is the discrete noise schedule and \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the independent noise injected at step i.
Song et al. [1] showed this discrete sequence is the Euler-Maruyama discretization of a continuous-time SDE [67], the scheme that replaces dt by a step \Delta t and dW_t by an increment \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t\, I). To apply the Itô calculus to it, we must recover that SDE.
With that goal in mind, we first write the sequence explicitly, then let the step size shrink to zero to obtain the continuous-time limit. This yields an SDE of the same form as Eq. 8, the Variance-Preserving SDE (VP-SDE), which exhibits the same drift-plus-diffusion structure as GBM.

7.5.1 The continuous-time form of the forward process
Partition the continuous interval [0, 1] into the N steps of even width \Delta t > 0:

0 = \tau_0 < \tau_1 < \cdots < \tau_N = 1, \qquad \tau_i = i\, \Delta t, \qquad \Delta t = \tfrac{1}{N}

Thus, continuous time \tau_i = i/N corresponds to step i. The step size \Delta t = 1/N \to 0 as N \to \infty.
We use the discrete noise schedule \beta_i = \beta(\tau_i)\, \Delta t, a function of \beta(t). To be able to apply the limit, from here we use the continuous time t in place of the grid point \tau_i i.e. \beta_i = \beta(t)\, \Delta t.
Substituting this into Eq. 38, 
x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, \epsilon_i

For small \Delta t, Taylor-expanding the square root gives

\sqrt{1 - \beta(t)\, \Delta t} \approx 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \Delta t

Substituting the expansion into the previous line,

x_i \;\approx\; \big(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \Delta t\big)\, x_{i-1} \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, \epsilon_i

Subtracting x_{i-1},

x_i - x_{i-1} \;\approx\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_{i-1}\, \Delta t \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)\, \Delta t}\, \epsilon_i

Factoring the noise term as \sqrt{\beta(t)}\big(\sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i\big),

x_i - x_{i-1} \;\approx\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_{i-1}\, \Delta t \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\,\big(\sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i\big)

The factor \sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon_i, with \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), is exactly a Brownian increment \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t\, I) over [\tau_{i-1}, \tau_i],

x_i - x_{i-1} \;\approx\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_{i-1}\, \Delta t \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, \Delta W_i

This difference equation is the Euler-Maruyama scheme of the SDE below, and such schemes converge to the SDE’s solution as \Delta t \to 0 under the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions of §2.1, with coefficients continuous in t as those of the VP-SDE are for a continuous \beta [67]. Taking that limit gives the VP-SDE,

\boxed{dx_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t}
\tag{39}
This is the continuous-time form of the DDPM forward process. \square


7.5.2 The structural parallel with GBM
Place the two SDEs side by side:

\begin{aligned}
\text{GBM (Black-Scholes stock):} \quad &dS_t = \mu S_t\, dt + \sigma S_t\, dW_t \\
\text{DDPM forward (VP-SDE):} \quad &dx_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t
\end{aligned}

Both are linear SDEs: the drift is linear in the state variable, and the diffusion is either linear in the state variable (GBM) or independent of it (VP-SDE). The drift sign is the essential difference: GBM has a positive expected return (+\mu S), DDPM forward has a contracting drift (-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t) x) that drives x toward zero. Combined with the diffusion term injecting noise, this drives x_t toward a standard normal as t \to 1 (Figure 19).








Figure 19: Sample paths of GBM (left) and the VP-SDE (right), both starting at 1 (S_0 = 1 and x_0 = 1) and both linear SDEs driven by Brownian motion. GBM exhibits geometric drift. The VP-SDE drives each path’s mean toward zero (dashed) while injecting noise, so the paths forget x_0 and converge to the unit-variance band \pm\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha(t)} \to \pm 1 (shaded): the distribution of x_t given x_0 approaches \mathcal{N}(0, 1), not a point.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
7.6 Derivation of the perturbation kernel
Here Itô’s lemma is applied as an integrating-factor transform: choosing the transform y_t = x_t / \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} makes Itô’s lemma collapse the drift, turning the VP-SDE Eq. 39 into a driftless process. Integrating that driftless process gives x_t \mid x_0 a closed-form Gaussian distribution, the perturbation kernel that is the central computational object of DDPM training.

7.6.1 Cumulative product \bar\alpha_i / \bar\alpha(t)
The discrete cumulative product of the factors 1 - \beta_j is:

\bar\alpha_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i}(1 - \beta_j)

Writing the product as the exponential of a log-sum,

\bar\alpha_i = \exp\!\big(\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{i}\log(1 - \beta_j)\big)

Using \log(1 - \beta_j) \approx -\beta_j for small \beta_j,

\bar\alpha_i \approx \exp\!\big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i}\beta_j\big)

Substituting the discrete schedule \beta_j = \beta(\tau_j)\, \Delta t, which makes the exponent a Riemann sum,

\bar\alpha_i \approx \exp\!\big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i}\beta(\tau_j)\, \Delta t\big)

Taking the continuum limit (N \to \infty, with t = i/N fixed), the Riemann sum becomes an integral,

\bar\alpha_i \to \exp\!\big(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\big)

which is the continuous cumulative product,

\boxed{\bar\alpha(t) = \exp\left(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\right)}
\tag{40}


7.6.2 Perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0)
Because the VP-SDE is linear, it admits a closed-form solution: the distribution of x_t \mid x_0 for a fixed x_0. With the intermediate states integrated out, conditional on x_0, the state at time t is Gaussian:

\boxed{x_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(t)) I\right)}
\tag{41}
This perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) lets us sample x_t for each t in a single step without simulating the SDE.


7.6.3 Derivation
The derivation restates the SDE, defines an integrating factor and applies Itô’s lemma to it to eliminate the drift, integrates the driftless process, then inverts the transform.

7.6.3.1 Use Itô to obtain the reduced SDE
The SDE:
The state x_t follows the VP-SDE Eq. 39,

dx_t \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\, dt \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma:
For a transform f(x_t, t) of a process with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b, that is, dx_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t, the lemma Eq. 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

Integrating factor:
Like OU, the standard technique for a linear SDE is to apply Itô’s lemma to the transform y_t = f(x_t, t) with f(x, t) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}.
Coefficients (from the VP-SDE):
a = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x and b = \sqrt{\beta(t)}.
Partials (from f = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}):
With \bar\alpha'(t) = -\beta(t)\,\bar\alpha(t), which follows from differentiating Eq. 40 by the chain rule,

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; \frac{x\,\beta(t)}{2\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} \;=\; 0

Substituting a = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x, b = \sqrt{\beta(t)}, and the three partials into the lemma,

dy_t \;=\; \left(\frac{x_t\, \beta(t)}{2\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}} \;+\; \left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x_t\right)\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\beta(t)\cdot 0\right) dt \;+\; \sqrt{\beta(t)}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}}\, dW_t

Simplifying (the explicit-time term and the drift term cancel),

dy_t \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{\beta(t)}{\bar\alpha(t)}}\, dW_t

so y_t is driftless.


7.6.3.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration
Integrating both sides of the driftless equation from 0 to t,

\int_0^t dy_s \;=\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s

Evaluating the left side by the fundamental theorem of calculus,

y_t - y_0 \;=\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s

Since y_0 = x_0/\sqrt{\bar\alpha(0)} and \bar\alpha(0) = 1, y_0 = x_0; substituting,

y_t - x_0 \;=\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s

Moving x_0 across,

y_t \;=\; x_0 \;+\; \int_0^t \sqrt{\frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}\, dW_s



7.6.3.3 Properties of the solution distribution
The Itô integral has a deterministic integrand g(s) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}}, so by Eq. 7 it is Gaussian, with mean 0 and variance \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds.
Conditioning on x_0, the offset x_0 is a deterministic constant; adding it to that Gaussian is an affine transformation, and an affine function of a Gaussian is Gaussian, hence

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\int_0^t \frac{\beta(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)}\, ds\right) I\right)

Substituting \beta(s) = -\dfrac{\bar\alpha'(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)} (from \bar\alpha'(s) = -\beta(s)\,\bar\alpha(s)) into the variance,

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\int_0^t \frac{-\bar\alpha'(s)}{\bar\alpha(s)^2}\, ds\right) I\right)

Recognizing the integrand as \dfrac{d}{ds}\!\left[\dfrac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)}\right],

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\int_0^t \frac{d}{ds}\!\left[\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(s)}\right] ds\right) I\right)

Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus,

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \left(\frac{1}{\bar\alpha(t)} \;-\; \frac{1}{\bar\alpha(0)}\right) I\right)

Evaluating, with \bar\alpha(0) = 1,

y_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_0,\;\, \frac{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}{\bar\alpha(t)}\, I\right)

Since x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, y_t,

\boxed{x_t \mid x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\;\, \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big)\, I\right)}

which is Eq. 41. \square


7.6.3.4 The terminal condition
The closed form delivers the endpoint the forward process was built to reach. Since \beta(s) > 0, the factor \bar\alpha(t) (Eq. 40) decreases monotonically from \bar\alpha(0) = 1 toward 0 as the accumulated noise \int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds grows; the schedule is chosen so that \int_0^1 \beta(s)\, ds is large enough to make \bar\alpha(1) \approx 0.
Under that choice, evaluating Eq. 41 at t = 1,

\mathbb{E}[x_{t=1} \mid x_0] = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1)}\, x_0 \;\approx\; 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}[x_{t=1} \mid x_0] = \big(1 - \bar\alpha(1)\big) I \;\approx\; I

Since Eq. 41 is Gaussian, these moments give

p_{01}(x_{t=1} \mid x_0) \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I)

for each starting point x_0; the marginal is the average of that kernel over x_0 \sim p_0, so it inherits the same distribution. With the continuous endpoint t = 1 corresponding to the discrete step N,

\boxed{p(x_N) \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}(0, I)}
\tag{42}
The data x_0 is almost completely forgotten: every starting point flows to nearly the same standard Gaussian, the approximation tightening as \int_0^1 \beta\, ds is made larger (Figure 20). The idealized exact value \bar\alpha(1) = 0 is never attained on [0, 1]. It is approached only as the schedule’s total noise \int_0^1 \beta(s)\, ds grows without bound.








Figure 20: As t \to 1 the schedule drives \bar\alpha(t) toward 0: the mean factor \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} (rose) decays toward 0, erasing the data’s contribution, while the variance 1 - \bar\alpha(t) (violet) rises toward 1. The perturbation kernel \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\,x_0,\,(1-\bar\alpha(t))I) therefore approaches \mathcal{N}(0, I) for every starting point x_0, the fixed prior the reverse process samples from. (Linear schedule \beta(t) from 0.1 to 20.)





This is the prior of §7.3, and it is what makes generation possible. To synthesize a sample, the reverse process starts from a sample from \mathcal{N}(0, I) (which is trivial to generate) and removes the noise; because the forward process sends every input to this one known distribution, the reverse process always has a fixed, data-independent place to begin.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
7.7 Why the perturbation kernel matters
The perturbation kernel Eq. 41 is what renders DDPM training tractable. Two consequences make this precise.
Constant-cost sampling: The reparameterized form of the perturbation kernel,

\boxed{x_t \;=\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon}
\tag{43}
evaluates the state at any time t in closed form: given a noise-free sample x_0, a time t, and a single noise sample \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), the state x_t is obtained by one affine combination, at cost O(1) in t, with no iteration through the intermediate states between x_0 and x_t.
Exact supervision: Because \epsilon is sampled explicitly when x_t is constructed, the noise realized in x_t is known exactly. It therefore serves as a ground-truth regression target, the known quantity the network, observing only (x_t, t), is trained to predict.
Neither property survives the loss of the closed form. Recovering x_t at a time t would then require simulating the forward process: iterating the transition Eq. 38, or an Euler-Maruyama step of the SDE, for \Theta(N) sequential steps per sample at each training iteration, against the closed form’s single O(1) evaluation, and with no available parallelism across steps. Moreover, the noise present in a simulated x_t is the cumulative effect of the per-step increments \epsilon_1, \ldots, \epsilon_i rather than a single \epsilon, so the exact regression target is no longer available. That target stands in for the score \nabla_x \log p_t. The perturbation kernel makes the conditional score a known multiple of the noise,

\nabla_{x_t} \log p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = -\epsilon / \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}

and post #2 shows that regressing on it recovers \nabla_x \log p_t. Without the closed form neither is available, and the score must be estimated by other means, such as implicit score matching [21].
The perturbation kernel thus reduces training to single-step sampling with an exact, analytically known target. The use of that target (the denoising network, the noise-prediction objective and its equivalence to score matching) concerns the reverse process and is developed in post #2. Part 7 establishes the object on which that construction depends.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
8.1 Marginal distribution p_t(x)
The marginal distribution is the perturbation kernel Eq. 41 marginalized over x_0 \sim p_0,

\boxed{p_t(x) = \int p_{0t}(x \mid x_0)\, p_0(x_0)\, dx_0}
\tag{44}
The two are different objects: the perturbation kernel fixes x_0, whereas the marginal distribution lets x_0 vary.

8.1.1 Why “Variance-Preserving”
The claim is about the variance of x_t under the marginal distribution, where both the data x_0 and the injected noise are random, so both contribute to its variance. In the reparameterized form,

x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon

the two terms are independent, so their variances add. Taking the variance,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \operatorname{Var}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0\big) + \operatorname{Var}\big(\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(t)}\, \epsilon\big)

Taking each deterministic factor out of its variance, squared,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \bar\alpha(t)\, \operatorname{Var}(x_0) + \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon) = I,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \bar\alpha(t)\, \operatorname{Var}(x_0) + \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) I

With standardized data, \operatorname{Var}(x_0) = I,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = \bar\alpha(t)\, I + \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) I

Adding the two terms,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = I

So \operatorname{Var}(x_t) is constant for each t. As we add more and more noise in each step of the forward process, the data term’s variance \bar\alpha(t)\, I shrinks toward 0 and the noise term’s variance \big(1 - \bar\alpha(t)\big) I grows toward I but the total stays constant at I; hence the variance is preserved.
Standardized data is the case the name describes. For data with any covariance V = \operatorname{Var}(x_0), rearranging the line before the standardized step,

\operatorname{Var}(x_t) = I + \bar\alpha(t)\, \big(V - I\big)

so the variance changes monotonically from V at t = 0 toward I as \bar\alpha(t) \to 0. Two properties hold whatever the data. The scale of the state stays bounded for each t, between that of the data and that of the noise, so one network sees inputs of comparable size at each noise level. And the variance converges to I, consistent with the data-free prior \mathcal{N}(0, I) at which the forward process ends, as the terminal condition above established. Real data is only approximately standardized (DDPM scales pixel values to [-1, 1] [2], and pixels are correlated), so exact preservation is an idealization, and these two properties are what the design delivers in practice.
The variance of the perturbation kernel behaves differently. With x_0 fixed, the data term \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0 is a constant and contributes nothing; only the injected noise does, so Eq. 41 has

\operatorname{Var}[x_t \mid x_0] = (1 - \bar\alpha(t))\, I

which is not constant but grows toward I as more noise is added. So “Variance-Preserving” is a statement about the marginal distribution, not the perturbation kernel at fixed x_0.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
8.2 Fokker-Planck equation
We state the result for an SDE on \mathbb{R}^d first, then specialize to the VP-SDE. The state is a vector, and its density is coupled across coordinates through the data, so the equation is derived in d dimensions rather than one coordinate at a time.
We write the process as X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d (capital, to mark it as the random state) with realized value x, the argument of its density p(x, t). Let it solve

dX_t = \mu(X_t, t)\, dt + \sigma(t)\, dW_t

with drift \mu(x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^d, a diffusion coefficient \sigma(t) that is the same for each coordinate and does not depend on the state, and W_t = (W^1_t, \dots, W^d_t) a d-dimensional Brownian motion, whose components are independent standard Brownian motions. The VP-SDE has this form.
Assume X_t has a density p(x, t) that is twice continuously differentiable in x and continuously differentiable in t, that \mu and \sigma are continuous, and that each \mu_k\, p is continuously differentiable in x. The density then satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation [68], [69]

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma(t)^2\, \Delta_x p}
\tag{45}
Here the divergence and the Laplacian are, respectively,

\nabla_x \cdot v = \sum_k \partial v_k / \partial x_k \qquad \Delta_x p = \sum_k \partial^2 p / \partial x_k^2

In one dimension the equation reads,

\partial_t p = -\partial_x(\mu\, p) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \partial_x^2 p

Setting \sigma \equiv 0 leaves the continuity equation of a deterministic flow,

\partial_t p + \nabla_x \cdot (\mu\, p) = 0

For the VP-SDE, with \mu = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x and \sigma = \sqrt{\beta(t)}, the equation reads

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \nabla_x \cdot \big(x\, p\big) + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \Delta_x p}
\tag{46}
The second-order term has the same origin as the second-order term in the Black-Scholes PDE: it is the consequence of (dW)^2 = dt.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
8.3 Derivation of the Fokker-Planck equation
We derive both Eq. 45 and Eq. 46 now (see also [68]). The strategy is the weak formulation: rather than analyzing p(x, t) directly, we test it against an arbitrary smooth \varphi, take expectations to eliminate the dW_t term, then integrate by parts to move every derivative off \varphi and onto \mu p and p, leaving an identity that must hold for all \varphi, which is the PDE.
Step 1 — Itô on a smooth test function:
Let \varphi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} be a smooth function with compact support (i.e. \varphi \equiv 0 outside some bounded region), so \varphi and all its derivatives vanish at the integration boundaries. Itô’s lemma Eq. 13 is stated for a scalar state. For a state in \mathbb{R}^d driven by the d independent components of W_t, its counterpart, derived in §A.8, reads, for f(x, t) twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t,

df = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \cdot \nabla_x f + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma(t)^2\, \Delta_x f\Big)\, dt + \sigma(t)\, \nabla_x f \cdot dW_t

It is the scalar lemma with the first derivative replaced by the gradient \nabla_x f and the second by the Laplacian \Delta_x f. A Taylor expansion in several coordinates also produces products of increments of two different components, and these vanish by the rule dW^i\, dW^j = \delta_{ij}\, dt of §A.8.1, so only the diagonal second derivatives survive.
Applying it to \varphi(X_t) (no explicit t-dependence in \varphi),

d\varphi(X_t) = \Big[\mu(X_t, t) \cdot \nabla_x \varphi(X_t) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma(t)^2\, \Delta_x \varphi(X_t)\Big]\, dt + \sigma(t)\, \nabla_x \varphi(X_t) \cdot dW_t

Step 2 — take expectations:
This differential is shorthand for its integral form; integrating from 0 to t,

\varphi(X_t) - \varphi(X_0) = \int_0^t \Big[\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \Delta_x \varphi\Big]\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma\, \nabla_x \varphi \cdot dW_s

Taking expectations of both sides,

\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] - \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] = \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^t \Big[\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \Delta_x \varphi\Big]\, ds + \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^t \sigma\, \nabla_x \varphi \cdot dW_s

The last term is a sum of d Itô integrals, \sum_k \int_0^t \sigma\, \partial \varphi / \partial x_k\, dW^k_s, each with zero expectation by the martingale property proved for adapted integrands in §A.4; each integrand is bounded, since \varphi has compact support and \sigma is continuous, so the square-integrability that property requires holds. Dropping it,

\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] - \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] = \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^t \Big[\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \Delta_x \varphi\Big]\, ds

Interchanging the expectation and the time integral, which Fubini’s theorem permits because the integrand is bounded on [0, t],

\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] - \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] = \int_0^t \mathbb{E}\Big[\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \Delta_x \varphi\Big]\, ds

Differentiating in t (the lower limit and \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_0)] are constant),

\frac{d}{dt}\, \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] = \mathbb{E}\Big[\mu(X_t, t) \cdot \nabla_x \varphi(X_t) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma(t)^2\, \Delta_x \varphi(X_t)\Big]

Writing each expectation as an integral against the density p(x, t),

\frac{d}{dt}\!\int \varphi(x)\, p(x, t)\, dx = \int \Big[\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \Delta_x \varphi\Big] p\, dx

Since \varphi is fixed and compactly supported and \partial p / \partial t is continuous, differentiation passes under the integral on the left, giving

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = \int \Big[\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \Delta_x \varphi\Big] p\, dx

Step 3 — integrate by parts:
The goal is to move the derivatives off \varphi and onto \mu p and p. The tool is integration by parts, whose full form in one variable over \mathbb{R} is

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u'\, v\, dx \;=\; \big[\, u\, v \,\big]_{-\infty}^{\infty} \;-\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u\, v'\, dx

In every application below, u is \varphi or one of its derivatives, which vanishes outside a bounded region, so the boundary term is 0. In d dimensions the rule acts one coordinate at a time. Writing \partial_k = \partial / \partial x_k, for u compactly supported and continuously differentiable and v continuously differentiable, integrating in x_k first with the one-variable rule and then over the remaining coordinates by Fubini’s theorem gives

\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \partial_k u\; v\, dx = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} u\; \partial_k v\, dx

Splitting the right side of Step 2 into its two terms,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = \int \big(\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi\big)\, p\, dx + \int \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \big(\Delta_x \varphi\big)\, p\, dx

Substituting the component forms

\mu \cdot \nabla_x \varphi = \sum_k \mu_k\, \partial_k \varphi \qquad \Delta_x \varphi = \sum_k \partial_k^2 \varphi

into the previous line,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = \sum_k \int \partial_k \varphi\; \mu_k\, p\, dx + \sum_k \int \partial_k^2 \varphi\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, p\, dx

Drift term:
Applying the rule to each term of the first sum, with u = \varphi and v = \mu_k\, p,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = -\sum_k \int \varphi\; \partial_k\big(\mu_k\, p\big)\, dx + \sum_k \int \partial_k^2 \varphi\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, p\, dx

Recognizing the divergence

\sum_k \partial_k(\mu_k\, p) = \nabla_x \cdot (\mu\, p)

in the previous line,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = -\int \varphi\, \nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big)\, dx + \sum_k \int \partial_k^2 \varphi\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, p\, dx

Diffusion term:
The second sum carries second derivatives of \varphi, so apply the rule twice. First, to each of its terms, with u = \partial_k \varphi and v = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, p,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = -\int \varphi\, \nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big)\, dx - \sum_k \int \partial_k \varphi\; \partial_k\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, p\big)\, dx

Applying it again with

u = \varphi \qquad v = \partial_k\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, p\big)

gives

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = -\int \varphi\, \nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big)\, dx + \sum_k \int \varphi\; \partial_k^2\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, p\big)\, dx

As \sigma(t) is independent of x,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = -\int \varphi\, \nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big)\, dx + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 \sum_k \int \varphi\; \partial_k^2 p\, dx

Recognizing \sum_k \partial_k^2 p = \Delta_x p,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = -\int \varphi\, \nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big)\, dx + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 \int \varphi\; \Delta_x p\, dx

Collecting under one integral,

\int \varphi\, \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\, dx = \int \varphi\, \Big[-\nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \Delta_x p\Big]\, dx

Step 4 — match integrands:
Since this identity holds for every smooth, compactly supported test function \varphi on \mathbb{R}^d, the two integrands must agree pointwise. This is the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations [70]: if \int h(x)\, \varphi(x)\, dx = 0 for each such \varphi, then h \equiv 0, since otherwise a bump function \varphi concentrated where h \neq 0 would make the integral nonzero. Thus, matching the integrands,

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot \big(\mu\, p\big) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma(t)^2\, \Delta_x p}

which is Eq. 45. \square

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 8.4 Specialization of the Fokker-Planck equation to the VP-SDE
text:
8.4 Specialization of the Fokker-Planck equation to the VP-SDE
Substituting \mu(x, t) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x and \sigma(t)^2 = \beta(t) into the Fokker-Planck equation Eq. 45,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot \Big[\big(-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x\big)\, p\Big] + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \Delta_x p

As \beta(t) is independent of x, it leaves the divergence,

\boxed{\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \nabla_x \cdot \big(x\, p\big) + \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, \Delta_x p}

which is Eq. 46. \square
The Fokker-Planck perspective will become essential in post #3 when we discuss the reverse-time SDE, because the reverse process depends on \nabla_x \log p(x, t), which depends on the density p itself, not on simulated paths.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 10.1 Which room you walked in from
text:
10.1 Which room you walked in from
This correspondence (one lemma, one second-order correction, behind both option pricing and the diffusion forward process) is worth your effort, because it reads differently depending on where you come from. If you came up through machine learning, the finance side is a ready-made vocabulary for objects you reinvented; if you came up through quantitative finance, the diffusion side is, under new names, machinery you already hold. Pick your reading below.

10.1.1 For the machine-learning practitioner
The quantitative finance vocabulary is worth a week of your time. Almost every object you meet on the diffusion side has a quant name and a history fifty years older: the VP-SDE is a time-dependent OU process, the same mean-reverting dynamics the Vasicek model [9] uses for interest rates; the closed-form perturbation kernel comes from the same integrating-factor transform we used to solve OU; and the -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 volatility drag in the GBM log-return (Eq. 15) is the same Itô correction appearing as the \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\,\Delta_x p diffusion term in the forward process’s Fokker-Planck equation (Eq. 46). What carries over is not any single formula but the habit it trains: moving fluently between an SDE and the PDE for its density, and between one sample path and the distribution it is sampled from.


10.1.2 For the quant
Diffusion models are closer than they look: re-application, not a pivot. If you can hedge an option, you already own the hard part: Itô’s lemma, the drift-plus-diffusion split, and the (dW)^2 = dt rule that keeps the second-order term alive. A diffusion model’s forward process is a linear SDE you would have recognized on sight, and deriving its perturbation kernel uses the same integrating-factor transform that solved OU in §2.4.2. What is genuinely new is built on top of the calculus, not underneath it: the question has changed from pricing a claim to generating a sample, and a neural network is introduced to learn one quantity classical pricing never needed, the score \nabla_x \log p. The machinery you would reach for is already in your hands.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
10.2 What comes next
I stopped here, deliberately, at the forward process, the easy direction: noise is added, with no need to train a model, and every conditional x_t \mid x_0 is a closed-form Gaussian. Generation is the hard direction. It must learn to undo that noise, and the distribution it needs is no longer a simple Gaussian but the unknown data distribution. It follows the dynamics backward in time, step by step, from pure noise to a sample. That reversal is the subject of posts #2 and #3: the score \nabla_x \log p that drives it (post #2), the one quantity the forward analysis here never had to compute, and Anderson’s reverse-time SDE [72] (post #3).
Writing the forward process as an SDE was the first step. In post #3 that viewpoint becomes a general framework, the single equation that unifies the two lineages of diffusion modeling, built with the machinery you now hold: Itô’s lemma and (dW)^2 = dt.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
Appendix

A.1 Random walks and the Brownian limit
The Definition called Brownian motion the “continuum limit of a random walk.” This appendix makes that precise: it defines a random walk, applies the diffusive scaling, and shows the rescaled walk reproduces every defining property of Brownian motion in the limit.
The random walk: Let \xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots be independent, identically distributed steps with mean 0 and variance 1 (for concreteness, \pm 1 coin flips, though any such distribution works). The random walk after n steps is the partial sum

R_n \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \xi_k, \qquad R_0 = 0

By independence its variance is \operatorname{Var}(R_n) = n: the walk spreads like \sqrt{n}.
The diffusive scaling: To pack N steps into one unit of time we rescale time by 1/N and space by 1/\sqrt{N}. The \sqrt{N} is forced by the variance growing like the step count. We define the continuous, piecewise-linear process

W^{(N)}_t \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\, R_{\lfloor N t \rfloor}, \qquad t \in [0, 1]

(linearly interpolated between steps). As N \to \infty the steps shrink like 1/\sqrt{N} and arrive N to a unit interval, the limit the Definition invoked.
Matching Brownian motion’s properties: We verify the rescaled walk reproduces the four defining properties in the limit.
Starts at zero:
W^{(N)}_0 = R_0/\sqrt{N} = 0 for each N, property 1, exactly.
Gaussian at each time:
Fixing t > 0 and writing n = \lfloor N t \rfloor, we have

W^{(N)}_t = \frac{R_n}{\sqrt{N}}

Multiplying and dividing by \sqrt{n},

W^{(N)}_t = \sqrt{\tfrac{n}{N}}\;\cdot\;\frac{R_n}{\sqrt{n}}

Since n/N \to t and, by the central limit theorem (CLT), R_n/\sqrt{n} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1),

W^{(N)}_t \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \sqrt{t}\,\cdot\,\mathcal{N}(0, 1) \;=\; \mathcal{N}(0, t)

matching W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t), the s = 0 case of property 2.
Independent, stationary increments:
At grid times s = j/N < t = m/N, the increment W^{(N)}_t - W^{(N)}_s is assembled from the steps \xi_k with j < k \le m, a block disjoint from the steps forming W^{(N)}_s, and disjoint blocks of i.i.d. steps are independent (property 3); at non-grid times the linear interpolation shares at most one straddling step, an overlap that vanishes as N \to \infty, and the same CLT argument applied to that block gives

W^{(N)}_t - W^{(N)}_s \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, t - s)

a distribution depending only on t - s, which completes property 2 and supplies its stationarity.
Continuous paths:
Each W^{(N)} is continuous by construction. That the limit has continuous sample paths, and that convergence holds for whole paths and not merely for fixed-time marginals, is Donsker’s invariance principle, the functional central limit theorem [7]: the distribution of W^{(N)} on the space of continuous functions converges to the distribution of standard Brownian motion. Property 4, and the full process-level statement, follow.
All four properties hold in the limit: Brownian motion is the diffusive-scaling limit of a random walk. The 1/\sqrt{N} space scaling set against the 1/N time scaling is the same \sqrt{\Delta t}-against-\Delta t balance that, read forward, yields the quadratic-variation identity (dW)^2 = dt (Eq. 3).


A.2 Solving the Black-Scholes PDE: heat-equation transform sketch
This appendix sketches the standard route from the Black-Scholes PDE Eq. 19 to the closed-form formula Eq. 27. The procedure converts the Black-Scholes PDE into the constant-coefficient heat equation, solves it with the Gaussian heat kernel, and transforms back. The treatment follows Wilmott, Howison and Dewynne [15].
Step 1 — change of variables:
We introduce the dimensionless coordinates

x \;=\; \log\!\big(S/K\big), \qquad \tau \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, (T - t)

and factor out an exponential prefactor,

V(S, t) \;=\; K\, e^{-\alpha x \,-\, \beta \tau}\, u(x, \tau)

with constants \alpha, \beta to be chosen below (local to this appendix, unrelated to the DDPM rate \beta(t) of Part 7). The terminal time t = T corresponds to \tau = 0.
Step 2 — choose \alpha, \beta to collapse the equation:
Substituting into Eq. 19 and computing the partials gives, with the abbreviation k := 2r/\sigma^2, a PDE for u(x, \tau) that still carries first- and zeroth-order terms:

\frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} \;=\; \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \;+\; \big[(k - 1) - 2\alpha\big]\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \;+\; \big[\alpha^2 + (1 - k)\alpha - k + \beta\big]\, u

Setting both lower-order coefficients to zero, (k-1) - 2\alpha = 0 and \alpha^2 + (1-k)\alpha - k + \beta = 0, forces

\alpha \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,(k - 1), \qquad \beta \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4}\,(k + 1)^2

What remains is the dimensionless heat equation

\frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} \;=\; \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R} \times (0, \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 T]

Step 3 — initial condition:
At \tau = 0 (i.e. t = T), the call payoff \max(S - K, 0) = K\, \max(e^x - 1, 0) becomes

u(x, 0) \;=\; \max\!\Big(e^{(\alpha + 1) x} \,-\, e^{\alpha x},\;\, 0\Big)

nonzero for x > 0.
Step 4 — solve via the heat kernel:
The solution of \partial_\tau u = \partial_{xx} u with initial data u(\cdot, 0) is the convolution

u(x, \tau) \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi \tau}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u(y, 0)\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - y)^2}{4\tau}\right) dy

Step 5 — evaluate the two Gaussian-tail integrals:
The initial data has two exponential terms, restricted to y > 0. Each contributes a Gaussian-times-half-line integral; completing the square in the exponent reduces each to a standard-normal CDF N(\cdot). The arithmetic yields

u(x, \tau) \;=\; e^{(\alpha + 1) x \,+\, (\alpha + 1)^2 \tau}\, N(d_1)
\;-\; e^{\alpha x \,+\, \alpha^2 \tau}\, N(d_2)

with

d_1 = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2\tau}} + (\alpha + 1)\sqrt{2\tau} \qquad d_2 = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2\tau}} + \alpha\sqrt{2\tau}

each affine in x with slope 1/\sqrt{2\tau}; the back-transform in Step 6 turns them into the familiar d_1, d_2 of Eq. 27.
Step 6 — transform back to (S, t):
We multiply through by the prefactor K\, e^{-\alpha x - \beta \tau}. The exponential terms in u pair against e^{-\alpha x - \beta \tau} to yield S and K\, e^{-r(T - t)} factors respectively. Substituting x = \log(S/K), \tau = \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2(T - t) in d_1, d_2 produces

d_1 \;=\; \frac{\log(S/K) + (r + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)(T - t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T - t}}, \qquad
d_2 \;=\; d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T - t}

and the option value collapses to

V(S, t) \;=\; S\, N(d_1) \;-\; K\, e^{-r(T - t)}\, N(d_2)

which is Eq. 27. (Two computations are omitted from this sketch and are standard: substituting the Step 1 ansatz into Eq. 19 to obtain the constant-coefficient equation for u, and completing the square in each of the two half-line Gaussian integrals of Step 5 to reach the two normal CDFs. Both are carried out in full in [15].)
Alternative route (Feynman-Kac / risk-neutral expectation): The same formula can be derived without solving a PDE. The Feynman-Kac formula identifies the Black-Scholes PDE solution with a conditional expectation:

V(S, t) \;=\; e^{-r(T-t)}\, \mathbb{E}^Q\!\Big[\,\max(S_T - K,\, 0)\;\Big|\; S_t = S\,\Big]

where the stock evolves under the risk-neutral measure Q (under which the drift is replaced by r; the change of measure is constructed via Girsanov’s theorem). Under Q, the log-return \log(S_T / S_t) is normal, an immediate consequence of applying Itô’s lemma to \log S as in §2.4.1, but with \mu \to r. Computing the expectation by direct lognormal integration reproduces the same expression, the route followed in Hull’s chapter 15 appendix [73], with N(d_2) now interpretable as the risk-neutral exercise probability Q(S_T > K) [74]; N(d_1) is not a Q-probability but the option’s delta \partial V / \partial S. Girsanov’s theorem is developed in full in P3:§A.3, with complete proofs in [7], [68]. That appendix serves the series twice: it gives an alternative, measure-theoretic route to the Black-Scholes formula, and it supplies the change of measure behind the reverse-time SDE of the diffusion posts.


A.3 The self-financing hedging portfolio
The hedging argument of §3.6 holds the hedge ratio fixed over each instant. In practice \Delta_t = \partial V / \partial S changes with the stock price, and rebalancing the stock position adds terms to the change in the portfolio’s value. This appendix computes those terms with the Itô product rule, then shows that a cash account absorbs them exactly when the hedge is self-financing, so the relation the main derivation used holds without approximation.
For the portfolio \Pi_t = V - \Delta_t S_t, §3.6 wrote d\Pi_t = dV - \Delta_t\,dS_t. With a time-varying hedge ratio, the change in the product \Delta_t S_t over dt is the product of the incremented factors minus the product itself,

d(\Delta_t S_t) \;=\; (\Delta_t + d\Delta_t)(S_t + dS_t) \;-\; \Delta_t S_t

Expanding the product,

d(\Delta_t S_t) \;=\; \Delta_t S_t \;+\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;+\; S_t\,d\Delta_t \;+\; d\Delta_t\,dS_t \;-\; \Delta_t S_t

Cancelling \Delta_t S_t, which leaves the Itô product rule,

d(\Delta_t S_t) \;=\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;+\; S_t\,d\Delta_t \;+\; d\Delta_t\,dS_t

The last term survives because both \Delta_t and S_t carry a dW term, so their product is of order dt by (dW)^2 = dt (Eq. 3).
Differencing the marked value \Pi_t = V - \Delta_t S_t, the value of the option and stock positions without a cash account,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV \;-\; d(\Delta_t S_t)

Substituting the product rule,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV \;-\; \big(\Delta_t\,dS_t + S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big)

Distributing the minus sign,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV \;-\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;-\; S_t\,d\Delta_t \;-\; d\Delta_t\,dS_t

which has two terms beyond what the main derivation used, -S_t\,d\Delta_t - d\Delta_t\,dS_t. They drop out once the hedge is run as a self-financing strategy rather than bought and held.
Make the cash explicit: hold the option, short \Delta_t shares, and a risk-free cash account C_t earning rate r,

\Pi_t \;=\; V_t \;-\; \Delta_t S_t \;+\; C_t

Self-financing means every rebalance is paid from within the portfolio, with no external cash in or out. Increasing the short by d\Delta_t releases S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t of cash, so

dC_t \;=\; \underbrace{r\,C_t\,dt}_{\text{interest}} \;+\; \underbrace{S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t}_{\text{cash from re-hedging}}

Taking the differential of the portfolio value,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; d(\Delta_t S_t) \;+\; dC_t

Substituting the Itô product rule derived above,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; \big(\Delta_t\,dS_t + S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big) \;+\; dC_t

Substituting the cash-account differential

dC_t = r\,C_t\,dt + \big(S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big)

into the previous line,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; \big(\Delta_t\,dS_t + S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big) \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt \;+\; \big(S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t\big)

The re-hedging terms S_t\,d\Delta_t + d\Delta_t\,dS_t cancel,

d\Pi_t \;=\; dV_t \;-\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt

The no-arbitrage condition d\Pi_t = r\, \Pi_t\, dt applies to this riskless portfolio. Substituting \Pi_t = V_t - \Delta_t S_t + C_t on the right,

dV_t \;-\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt \;=\; r\,\big(V_t - \Delta_t S_t\big)\,dt \;+\; r\,C_t\,dt

Cancelling the r\,C_t\,dt terms on both sides,

dV_t \;-\; \Delta_t\,dS_t \;=\; r\,\big(V_t - \Delta_t S_t\big)\,dt

This is the relation the main derivation used, and it holds for each cash balance C_t. The -S_t\,d\Delta_t - d\Delta_t\,dS_t terms are not neglected; they are paid for by the cash leg.


A.4 The Itô integral, constructed
The main text (§1.8) used the fact that an Itô integral of a deterministic integrand is Gaussian, with a variance fixed by the Itô isometry. This appendix constructs the integral \int_0^T H_s\, dW_s for adapted, random integrands and proves the isometry it rests on, following Itô’s original construction [75], [76]. The non-anticipating requirement invoked below is made precise in §A.5.
Step 1 — simple integrands:
Call H simple if it is piecewise constant on a partition 0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = T, with H_s = \xi_i for s \in [t_i, t_{i+1}) and each \xi_i square-integrable and measurable with respect to the information available at t_i (it may depend on the path up to t_i, never beyond). For such H define the integral as the obvious sum:

\int_0^T H_s\, dW_s \;:=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \xi_i \,\big(W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i}\big)

Each increment \Delta W_i = W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i} is independent of \xi_i (which is fixed by time t_i), with mean 0 and variance t_{i+1} - t_i.
Step 2 — the Itô isometry for simple integrands:
Taking the expected square and expanding,

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i^2\, (\Delta W_i)^2\big] + \sum_{i \ne j} \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i\, \xi_j\, \Delta W_i\, \Delta W_j\big]

The cross terms vanish because increments over disjoint intervals are independent and mean-zero, and \xi_i is known by t_i,

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i^2\, (\Delta W_i)^2\big]

Substituting \mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_i)^2] = \Delta t_i (\Delta W_i independent of \xi_i),

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}\big[\xi_i^2\big]\,\Delta t_i

Recognizing the right side as the integral of the simple process H^2,

\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\sum_i \xi_i\, \Delta W_i\Big)^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^T H_s^2\, ds

That is the Itô isometry.

\boxed{\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\textstyle\int_0^T H_s\, dW_s\Big)^2\Big] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^T H_s^2\, ds\;}
\tag{47}
The integral preserves the L^2 norm.
Step 3 — extension to general integrands:
For each adapted H with \mathbb{E}\!\int_0^T H_s^2\, ds < \infty, we choose simple processes H^{(n)} \to H in L^2. By the isometry Eq. 47 the integrals \int H^{(n)}\, dW form a Cauchy sequence in L^2(\Omega), which is complete, so they converge to a limit that does not depend on the approximating sequence. We define \int_0^T H_s\, dW_s as that limit. The isometry passes to the limit, so it holds for each such H.
Step 4 — the integral is a martingale:
For simple H and s \le t,

\mathbb{E}\big[\int_0^t H\, dW \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big] = \int_0^s H\, dW

where \mathcal{F}_s is the information available at time s, made precise in §A.5. The identity holds because the increments after s have conditional mean zero. The property survives the L^2 limit, so M_t := \int_0^t H_s\, dW_s is a martingale with \mathbb{E}[M_t] = 0: it has no drift. This is the precise sense in which a dW term carries no trend.
Step 5 — connection to the main text:
When H_s = h(s) is deterministic, the integral is a limit of sums of independent Gaussians, hence itself Gaussian (§A.6), with mean 0 and, by Eq. 47, variance \int_0^T h(s)^2\, ds. That is the statement used in §1.8. The infinitesimal shadow of the isometry, \mathbb{E}[(dW)^2] = dt, is the (dW)^2 = dt rule of the main text; quadratic variation is the same fact seen pathwise.
A construction at this level of detail is standard; see [7], [68].


A.5 Filtrations, adapted processes, and martingales
The two constructions above rely on a notion of “information available at time t” and on the integrand not peeking into the future. This appendix collects that scaffolding and makes precise the phrase used throughout, that a dW term is a martingale and so carries no drift.
Filtration: On a probability space (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}), a filtration (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0} is an increasing family of \sigma-algebras, \mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t for s \le t. Read \mathcal{F}_t as everything observable up to time t. For Brownian motion the natural choice is \mathcal{F}_t = \sigma(W_s : s \le t), the information generated by the path so far.
Adapted / non-anticipating: A process H_t is adapted if H_t is \mathcal{F}_t-measurable for each t. Its value at t depends only on information up to t, never on the future. This is the requirement placed on Itô integrands in §A.4, and it is not cosmetic: evaluating the integrand at the left endpoint t_i of each interval, so it cannot see the increment \Delta W_i it multiplies, is what makes the cross terms vanish, delivers the Itô isometry, and yields a martingale. Evaluating at the midpoint instead gives the Stratonovich integral [77], with an extra drift term and the ordinary chain rule, a different calculus.
Martingale: An adapted, integrable process M_t is a martingale if

\mathbb{E}[\, M_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s \,] = M_s \qquad (s \le t)

i.e. the best forecast of a future value, given the present, is the present value, no expected drift. Brownian motion is a martingale, and by §A.4 so is the Itô integral \int_0^t H_s\, dW_s. (Conditional expectation \mathbb{E}[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_s\,] is the L^2-orthogonal projection onto \mathcal{F}_s-measurable variables, the least-squares forecast given the present.)
Why this underlies Itô’s lemma: Itô’s lemma writes a transformed process as

df(X_t, t) = \underbrace{\big(\partial_t f + \mu\, \partial_x f + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, \partial_{xx} f\big)\, dt}_{\text{drift}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sigma\, \partial_x f\, dW_t}_{\text{martingale part}}

The dW term is a martingale increment: conditioned on the present it has mean zero. Taking expectations therefore annihilates it and leaves only the drift, the step used (often silently) whenever the main text computes a mean, derives a moment equation, or passes from an SDE to the Fokker-Planck equation. “A martingale has no drift” is the statement that the dW part contributes nothing to the expected change.
These three notions (filtration, adapted integrand, martingale) are the measure-theoretic scaffolding beneath the heuristic (dW)^2 = dt calculus of the main text. For complete treatments see [7], [68].


A.6 Gaussian limits in L^2
§1.8 built the Itô integral as an L^2 limit of Gaussian partition sums and asserted that the limit is itself Gaussian. This appendix proves that closure fact.
Claim: Let X_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \sigma_n^2) and suppose X_n \to X in L^2, i.e. \mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2] \to 0. Then \mu_n and \sigma_n^2 converge, and X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) with \mu = \lim_n \mu_n and \sigma^2 = \lim_n \sigma_n^2.
Step 1 — the moments pass to the limit:
By linearity of expectation,

|\mu_n - \mathbb{E}[X]| \;=\; \big|\mathbb{E}[X_n - X]\big|

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

\mathbb{E}|YZ| \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[Y^2]}\,\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[Z^2]}

applied with Z = 1,

|\mu_n - \mathbb{E}[X]| \;\le\; \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2]}

By the L^2 hypothesis the right-hand side tends to zero,

|\mu_n - \mathbb{E}[X]| \;\xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;}\; 0

so \mu_n \to \mu := \mathbb{E}[X]. For the second moment, expanding X_n = (X_n - X) + X,

\mathbb{E}[X_n^2] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2] \;+\; 2\,\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)\,X] \;+\; \mathbb{E}[X^2]

The first term vanishes by assumption, and the cross term is bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz,

|\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)\,X]| \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2]}\,\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]} \to 0

so \mathbb{E}[X_n^2] \to \mathbb{E}[X^2] and therefore

\sigma_n^2 = \mathbb{E}[X_n^2] - \mu_n^2 \to \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X) =: \sigma^2

Step 2 — X_n \to X in distribution:
L^2 convergence implies convergence in probability. Since

\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y| > \epsilon\}} \le Y^2 / \epsilon^2

pointwise, taking expectations gives

\mathbb{P}\big(|X_n - X| > \epsilon\big) \;\le\; \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X_n - X)^2]}{\epsilon^2} \;\xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;}\; 0

Convergence in probability in turn implies convergence of the distribution functions at continuity points: the event \{X_n \le x\} is contained in \{X \le x + \epsilon\} \cup \{|X_n - X| > \epsilon\}, and \{X \le x - \epsilon\} is contained in \{X_n \le x\} \cup \{|X_n - X| > \epsilon\}, so

\mathbb{P}(X \le x - \epsilon) - \mathbb{P}\big(|X_n - X| > \epsilon\big) \;\le\; \mathbb{P}(X_n \le x) \;\le\; \mathbb{P}(X \le x + \epsilon) + \mathbb{P}\big(|X_n - X| > \epsilon\big)

Letting n \to \infty and then \epsilon \to 0, at each continuity point x of the distribution function of X, \mathbb{P}(X_n \le x) \to \mathbb{P}(X \le x).
Step 3 — identify the limit distribution:
Suppose \sigma > 0. For each n large enough that \sigma_n > 0, which is all but finitely many since \sigma_n \to \sigma > 0, the distribution function of X_n is N\!\big((x - \mu_n)/\sigma_n\big), with N(\cdot) the standard normal CDF of §3.7.1. Since \mu_n \to \mu and \sigma_n \to \sigma > 0 (Step 1) and N is continuous,

N\!\left(\frac{x - \mu_n}{\sigma_n}\right) \;\xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;}\; N\!\left(\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right) \quad \forall x

Step 2 gives the same sequence the limit \mathbb{P}(X \le x) at continuity points, and limits are unique, so

\mathbb{P}(X \le x) = N\!\big((x - \mu)/\sigma\big)

at each continuity point of the left side; both sides are non-decreasing and the right side is continuous everywhere, so the two agree for each x. That is, X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).
The degenerate case \sigma = 0:
Step 1 gives \operatorname{Var}(X) = 0 and \mathbb{E}[X] = \mu, so X = \mu almost surely, the constant limit, consistent with reading \mathcal{N}(\mu, 0) as a point mass.
Applied to §1.8: the partition sums are Gaussian with \mu_n = 0 and

\sigma_n^2 = \sum_i g(t_i)^2\, \Delta t_i \to \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds

They converge in L^2 to the integral, so the integral is \mathcal{N}\big(0, \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds\big), which is Eq. 7. \square
For the general theory see [68].


A.7 Composing the forward transitions: the discrete perturbation kernel
The Definitions of Part 7 assert that composing the forward transitions

p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1},\ \beta_i I\big)

and marginalizing out the intermediate states yields the discrete perturbation kernel of DDPM [2],

p(x_i \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_i)\, I\big)

This appendix derives it by induction on i, working in the reparameterized form

x_i = \sqrt{\alpha_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i

with \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) independent across steps.
Base case i = 1:
The kernel is the first transition,

x_1 = \sqrt{\alpha_1}\, x_0 + \sqrt{\beta_1}\, \epsilon_1

and since \bar\alpha_1 = \alpha_1 and \beta_1 = 1 - \alpha_1 = 1 - \bar\alpha_1, this is the claimed form,

x_1 = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_1}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_1}\, \epsilon_1

Induction step:
Assume the claim at step i-1,

x_{i-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, \bar\epsilon

where \bar\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) collects the noise of steps 1, \dots, i-1 and is therefore independent of the fresh step-i noise \epsilon_i. Substituting the induction hypothesis into the reparameterized transition,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i}\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, \bar\epsilon\right) + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i

Expanding,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha_i (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1})}\, \bar\epsilon \;+\; \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i

Combining the two independent zero-mean Gaussian noise terms into a single \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) (a linear combination of independent Gaussians is Gaussian and their variances add, the fact used for the partition sums of §1.8),

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha_i (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}) + \beta_i}\, \epsilon

Substituting \beta_i = 1 - \alpha_i,

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{\alpha_i (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}) + 1 - \alpha_i}\, \epsilon

Expanding the product under the square root (the \pm\alpha_i cancel),

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{1 - \alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, \epsilon

Recognizing the cumulative product \bar\alpha_i = \alpha_i \bar\alpha_{i-1},

x_i \;=\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 \;+\; \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\, \epsilon

which is the claimed form at step i, so the induction closes and

p(x_i \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_i)\, I\big)

holds for each i. \square


A.8 Itô calculus in d dimensions
Itô’s lemma Eq. 13 transforms a scalar state driven by one Brownian motion. Generative models act on vectors. The Fokker-Planck derivation of §8 applies the lemma to a test function of every coordinate of the state, and the d-dimensional Girsanov theorem of the later posts applies it to a function of a scalar process driven by several independent Brownian motions. This appendix develops what those uses need: the multiplication rule for the increments of two different Brownian components, then Itô’s lemma for a vector state, then the special case the series uses.
Throughout, W_t = (W^1_t, \dots, W^m_t) is an m-dimensional Brownian motion, whose components are independent standard Brownian motions, and X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d solves

dX_t = \mu(X_t, t)\, dt + G(X_t, t)\, dW_t

with drift \mu(x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^d and a d \times m diffusion matrix G(x, t). The derivation below uses \mu and G only through their values at time t, so it and the lemma it gives hold verbatim for an Itô process whose coefficients \mu_t \in \mathbb{R}^d and G_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times m} are adapted processes rather than functions of the state, the form the Girsanov theorem of the later posts uses.
In coordinates,

dX^k_t = \mu_k\, dt + \sum_{i=1}^{m} G_{ki}\, dW^i_t


A.8.1 The cross rule
The rule (dW)^2 = dt of Eq. 3 concerns a single Brownian motion. Itô’s lemma for a function of several coordinates also meets products dW^i\, dW^j of the increments of two different components. Those products vanish, which completes the multiplication rules to

\boxed{dW^i\, dW^j = \delta_{ij}\, dt}
\tag{48}
with \delta_{ij} the Kronecker delta, equal to 1 if i = j and 0 otherwise. The diagonal case i = j is Eq. 3 applied to the component W^i. For i \neq j the content is again an integral statement. We take a partition \Pi of [0, t] and write \Delta W^i_k = W^i_{t_{k+1}} - W^i_{t_k} for the increment of component i over the k-th interval. Let f be a bounded, Riemann-integrable deterministic weight on [0, t]. Then

\int_0^t f(s)\, dW^i_s\, dW^j_s \;:=\; \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(t_k)\, \Delta W^i_k\, \Delta W^j_k \;=\; 0

with convergence in L^2. The proof is the mean-and-variance argument of Eq. 4. We write S = \sum_k f(t_k)\, \Delta W^i_k\, \Delta W^j_k for the partition sum.
Step 1 — the mean:
By linearity of expectation,

\mathbb{E}[S] = \sum_k f(t_k)\, \mathbb{E}\big[\Delta W^i_k\, \Delta W^j_k\big]

Substituting the value

\mathbb{E}\big[\Delta W^i_k\, \Delta W^j_k\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\Delta W^i_k\big]\, \mathbb{E}\big[\Delta W^j_k\big] = 0

into the previous line, since the two components are independent and each increment has mean zero,

\mathbb{E}[S] = 0

Step 2 — the variance:
The summands are independent across k, because increments over non-overlapping intervals are independent, so variances add,

\operatorname{Var}(S) = \sum_k \operatorname{Var}\big(f(t_k)\, \Delta W^i_k\, \Delta W^j_k\big)

Taking each deterministic factor out squared,

\operatorname{Var}(S) = \sum_k f(t_k)^2\, \operatorname{Var}\big(\Delta W^i_k\, \Delta W^j_k\big)

Substituting the value

\operatorname{Var}\big(\Delta W^i_k\, \Delta W^j_k\big) = \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W^i_k)^2\big]\, \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W^j_k)^2\big] = (\Delta t_k)^2

into the previous line, since the product has mean zero by Step 1 and its two factors are independent, each with second moment \Delta t_k,

\operatorname{Var}(S) = \sum_k f(t_k)^2\, (\Delta t_k)^2

Bounding f(t_k)^2 \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2,

\operatorname{Var}(S) \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2 \sum_k (\Delta t_k)^2

Step 3 — shrink the mesh:
Bounding \sum_k (\Delta t_k)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t by the mesh,

\operatorname{Var}(S) \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\operatorname{Var}(S) \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

Step 4 — conclude:
The partition sum has mean zero and a variance vanishing as the mesh refines, so it converges to zero in L^2, since

\mathbb{E}[S^2] = \operatorname{Var}(S) + \mathbb{E}[S]^2

Hence

\int_0^t f(s)\, dW^i_s\, dW^j_s = 0, \qquad i \neq j

whose differential form, together with the diagonal case, is

\boxed{dW^i\, dW^j = \delta_{ij}\, dt}

which is Eq. 48. \square
As with Eq. 4, Itô’s lemma applies the rule with a random weight that depends only on the path up to that time. The argument goes through conditionally on that past, because the increments \Delta W^i_k and \Delta W^j_k are independent of it. The companion rules Eq. 5 and Eq. 6 hold for each component, since each is a standard Brownian motion.


A.8.2 Itô’s lemma for a vector state
Let f(x, t) be twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t. We write its partial derivatives as

\partial_k f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_k}, \qquad \partial_{kl} f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_k\, \partial x_l}

with \nabla_x f the gradient and \nabla_x^2 f the Hessian, the matrix of the \partial_{kl} f. Then Y_t = f(X_t, t) satisfies

\boxed{df = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \cdot \nabla_x f + \tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr}\!\big(G G^\top\, \nabla_x^2 f\big)\Big)\, dt + \nabla_x f \cdot G\, dW}
\tag{49}
where \operatorname{tr} is the trace, the sum of the diagonal entries. For d = m = 1 it is Eq. 13.
Derivation:
Taylor-expand f(X_{t+dt}, t+dt) to second order in x and first order in t, as in the scalar derivation. The omitted terms are of order dt\, dX^k and (dt)^2, which the companion rules annihilate, and the remainder is of smaller order than the second-order terms, which are themselves of order dt,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, dX^k + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} \partial_{kl} f\, dX^k\, dX^l

Substituting dX^k = \mu_k\, dt + \sum_i G_{ki}\, dW^i into the product,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, dX^k + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} \partial_{kl} f\, \Big(\mu_k\, dt + \sum_i G_{ki}\, dW^i\Big)\Big(\mu_l\, dt + \sum_j G_{lj}\, dW^j\Big)

Expanding the product,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, dX^k + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} \partial_{kl} f\, \Big(\mu_k \mu_l\, (dt)^2 + \mu_k \sum_j G_{lj}\, dt\, dW^j + \mu_l \sum_i G_{ki}\, dt\, dW^i + \sum_{i,j} G_{ki}\, G_{lj}\, dW^i\, dW^j\Big)

Reducing by the companion rules (dt)^2 = 0 and dt\, dW^i = 0,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, dX^k + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} \partial_{kl} f \sum_{i,j} G_{ki}\, G_{lj}\, dW^i\, dW^j

Substituting dW^i\, dW^j = \delta_{ij}\, dt from Eq. 48,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, dX^k + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} \partial_{kl} f \sum_{i,j} G_{ki}\, G_{lj}\, \delta_{ij}\, dt

Summing over j, which keeps only the term j = i,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, dX^k + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} \partial_{kl} f \sum_{i} G_{ki}\, G_{li}\, dt

Recognizing \sum_i G_{ki}\, G_{li} = (G G^\top)_{kl},

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, dX^k + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} (G G^\top)_{kl}\, \partial_{kl} f\, dt

Substituting dX^k = \mu_k\, dt + \sum_i G_{ki}\, dW^i into the first-order term,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \partial_k f\, \Big(\mu_k\, dt + \sum_i G_{ki}\, dW^i\Big) + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} (G G^\top)_{kl}\, \partial_{kl} f\, dt

Distributing \partial_k f across the bracket,

df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt + \sum_k \mu_k\, \partial_k f\, dt + \sum_{k,i} \partial_k f\, G_{ki}\, dW^i + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} (G G^\top)_{kl}\, \partial_{kl} f\, dt

Grouping by dt and dW,

df = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \sum_k \mu_k\, \partial_k f + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{k,l} (G G^\top)_{kl}\, \partial_{kl} f\Big)\, dt + \sum_{k,i} \partial_k f\, G_{ki}\, dW^i

Writing the sums as vector and matrix products with the identities

\begin{aligned}
\sum_k \mu_k\, \partial_k f &= \mu \cdot \nabla_x f \\[4pt]
\sum_{k,l} (G G^\top)_{kl}\, \partial_{kl} f &= \operatorname{tr}\big(G G^\top\, \nabla_x^2 f\big) \\[4pt]
\sum_{k,i} \partial_k f\, G_{ki}\, dW^i &= \nabla_x f \cdot G\, dW
\end{aligned}

where the second holds because the Hessian is symmetric,

\boxed{df = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \cdot \nabla_x f + \tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr}\!\big(G G^\top\, \nabla_x^2 f\big)\Big)\, dt + \nabla_x f \cdot G\, dW}

which is Eq. 49. \square


A.8.3 The isotropic case
The VP-SDE of Part 7, and the forward SDEs in the main text of the later posts, have m = d and the diffusion matrix G(x, t) = \sigma(t)\, I, a scalar \sigma(t) times the identity, which is the same for each coordinate and independent of the state. Substituting G = \sigma(t)\, I into Eq. 49, so that G G^\top = \sigma(t)^2 I and G\, dW = \sigma(t)\, dW,

df = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \cdot \nabla_x f + \tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr}\!\big(\sigma(t)^2\, \nabla_x^2 f\big)\Big)\, dt + \sigma(t)\, \nabla_x f \cdot dW

Taking the scalar \sigma(t)^2 out of the trace,

df = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \cdot \nabla_x f + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma(t)^2 \operatorname{tr}\!\big(\nabla_x^2 f\big)\Big)\, dt + \sigma(t)\, \nabla_x f \cdot dW

Recognizing the Laplacian

\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x^2 f\big) = \sum_k \partial_{kk} f = \Delta_x f

in the previous line,

\boxed{df = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \cdot \nabla_x f + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma(t)^2\, \Delta_x f\Big)\, dt + \sigma(t)\, \nabla_x f \cdot dW}
\tag{50}
