title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
In the late 2000s, the anti-malware industry faced a submission rate that substantially exceeded its analysis capacity. Novel malware samples, together with a continuous stream of variants derived from existing families, arrived faster than human analysts could examine them. The scale of the increase is documented in the AV-TEST Institute’s collection statistics, which record an average monthly growth rate of 9.5% over this period (Figure 1). This growth produced three consequences:

Processing time increased — each sample required individual analysis, and analyst capacity did not scale with submission volume.
Definition content expanded — each newly identified threat required an additional signature to be distributed to customers.
Scan durations lengthened — larger signature databases increased scan time on every protected endpoint.







Figure 1: Total unique samples in AV-TEST’s malware collection, January 2007 to March 2009. The rose line is AV-TEST’s own forecast. Data: AV-TEST GmbH, Malware Collection Statistics, 2009-07-24.



The conventional practice of authoring one signature per sample was therefore not scalable, and a fundamentally different formulation of the problem was required.



The governing observation is that not all samples exhibit unique behavior. The majority of newly submitted malware consists of variants of previously observed specimens: repacked, modified, or lightly mutated instances of the same underlying families.
This redundancy motivates an alternative strategy: rather than analyzing every sample individually, group samples exhibiting similar behavior into clusters, analyze a single representative from each cluster, and infer the behavior of the remaining members by extension. A single generic signature can then be authored to detect the entire cluster. One signature then provides the coverage previously requiring hundreds, reversing each of the three consequences above.



The conventional choice for a task of this shape is hierarchical agglomerative clustering. Each item begins as its own cluster; the closest pair is merged; the process repeats until a stopping criterion is met. It is well understood, requires no advance specification of the number of clusters, and produces a dendrogram from which groupings may be cut at any desired granularity. Its complexity, however, is prohibitive at this scale.
For N_F files, hierarchical clustering requires the full pairwise similarity matrix:

Space complexity: O(N_F^2). All pairwise similarities are retained, since any pair may become the next merge candidate.
Time complexity: O(N_F^3) for the naive formulation, reducible to O(N_F^2 \log N_F) with priority-queue variants. Every merge alters the distances from the new cluster to all others, so similarities are recomputed repeatedly.

The quadratic space term is the decisive obstacle. At N_F = 194{,}802, the pairwise matrix contains approximately 1.9 \times 10^{10} entries, requiring on the order of 75 GB at four bytes per entry before any file content is stored. The cubic time term compounds this: doubling the corpus increases the work eightfold.
A second objection is structural. Hierarchical clustering is inherently a batch method: the complete corpus must be present before clustering begins, and the arrival of new samples requires re-clustering from the start. Given a submission stream of millions of samples per year, a method requiring full recomputation on each arrival is unusable irrespective of its complexity.
These two objections, quadratic memory and batch operation, motivate the streaming formulation described in the remainder of this post.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
2.1 Method overview
The method rests on a single feature source: the ASCII strings contained within the files themselves. Malware samples encode a substantial degree of identity in their embedded strings, including DLL names, API identifiers, file paths, registry entries, URLs, packer artifacts, and compiler fingerprints. Variants belonging to a common family typically share a large proportion of this string content.
The processing pipeline comprises three stages:

String extraction. All ASCII strings are extracted from every sample and consolidated into an exhaustive set of unique strings, S (Figure 2).






Figure 2: Representative ASCII strings extracted per file, comprising section names and imported DLL names, which constitute the shared residue characteristic of variants.



Sorting and deduplicating the extracted strings yields the set S. Each member is assigned a fixed index j as per its position in the sorted order (Figure 3).






Figure 3: The unique string set S, with the index assigned to each member.



File-Vector construction. A File-Vector is a binary vector of length \left| S \right| and represents the subset of the string set S present in its corresponding file. As each string is assigned a unique index in the previous step, a 1 or 0 at each index denotes the presence or absence of the corresponding string in that file (Figure 4).






Figure 4: The same five files as binary File-Vectors, over the columns of S established above.



The file clustering problem is thereby reduced to a vector clustering problem.
Cluster generation. The resulting vectors are streamed into the clustering algorithm sequentially.

As with any clustering scheme, three components are required: the items to be clustered (File-Vectors), a similarity measure (designated Simile), and a cutoff threshold (the Floor-Value).

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
section: 2.2 Simile: a similarity measure between two files
text:
2.2 Simile: a similarity measure between two files
Simile is a correlation measure defined on the interval [0, 1]. It is defined as the number of strings present in both files (the intersection) divided by the number of unique strings present in either file (the union), and is therefore equivalent to the Jaccard index computed over the corresponding string sets. Writing S_1 and S_2 for the string sets of the two files:
\boxed{\,\text{Simile} = \frac{\left| S_1 \cap S_2 \right|}{\left| S_1 \cup S_2 \right|}\,} \tag{1}
The union may be decomposed as the intersection plus the elements belonging to exactly one of the two sets, which gives the equivalent form:
\text{Simile} = \frac{\left| S_1 \cap S_2 \right|}{\underbrace{\left| S_1 \cap S_2 \right|}_{\text{in both files}} + \underbrace{\left\{ \left| S_1 \cup S_2 \right| - \left| S_1 \cap S_2 \right| \right\}}_{\text{in exactly one file}}}
The denominator is now a sum of two quantities that are directly countable:

The first, \left| S_1 \cap S_2 \right|, is the number of strings present in both files. This is the green region of Figure 5, and it is identical to the numerator.
The second, \left| S_1 \cup S_2 \right| - \left| S_1 \cap S_2 \right|, is the number of strings present in exactly one of the two files. This is the pair of rose regions.

On File-Vectors, each quantity is one bitwise operation: AND (\wedge), which yields 1 only where both operands are 1, marks the first; XOR (\oplus), which yields 1 only where the operands differ, marks the second. Writing f_s for the function returning the sum of a vector’s elements, the measure for two vectors V_1 and V_2 becomes:
\boxed{\,\text{Simile}(V_1, V_2) = \frac{f_s(V_1 \wedge V_2)}{f_s(V_1 \wedge V_2) + f_s(V_1 \oplus V_2)}\,} \tag{2}






Figure 5: Simile as a set relation over the universe S of all extracted strings. The amber region holds strings appearing in neither file but occurring elsewhere in the corpus.



On a binary vector, f_s returns the count of its 1’s, conventionally the Hamming weight or population count, which on modern hardware is a single instruction. For two 8-bit vectors sharing 3 strings and differing in 2 positions, \text{Simile} = \frac{3}{3+2} = 0.6 (Figure 6).






Figure 6: Worked Simile computation. Columns are coloured green where the string is present in both files, rose where present in exactly one, and amber where absent from both.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
section: 2.3 Simile between a file and a cluster
text:
2.3 Simile between a file and a cluster
Pairwise similarity is insufficient on its own, since the streaming algorithm must compare an incoming vector against entire clusters. The definition is therefore extended: the Simile between a vector and a cluster pools the pairwise counts across the members — total shared strings over total compared strings. For a cluster C containing N File-Vectors \{C_1, \ldots, C_N\}:
\boxed{\,\text{Simile}(V, C) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_s(V \wedge C_i)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_s(V \wedge C_i) + \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_s(V \oplus C_i)}\,} \tag{3}
where C_i denotes the i-th File-Vector in the cluster and N the cluster cardinality. The pooled form preserves the range [0, 1], reduces to Equation 2 for N = 1, and reflects all of the cluster’s members rather than the single closest one. It is a weighted mean of the pairwise Similes: writing u_i = f_s(V \wedge C_i) + f_s(V \oplus C_i) for the number of strings in the union of V and C_i, the definition equals \sum_i u_i\, \text{Simile}(V, C_i) \,/\, \sum_i u_i, so member i carries the weight w_i = u_i / \sum_j u_j — its share of all compared strings. A member that shares more compared strings carries more evidence and counts proportionally more, whereas an equal-weight arithmetic mean would give a three-string member the same vote as a three-thousand-string one. The pooled form is also what collapses into the constant-size per-cluster summary that the optimizations below exploit; the equal-weight mean admits no summary smaller than the member list itself.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
2.4 The streaming algorithm
The clustering procedure operates as a single pass over the incoming stream of File-Vectors. For each new vector:

Compute the Simile against every existing cluster.
If the maximum Simile is greater than or equal to the Floor-Value, assign the vector to the corresponding cluster.
Otherwise, instantiate a new cluster with this vector as its sole initial member.

The procedure requires no iteration, no re-clustering, and no retention of the full pairwise distance matrix in memory. Each sample is assigned exactly once, which is the defining property of the streaming formulation and the principal reason it remains tractable at industrial scale (Figure 7).






Figure 7: Assignment procedure for the streaming algorithm. Each incoming File-Vector is either assigned to its best-matching cluster or used to instantiate a new one.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
3.1 Inherent computational complexity
Notwithstanding the simplicity of the algorithm, a naive implementation proves computationally prohibitive. With N_F files, N_C clusters, and N_S = \left| S \right| unique strings:

Space complexity: O(N_F \times N_S), since the complete vector for every file is retained in memory.
Time complexity: O(N_F^2 \times N_S), since each incoming vector is compared against all others, traversing the full vector length in every comparison.

For a representative workload of 68,000 files and 135,000 unique strings, these bounds correspond to approximately 2 GB of memory and 9 hours of computation. A workload of this size could be completed by allocating sufficient hardware to it, but not at a cost proportionate to its value, and not on the daily cadence that production operation required.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
3.2 Binary representation and complexity reduction
The reduction in complexity derives from exploiting the binary representation of File-Vectors through three successive optimizations. All three are exact: none alters the resulting clustering, only the computational and memory cost of obtaining it.

3.2.1 Optimization 1: discard if poor
This optimization applies to clusters containing exactly one File-Vector. Prior to computing a full Simile between a new vector and a singleton cluster, a less expensive question is posed: what is the maximum Simile the pair could attain? Since the 1-count f_s(V) of each vector is recorded once at construction time, an upper bound is obtained at negligible cost.
Dividing numerator and denominator by the intersection term yields:
\text{Simile}(V_1, V_2) = \frac{f_s(V_1 \wedge V_2)}{f_s(V_1 \wedge V_2) + f_s(V_1 \oplus V_2)} = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{f_s(V_1 \oplus V_2)}{f_s(V_1 \wedge V_2)}}
Simile attains its maximum when the \wedge term is as large as possible and the \oplus term as small as possible. Given only the 1-counts, the extremal cases are:
f_s(V_1 \wedge V_2)_{\max} = \min\big(f_s(V_1),\, f_s(V_2)\big) \qquad \text{(one string set wholly contained in the other)}
f_s(V_1 \oplus V_2)_{\min} = \big|\, f_s(V_1) - f_s(V_2) \,\big| \qquad \text{(only the surplus strings differ)}
Substituting both bounds, and assuming f_s(V_2) \le f_s(V_1) without loss of generality:
\text{Simile}(V_1, V_2)_{\max} = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{f_s(V_1) - f_s(V_2)}{f_s(V_2)}}
Simplifying,
\boxed{\,\text{Simile}(V_1, V_2)_{\max} = \frac{f_s(V_2)}{f_s(V_1)}\,} \tag{4}
The maximum attainable Simile is therefore the ratio of the smaller 1-count to the larger, computable in constant time without vector traversal. If \text{Simile}_{\max} < \text{Floor-Value}, the full computation is omitted. This single test eliminated approximately 30% of all Simile computations.


3.2.2 Optimization 2: N_F \rightarrow N_C
The second optimization is algebraic. The cluster Simile Equation 3 already aggregates the pairwise counts into summations, but evaluated as written it still requires accessing every member vector individually — each term traverses one member. Expanding \oplus into its two one-sided differences, namely strings in V but not in C_i and strings in C_i but not in V:
\text{Simile}(V, C) = \frac{\sum_{i} f_s(V \wedge C_i)}{\sum_{i} f_s(V \wedge C_i) + \sum_{i} f_s(V \wedge \overline{C_i}) + \sum_{i} f_s(\overline{V} \wedge C_i)}
Consider now the sequence of operations. Each term evaluates: \wedge \rightarrow f_s \rightarrow summation over members. Because the vectors are binary, this sequence admits reordering to: summation over members \rightarrow multiplication \rightarrow count. This is an instance of the sum of products versus product of sums equivalence, and the reordering is justified by the distributive law of multiplication over addition,
x\,y_1 + x\,y_2 + \cdots + x\,y_N \;=\; x\,(y_1 + y_2 + \cdots + y_N)
applied independently at each string index j, in conjunction with the interchange of the two finite summations, which is permitted by the commutativity and associativity of addition. Noting further that for binary vectors \wedge is identical to element-wise multiplication:
\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_s(V \wedge C_i) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j} V[j]\, C_i[j] \;=\; \sum_{j} V[j] \sum_{i=1}^{N} C_i[j] \;=\; f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} C_i\right)
where \sum_i C_i denotes the element-wise sum of all member vectors, that is, a single vector of per-string membership counts, and the product is evaluated index by index. Here f_s is read as the component sum, f_s(x) = \sum_j x[j] — on binary vectors this coincides with the Hamming weight, while V \cdot \sum_i C_i is in general integer-valued. The same rewriting applies to every term, so the complete cluster Simile may be expressed solely in terms of the two summation vectors:
\boxed{\,\text{Simile}(V, C) = \frac{f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i C_i\right)}{f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i C_i\right) + f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i \overline{C_i}\right) + f_s\!\left(\overline{V} \cdot \sum_i C_i\right)}\,} \tag{5}
The consequence is that computing the Simile against a cluster requires no access to the individual member vectors. Retaining only two summation vectors per cluster, \sum_i C_i (the One_Count vector) and \sum_i \overline{C_i} (the Zero_Count vector), is sufficient. The resulting complexity bounds are:

Space: O(N_F \times N_S) \rightarrow \mathbf{O(N_C \times N_S)}
Time: O(N_F^2 \times N_S) \rightarrow \mathbf{O(N_C \times N_F \times N_S)}

Since the number of clusters was substantially smaller than the number of files, this was a considerable improvement, though memory did not fall proportionately: on the 68,000-file workload, N_C was observed to be approximately N_F/3.


3.2.3 Optimization 3: sparse matrix
The final improvement follows from a property of the data: the strings present in any single cluster constitute a small subset of the exhaustive string set S, so the One_Count vector \sum_i C_i is highly sparse, with a measured density of approximately 0.06%. Retaining only its non-zero values therefore offers a substantial saving.
One obstacle remained: the rewritten formula from Optimization 2 also requires the Zero_Count vector \sum_i \overline{C_i}, which is by construction dense precisely where One_Count is sparse. The algebra was therefore extended one step further, proceeding again from that form:
\text{Simile}(V, C) = \frac{f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i C_i\right)}{f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i C_i\right) + f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i \overline{C_i}\right) + f_s\!\left(\overline{V} \cdot \sum_i C_i\right)}
The first two denominator terms may be combined, since the element-wise sum \sum_i C_i + \sum_i \overline{C_i} is a vector containing N at every index, each member contributing a 1 to exactly one of the two terms. Denoting this vector V_N:
f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i C_i\right) + f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i \overline{C_i}\right) = f_s(V \cdot V_N) = N \cdot f_s(V)
which reduces the expression to its final form:
\boxed{\,\text{Simile}(V, C) = \frac{f_s\!\left(V \cdot \sum_i C_i\right)}{N \cdot f_s(V) + f_s\!\left(\overline{V} \cdot \sum_i C_i\right)}\,} \tag{6}
The dense Zero_Count vector has been eliminated: N is a single integer per cluster and f_s(V) is already available. Every remaining term references only \sum_i C_i, and any index at which it holds a zero contributes nothing to the summations. A linked-list sparse representation storing only non-zero values therefore reduces both memory consumption and computation time.


3.2.4 The result
The combined effect of the three optimizations on the same 68,000-file workload was as follows:

Memory: approximately 2 GB reduced to approximately 20 MB, a factor of 100.
Time: approximately 9 hours reduced to approximately 12 minutes, a factor of 45.

The output is unchanged. All three optimizations are exact, so the clustering produced after them is identical to the clustering produced before. What changed is the cost of obtaining it, which is what determines whether the method can be run daily on a growing corpus rather than occasionally on a favourable one.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
4.1 Comparison with hierarchical clustering
Streaming clustering addresses both of the objections raised earlier. Each sample is examined once and assigned immediately, so no pairwise matrix is ever formed and no re-clustering occurs. The cost is a known trade-off: the result depends on the order of arrival, and an assignment once made is never revisited, so the partition is not guaranteed optimal in the sense a hierarchical method would provide. In this application that trade-off is acceptable, since the objective is to group samples closely enough to support a shared generic signature, not to recover a canonical taxonomy (Figure 8).

The optimized streaming curve incorporates the measured 0.06% matrix density. The dotted line marks the 68,000-file corpus used for the timing measurements.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
4.2 Experimental evaluation
The system was evaluated on a corpus of 194,802 samples with a Floor-Value of 75%. The procedure produced well-populated groupings: the largest cluster contained 32,499 samples, just 403 clusters lay entirely within the first half of the covered samples, and the full set resolved into 44,909 clusters. The observed cluster quality supports the central hypothesis: string-based similarity captures family relationships among malware variants to a degree sufficient both for generic signature construction and for disposing of non-malicious clusters in bulk (Figure 9).






Figure 9: Cluster size against percentage sample coverage for the 194,802-sample evaluation. A small number of large clusters account for the majority of samples.



The operational effect was evident in analyst throughput. Relative to the preceding normalized-name approach, streaming clustering enabled a single analyst to process nearly ten times as many samples per day (approximately 307 against 33). The largest gain was in clearing samples as non-malicious, which rose from approximately 14 to 268 per day, since an entire cluster determined to be clean could be dispensed with in a single decision. In one such case, analysis of 15 clean or disputed clusters cleared 64,120 samples (Figure 10).






Figure 10: Analyst throughput under streaming clustering compared with the preceding normalized-name workflow, measured in samples handled per person-day. Cleared as non-malicious denotes samples determined to require no signature; signature written denotes samples for which a definition was authored and shipped.




4.2.1 Detections per signature
The clearest measure of the method’s value is the number of detections obtained per signature authored. Across the malicious clusters, signatures fell into two categories. Where cluster coherence permitted a hand-written generic signature, one signature covered a large number of samples. Where it did not, samples were covered in bulk by script-generated automated signatures, each of which covers essentially one sample.

Twenty-eight generic signatures produced 8,719 detections, while 1,525 automated signatures produced 1,557: a comparable order of detections from roughly one fifty-fourth as many signatures, or 307 detections per signature against 1.02. This is the mechanism by which the method attacks all three consequences identified at the outset. Detections protect the customer; signatures occupy the definition file and lengthen every scan. Raising the ratio between them increases coverage while holding definition content approximately constant.
Several qualifications arise from operational experience:

The method successfully clustered many files processed with unsupported packers, as the residual strings remained discriminative.
Installer files constituted the principal weakness, with cluster quality varying considerably.
Execution over sample sets restricted to malicious files yielded the highest-quality generic signatures.
String extraction became the limiting stage of the pipeline, processing approximately 10,000 files per hour.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
4.3 Relation to existing work
The ingredients are long-established. Binary presence/absence vectors compared by the Jaccard index are the classic set-of-words model from information retrieval, applied to near-duplicate document detection at web scale since the late 1990s [1], [2]. The clustering schema is Hartigan’s Leader algorithm [3]: assign each arriving item to its best-matching cluster if a threshold is met, otherwise start a new one, carrying the same two limitations noted earlier, order dependence and threshold sensitivity. This work arrived at both independently, from the constraints of the problem; given presence/absence features, a corpus too large to hold pairwise, and a stream that does not stop, the design space is narrow.
Contemporaneous malware work reached the same objective by a different route. BitShred [4] also computes Jaccard similarity over bit vectors, but reduces dimensionality by feature hashing, trading a bounded error rate for fixed-size fingerprints; MutantX-S [5] applied the same trick to million-dimensional n-gram vectors and then clustered hierarchically over prototypes rather than over all samples. Complementary work addressed the downstream step rather than this one: Griffin et al. [6] automated the generation of string signatures for samples already known to be malicious and already grouped into families, taking as input the clusters that a method like this one produces.
The contribution here is therefore neither the representation nor the clustering schema, but the exact algebraic reduction that makes their combination tractable: expressing cluster-level similarity through summation vectors so that member vectors need never be retained, then eliminating the dense complement term so that sparsity can be exploited. Where the hashing approaches trade accuracy for scale, this route preserves the exact result.

title: Scaling Malware Analysis: A Streaming Clustering Method Reducing Computation from 9 Hours to 12 Minutes
text:
4.4 Patent disclosure and citation impact
The method described here was filed with the USPTO and granted in 2013.
It has since accumulated 69 forward citations, placing it in roughly the 92nd to 94th percentile among the approximately 8,000 US malware and malicious-software patents filed around that time. Citing organisations include Palo Alto Networks, Cisco, McAfee, and CrowdStrike, indicating that string-based clustering has remained an established technique within malware analysis.
Citation count and peer cohort are both taken from PatSnap; the percentile is an estimate obtained by fitting a log-normal distribution to that cohort, the standard approach in the patent citation literature.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
This series — Continuous-Time Generative Models
The forward process is the easy direction: it gradually adds Gaussian noise to a real image until it becomes pure noise, without requiring a neural network. The challenge lies in the reverse process, which starts with random noise and progressively removes it step by step to generate a meaningful image.
Post #1 developed the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) forward process end to end as a continuous-time object. It introduced the generative-modeling framing and diffusion models, defined Ho et al.’s DDPM forward process [1], and used the continuum limit to recover the continuous-time forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). It used Itô’s lemma to derive its closed-form perturbation kernel and established why it matters: tractable training, by allowing single-step sampling of any x_t with an exact, known noise target.
It again used Itô’s lemma to derive the Fokker-Planck equation [2], [3], which governs how the marginal distribution spreads. It named, but deliberately deferred, the details of the reverse direction.
This post picks up from there. It focuses entirely on generative AI and develops the generative direction along the two main lineages of diffusion modeling.
The variational route starts from latent-variable models, which explain data through unobserved variables, with the Gaussian mixture model as a first example. For a deep model the marginal likelihood is intractable. Naive Monte Carlo estimates it with high variance, and the logarithm of the unbiased importance-sampling estimate is biased. The variational autoencoder (VAE) [4] trains instead on the evidence lower bound (ELBO), whose gap is a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. Variational inference, the reparameterization gradient and an encoder shared by all training images make the bound trainable, and stacking several latent variables gives hierarchical VAEs.
DDPM is a hierarchical VAE whose encoder, the forward process, is fixed, so the same bound trains its reverse process. The post derives that training objective from the ELBO and reduces it to the noise-prediction loss. It also describes the denoising network the bound calls for and the ancestral sampling procedure to generate samples, completing the reverse process of the DDPM.
It then builds the other lineage in parallel. Energy-based models define a density only up to a normalizing constant that cannot be computed, and the gradient of the log-density (\nabla_x \log p(x)), the score, does not depend on that constant. The score is a compass that shows in which direction the data density increases. The post then shows that estimating it directly, by explicit and then implicit score matching, and sampling with Langevin dynamics work in principle but meet four pitfalls on real data.
Denoising score matching [5] resolves them by perturbing the data and trading the marginal score for a conditional one known in closed form, which cuts the cost per example from O(d) to O(1). Vincent’s theorem shows that it has the same minimizer as score matching on the perturbed data, the score of the perturbed data density. By Tweedie’s formula, that minimizer gives the posterior mean of the training sample given its perturbed version, and an unbiased estimate of the denoising risk shows why denoising and score matching coincide.
A single noise level still forces a dilemma, since no level serves both signal and fidelity. Song and Ermon’s score matching with Langevin dynamics [6] resolves it by perturbing the data at a finite sequence of noise levels, training one noise-conditional score network across them, and sampling with annealed Langevin dynamics.
It closes by weighing what the reformulation from densities to scores gained and what it cost. Post #1 built the forward process and the objects the reverse process would need; this post reverses that process by two methods, leaving the unification of the two lineages to post #3.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
Roadmap

Part 1: Introduces the variational route. It motivates models that explain data through unobserved variables, develops the VAE and the ELBO that trains it, from variational inference to the gradients that maximize the bound, and closes with VAEs that stack several such variables.
Part 2: Develops the variational route for DDPM end to end. It defines the DDPM reverse process, shows that DDPM is a VAE with many latent levels and a fixed encoder, derives the ELBO that trains it, describes the denoising network the bound produces, and closes with ancestral sampling.
Part 3: Develops the score-based route, which grew from a different question: how to model a density whose normalizing constant cannot be computed. It defines the score, trains it by score matching, samples with Langevin dynamics, and diagnoses the four pitfalls that hinder its effectiveness and scalability on real data.
Part 4: Discusses denoising score matching in depth, which resolves those pitfalls by perturbing the data with noise and replacing the computationally inefficient marginal score with a closed-form conditional one (O(d) \to O(1)), but introduces the \sigma dilemma.
Part 5: Resolves the \sigma dilemma by perturbing the data at a finite sequence of noise levels, since no single level serves both fidelity and signal. This is Song and Ermon’s score matching with Langevin dynamics, which trains one noise-conditional score network across all the levels and samples with annealed Langevin dynamics.
Part 6: Weighs what the reformulation from densities to scores gained, and hands the two routes to post #3, which unifies them.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
section: 1.1 Latent-variable models: explaining data through unobserved factors
text:
1.1 Latent-variable models: explaining data through unobserved factors

1.1.1 The case for latent variables
Images vary according to underlying factors that are not explicitly represented by their pixel values. For example, the images in a dataset of faces may differ in the age of each person, the orientation of the head, and the colors of the hair and eyes [7]. Without annotations, these factors remain unobserved, leaving the model with only the pixel data x from which to learn.
A latent variable is a random variable of a model that is never observed. A latent-variable model represents the factors of variation explicitly, by latent variables z_1, z_2, \ldots collected in a vector z, and generates x from z, as Figure 1 shows below.








Figure 1: Latent-variable models as graphs, after Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. A shaded node is observed in the data and an open node is not, and an arrow points from a variable to the variable it generates. Left: The latent variable z generates the observed x. Right: The same structure for face images, with the factors of variation age, pose, hair color and eye color as the latent variables z_1, \ldots, z_4 and the image as the observed x.





Only the pixel values x are observed, while the latent variables z represent the image’s underlying, high-level features. A well-designed latent representation offers two main advantages:

Simpler conditional distributions: The conditional density p(x \mid z) can be much simpler than the overall data distribution p(x), because images sharing the same latent features vary less than the dataset as a whole.
Meaningful feature representations: Once trained, the model’s posterior distribution p(z \mid x) describes the latent features of a given image. For example, it can estimate the probability that the eyes in an image are blue, p(\text{eye color} = \text{blue} \mid x). These features provide a compact representation of the image, with far fewer dimensions than its pixels.

The main difficulty is that these conditional distributions are hard to define explicitly. For instance, specifying the pixel distribution of a face given its age, head pose, hair color, and eye color is a hard task.


1.1.2 Gaussian mixture model: a shallow latent-variable model
The simplest latent-variable model is the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) [8]. It avoids the difficulty of specifying complex conditional distributions by assuming that each latent state corresponds to a Gaussian distribution. A single discrete latent variable z \in \{1, \ldots, K\} selects one of K Gaussian components, from which the observed data x \in \mathbb{R}^d is generated. The model is represented by the directed graph z \to x, shown on the left of Figure 1, and is defined by two distributions:

Prior: The latent variable z follows a categorical distribution, with each component k selected with probability p(z = k) > 0. These probabilities sum to one: 
\sum_{k=1}^{K} p(z = k) = 1

Components: Given z = k, the observation x follows a Gaussian distribution with mean \mu_k \in \mathbb{R}^d and covariance matrix \Sigma_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, symmetric and positive definite, 
p(x \mid z = k) = \mathcal{N}(x;\ \mu_k,\ \Sigma_k)


The model’s parameters consist of the K component probabilities p(z = k), the means \mu_k, and the covariance matrices \Sigma_k. These parameters are stored explicitly, with one set for each component, rather than being computed by a neural network. For this reason, the model is considered shallow [7].

1.1.2.1 Sampling from a GMM
Sampling from a GMM follows the graph’s direction in two steps. First, a component k is sampled from the prior distribution p(z). Then, an observation x is sampled from the corresponding Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma_k). Figure 2 illustrates this process for a mixture of three Gaussian components in two dimensions.








Figure 2: Samples from a three-component Gaussian mixture in two dimensions, adapted from Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. Each point is generated by first sampling a component k from p(z), then sampling x from \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma_k). The point’s color indicates its selected component, while the ellipses show contours of the component densities centered at their respective means \mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3.





Each component forms a group of points centered at its mean \mu_k, with its shape and spread determined by the covariance matrix \Sigma_k. Because the Gaussian components can overlap, a point in an overlapping region may plausibly have been generated by either component.


1.1.2.2 The tractable marginal density
Because the component assignment z is not observed, the model must describe the data using the marginal density p(x), which accounts for each component that could have generated the observation.
Summing the joint density over the K values of z,

p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p(x, z = k)

Factorizing each term by the product rule,

p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p(z = k)\, p(x \mid z = k)

Substituting the Gaussian components,

\boxed{p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p(z = k)\, \mathcal{N}(x;\ \mu_k,\ \Sigma_k)}
\tag{1}
This illustrates the first advantage of latent-variable models listed in the motivation, as the model combines simple conditional distributions into a more expressive overall distribution [7]. Although each Gaussian component is unimodal and has an elliptical shape, their weighted sum can exhibit multiple modes and a much more complex shape, as illustrated in Figure 3 for a one-dimensional mixture.








Figure 3: A mixture of three one-dimensional Gaussians, adapted from Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. The shaded curves represent the weighted component densities p(z = k)\, \mathcal{N}(x;\ \mu_k,\ \Sigma_k), where each covariance \Sigma_k is a scalar variance. The dark curve represents their sum, the marginal density p(x) defined in Eq. 1.





The resulting distribution cannot generally be represented by a single Gaussian. However, because the marginal density consists of K Gaussian terms, each of which can be evaluated in closed form, the likelihood of a GMM can be computed exactly.


1.1.2.3 Clustering: unsupervised learning using the posterior
The posterior distribution p(z = k \mid x), which represents the probability that component k generated an observation x, can also be computed exactly. It provides a way to assign observations to components based on their inferred probabilities, enabling the GMM to group observations without requiring labeled data.
By the definition of conditional probability,

p(z = k \mid x) = \frac{p(x, z = k)}{p(x)}

Factorizing the numerator by the product rule,

p(z = k \mid x) = \frac{p(z = k)\, p(x \mid z = k)}{p(x)}

Substituting the Gaussian component in the numerator,

p(z = k \mid x) = \frac{p(z = k)\, \mathcal{N}(x;\ \mu_k,\ \Sigma_k)}{p(x)}

Substituting Eq. 1 for the denominator,

\boxed{p(z = k \mid x) = \frac{p(z = k)\, \mathcal{N}(x;\ \mu_k,\ \Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} p(z = j)\, \mathcal{N}(x;\ \mu_j,\ \Sigma_j)}}
\tag{2}
Assigning each observation x to the component with the highest posterior probability partitions the dataset into K clusters. A fitted GMM can therefore perform clustering, the task of grouping unlabeled observations according to their similarities [7]. Figure 4 compares a single Gaussian with a mixture of two Gaussians fitted to the same unlabeled dataset.








Figure 4: A single Gaussian and a two-component GMM fitted to the same data, adapted from the Old Faithful example in Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. The observations form two distinct groups. Left: The raw data. Middle: A single Gaussian fitted by maximum likelihood, with its sample mean and covariance represented by two density contours. Right: A two-component GMM fitted by maximum likelihood using the expectation-maximization algorithm [9]. Each component is represented by two density contours, and each point is colored according to the component with the highest posterior probability, as defined in Eq. 2.





A single Gaussian spreads across both groups and assigns substantial density to the empty region between them, while the mixture places one Gaussian over each group, and its posterior recovers the two groups without labeled data. This is unsupervised learning, in which a model learns patterns from unlabeled data, and it is ill-posed, because no label specifies the correct grouping [7]. Both the marginal density and the posterior of a GMM are exact, and this exactness is what the VAE of the next section gives up.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
section: 1.2 Variational autoencoder: a deep latent-variable model
text:
1.2 Variational autoencoder: a deep latent-variable model
A GMM stores its parameters explicitly in a table and uses a discrete latent variable with only K possible values. These limitations make it difficult to capture the diverse, continuous factors of variation present in complex data such as face images. A deep latent-variable model overcomes these restrictions by using neural networks to parameterize the conditional distributions [7].
The VAE [4] is a deep latent-variable model in which the latent variable z \in \mathbb{R}^{d_z} follows a standard Gaussian prior, while the observed data x, conditioned on z, also follows a Gaussian distribution. This provides a continuous latent representation and allows neural networks to learn how latent variables map to the observed data. The model is defined by two distributions:

Prior: z is standard Gaussian, p(z) = \mathcal{N}(z;\ 0,\ I), where I is the d_z \times d_z identity matrix.
Conditional: Given z, x is Gaussian with mean \mu_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to \mathbb{R}^d and covariance \Sigma_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, whose values are symmetric positive-definite matrices. Both are neural networks with parameters \theta.

Together,

\boxed{z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \qquad p_\theta(x \mid z) = \mathcal{N}\big(x;\ \mu_\theta(z),\ \Sigma_\theta(z)\big)}
\tag{3}
The VAE can be viewed as a mixture of infinitely many Gaussian distributions [7]. Unlike a GMM with K discrete components, its latent variable z takes values in a continuous space, with each value defining a Gaussian distribution over the observed data x.
The model’s generative structure follows the directed graph z \to x, as illustrated in Figure 5. Neural networks map the latent vector z to the parameters of the conditional distribution, namely the mean \mu_\theta(z) and covariance \Sigma_\theta(z).








Figure 5: A deep latent-variable model, adapted from Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. Left: The graphical model z \to x, where the latent variable z is unobserved and the data x are observed. Right: The same structure expanded, in which the coordinates of z feed into neural networks that compute \mu_\theta(z) and \Sigma_\theta(z), which together define the Gaussian distribution p_\theta(x \mid z) over the generated image x.





For an observed image x, the posterior distribution p_\theta(z \mid x) describes the latent factors that could have generated it [7]. Although the conditional distribution p_\theta(x \mid z) is Gaussian and therefore relatively simple, marginalizing over the continuous latent space produces a much richer and more flexible distribution p_\theta(x) [7]. This expressive power, however, introduces additional challenges during training, as the next section explains.

1.2.1 The intractable marginal likelihood
Training a VAE requires evaluating how much probability the model assigns to each training image. The image x is observed, but its latent variable z is unknown because the data do not include information about which latent state generated each image [7]. The model defines the joint density of x and z by the product rule,

p_\theta(x, z) = p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)

To obtain the probability of observing x alone, we must account for each latent value that could have generated it. This is done by marginalizing over z [7]. For a discrete latent variable, marginalization involves a finite sum, as in the GMM of Eq. 1. Since the VAE uses a continuous latent variable, the sum becomes an integral,

\boxed{p_\theta(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_z}} p_\theta(x, z)\, dz}
\tag{4}
This quantity is called the marginal likelihood of x.
Factorizing the joint density in Eq. 4 by the product rule,

p_\theta(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_z}} p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz
\tag{5}
Substituting the conditional of Eq. 3,

p_\theta(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_z}} \mathcal{N}\big(x;\ \mu_\theta(z),\ \Sigma_\theta(z)\big)\, p(z)\, dz

The difficulty is that this marginal likelihood is generally intractable. Because the mean \mu_\theta(z) and the covariance \Sigma_\theta(z) of the Gaussian in the integrand are neural networks of z, the integral typically has no closed form. Numerical integration over a grid is also impractical in high-dimensional latent spaces, since the number of grid points required grows exponentially with the latent dimension d_z.


1.2.2 Monte Carlo estimates of the marginal likelihood
Since the integral in Eq. 4 cannot in general be computed, this section estimates it from samples of z, first from the prior and then from a chosen density. The second estimate then leads to a lower bound on the log-likelihood.

1.2.2.1 Naive Monte Carlo
The marginal likelihood can be expressed as an expectation, allowing the Monte Carlo method [10] to approximate it using a sample average.
The integral in Eq. 5 is an expectation over the prior distribution,

p_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}_{p(z)}\big[p_\theta(x \mid z)\big]

We can estimate this expectation by independently sampling z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} from p(z) and replacing the expectation with the sample average,

p_\theta(x) \approx \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} p_\theta\big(x \mid z^{(j)}\big)

Although this estimator is theoretically valid, it is often ineffective in practice [7]. For most values of z, p_\theta(x \mid z) is extremely small because those latent values generate images that differ substantially from the observed image x. Only a small region of the latent space produces values of z for which p_\theta(x \mid z) is large. Samples from the prior rarely fall into this region, resulting in an estimate with high variance. Reducing this variance requires a better strategy for selecting the samples z^{(j)}.


1.2.2.2 Importance sampling
Importance sampling [11] addresses this problem by sampling from a chosen density q: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to (0, \infty) rather than from the prior.
Multiplying the integrand in Eq. 4 by q(z)/q(z) = 1 gives

p_\theta(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_z}} q(z)\, \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\, dz

Recognizing this integral as an expectation under q,

p_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right]
\tag{6}
We can again approximate the expectation using a sample average. Sampling z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} from q, independently of one another, yields

\boxed{p_\theta(x) \approx \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big)}{q\big(z^{(j)}\big)} = \hat{p}_k(x)}
\tag{7}
Here \hat{p}_k(x) denotes the importance-sampling estimator of p_\theta(x). Its accuracy depends strongly on the choice of q. It performs well when q frequently samples latent values that are likely given the observation x under p_\theta(x, z) [7]. This is where naive Monte Carlo, which samples from the prior p(z), can fail, because the prior may rarely generate latent values that explain the observed image well. Importance sampling therefore provides a more effective approach when q is chosen to concentrate samples in the relevant regions of the latent space.

Unbiasedness of the importance-sampling estimator
The samples z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} are random, so \hat{p}_k(x) is a random variable, and its expected value is taken over the samples. The estimator is unbiased, meaning that this expected value equals p_\theta(x).
Substituting the definition of \hat{p}_k(x) from Eq. 7,

\mathbb{E}_{z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} \sim q}\big[\hat{p}_k(x)\big] = \mathbb{E}_{z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} \sim q}\!\left[\frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big)}{q\big(z^{(j)}\big)}\right]

By the linearity of expectation,

\mathbb{E}_{z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} \sim q}\big[\hat{p}_k(x)\big] = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} \sim q}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big)}{q\big(z^{(j)}\big)}\right]

Since the j-th term depends only on z^{(j)}, its expectation is over q(z^{(j)}) alone,

\mathbb{E}_{z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} \sim q}\big[\hat{p}_k(x)\big] = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{q(z^{(j)})}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big)}{q\big(z^{(j)}\big)}\right]

Since each z^{(j)} is sampled from q, substituting Eq. 6 for each expectation on the right-hand side,

\mathbb{E}_{z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} \sim q}\big[\hat{p}_k(x)\big] = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} p_\theta(x)

Summing the k equal terms,

\mathbb{E}_{z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} \sim q}\big[\hat{p}_k(x)\big] = p_\theta(x)

Therefore the importance-sampling estimator is unbiased. \square




1.2.3 ELBO: a surrogate objective for the log-likelihood

1.2.3.1 The log-likelihood objective
Training a VAE involves fitting the parameters \theta to a dataset of n images, \mathcal{D} = \{x^{(1)}, \ldots, x^{(n)}\} [7]. Under maximum-likelihood estimation (P1:§4.1.2), the objective is to maximize the likelihood of the entire dataset, the product of the probabilities assigned to each image,

p_\theta\big(x^{(1)}, \ldots, x^{(n)}\big) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_\theta\big(x^{(i)}\big)

Taking the logarithm converts this product into a sum, the log-likelihood of the dataset as a function of \theta,

\ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p_\theta\big(x^{(i)}\big)
\tag{8}
Substituting the marginal likelihood from Eq. 4,

\ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_z}} p_\theta\big(x^{(i)}, z\big)\, dz

Each term contains the intractable integral discussed in §1.2.1, so evaluating the objective requires evaluating one such integral for each training image. Calculating the gradient with respect to \theta is similarly challenging [7].
Training therefore requires an approximation to the maximum-likelihood objective. Since optimization evaluates gradients repeatedly across training examples, this approximation must be computationally efficient enough to make large-scale training practical [7].
The training objective is the log-likelihood \log p_\theta(x), rather than the likelihood p_\theta(x) itself [7]. Although importance sampling provides an unbiased estimate of the likelihood, taking the logarithm of this estimate introduces bias.
Using Eq. 7, we can estimate the log-likelihood as

\log p_\theta(x) \approx \log\!\left(\frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big)}{q\big(z^{(j)}\big)}\right)

With a single sample, k = 1, this becomes

\log p_\theta(x) \approx \log \frac{p_\theta\big(x, z^{(1)}\big)}{q\big(z^{(1)}\big)}

The problem is that the logarithm is nonlinear, so the logarithm of an unbiased estimate is not generally an unbiased estimate of the logarithm. In particular, unless p_\theta(x, z)/q(z) is constant in z,

\mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right] \neq \log \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right]

By Eq. 6, the right-hand side equals \log p_\theta(x). Jensen’s inequality explains the direction of this difference.


1.2.3.2 Jensen’s inequality
The logarithm is a concave function. For y_1, y_2 > 0 and w \in [0, 1],

\log\big(w y_1 + (1 - w) y_2\big) \ge w \log y_1 + (1 - w) \log y_2

In other words, the logarithm of an average is at least as large as the average of the logarithms. Jensen’s inequality [12] generalizes this property to expectations. For a density q on \mathbb{R}^{d_z} and a function f: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to (0, \infty) whose expectation under q is finite,

\log \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\big[f(z)\big] \ge \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\big[\log f(z)\big]

Figure 6 shows the two-point case below.








Figure 6: Jensen’s inequality for the logarithm, after Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. For Y equal to y_1 = 1 or y_2 = 5 with probability w = 1/2 each, the logarithm of the mean, \log \mathbb{E}[Y], lies on the curve, and the mean of the logarithms, \mathbb{E}[\log Y], lies on the chord below it.







1.2.3.3 Deriving the bound using Jensen’s inequality
Taking the logarithm of Eq. 6 gives

\log p_\theta(x) = \log \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right]
\tag{9}
Applying Jensen’s inequality with f(z) = p_\theta(x, z)/q(z), which is positive because p_\theta(x, z) and q(z) are, and whose expectation is the finite p_\theta(x) by Eq. 6,

\boxed{\log p_\theta(x) \ge \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right]}
\tag{10}
The right-hand side is a lower bound on the log-likelihood, called the ELBO [13]. The VAE is trained by maximizing this bound [4], which makes it a surrogate objective for the log-likelihood.


1.2.3.4 Unbiased estimates of the ELBO
The ELBO places the expectation outside the logarithm, so it can be estimated by averaging over samples of z. Sampling z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} from q, independently of one another, and replacing the expectation by the sample average,

\mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right] \approx \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \log \frac{p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big)}{q\big(z^{(j)}\big)}

By the linearity of expectation, this sample average is an unbiased estimate of the ELBO. By contrast, the logarithm of a sample average estimates the log-likelihood with a bias that vanishes only as the number of samples tends to infinity, under suitable conditions, by the law of large numbers [14].
The ELBO equals the log-likelihood only when q(z) matches the posterior p_\theta(z \mid x), as shown in §1.2.4. Otherwise, maximizing the ELBO raises a lower bound on the log-likelihood rather than maximizing the log-likelihood directly.



1.2.4 The ELBO gap as a KL divergence
The bound of Eq. 10 holds for each density q on \mathbb{R}^{d_z} that is positive at each z, so the choice of q is free, and how far the ELBO lies below \log p_\theta(x) depends on it [7]. This section measures the gap for each q, which identifies the q for which the bound is an equality.
By the definition of conditional density, the model’s posterior is

p_\theta(z \mid x) = \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{p_\theta(x)}
\tag{11}
The KL divergence [15] of q from the posterior measures the gap [7]. For densities r and s on the same space it is D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) = \mathbb{E}_r[\log r - \log s] (P1:Eq. 29).
By that definition, with r = q and s = p_\theta(z \mid x),

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\big[\log q(z) - \log p_\theta(z \mid x)\big]

Substituting \log p_\theta(z \mid x) = \log p_\theta(x, z) - \log p_\theta(x), the logarithm of Eq. 11,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\big[\log q(z) - \log p_\theta(x, z) + \log p_\theta(x)\big]

By linearity of the expectation, with \log p_\theta(x) constant in z,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\big[\log q(z) - \log p_\theta(x, z)\big] + \log p_\theta(x)

Combining the two logarithms into the logarithm of a quotient,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log \frac{q(z)}{p_\theta(x, z)}\right] + \log p_\theta(x)

Inverting the quotient, which negates its logarithm,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) = -\mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right] + \log p_\theta(x)

Rearranging for \log p_\theta(x),

\boxed{\log p_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)}\right] + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big)}
\tag{12}
The first term on the right is the ELBO from Eq. 10. \square
Therefore, the gap between the log-likelihood \log p_\theta(x) and the ELBO is the KL divergence of q(z) from the posterior p_\theta(z \mid x). Since the KL divergence is non-negative and equals zero only when the two distributions are equal [15], removing this term recovers the lower bound in Eq. 10.






NoteProof: the KL divergence is non-negative





Let r and s be densities on \mathbb{R}^{d_z}, each positive at each z.
Writing the negative KL divergence with the quotient inverted,

-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) = \mathbb{E}_{r(z)}\!\left[\log \frac{s(z)}{r(z)}\right]

By Jensen’s inequality, with f(z) = s(z)/r(z),

-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) \le \log \mathbb{E}_{r(z)}\!\left[\frac{s(z)}{r(z)}\right]

Writing the expectation as an integral,

-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) \le \log \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_z}} r(z)\, \frac{s(z)}{r(z)}\, dz

Cancelling r(z),

-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) \le \log \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_z}} s(z)\, dz

Since s integrates to 1,

-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) \le \log 1

Since \log 1 = 0,

-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) \le 0

Multiplying by -1,

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r \,\|\, s) \ge 0

The logarithm is strictly concave, so Jensen’s inequality is an equality only when f is constant [12]. Here that means s = c\, r for a constant c, and integrating both sides gives c = 1. The KL divergence is therefore zero exactly when r = s. \square



Thus, the ELBO equals the log-likelihood exactly when q(z) = p_\theta(z \mid x). More generally, the closer q(z) is to the posterior, the tighter the ELBO and the closer it lies to the true log-likelihood [7]. This confirms the intuition behind importance sampling, that the best q samples the values of z that are likely given x [7].
The posterior in Eq. 11 cannot be used as q because, although its numerator p_\theta(x, z) can be evaluated for each z, its denominator p_\theta(x) is the intractable marginal likelihood, as discussed in §1.2.1. Consequently, the posterior is only known up to an unknown normalizing constant.


1.2.5 Variational inference: approximating the posterior
Since the posterior p_\theta(z \mid x) of the VAE is known only up to its normalizing constant, it can be neither evaluated nor sampled directly [7]. It is therefore approximated by the member of a family of densities that can be sampled and evaluated, the member that lies closest to it.
The family is indexed by parameters \phi, the variational parameters, and each member is a density q(\cdot\,; \phi): \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to (0, \infty). For example, q may be a Gaussian whose mean \phi_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_z} and symmetric positive-definite covariance \phi_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_z \times d_z} make up \phi = (\phi_1, \phi_2),

q(z; \phi) = \mathcal{N}(z;\ \phi_1,\ \phi_2)

Variational inference chooses \phi so that q(z; \phi) is as close as possible to the posterior p_\theta(z \mid x) [13], where closeness is measured by the KL divergence of Eq. 12. For example, with d_z = 1 and a posterior with two modes, one of two Gaussians with different means and variances approximates it much better than the other, as Figure 7 shows below.








Figure 7: Two Gaussian choices of q(z; \phi) for a posterior p_\theta(z \mid x) with two modes, in one dimension, after Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. The posterior here is the mixture \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(z; 1.5, 1) + \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{N}(z; 4, 0.3). The Gaussian \mathcal{N}(z; 2, 2) covers both modes, and its KL divergence from the posterior is about 0.24. The Gaussian \mathcal{N}(z; -4, 0.75) places its mass where the posterior has almost none, and its KL divergence is about 15.8.





The Gaussian centered between the two modes places its mass where the posterior has mass, so its KL divergence from the posterior is small. The narrow Gaussian at z = -4 proposes values of z that the posterior almost never produces, and its KL divergence is large. Neither Gaussian has two modes, so the ELBO stays below \log p_\theta(x) even for the better one.
Writing \operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) for the right-hand side of Eq. 10 with q = q(\cdot\,; \phi),

\boxed{\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z; \phi)}\right]}
\tag{13}
Substituting \operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) for the first term of Eq. 12 with q = q(\cdot\,; \phi),

\boxed{\log p_\theta(x) = \operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(\cdot\,; \phi) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big)}
\tag{14}
As a function of the variational parameters \phi, the log-likelihood is constant and the ELBO lies below it by that KL divergence, as Figure 8 shows below.








Figure 8: The ELBO, the KL divergence and the log-likelihood as functions of the variational parameters \phi for a fixed x and \theta, after Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. The log-likelihood \log p_\theta(x) does not depend on \phi, and the ELBO lies below it by D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(z; \phi) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)), as Eq. 14 states. The curve is schematic.





The better q(z; \phi) approximates the posterior, the smaller the KL divergence and the closer the ELBO is to \log p_\theta(x) [7]. Since \log p_\theta(x) does not depend on \phi, minimizing the KL divergence over \phi is the same as maximizing the ELBO over \phi. The ELBO needs only the joint density p_\theta(x, z) and q(z; \phi), never the posterior, so variational inference is carried out by maximizing the ELBO in \phi.


1.2.6 Variational learning: joint optimization of the model and the approximation
The ELBO serves two ends at once. Raising it in \phi tightens the bound, as the previous section showed, and raising it in \theta raises the bound on the log-likelihood of the data. Variational learning maximizes it over the model parameters \theta and the variational parameters \phi together [7]. For a fixed \phi, \operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) is a function of \theta that lies below \log p_\theta(x) at each \theta, and it touches \log p_\theta(x) at the \theta for which q(z; \phi) equals the posterior p_\theta(z \mid x). Two values, \phi and \phi', give two such lower bounds, as Figure 9 shows below.








Figure 9: Two ELBOs as functions of \theta for a fixed x, after Ermon and Grover’s CS236 notes [7]. Each lies below the log-likelihood \log p_\theta(x) and touches it at one value of \theta. Maximizing \mathrm{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi), which touches at \theta_{\mathrm{old}}, gives \theta_{\mathrm{new}}, where the log-likelihood is higher. The ELBO with \phi' touches at \theta_{\mathrm{new}}. The curves are schematic.





At \theta_{\mathrm{old}} the bound with \phi equals the log-likelihood. Maximizing that bound in \theta gives \theta_{\mathrm{new}}, where the bound is higher than at \theta_{\mathrm{old}}, and the log-likelihood at \theta_{\mathrm{new}} lies above the bound. So, starting from a \theta at which the bound is tight, raising the ELBO in \theta raises the log-likelihood. At \theta_{\mathrm{new}} the bound with \phi is no longer tight, and the bound with \phi' is. Each update of \theta therefore calls for a new \phi, which is why learning optimizes the two jointly [7].

1.2.6.1 A bound for the whole dataset
So far the ELBO bounds the log-likelihood of a single image. Training maximizes the log-likelihood \ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) of the whole dataset, Eq. 8. Substituting Eq. 14 for each of its terms, with its own variational parameters \phi^{(i)} for x^{(i)},

\ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big[\operatorname{ELBO}\big(x^{(i)}; \theta, \phi^{(i)}\big) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q(\cdot\,; \phi^{(i)}) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x^{(i)})\big)\Big]

Dropping the non-negative KL divergences,

\ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) \ge \sum_{i=1}^{n} \operatorname{ELBO}\big(x^{(i)}; \theta, \phi^{(i)}\big)

The inequality holds for each \theta and each \phi^{(1)}, \ldots, \phi^{(n)}, so it holds between the maxima. Maximizing the left-hand side over \theta and the right-hand side over \theta and \phi^{(1)}, \ldots, \phi^{(n)},

\boxed{\max_{\theta}\, \ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) \ge \max_{\theta,\, \phi^{(1)}, \ldots, \phi^{(n)}}\, \sum_{i=1}^{n} \operatorname{ELBO}\big(x^{(i)}; \theta, \phi^{(i)}\big)}
\tag{15}
Each training image has its own variational parameters \phi^{(i)}, because the posterior p_\theta(z \mid x^{(i)}) differs from one training image to another [7].


1.2.6.2 Stochastic variational inference: one training image per update
Stochastic variational inference (SVI) [16] maximizes the right-hand side of Eq. 15 by stochastic gradient ascent, which updates the parameters with the gradient on one randomly chosen training image at a time [7]. It writes the ELBO of each training image as one expectation.
Splitting the logarithm of the quotient in Eq. 13 for x^{(i)} and \phi^{(i)},

\operatorname{ELBO}\big(x^{(i)}; \theta, \phi^{(i)}\big) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi^{(i)})}\big[\log p_\theta\big(x^{(i)}, z\big) - \log q\big(z; \phi^{(i)}\big)\big]

The algorithm alternates between the variational parameters of one training image and the model parameters. Its step size is \eta > 0.
Algorithm 1 — Stochastic variational inference [7]:
1: Initialize \theta, \phi^{(1)}, \ldots, \phi^{(n)}
2: repeat
    3: Sample i uniformly from \{1, \ldots, n\}
    4: repeat
        5: \phi^{(i)} \leftarrow \phi^{(i)} + \eta\, \nabla_{\phi} \operatorname{ELBO}\big(x^{(i)}; \theta, \phi^{(i)}\big)
    6: until \phi^{(i)} converges to \phi^{(i),*} \approx \arg\max_{\phi} \operatorname{ELBO}\big(x^{(i)}; \theta, \phi\big)
    7: Compute \nabla_\theta \operatorname{ELBO}\big(x^{(i)}; \theta, \phi^{(i),*}\big)
    8: Update \theta in the direction of that gradient
9: until converged
Lines 5 and 7 need gradients of the ELBO, an expectation over q(z; \phi^{(i)}) that often has no closed form. The next section estimates them by Monte Carlo sampling [7].



1.2.7 Gradient estimates for training
Algorithm 1 needs \nabla_\theta \operatorname{ELBO} and \nabla_\phi \operatorname{ELBO} for one training image. Dropping the superscript (i) from x and \phi for compactness, the ELBO of the previous section is [7]

\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\big[\log p_\theta(x, z) - \log q(z; \phi)\big]


1.2.7.1 The gradient with respect to the model parameters
The family q(z; \phi) was chosen so that it can be sampled and evaluated, and this makes the ELBO easy to estimate [7]. Sampling z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)} independently from q(z; \phi) and replacing the expectation by the sample average,

\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) \approx \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \Big[\log p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big) - \log q\big(z^{(j)}; \phi\big)\Big]

The gradient with respect to \theta is easy, because the density q(z; \phi) that the expectation averages over does not depend on \theta. Exchanging the gradient and the expectation, which holds when \log p_\theta(x, z) is differentiable in \theta with a gradient bounded by a function integrable under q(z; \phi), by dominated convergence,

\nabla_\theta \operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\big[\nabla_\theta \big(\log p_\theta(x, z) - \log q(z; \phi)\big)\big]

Since \log q(z; \phi) does not depend on \theta,

\nabla_\theta \operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\big[\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x, z)\big]

Replacing the expectation by the sample average over z^{(1)}, \ldots, z^{(k)},

\nabla_\theta \operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) \approx \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta\big(x, z^{(j)}\big)

The gradient with respect to \phi is harder, because the density of the expectation depends on \phi, so the gradient cannot be exchanged with an expectation over q(z; \phi) in the same way [7]. A Monte Carlo average is still the goal. A general estimator, REINFORCE [17], works for each family q(z; \phi). A less general one, which needs a continuous z and only some families, typically has a lower variance [7], and the following subsection develops it.


1.2.7.2 Reparameterization: the gradient with respect to the variational parameters
The estimator rewrites a sample of q(z; \phi) as a deterministic function of \phi and of noise that does not depend on \phi [4], [18]. The simpler case is the gradient with respect to \phi of \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}[h(z)] for a function h: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to \mathbb{R} that does not depend on \phi [7].
Let q(z; \phi) = \mathcal{N}(z;\ \mu,\ \sigma^2 I) be a Gaussian with a mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{d_z} and a standard deviation \sigma > 0, the isotropic case of the Gaussian example, with mean \phi_1 = \mu and covariance \phi_2 = \sigma^2 I, parameterized here by \phi = (\mu, \sigma). It can be sampled in two equivalent ways.

Sampling z \sim q(z; \phi) directly.
Sampling \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and setting z = z_\phi(\epsilon), where z_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{d_z} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_z}, z_\phi(\epsilon) = \mu + \sigma \epsilon, is deterministic.

They are equivalent because \mu + \sigma \epsilon is Gaussian, as an affine function of a Gaussian, with mean \mu and covariance \sigma^2 I. This rewriting is the reparameterization of z.
By the equivalence of the two ways of sampling,

\mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\big[h(z)\big] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(\epsilon; 0, I)}\big[h\big(z_\phi(\epsilon)\big)\big]

Taking the gradient with respect to \phi of both sides,

\nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\big[h(z)\big] = \nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(\epsilon; 0, I)}\big[h\big(z_\phi(\epsilon)\big)\big]

The density of \epsilon does not depend on \phi. Exchanging the gradient and the expectation, under the same dominated-convergence condition as for \theta,

\nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\big[h(z)\big] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(\epsilon; 0, I)}\big[\nabla_\phi\, h\big(z_\phi(\epsilon)\big)\big]

Sampling \epsilon^{(1)}, \ldots, \epsilon^{(k)} independently from \mathcal{N}(0, I) and replacing the expectation by the sample average,

\boxed{\nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{q(z; \phi)}\big[h(z)\big] \approx \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \nabla_\phi\, h\big(z_\phi(\epsilon^{(j)})\big)}
\tag{16}
Each term is computed by the chain rule through h and z_\phi, which needs both to be differentiable. This estimate typically has a lower variance than REINFORCE [7].
The ELBO adds one complication, because the function inside its expectation, \log p_\theta(x, z) - \log q(z; \phi), depends on \phi as well as on z [7]. Writing it as h(z, \phi), the reparameterization still applies. By the equivalence of the two ways of sampling,

\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(\epsilon; 0, I)}\big[h\big(z_\phi(\epsilon), \phi\big)\big]

Replacing the expectation by the sample average over \epsilon^{(1)}, \ldots, \epsilon^{(k)},

\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) \approx \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} h\big(z_\phi(\epsilon^{(j)}), \phi\big)

Its gradient with respect to \phi is the average of the gradients of the terms, each computed by the chain rule through both arguments of h.
With these estimates, each line of Algorithm 1 can be computed. The algorithm is still expensive, because it stores variational parameters \phi^{(1)}, \ldots, \phi^{(n)}, one set for each training image, and runs an inner optimization of \phi^{(i)} at each update. The next section replaces both by a single network.



1.2.8 The encoder: one network for all training images
The VAE replaces the variational parameters \phi^{(1)}, \ldots, \phi^{(n)} by a network, its encoder, which computes the parameters of q from x [4].
Post #1 describes a VAE with a single latent variable z (P1:§5.1). Its computation graph encodes from x to z and decodes back from z to x, as Figure 10 shows below.








Figure 10: Computation graph of a VAE, after Lai et al. [19], Figure 2.1. The encoder q_\phi maps x to the latent z along the upper arrow, and the decoder p_\theta maps z back to x along the lower one. Both directions are learned.





The encoder of the VAE follows the upper arrow,

q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(z;\ \mu_\phi(x),\ \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_\phi(x)^2)\big)

a Gaussian whose mean \mu_\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d_z} and standard deviations \sigma_\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to (0, \infty)^{d_z} are computed by the network. Here the square is taken elementwise, and \operatorname{diag}(v) is the diagonal matrix with the vector v on its diagonal, so the coordinates of z are independent given x. From here on, \phi denotes the parameters of this network rather than the variational parameters of a single density. The decoder follows the lower arrow, the factor p_\theta(x \mid z) of the joint density in §1.2.1.
With q_\phi(z \mid x) in place of q(z; \phi), the ELBO of an image x is [7]

\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x, z) - \log q_\phi(z \mid x)\big]
\tag{17}
Reparameterization carries over to the encoder. Its Gaussian is the affine image of a standard Gaussian, so sampling z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x) is the same as sampling \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and setting

z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \epsilon

where \odot is the elementwise product [4]. The gradient with respect to \phi then follows as in §1.2.7, now through the encoder network. Training no longer needs an inner loop, because one gradient step updates \theta and \phi together, on a random set of m training images at a time, with the step size \eta of Algorithm 1.
Algorithm 2 — VAE training [4]:
1: Initialize \theta, \phi
2: repeat
    3: Sample a set \mathcal{B} of m indices uniformly from \{1, \ldots, n\}
    4: For each i \in \mathcal{B}, sample \epsilon^{(i)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and set z^{(i)} = \mu_\phi\big(x^{(i)}\big) + \sigma_\phi\big(x^{(i)}\big) \odot \epsilon^{(i)}
    5: Compute \widehat{\operatorname{ELBO}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} \Big[\log p_\theta\big(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}\big) - \log q_\phi\big(z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}\big)\Big]
    6: (\theta, \phi) \leftarrow (\theta, \phi) + \eta\, \nabla_{\theta, \phi}\, \widehat{\operatorname{ELBO}}
7: until converged
Line 5 uses one sample of z for each training image, as Kingma and Welling do with m = 100 [4]. Compared with Algorithm 1, the n separate sets of variational parameters and the inner loop are gone.


1.2.9 The VAE objective as an autoencoder
The ELBO of Eq. 17 splits into two terms, each with a direct role in the model.
Substituting \log p_\theta(x, z) = \log p_\theta(x \mid z) + \log p(z), the logarithm of the factorization of the joint density in §1.2.1,

\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z) + \log p(z) - \log q_\phi(z \mid x)\big]

By linearity of the expectation,

\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p(z) - \log q_\phi(z \mid x)\big]

Recognizing the second expectation as the negative of the KL divergence of the encoder from the prior,

\boxed{\operatorname{ELBO}(x; \theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\big)}
\tag{18}
The first term is the expected log-likelihood of x under the decoder, and the second is the KL divergence of the encoder from the prior. \square
This form can be interpreted as an autoencoder [7]. For a training image x^{(i)}, the two terms evaluate two steps:

Encoding: Mapping x^{(i)} to a latent value z' by sampling z' \sim q_\phi(z \mid x^{(i)}), the Gaussian with mean \mu_\phi(x^{(i)}) and standard deviations \sigma_\phi(x^{(i)}).
Decoding: Reconstructing an image x' by sampling from p_\theta(x \mid z'), the Gaussian with mean \mu_\theta(z') and covariance \Sigma_\theta(z').

The first term of Eq. 18 is large when x^{(i)} is likely under p_\theta(x \mid z'), so it encourages the reconstruction x' to be close to x^{(i)}. Its negative plays the part of the reconstruction loss of an autoencoder. The second term encourages the latent values z' to follow a distribution similar to the prior p(z) [7].
A communication analogy: Alice compresses an image x^{(i)} into a message z' \sim q_\phi(z \mid x^{(i)}) and sends it, and Bob reconstructs the image with p_\theta(x \mid z') [7]. The first term of Eq. 18 rewards accurate reconstructions, and the KL divergence forces the messages to follow p(z), so Bob can also sample messages z' \sim p(z) and decode them into realistic images. A trained VAE generates in the same way, by sampling z from the prior p(z) and decoding it with p_\theta(x \mid z).

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
section: 1.3 Hierarchical VAE: posteriors with several modes
text:
1.3 Hierarchical VAE: posteriors with several modes
Making the encoder and decoder deeper does not remove the limit of this design. For each x, the encoder q_\phi(z \mid x) outputs one Gaussian over z. Deeper networks make its mean and variance more accurate but leave it one Gaussian, so it cannot match a posterior of z given x that has several modes. This is the limit Figure 7 showed for a single density, where neither Gaussian has two modes and the gap stays open.
A hierarchical VAE stacks M latent variables z_1, \ldots, z_M, each conditioning the one below it [18], [20]. Its computation graph encodes upward from x through z_1, \ldots, z_M and decodes back down from z_M to x, as Figure 11 shows below.








Figure 11: Computation graph of a hierarchical VAE, drawn as the VAE’s graph above with M latent levels, after Lai et al. [19], Figure 2.2. The encoder q_\phi maps x up through the latents z_1, \ldots, z_M along the upper arrows, and the decoder p_\theta maps z_M back down to x along the lower ones. Both directions are learned.





The decoder of the hierarchical VAE follows the lower arrows, so it factorizes from the top down,

p_\theta(x, z_{1:M}) = p_\theta(x \mid z_1) \prod_{i=2}^{M} p_\theta(z_{i-1} \mid z_i)\, p(z_M)

so generation samples z_M from the prior and decodes it level by level down to x. Its encoder follows the upper arrows from the bottom up,

q_\phi(z_{1:M} \mid x) = q_\phi(z_1 \mid x) \prod_{i=2}^{M} q_\phi(z_i \mid z_{i-1})

Each factor is a Gaussian of the VAE encoder’s form, with a mean and standard deviations that are computed from the level below using a network with parameters \phi. Such a chain is no longer one Gaussian, so it can represent a posterior with several modes.
It is trained through its ELBO, which follows from the derivation of Eq. 10, with z_{1:M} and the encoder chain in place of z and q,

\log p_\theta(x) \ge \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z_{1:M} \mid x)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z_{1:M})}{q_\phi(z_{1:M} \mid x)}\right]

Negating both sides gives an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood, the form in which Part 2 trains DDPM,

-\log p_\theta(x) \le \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z_{1:M} \mid x)}\!\left[-\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z_{1:M})}{q_\phi(z_{1:M} \mid x)}\right]
\tag{19}
Part 1 has assembled the four elements of variational training: a lower bound on the log-likelihood, the ELBO; an encoder that approximates the posterior; a decoder that generates; and a training loop that maximizes the bound over both networks (Algorithm 2). DDPM keeps the bound, the decoder and the training loop, and replaces the learned encoder by a fixed one. Part 2 shows that it is a hierarchical VAE whose encoder is fixed to adding Gaussian noise and whose latent levels have the dimension of the data.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
2.1 Definitions
The DDPM sections of this Part use the objects below. The first group recaps the construction of post #1; the second group is new to this post and is developed in the sections that follow.
