The table supports three conclusions. Predicting the posterior mean \tilde\mu_i works only with the true bound. A learned diagonal \Sigma_\theta trains worse than a fixed one, or not at all. Predicting the noise \epsilon matches predicting \tilde\mu_i under the bound, with an FID of 13.51 against 13.22, and is far better under L_{\text{simple}}, with 3.17.
The price is likelihood, measured in bits per dimension, the negative base-2 log-likelihood of an image divided by its number of coordinates (3072 for a CIFAR-10 image), so lower is better. On the CIFAR-10 test set, the model trained on the bound reaches a codelength of at most 3.70 bits per dimension, against 3.75 for the model trained on L_{\text{simple}} (their Table 1).
Ho et al. interpret the terms of Eq. 22 as a code [1]. The sum L_1 + \cdots + L_N is the rate, the codelength of x_N, x_{N-1}, \ldots, x_1 under the reverse Markov chain, and L_0 is the distortion, the codelength of x_0 given x_1. Their model with the best samples has a rate of 1.78 bits per dimension and a distortion of 1.97, which corresponds to a root-mean-square error of 0.95 on the pixel scale from 0 to 255. More than half of the codelength therefore describes differences too small to see, and they sit at the small-noise end of the chain, which the true weight emphasizes.
The sampler shows the same order. During sampling, the network’s estimate of x_0 from the current state shows large-scale features of the image first and fine details last (their Fig. 6).


2.3.2 The two extremes of the reverse variance
Step 4 fixed the reverse variance to \beta_i or \tilde\beta_i and called the two values the extremes. Ho et al. state that \beta_i is optimal for x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and \tilde\beta_i for a single fixed x_0 [1]. They identify the two values with the upper and lower bounds on the entropy of a reverse step that Sohl-Dickstein et al. derived [21], for data whose coordinates have unit variance.
The theorem below makes the optimality precise. For each i \ge 2 one fixed variance minimizes the expected KL divergence \mathbb{E}_p[L_{i-1}] of Eq. 25, and the two values bound it. Here L_{i-1} is the KL term of Eq. 22 with the variance term C of Step 4 kept, since C depends on \sigma_i^2.
Definitions:

Reverse mean: \bar\mu_i: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, \bar\mu_i(x_i) = \mathbb{E}[x_{i-1} \mid x_i], is the mean of the true reverse conditional q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i).
Average reverse variance: The variance of q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) per coordinate, averaged over x_i, is 
\bar\sigma_i^2 = \frac{1}{d}\, \mathbb{E}_p \big\lVert x_{i-1} - \bar\mu_i(x_i) \big\rVert^2


Assumptions:

The data has a finite second moment, and the expectations in the proof are finite.
The variances of the coordinates of x_0 average at most 1, \operatorname{tr} \operatorname{Cov}(x_0) \le d.

Theorem:
Under these assumptions, for each i \ge 2, among the reverse steps q_\theta(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_{i-1};\, \bar\mu_i(x_i),\, \sigma_i^2 I\big) the expected KL divergence \mathbb{E}_p[L_{i-1}] of Eq. 25 is smallest at \sigma_i^2 = \bar\sigma_i^2, and

\boxed{\tilde\beta_i \le \bar\sigma_i^2 \le \beta_i}
\tag{33}
The lower bound needs only assumption 1 and is attained when p_0 is a single point. The upper bound is attained when p_0 = \mathcal{N}(0, I). The proof has three steps.

Splitting the error of \bar\mu_i around the posterior mean \tilde\mu_i adds a non-negative term to d\, \tilde\beta_i, which gives the lower bound.
The error of \bar\mu_i is at most that of an estimator linear in x_i, and a concavity argument bounds that error by d\, \beta_i.
The part of \mathbb{E}_p[L_{i-1}] that depends on \sigma_i^2 is a function of one variable, smallest at \bar\sigma_i^2.







NoteProof: the two extremes of the reverse variance





Step 1 — the lower bound:
We write \tilde\mu_i for \tilde\mu_i(x_i, x_0) and \bar\mu_i for \bar\mu_i(x_i). Adding and subtracting \tilde\mu_i inside the error,

\mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2 = \mathbb{E}_p \big\lVert (x_{i-1} - \tilde\mu_i) + (\tilde\mu_i - \bar\mu_i) \big\rVert^2

Expanding the square,

\mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2 = \mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \tilde\mu_i \rVert^2 + 2\, \mathbb{E}_p\big[(x_{i-1} - \tilde\mu_i)^\top (\tilde\mu_i - \bar\mu_i)\big] + \mathbb{E}_p \lVert \tilde\mu_i - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2

Conditioning the cross term on (x_i, x_0), which fixes its second factor and, by Eq. 23, gives its first factor the mean zero, the cross term vanishes,

\mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2 = \mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \tilde\mu_i \rVert^2 + \mathbb{E}_p \lVert \tilde\mu_i - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2

Substituting \mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \tilde\mu_i \rVert^2 = d\, \tilde\beta_i, the trace of the posterior covariance \tilde\beta_i I,

\mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2 = d\, \tilde\beta_i + \mathbb{E}_p \lVert \tilde\mu_i - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2

Dividing by d, which turns the left side into \bar\sigma_i^2 by its definition,

\bar\sigma_i^2 = \tilde\beta_i + \frac{1}{d}\, \mathbb{E}_p \lVert \tilde\mu_i - \bar\mu_i \rVert^2

The last term is non-negative, which gives the lower bound. When p_0 is a single point x^\ast, x_0 = x^\ast always, so q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) = q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i, x^\ast), whose mean is \tilde\mu_i(x_i, x^\ast). Then \bar\mu_i = \tilde\mu_i, the last term is zero and \bar\sigma_i^2 = \tilde\beta_i.
Step 2 — the upper bound:
We write S = \operatorname{Cov}(x_{i-1}) = U \Omega U^\top, with U orthogonal and \Omega = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_d), \omega_k \ge 0, and compare \bar\mu_i with the estimator h: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d that is affine in x_i and diagonal in that basis,

h(x_i) = \mathbb{E}[x_{i-1}] + U \operatorname{diag}(c_1, \ldots, c_d)\, U^\top \big(x_i - \mathbb{E}[x_i]\big), \qquad c_k = \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_i}\, \omega_k}{\alpha_i \omega_k + \beta_i}

The expansion of Step 1, around \bar\mu_i instead of \tilde\mu_i and with the cross term conditioned on x_i, shows that \bar\mu_i(x_i) = \mathbb{E}[x_{i-1} \mid x_i] has the smallest mean squared error among the functions of x_i. Comparing with h,

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le \mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - h(x_i) \rVert^2

We write y = U^\top (x_{i-1} - \mathbb{E}[x_{i-1}]) and z = U^\top \epsilon_i, so that the forward step x_i = \sqrt{\alpha_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i gives U^\top (x_i - \mathbb{E}[x_i]) = \sqrt{\alpha_i}\, y + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, z. Rotating by U^\top, which preserves the norm,

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le \sum_{k=1}^{d} \mathbb{E}\big[\big(y_k - c_k (\sqrt{\alpha_i}\, y_k + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, z_k)\big)^2\big]

Expanding each square, with \mathbb{E}[y_k^2] = \omega_k, \mathbb{E}[z_k^2] = 1 and \mathbb{E}[y_k z_k] = 0, since \epsilon_i is independent of x_{i-1},

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le \sum_{k=1}^{d} \Big(\omega_k - 2 c_k \sqrt{\alpha_i}\, \omega_k + c_k^2 (\alpha_i \omega_k + \beta_i)\Big)

Substituting c_k,

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le \sum_{k=1}^{d} \Big(\omega_k - \frac{\alpha_i \omega_k^2}{\alpha_i \omega_k + \beta_i}\Big)

Combining each term over its denominator,

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le \sum_{k=1}^{d} \frac{\beta_i\, \omega_k}{\alpha_i \omega_k + \beta_i}

The function f: [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty), f(\omega) = \beta_i \omega / (\alpha_i \omega + \beta_i), is increasing and concave, since

f''(\omega) = -\frac{2 \alpha_i \beta_i^2}{(\alpha_i \omega + \beta_i)^3} < 0

Since a concave f lies below its tangent line at m = \operatorname{tr} S / d, the average of the \omega_k, each f(\omega_k) \le f(m) + f'(m)(\omega_k - m). Summing over k, which cancels the linear terms (Jensen’s inequality for a finite average),

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le d\, f\big(\operatorname{tr} S / d\big)

The closed form x_{i-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\, \epsilon, with \epsilon independent of x_0, gives

\operatorname{tr} S = \bar\alpha_{i-1} \operatorname{tr} \operatorname{Cov}(x_0) + (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1})\, d

which is at most d by assumption 2. As f is increasing, substituting \operatorname{tr} S / d \le 1,

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le d\, f(1)

Substituting f(1) = \beta_i / (\alpha_i + \beta_i) = \beta_i, since \alpha_i + \beta_i = 1,

d\, \bar\sigma_i^2 \le d\, \beta_i

Dividing by d gives the upper bound. When p_0 = \mathcal{N}(0, I), the closed form makes x_{i-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) as well, so by Bayes’ rule the density of x_{i-1} given x_i satisfies

q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) \propto \exp\Big(-\frac{\lVert x_{i-1} \rVert^2}{2} - \frac{\lVert x_i - \sqrt{\alpha_i}\, x_{i-1} \rVert^2}{2 \beta_i}\Big)

The coefficient of -\lVert x_{i-1} \rVert^2 / 2 in the exponent is 1 + \alpha_i / \beta_i = 1 / \beta_i, so q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) is Gaussian with covariance \beta_i I and \bar\sigma_i^2 = \beta_i.
Step 3 — the best fixed variance:
By Eq. 25, only the first term of \mathbb{E}_p[L_{i-1}] depends on \sigma_i^2. We write it K(\sigma_i^2). Under the forward process x_{i-1} given x_i has density q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i), so it is an expected log-ratio over the pair,

K(\sigma_i^2) = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\log q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) - \log q_\theta(x_{i-1} \mid x_i)\big]

Substituting the Gaussian log-density of q_\theta,

K(\sigma_i^2) = \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\log q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i) + \frac{d}{2} \log(2\pi \sigma_i^2) + \frac{\lVert x_{i-1} - \bar\mu_i(x_i) \rVert^2}{2 \sigma_i^2}\Big]

By linearity,

K(\sigma_i^2) = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\log q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i)\big] + \frac{d}{2} \log(2\pi \sigma_i^2) + \frac{\mathbb{E}_p \lVert x_{i-1} - \bar\mu_i(x_i) \rVert^2}{2 \sigma_i^2}

Substituting the definition of \bar\sigma_i^2,

K(\sigma_i^2) = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\log q(x_{i-1} \mid x_i)\big] + \frac{d}{2} \log(2\pi \sigma_i^2) + \frac{d\, \bar\sigma_i^2}{2 \sigma_i^2}

Differentiating in \sigma_i^2,

\frac{dK}{d\sigma_i^2} = \frac{d}{2 \sigma_i^2} - \frac{d\, \bar\sigma_i^2}{2 \sigma_i^4}

The derivative is negative below \bar\sigma_i^2 and positive above it, and \bar\sigma_i^2 \ge \tilde\beta_i > 0 for i \ge 2 by Step 1, so K is smallest at \sigma_i^2 = \bar\sigma_i^2. \square





2.3.3 Learning the reverse variance
The two extremes nearly coincide over most of the chain. Their ratio \tilde\beta_i / \beta_i = (1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}) / (1 - \bar\alpha_i), from Eq. 24, is 0 at i = 1 and close to 1 after the first few percent of the chain (Nichol and Dhariwal’s Fig. 1), so the choice between them barely changes the samples, as Ho et al. observed. Nichol and Dhariwal add that the first few terms of the bound carry most of its value, so the variance matters for the likelihood [23].
The range of sensible variances is narrow, so they do not predict \Sigma_\theta directly. For i \ge 2 the network outputs a vector field \nu_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \times \{1, \ldots, N\} \to \mathbb{R}^d that interpolates between the two extremes in the logarithm, coordinate by coordinate,

\Sigma_\theta(x_i, i) = \exp\big(\nu_\theta(x_i, i) \log \beta_i + (1 - \nu_\theta(x_i, i)) \log \tilde\beta_i\big)

with the exponential applied to each coordinate and the result placed on the diagonal of \Sigma_\theta. The vector \nu_\theta is unconstrained, yet the trained network kept the variances between the two extremes.
L_{\text{simple}} does not depend on \Sigma_\theta, so they train with the hybrid objective

L_{\text{hybrid}} = L_{\text{simple}} + 0.001\, L

where L is the bound Eq. 21, with each L_{i-1} the KL divergence between Gaussians computed with the learned variance. In L the predicted mean is held fixed in the gradient, so the bound trains the variance and L_{\text{simple}} the mean.
Combined with a change of noise schedule, the hybrid objective improves the log-likelihood while keeping the FID close to Ho et al.’s (their Tables 1 and 2) [23]. The learned variances also keep the sample quality when sampling uses fewer steps than training. For their fully trained models, 100 sampling steps reach a near-optimal FID, while the L_{\text{simple}} models with either fixed variance degrade much more (their Fig. 8).

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
2.4 The denoising network
Input: The model is a neural network with parameters \theta, the denoising network. Its input is a noised state x_i together with the step index i that says how noised it is.
Output: The network outputs a vector of the same shape as x_i: a prediction of the noise that was mixed into x_0 to produce x_i. We write this output \epsilon_\theta(x_i, i).
Prediction: When we built x_i by one-step sampling, we sampled the noise \epsilon ourselves, so we know the true value exactly. The network does not see \epsilon; it sees only x_i and i, and must predict it. Its prediction \epsilon_\theta(x_i, i) is compared against the \epsilon we sampled, the ground truth (Figure 14).








Figure 14: The denoising network as a supervised regressor. We build a training example by one-step sampling: an image x_0 and a sampled noise \epsilon combine into the noised state x_i. The network sees only x_i and the step index i, not \epsilon, and outputs a prediction \epsilon_\theta(x_i, i) of that noise. Training minimizes the squared gap between the prediction and the noise we sampled, \|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_i, i)\|^2.





Algorithm 3 — DDPM training [1]:
1: repeat
    2: x_0 \sim p_0(x_0)
    3: i \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(\{1, \ldots, N\})
    4: \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
    5: Take gradient descent step on \nabla_\theta \big\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\epsilon,\ i\big)\big\rVert^2
6: until converged
Predicting x_0: The mean \mu_\theta of Eq. 20 can also come from a network that predicts x_0 instead of the noise [1], [19]. Writing \hat x_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \times \{1, \ldots, N\} \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x_i, i) \mapsto \hat x_\theta(x_i, i), for that prediction and putting it in place of x_0 in Eq. 24,

\mu_\theta(x_i, i) = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\beta_i}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, \hat x_\theta(x_i, i) + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_i}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{i-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, x_i

Subtracting it from \tilde\mu_i of Eq. 24,

\begin{aligned}
\tilde\mu_i - \mu_\theta = {} & \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\beta_i}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_i}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{i-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, x_i \\[4pt]
& - \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\beta_i}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, \hat x_\theta(x_i, i) - \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_i}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{i-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, x_i
\end{aligned}

Cancelling the x_i terms,

\tilde\mu_i - \mu_\theta = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\beta_i}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 - \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\beta_i}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\, \hat x_\theta(x_i, i)

Factoring out the common coefficient,

\tilde\mu_i - \mu_\theta = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\beta_i}{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\big(x_0 - \hat x_\theta(x_i, i)\big)

so matching the means is regressing \hat x_\theta onto x_0, with a weight for each step. The two predictions determine each other through x_i = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\epsilon. A noise prediction gives

\hat x_\theta = \frac{x_i - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\epsilon_\theta}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}}

so the two are equivalent parameterizations of one network. §4.10 shows that the minimizer of this regression is the posterior mean of x_0 given x_i.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
2.5 Sampling: ancestral sampling
With \epsilon_\theta trained, generation runs the reverse Markov chain: start from noise and, for i = N down to 1, take one learned reverse step.
Algorithm 4 — DDPM sampling [1]:
1: x_N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
2: for i = N, \ldots, 1 do
    3: z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) if i > 1, else z = 0
    4: x_{i-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_i}}\left(x_i - \frac{\beta_i}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_i, i)\right) + \sigma_i z
5: end for
6: return x_0
Line 4 is one step of the learned reverse Markov chain. The expression before \sigma_i z is its mean \mu_\theta(x_i, i), parameterized as in Eq. 28. The factor \sigma_i scales the noise, so the step’s variance \sigma_i^2 matches the fixed schedule constant, as Step 4 of the ELBO loss derivation established. Line 4 is therefore, for i > 1, the reparameterized sample

x_{i-1} \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\theta(x_i, i),\, \sigma_i^2 I\big)

At i = 1 it returns the mean \mu_\theta(x_1, 1). The only unknown in \mu_\theta is \epsilon_\theta, which the network predicts. This stepwise sample-from-each-conditional scheme is ancestral sampling, the native sampler of the reverse Markov chain.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
section: 3.1 Energy-based models and the partition function
text:
3.1 Energy-based models and the partition function
Energy-based models rely on a constraint-free representation of probability densities, so it is worth examining what any such representation must satisfy.
The requirement on a given model to be a probability distribution is twofold:

Non-negative, p(x) \ge 0: This is easy to satisfy, since given any function f_\theta(x), each of g_\theta(x) = f_\theta(x)^2 and \exp(f_\theta(x)) is non-negative.
Sum-to-one, \sum_x p(x) = 1 (or \int p(x)\, dx = 1 for continuous variables): This is the binding constraint, and it matters because a fixed total volume is what makes training meaningful. Increasing p(x_{\text{train}}) then guarantees that x_{\text{train}} becomes relatively more likely than the rest. A generic non-negative g_\theta has \int g_\theta(x)\, dx = Z(\theta) \ne 1, so it is not a valid probability mass function or density.

The generic repair is to divide by the volume,

p_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\, g_\theta(x)

where the normalizer is the total volume under g_\theta,

Z(\theta) = \int g_\theta(x)\, dx

The integral is assumed finite and positive, so g_\theta must decay fast enough at infinity for it to converge. Then \int p_\theta(x)\, dx = 1 by construction.
Choosing the exponential as the non-negativity transform, and writing the exponent as -E_\theta(x), where E_\theta(x) is the energy function, so that low energy values are assigned high probability, gives the energy-based model (EBM) [27], [28]:

p_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp(-E_\theta(x))

They are inspired by principles of thermodynamics, where systems evolve toward lower-energy states, so lower-energy states are more likely than higher ones.
Here, the normalization constant

Z(\theta) = \int \exp(-E_\theta(x))\, dx

is called the partition function.
This partition function was one of the deepest obstacles in generative modeling because it is central to turning an energy function into a valid probability distribution. As we can see, Z requires summing or integrating over the entire, astronomically high-dimensional data space, which amounts to accounting for each possible image, configuration, or state in order to assign probabilities to the ones we care about. This made likelihood-based learning extraordinarily difficult: researchers tried to avoid the problem through contrastive divergence [29], Metropolis-Hastings Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) [30], [31], importance sampling [11], variational approximations [13], pseudo-likelihood [32], autoregressive factorizations [33], and other approximate inference schemes, but these approaches either remained computationally expensive, introduced bias, mixed poorly in high dimensions, or sacrificed the attractive properties of an explicit normalized likelihood. The fundamental difficulty was not simply that Z was “large”; it was that changing the model parameters changes the entire integral, so the normalization had to be repeatedly accounted for during learning.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
3.2 The score

3.2.1 Intuition: electric fields
Before defining the score formally, it helps to borrow an analogy from electrostatics, where the same relationship between a scalar field and its gradient appears in a setting most readers already have intuition for.
In electrostatics, a distribution of charge sets up a scalar potential \phi(x), one number at each point in space. Its value measures how much potential energy a positive test charge would have there: high near like charges it is repelled from, low near opposite charges it is drawn toward. From that potential comes a vector field \mathcal{E}(x), the electric field, defined as the negative of its gradient, \mathcal{E} = -\nabla_x \phi. The field has a direction and a magnitude at each point: it points “downhill,” toward lower potential, and it is strong where the potential varies sharply and weak where the potential is flat (Figure 16).
The key relationship is that the field is the negative gradient of the potential. Knowing the potential everywhere, we obtain the field by differentiating. The field tells us, at any point, which way is downhill in potential most steeply and how steep that descent is. A test charge released into the field feels a force along it and drifts accordingly. It is pushed by the local gradient, without ever needing to know the global shape of the potential.








Figure 16: The electric field of a pair of opposite charges. Each line leaves the positive charge and enters the negative one; at any point the local arrow gives the field’s direction, and the spacing of the lines encodes its strength. A test charge responds to the local arrow alone, and no global knowledge of the potential is required. The score plays the same role over data space.







3.2.2 Score definition
Generative modeling follows the electrostatics analogy given above, with the log-density playing the role of the potential. A data distribution defines a log-density \log p(x) at each point, high where data is dense and low where data is sparse. Its gradient,

\boxed{s(x) \;=\; \nabla_x \log p(x)}
\tag{34}
is the score. The score plays the role of the field, with one difference in convention: where the electric field is the negative gradient of the potential and points downhill toward lower potential, the score is the positive gradient of the log-density and points uphill, toward regions where data is more likely. Both are gradient fields of a scalar. At each point the vector is aligned with the direction the scalar changes fastest, and its magnitude is the rate of that change. They differ only in sign, and so in whether they point down the potential or up the density.
The analogy extends to how each field moves the object it acts on. In electrostatics, a test charge released into the field drifts along \mathcal{E}. At each point it feels a force in the field’s direction and is carried downhill in potential, from high potential energy toward low. The field alone determines the motion, since the charge follows the local vectors and needs nothing else. The score does the same for a sample, in the opposite direction. A point released into the score field is carried uphill in log-density, from sparse regions toward dense ones, moving at each step along the local score vector (Figure 17). In both cases the field is sufficient to transport the object across the landscape (the charge from high potential to low, the sample from low density to high) by following its vectors step by step.
That transport is what the reverse process will do: a sample released in a low-density region (pure noise) is carried by the score toward the high-density region where the data lie.








Figure 17: The score field of a two-mode density. Contours show the density p; at each point the score s(x) = \nabla_x \log p(x) is a vector pointing uphill in log-density, toward the nearest concentration of data, with the two mode centers as the field’s sinks. The dashed path is a sample released in a sparse region and transported by the field alone: at each step it follows the local score vector and is carried into the high-density region, which is the transport the reverse process will perform.







3.2.3 How the score helps
As we saw at the start of this Part, while trying to model the density using an arbitrary function, the presence of the intractable partition function Z(\theta) prohibits density evaluation. But if we look carefully:

p_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp(-E_\theta(x))

By the definition of the score,

s_\theta(x) = \nabla_x \log p_\theta(x)

Substituting the EBM for p_\theta(x),

s_\theta(x) = \nabla_x \log \frac{\exp(-E_\theta(x))}{Z(\theta)}

Expanding the logarithm of the quotient,

s_\theta(x) = \nabla_x \big(-E_\theta(x) - \log Z(\theta)\big)

By linearity of the gradient,

s_\theta(x) = -\nabla_x E_\theta(x) - \nabla_x \log Z(\theta)

Since Z(\theta) does not depend on x, its gradient vanishes,

s_\theta(x) = -\nabla_x E_\theta(x)

The gradient of Z(\theta) with respect to x is zero, which makes the log-density gradient, i.e. the score, independent of Z(\theta) and thus makes it tractable.
Score-based modeling therefore escapes the obstacle. Rather than learning or evaluating the normalized density itself, it learns its score, \nabla_x \log p(x). Because differentiation annihilates the unknown constant, the partition function disappears entirely. That shift, from modeling probability values to modeling the geometry of the probability landscape, is what turned a problem that had resisted generations of generative-modeling research into something that could be learned locally from data.
The structure of that escape is worth pausing on. Normalization was the source of the difficulty, since \int p_\theta(x)\, dx = 1 is what forces the intractable Z(\theta). Differentiating the log-density removes Z(\theta), but differentiation discards information, so recovering the density from the score means integrating it back and picking up an unknown constant. That constant is fixed by the same constraint that caused the difficulty. On a connected domain where the density is positive, requiring it to integrate to one determines it uniquely, so the score carries as much information as the density, and score-based modeling is an equivalent formulation of density estimation rather than a lossy substitute for it. The argument does not extend further, because normalization supplies exactly one constraint, and a second derivative of the log-density would discard more than one constant can restore.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
3.3 Modeling using score matching
This section builds the simplest score-based generative model. The KL divergence compares two distributions through their densities, so comparing them through their scores calls for a different quantity, the Fisher divergence. Explicit score matching minimizes it directly, comparing the model’s score with the true score of the data distribution. That objective is not computable, because the true score is unknown. Implicit score matching removes the unknown target, leaving a quantity computable from samples alone. The section then discusses sampling with Langevin MCMC driven by the learned score. Four pitfalls close it, and together they show that replacing the density with the score was not free.

3.3.1 Training: score matching
Since scores are computable without Z(\theta), a training objective that compares scores rather than densities avoids the partition function entirely. The Fisher divergence is one such objective, and it measures the difference between two distributions p(x) and q(x) as:

D_F(p, q) := \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_p\big[\lVert\nabla_x \log p(x) - \nabla_x \log q(x)\rVert^2\big]

Throughout, the subscript of \mathbb{E} names the density the expectation averages over.

3.3.1.1 Explicit score matching
Hyvärinen’s score matching [34] fits a model by minimizing the Fisher divergence between the data distribution p_0 and the model p_\theta. The model enters only through its score, so from here s_\theta may be a network that outputs the score vector directly, a score-based model, rather than the gradient of an energy. The objective is:

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}}(\theta) := \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\lVert s_\theta(x) - \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\rVert^2\big]}
\tag{35}
In Vincent’s terminology [5] this is the explicit score matching (ESM) objective, explicit because the target score is written out in the open.
For an EBM the score is s_\theta = -\nabla_x E_\theta. Substituting it,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}}(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\lVert -\nabla_x E_\theta(x) - \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\rVert^2\big]

Passing from densities to scores removed one unknown but introduced another. The objective no longer requires p_0(x), but it now requires \nabla_x \log p_0(x), which we do not have access to as we have only samples. So \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} is no more computable than a density-based objective such as the KL divergence.


3.3.1.2 Implicit score matching
Hyvärinen’s theorem removes that unknown. An integration-by-parts identity [34] eliminates \nabla_x \log p_0 from Eq. 35, leaving the implicit score matching (ISM) form [5], computable from samples alone:

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(x)\big\rVert^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)\right],\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}+C_1}
\tag{36}
Here the constant is

C_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\lVert \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\rVert^2\big]

which does not depend on \theta, so the two objectives share a minimizer.
The equivalence holds under three regularity conditions:

Differentiability: p_0 and s_\theta are differentiable.
Finite second moments: For each \theta, 
\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\lVert \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\rVert^2\big] < \infty \qquad \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\lVert s_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big] < \infty
 so that C_1 is finite and, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so is the cross term \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[s_\theta(x) \cdot \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\big] that the proof integrates by parts.
Decay at infinity: p_0(x)\, s_\theta(x) \to 0 as \lVert x \rVert \to \infty, which is what makes the boundary term of the integration by parts vanish in the proof below.

Proof:
We write s_\theta for s_\theta(x) throughout. By definition,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta - \nabla_x\log p_0\rVert^{2}\right]

Expanding \lVert a-b\rVert^2 inside the expectation,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2} - s_\theta \cdot \nabla_x\log p_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \nabla_x\log p_0\rVert^{2}\right]

By linearity of expectation,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] - \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[s_\theta \cdot \nabla_x\log p_0\right] + \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \nabla_x\log p_0\rVert^{2}\right]

The last term is free of \theta; naming it C_1,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] - \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[s_\theta \cdot \nabla_x\log p_0\right] + C_1

Writing the cross term’s expectation as an integral,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] - \int p_0(x)\; s_\theta(x)\cdot \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\,dx + C_1

Using \nabla_x\log p_0 = \nabla_x p_0/p_0,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] - \int p_0(x)\; s_\theta(x)\cdot \frac{\nabla_x p_0(x)}{p_0(x)}\,dx + C_1

Cancelling p_0,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] - \int s_\theta(x)\cdot \nabla_x p_0(x)\,dx + C_1

Writing the dot product as a sum over the d coordinates of x \in \mathbb{R}^d, with s_{\theta,k} the k-th component of s_\theta,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] - \sum_{k=1}^{d}\int s_{\theta,k}(x)\,\frac{\partial p_0(x)}{\partial x_k}\,dx + C_1

Integrating by parts in x_k, with x_{\setminus k} the remaining coordinates,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] - \sum_{k=1}^{d}\left(\int \Big[s_{\theta,k}\,p_0\Big]_{x_k=-\infty}^{+\infty} dx_{\setminus k} - \int p_0(x)\,\frac{\partial s_{\theta,k}(x)}{\partial x_k}\,dx\right) + C_1

The boundary term vanishes, since s_{\theta,k}\, p_0 \to 0 as x_k \to \pm\infty,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] + \sum_{k=1}^{d}\int p_0(x)\,\frac{\partial s_{\theta,k}(x)}{\partial x_k}\,dx + C_1

The sum of the diagonal entries is the trace,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] + \int p_0(x)\,\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)\,dx + C_1

Writing the integral back as an expectation,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta\rVert^{2}\right] + \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)\right] + C_1

Combining the two expectations by linearity,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(x)\big\rVert^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)\right] + C_1

Naming the \theta-dependent part \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}(\theta),

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(x)\big\rVert^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)\right],\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}+C_1}

which is Eq. 36. \square


3.3.1.3 The two terms of the implicit objective
The two terms of Eq. 36 determine the learned field where the data lie [19]. The expectation is taken under p_0, so points of high data density dominate the loss.
The norm term \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(x)\rVert^2 penalizes large values of the learned score, most heavily where the data are dense. Together with the trace term, it does not set s_\theta(x) = 0 there, because the minimizer of Eq. 36, when the model family contains it, is the true score \nabla_x \log p_0, which vanishes only where \nabla_x p_0 = 0.
The trace term \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big) is the divergence of s_\theta,

\nabla_x \cdot s_\theta = \sum_{k=1}^{d} \frac{\partial s_{\theta,k}}{\partial x_k}

a vector-calculus quantity unrelated to the KL and Fisher divergences. It enters with a positive sign, so minimizing the loss favors a negative divergence of s_\theta where the data are dense. When the field is the gradient of a scalar function u: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}, s_\theta = \nabla_x u, as the score of a density is, its divergence is the trace of the Hessian, \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x^2 u\big). At a stationary point x_\star, where \nabla_x u(x_\star) = 0, for u twice continuously differentiable, Taylor’s theorem [35] gives

u(x) = u(x_\star) + \tfrac{1}{2}(x - x_\star)^\top \nabla_x^2 u(x_\star)\,(x - x_\star) + o\big(\lVert x - x_\star\rVert^2\big)

If the Hessian \nabla_x^2 u(x_\star) is negative definite, u has a strict local maximum at x_\star, and the trace of the Hessian is negative. A negative trace alone does not force a maximum, since some eigenvalues could still be positive, but it is what the loss rewards. The objective therefore favors negative divergence where the data density is high. A stationary point of u in such a region is a strict local maximum of u (the learned log-density, when s_\theta is the gradient of \log p_\theta) wherever the Hessian there is negative definite.


3.3.1.4 Training procedure
For the EBM, s_\theta = \nabla_x \log p_\theta and \nabla_x s_\theta = \nabla_x^2 \log p_\theta, so substituting these in Eq. 36,

\begin{aligned}
&\tfrac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\lVert\nabla_x \log p_\theta(x) - \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\rVert^2\big] \\[4pt]
&\qquad = \mathbb{E}_{p_0}\Big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla_x \log p_\theta(x)\rVert^2 + \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x^2 \log p_\theta(x)\big)\Big] + \text{const}
\end{aligned}

Training is then standard: sample a mini-batch \{x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \cdots, x^{(m)}\} \sim p_0(x) and estimate the loss by the empirical mean \hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}(\theta)

\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{j=1}^m \Big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla_x \log p_\theta(x^{(j)})\rVert^2 + \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x^2 \log p_\theta(x^{(j)})\big)\Big]

Substituting \nabla_x \log p_\theta = -\nabla_x E_\theta, which leaves the squared norm unchanged and flips the sign of the trace,

\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{j=1}^m \Big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla_x E_\theta(x^{(j)})\rVert^2 - \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x^2 E_\theta(x^{(j)})\big)\Big]

and this is the loss used to run stochastic gradient descent for training.



3.3.2 Sampling: Langevin MCMC
The Langevin MCMC method obtains random samples from a probability distribution for which direct sampling is difficult. It uses overdamped Langevin dynamics [36] to generate the states of a random walk that has the target distribution as its stationary distribution. Each new state is generated from the previous one using evaluations of the score of the target density. Informally, the Langevin dynamics drives the random walk toward regions of high probability in the manner of a gradient flow.
We want samples from p_0, so the overdamped Langevin Itô diffusion for it is,

dX_t = \nabla_x \log p_0(X_t)\, dt + \sqrt{2}\, dW_t

where \nabla_x \log p_0(X_t) is its drift and W_t is a standard Brownian motion.
How p_0 is stationary:
A Fokker-Planck check confirms it. For a diffusion dX_t = f(X_t, t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW_t whose diffusion coefficient does not depend on the state, the density of X_t satisfies the d-dimensional Fokker-Planck equation, P1:Eq. 45,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot \big[f(x, t)\, p(x, t)\big] + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \Delta_x p(x, t)

with \Delta_x the Laplacian. Substituting the drift f = \nabla_x \log p_0 and the constant diffusion coefficient g = \sqrt{2},

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla_x \cdot \big(p\, \nabla_x \log p_0\big) + \Delta_x p

Evaluating the right-hand side at p = p_0,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\bigg|_{p = p_0} = -\nabla_x \cdot \big(p_0\, \nabla_x \log p_0\big) + \Delta_x p_0

Using p_0 \nabla_x \log p_0 = \nabla_x p_0,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\bigg|_{p = p_0} = -\nabla_x \cdot \nabla_x p_0 + \Delta_x p_0

Using \nabla_x \cdot \nabla_x = \Delta_x, the two terms cancel,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\bigg|_{p = p_0} = 0

So p_0 does not change under the dynamics. That the distribution of X_t converges to it from any starting point is the ergodicity result of Roberts and Tweedie [37].
Approximate sample paths of this Langevin diffusion can be generated by the Euler-Maruyama method, the discrete-time scheme for SDEs, with a fixed time step \varepsilon > 0. That discretization is known as the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) [37].
Initialize x^{(0)} \sim \pi from any distribution, and repeat for k \leftarrow 1, 2, \ldots, K,

\begin{aligned}
z_k &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \\[4pt]
x^{(k)} &\leftarrow x^{(k-1)} + \varepsilon\, \nabla_x \log p_0\big(x^{(k-1)}\big) + \sqrt{2\varepsilon}\, z_k
\end{aligned}

The iterates form a Markov chain, each state depending only on the one before it, and the chain is built so that its stationary distribution approaches the target as the step shrinks. Running it long and treating late states as samples is MCMC, and ULA is its Langevin instance. As \varepsilon \to 0 and K \to \infty, x^{(K)} \sim p_0 under regularity conditions on p_0. At a fixed \varepsilon the chain equilibrates to a distribution that differs from p_0 by an error of order \varepsilon.
Replacing the score \nabla_x \log p_0 with the score estimated by the trained model s_\theta(x) gives a sampler that needs neither the partition function nor a density evaluation, and completes the generative process (Figure 18).








Figure 18: Langevin MCMC sampling from a two-mode density using only its score (the same density whose score field the previous figure displays). Two chains, initialized far from the data, ascend the log-density with a fresh noise term at each step and concentrate in the modes. The dots are the final states of 250 independent chains after K = 900 steps: samples from p_0, spread across both modes.







3.3.3 Pitfalls
The basic approach fails in practice for four reasons, and diagnosing them determines the fix. The first three are Song and Ermon’s diagnosis [6]; the fourth is the cost of the trace term.

3.3.3.1 The manifold hypothesis
Real data concentrate on a low-dimensional manifold of the ambient space. When the data lie on a manifold, the ambient data score \nabla_x \log p_0(x) is undefined (Figure 19).








Figure 19: The manifold hypothesis. The data (dots) concentrate on a thin curve inside the two-dimensional ambient space. On the curve the density is significant; off it the density is zero, \log p_0 = -\infty, and the ambient score is undefined; the question marks are placed at points where there is no gradient to point anywhere.







3.3.3.2 Low data density regions
The score-matching objective

\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_0}\big[\lVert s_\theta(x) - \nabla_x \log p_0(x)\rVert^2\big]

weights the error at each point by the data density. Langevin MCMC must cross the low-density regions to travel between modes, so an accurate score is needed most where samples are few, and that is where the estimate is worst (Figure 20).








Figure 20: Low data density regions. The shaded band is the data density, and the objective weights score errors by it. The learned estimate (dashed) tracks the true score (solid) closely where the density is high and degrades in the low-density gap between the modes. That gap is the region a Langevin chain must cross to travel from one mode to the other, so the sampler depends on the score most where the estimate is worst.







3.3.3.3 Slow mixing between modes
The score is local. It tells a chain which way is uphill from where it stands, and nothing about how much probability lies beyond the next valley. Assume a dataset that is 90% cats and 10% dogs, with the two classes occupying separated regions. A chain started near the cats stays there, because leaving requires a long run of noise steps against the drift, so for a long time the class ratio of the samples reflects where the chains started rather than the data density.
The tilted double well shows this concretely (Figure 21),

U(x) = \frac{x^4}{4} - \frac{x^2}{2} + h\,x, \qquad p_0(x) \propto e^{-U(x)/T}

with two wells separated by a barrier near x = 0 (the root of U'(x) = x^3 - x + h = 0 closest to the origin, at x \approx h), a tilt h > 0 that makes the left well deeper, and a temperature T that sets how sharply p_0 concentrates in them.








Figure 21: The tilted double-well density p_0 \propto e^{-U/T} with h = 0.055 and T = 0.05. The tilt makes the left well deeper, and that well holds most of the mass; the barrier between the wells lies near x = 0.





The score -(x^3 - x + h)/T is defined everywhere and depends on h, so the chain lacks no information. What it lacks is time. The expected time to cross the barrier grows as e^{\Delta U/T}, with \Delta U the barrier height, as Kramers showed [38]. For each number of steps short of that crossing time a chain therefore stays in the well it started in, and the share of samples in each well is set by the initialization rather than by p_0 (Figure 22).








Figure 22: Slow mixing between modes, on the double well above. Top: One Langevin chain over 4,000 time units. It dwells in a well for long stretches, about ten times longer in the deeper left well than in the right one, and crosses the barrier only when a rare fluctuation carries it over. Bottom: End points of 400 chains started uniformly across the axis and run for 1,000 steps, one time unit on the axis above. That is the order of a real sampler’s step count, and far short of the tens of thousands to a hundred thousand steps a barrier crossing requires at this step size. The left share of the samples stays close to the one half fixed by the uniform initialization, against the left well’s true share printed in the panel: each chain enters the well nearest its start and stays there.







3.3.3.4 Poor computational efficiency
The \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}} objective Eq. 36 contains the trace of the Jacobian of s_\theta, and with a deep network as the score-based model, that term is the bottleneck. The governing fact about reverse-mode automatic differentiation is that one backward pass computes the gradient of one scalar with respect to all of its inputs, at approximately the cost of a forward pass, no matter how many inputs there are. A vector-valued output needs one pass per component (Table 2).
The trace is a sum of d diagonal entries (with d the dimension of x),

\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\frac{\partial s_{\theta,k}(x)}{\partial x_k}

and each s_{\theta,k} is a separate scalar, so each needs its own backward pass. Written out for d = 3,

\nabla_x s_\theta(x) = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,1}(x)}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,1}(x)}{\partial x_2} & \dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,1}(x)}{\partial x_3} \\[6pt]
\dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,2}(x)}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,2}(x)}{\partial x_2} & \dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,2}(x)}{\partial x_3} \\[6pt]
\dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,3}(x)}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,3}(x)}{\partial x_2} & \dfrac{\partial s_{\theta,3}(x)}{\partial x_3}
\end{pmatrix}

The trace therefore needs one backward pass per diagonal entry. Worse, each pass produces a full row of the Jacobian (d numbers), of which we keep one. We compute order d^{2} quantities to use d of them. Computing \operatorname{tr}(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)) therefore requires O(d) backward passes.



Table 2: What each quantity costs in backward passes. Ordinary training and the score itself differentiate a scalar, so one pass suffices; the trace differentiates a vector field component by component, so its cost scales with the data dimension.










Quantity
Differentiating what
Backward passes




\nabla_\theta L (ordinary training)
scalar loss L

For a modest 32\times32\times3 image, d=3072: about three thousand backward passes per training example, against one for ordinary supervised learning. That cost is unusable at image dimensionality.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.1 Intuition






Figure 23: An alley on a cold, dark, foggy night. Several street lamps light up the street. Their rays start at the lamps and spread into the fog, which is dense enough to dilute the light but not to hide its path. The lamps are the sources; the glow is all that a viewer standing in the street can see.




4.1.1 A cold, dark night
Imagine a foggy street where someone has been placing many poles following a pattern. We want to learn that pattern, so that we can predict where the upcoming poles will stand. To learn the pattern, we remove all random light sources on the street and attach a light source to every pole, turning each into a lamp (Figure 23).
There are two important restrictions. First, our vision is very narrow: we cannot see far away places and can only observe the light as it spreads around us in our closest neighborhood. Second, the light sources we are using have one special property, their intensity does not directly fall with distance as we move away from the source, but only due to fog. The fog is unusual too. It thins a lamp’s light by the exponential of the squared distance the light has traveled (e^{-r^2/2\ell^2}, for a distance r and a fog thickness \ell), so intensity falls off far more sharply with range than ordinary light would. Light from a lamp across the road reaches us strongly, but light from a lamp three blocks away has diminished to almost nothing.
As there are multiple sources, what we observe at a point is the cumulative sum of all the light every lamp contributes, each thinned by the fog it crossed, with the cumulative light carrying no label saying which source sent which part of it.


4.1.2 Where is the light coming from?
As we saw, we cannot separate the light into its individual sources, yet we can ask a simpler question: in which direction does it grow stronger?
The answer to that question needs no decomposition. We take a step in some direction and see whether light intensity increases or decreases; we can find the answer to this question, irrespective of what produced it. Doing this in every direction, one of them wins, and we take a small step in that direction.
And that direction, though we never needed individual lamp locations to find it, is not arbitrary. The light grows stronger as we move toward the lamps, because the lamps are the source. A lamp across the road contributes strongly to the direction, because much of its light survives the fog to reach us. A lamp three blocks away contributes too, but weakly, because almost none of its light reached us. Every lamp contributes on which way to go, and each contribution matches the amount of light that lamp contributed in the total light observed by us.
As the direction of increasing light is a weighted average of the vectors connecting the point to each lamp, it points toward their center of mass, almost surely a place where no actual lamp is present.
If we do not control the light on each individual lamp, finding the direction at a point means accounting for each lamp that contributed to the light there, as many terms as there are lamps, a costly operation.
However, we are in control of which light to turn on and which one to leave off. We switch on one light source at a time and pick a random point inside its glow to find the direction of that source, a direction we know exactly, because we chose which lamp was lit. If we do this for each lamp, over many points, the average direction at a point converges to the same one the cumulative light would have given. To generate a new pole location matching the pattern, we pick a random point and from there take small steps following the direction we learned, with a little randomness in each step. After enough steps the point we are standing on is a plausible pole location, blurred by the fog we added.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.2 Definitions
The denoising score matching derivation uses the objects below.

p_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sigma^d}\, e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\lVert \tilde{x} - x \rVert^2}

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
section: 4.3 Where is the score pointing to?
text:
4.3 Where is the score pointing to?
With the notation of Table 3 in place, let us see how the light-driven search for the pole pattern helps us. In generative modeling we have a similar setup: we are given a set of training samples with no knowledge of the distribution they were sampled from, so we do not know how to generate new samples matching the given ones.
To solve this we follow a similar approach, where each sample is equivalent to a pole and its value x^{(i)} to the pole’s location. Like a light source attached to a pole and spreading light on the street, we perturb each given sample by adding Gaussian noise of scale \sigma, which turns the samples into sources of probability spreading it in space as a perturbation kernel p_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x^{(i)}), with \sigma controlled noise acting as the fog. Like the cumulative light at a given point, the total probability density at a given point (\tilde{x}) is the sum of the kernel densities, giving p_\sigma(\tilde{x}).
In the case of the light, moving a little in various directions and observing the change gave us the direction in which the light increases the most. Doing the same here, but evaluating the probability density instead of the light, gives the direction in which the density increases the most. Like the light, it is a weighted average of the vectors connecting \tilde{x} to each sample, each weighted by that sample’s share of the density arriving at \tilde{x}, and it is represented by the score \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}).
As with the light, obtaining that average direction costs a term per sample at each point. But like turning on one light source at a time, denoising score matching uses one sample at a time, perturbs it with noise to convert it into a source, and then the direction back is known exactly, because we know which particular sample was switched on.
If we do this for each sample x^{(i)}, over many perturbed points \tilde{x}, and fit a single score-based model to the results, it converges to the same score the cumulative density would have given. To generate a new sample, we pick a random \tilde{x} and from there take small steps following the score, with a little randomness in each step. After enough steps the value we reach is a plausible sample, scattered by the noise we added.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.4 The Parzen window density
As we discussed earlier, score matching wants us to compare our model’s gradient field against the data’s gradient field, but the trouble is that we have never seen the data’s gradient field. We only have samples: a finite set of points, each sitting at its own location, with nothing in between. A finite set of points has no gradient. There is nothing to differentiate, and so nothing to compare against. The way out begins by giving the data something to be a gradient of. So, in the next few steps we try to find a density we can use to replace the unknown true probability distribution p_0.
The first step starts with replacing p_0 with the most basic pdf we can create using the samples:

\hat{p}(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta\big(x - x^{(i)}\big)
\tag{37}
which is the empirical distribution, the pdf for a discrete distribution represented by discrete sample points expressed with Dirac deltas (Figure 24). It is zero almost everywhere and infinite on a finite set of points. Thus, it has no density in the ordinary sense and as it is still not differentiable, \nabla_x \log \hat{p} does not exist anywhere that matters.








Figure 24: From samples to the empirical distribution. Left: The training samples are isolated points, with nothing in between. Right: The empirical distribution \hat p places a Dirac spike of mass 1/n at each training point, so \nabla_x \log \hat p does not yet exist anywhere useful.





To fix that deficiency, we use kernel density estimation (KDE) [39]. KDE is the application of kernel smoothing for probability density estimation, a non-parametric method to estimate the pdf of a random variable based on kernels as weights. KDE answers a fundamental data smoothing problem where inferences about the population are made based on a finite data sample, something we desire here as we are looking for an appropriate replacement of p_0 using the data samples.
To do it, we perturb a sample with additive Gaussian noise of covariance \sigma^{2}I, which yields the perturbed sample,

\tilde{x} \;=\; x + \sigma\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\big(0,\, I\big)

In terms of \hat{p}, this implies replacing the spike corresponding to that sample with a Gaussian kernel:

p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\;=\;\mathcal{N}\big(\tilde{x};\,x,\,\sigma^{2}I\big)\;=\;(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert \tilde{x}-x\rVert^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)
\tag{38}
which is a conditional distribution conditioned on the sample x, an isotropic Gaussian centered at x with variance \sigma^2, the perturbation kernel. This converts that single point into a cloud, which is densest at the original sample location and gradually thinning outward.
If we do this for each sample and replace each spike with the corresponding kernel, we obtain:

p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\;=\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_\sigma\big(\tilde{x}\mid x^{(i)}\big)\;=\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert \tilde{x}-x^{(i)}\rVert^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)
\tag{39}
This estimated density obtained by perturbing all the samples of a distribution with a kernel and taking their equi-weight average is called the Parzen window density estimator. It results in the isolated points becoming overlapping clouds and the total density at a given point becoming the sum of n densities, one corresponding to each sample. What was a scatter of locations is now a continuous field of probability, defined everywhere, strictly positive, and differentiable everywhere with a score (Figure 25).








Figure 25: The Parzen density and its score. Left: Convolving with a Gaussian kernel of width \sigma produces the Parzen density p_\sigma, one peak per point summed, which is smooth and strictly positive; the dashed curve is the true data density p_0, which p_\sigma reproduces only up to the smoothing and the finite training set. Right: p_\sigma therefore has a score, defined for each x. It vanishes at the peaks of p_\sigma and points toward the data from either side.





The Parzen window density estimator fixes our issue of no gradients, however p_\sigma is not the density we wanted as it is \hat{p} convolved with a Gaussian. It is a smoothed version of p_0 only in expectation over the training set.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.5 Back to score matching
Having converted p_0(x) with intractable scores into the sample-based but perturbed and approximate Parzen density p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) with tractable scores, let’s see what impact this change has on our score-matching objectives of §3.3.1.
Using the same convention, we can write the ESM objective for \hat{p} as:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{\hat{p}}}(\theta) := \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_{\hat{p}}\big[\lVert s_\theta(x) - \nabla_x \log \hat{p}(x)\rVert^2\big]
\tag{40}
But its target \nabla_x \log \hat{p} does not exist, as the previous section established, so \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{\hat{p}}} cannot be computed.
Similarly, the ISM objective for \hat{p} is:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{\hat{p}}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\hat{p}}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(x)\big\rVert^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x)\big)\right]

Writing the expectation under \hat{p} as the average over the training set,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{\hat{p}}}(\theta)\;=\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(x^{(i)})\big\rVert^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_x s_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)\right]
\tag{41}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{\hat{p}}} remains well-defined, because it contains only the model’s quantities, and the density enters only as the averaging measure. Its summand has finite mean under p_0, so by the law of large numbers it converges to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}} as n \to \infty for each fixed \theta. It is hence asymptotically equivalent to the objective \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}}.
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{\hat{p}}} cannot be computed while \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{\hat{p}}} can. Thus, in the case of \hat{p} the ESM and ISM objectives are not equivalent. The reason is that \hat{p} fails the regularity conditions: Hyvärinen’s theorem can’t repair its non-differentiability, as the objective its integration by parts would transform does not exist.
Following the same convention, the ESM objective for p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) is:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta) := \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\big[\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x}) - \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\rVert^2\big]
\tag{42}
Similarly, the ISM objective for p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) is:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\big\rVert^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_{\tilde{x}} s_\theta(\tilde{x})\big)\right]
\tag{43}
For \sigma > 0, p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) is differentiable and decreases to 0 at infinity, and its score has a finite second moment,

\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\big[\lVert \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) \rVert^2\big] < \infty

The model-side conditions hold as before. The network s_\theta is differentiable, \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\big[\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x}) \rVert^2\big] is finite, and the product p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\, s_\theta(\tilde{x}) vanishes at infinity, since p_\sigma’s Gaussian tails dominate any polynomially bounded network. Thus, all regularity conditions are satisfied, so like Eq. 36, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_\sigma}} is also equivalent to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}.
As \sigma \to 0 the perturbation vanishes. Then \tilde{x} = x, every cloud collapses back to its spike, and p_\sigma falls back to \hat{p}. There, as we saw, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{\hat{p}}} cannot be computed, and the ESM and ISM objectives are not equivalent. So \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{\hat{p}}}, though computable, loses the guarantee that minimizing it matches the score it is meant to target, \nabla_x \log \hat{p}. For each \sigma > 0 the two objectives still differ by a finite \theta-free constant and share a minimizer. That constant is

\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\big[\lVert \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) \rVert^{2}\big]

The score of a width-\sigma cloud is of order 1/\sigma near a training point, so the constant \to \infty as \sigma \to 0. Keeping \sigma > 0 preserves both the target and the equivalence.
