The generative goal is a single gradient: \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_0}}, the direction that matches the model to the score of the data distribution. Below, we pick each of the other five objectives and, using Table 4, discuss how its gradient relates to that goal:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}}: Equivalent to the goal but not computable exactly, estimable by sampling at inefficient O(d) trace cost.
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{\hat{p}}}: The objective is undefined as the density’s gradient does not exist, nothing to match to the goal.
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{\hat{p}}}: Computable exactly, gradient is an unbiased estimator of the goal [5] but the issues are higher variance, the failed equivalence, and inefficiency due to the O(d) trace cost.
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}: Density and gradient both are available thus well-defined and estimable by sampling but gradient is a biased (smoothing) estimator of the goal, likely with lower variance [5]; computationally inefficient due to the n-kernel target.
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_\sigma}}: The equivalence holds, so the gradient equals \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} and, like \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}, density and gradient both are available thus well-defined and estimable by sampling but gradient is a biased (smoothing) estimator of the goal, likely with lower variance; computationally inefficient due to the O(d) trace cost.

If we focus on the last objective, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_\sigma}}, it is an expectation under p_\sigma that must be estimated by sampling perturbed points, with the same inefficient O(d) trace term as \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}} but in addition to that it is a biased estimator of the goal while \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_0}} was not. So it appears that we created an objective which has made the problem worse but hold that judgment for a while as the payoff for this hard work comes in the next section.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.7 Marginal to joint
The final element of the setup is a new object: the joint distribution over pairs of a training sample and its perturbed version,

p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x}) = \hat{p}(x)\,p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)

The issue: the marginal score \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) is an n-kernel mixture, inefficient as we saw in the previous section. The observation: because we perturb the samples ourselves, the pair (x, \tilde{x}) is available, not merely \tilde{x}, so the conditional score \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x), the score of a single Gaussian in closed form, is available too. The solution: average over the joint and match the conditional score, which the next section develops.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.8 The denoising score matching objective
Let us now consider the denoising score matching (DSM) objective [5], which was inspired by both the score-matching principle and the denoising-autoencoder approach [40] of using pairs of training examples and their perturbed versions, (x, \tilde{x}). For the joint density

p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x}) = \hat{p}(x)\,p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)

it is defined as:

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})-\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\big\rVert^{2}\right]}
\tag{44}
If we compare this objective with the \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} objective (Eq. 42), two elements changed: the averaging distribution changed from the marginal p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) to the joint p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x}), and the density whose score s_\theta(\tilde{x}) targets changed from the marginal p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) to the conditional p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x). At first glance, the two objectives appear very different but as we show below they differ by a constant.
Theorem:
Under the standing regularity assumptions, for each perturbation kernel p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x) that is differentiable in \tilde{x} [5],

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)\;+\;C,\qquad \frac{\partial C}{\partial \theta}=0}
\tag{45}
and consequently

\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)\;=\;\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)

Proof:
By the definition Eq. 42,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})-\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\big\rVert^{2}\right]

Expanding the square inside the expectation,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2} - s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right]

By linearity of expectation,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\right] + \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right]

The last term is free of \theta; naming it C_{\mathrm{E}},

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\right] + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Writing the cross term’s expectation as an integral,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \int p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\; s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\;d\tilde{x} + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Using the identity

\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma=\nabla_{\tilde{x}} p_\sigma/p_\sigma

in the previous line,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \int p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\; s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\frac{\nabla_{\tilde{x}}p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\;d\tilde{x} + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Cancelling p_\sigma(\tilde{x}),

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \int s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\;d\tilde{x} + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Since the Parzen density is a marginal, substituting

p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) = \int p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})\,dx

into the previous line,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \int s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\!\left(\int p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})\,dx\right)d\tilde{x} + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Differentiating under the integral,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \iint s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\,p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})\;dx\,d\tilde{x} + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Since

p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})=\hat{p}(x)\,p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x), \qquad \nabla_{\tilde{x}} g = g\,\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log g

with \hat{p}(x) free of \tilde{x}, the gradient of the joint is

\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\,p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x}) = p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})\,\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)

Substituting it into the previous line,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \iint p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})\; s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\;dx\,d\tilde{x} + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Reading the double integral back as an expectation over the joint,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\right] + C_{\mathrm{E}}

The quadratic term is likewise an expectation over the joint, since its integrand has no x and p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) is p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x}) marginalized over x,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\right] + C_{\mathrm{E}}

Adding and subtracting

C_{\mathrm{D}} := \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\rVert^{2}\right]

which is free of \theta,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}\right] - \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\right] + C_{\mathrm{D}} + \big(C_{\mathrm{E}}-C_{\mathrm{D}}\big)

By linearity of expectation, collecting the three joint expectations under one,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2} - s_\theta(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x) + \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\rVert^{2}\right] + \big(C_{\mathrm{E}}-C_{\mathrm{D}}\big)

Completing the square, now with the conditional score,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert s_\theta(\tilde{x})-\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}\mid x)\big\rVert^{2}\right] + \big(C_{\mathrm{E}}-C_{\mathrm{D}}\big)

By the definition Eq. 44, with C := C_{\mathrm{E}}-C_{\mathrm{D}},

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta)\;+\;C}

which is Eq. 45. \square
The cancellation of p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) against the denominator of \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma is the key identity: it leaves a bare \nabla_{\tilde{x}} p_\sigma, and only then can the marginalization be unfolded and the derivative moved inside. A related cancellation, of the normalizer in a ratio of two density values, makes Metropolis acceptance ratios computable without that normalizer [30].

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
section: 4.10 The optimum: posterior mean and Tweedie
text:
4.10 The optimum: posterior mean and Tweedie
The constructed distribution (p_\sigma(\tilde{x})) is continuous because each spike was replaced by a Gaussian cloud. It is a mixture: every sample contributes one component to it, its cloud (p_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x^{(i)})). Each perturbed point (\tilde{x}) came from exactly one original sample (x), and since we perturbed it ourselves, we can trace that origin. The density cannot. At any location it holds only the summed density, every component’s contribution already merged, and the score (\nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})) inherits that: it is a property of the sum alone. So given only the density, if we ask which component produced a given point, we are the fog viewer again. The point could have come from any of the components, some far more plausibly than others, and nothing in the sum says which one.
Since the DSM objective Eq. 46 is a squared error and s_\theta is unconstrained, its minimizer s^\star can be found separately at each \tilde{x}: the value the network assigns at one point does not affect the loss at any other. Fixing \tilde{x} and writing v for the vector the network outputs there, v = s_\theta(\tilde{x}), the objective restricted to that \tilde{x} is

g(v) = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x \mid \tilde{x})}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert v-\tfrac{x-\tilde{x}}{\sigma^{2}}\big\rVert^{2}\right]

The expectation is over the posterior

p_\sigma(x \mid \tilde{x}) := p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})/p_\sigma(\tilde{x})

which assigns every training sample a weight measuring how plausibly it produced this \tilde{x}. Splitting the joint expectation of Eq. 44 as

\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x,\tilde{x})} = \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(x \mid \tilde{x})}

is what leaves g(v) as the inner objective at each \tilde{x}. Differentiating with respect to v,

\nabla_v\, g = v-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{x-\tilde{x}}{\sigma^{2}}\,\Big|\,\tilde{x}\right]

Setting the gradient to zero and solving for v, with \tilde{x} fixed,

v = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{x-\tilde{x}}{\sigma^{2}}\,\Big|\,\tilde{x}\right]

By linearity, with \tilde{x} fixed under the conditioning,

v = \frac{\mathbb{E}[x\mid\tilde{x}]-\tilde{x}}{\sigma^{2}}

Writing s^{\star}(\tilde{x}) for that minimizing value,

s^{\star}(\tilde{x}) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[x\mid\tilde{x}]-\tilde{x}}{\sigma^{2}}

Here \mathbb{E}[x\mid\tilde{x}] is the posterior mean: the average over every training sample, each weighted by how plausibly it produced \tilde{x}.
At fixed \tilde{x} the inner objective of Eq. 42 is

\frac{1}{2}\lVert v-\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\rVert^{2}

which is minimized at v = \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}). By Vincent’s theorem Eq. 45 the two objectives differ by a \theta-free constant, so that value is the s^\star just computed,

\boxed{\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})\;=\;\frac{\mathbb{E}[x\mid\tilde{x}]-\tilde{x}}{\sigma^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \mathbb{E}[x\mid\tilde{x}]\;=\;\tilde{x}+\sigma^{2}\,\nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x})}
\tag{47}
That is Tweedie’s formula presented by Efron [41]. \square
It says that the best estimate of the training sample behind \tilde{x}, \mathbb{E}[x\mid\tilde{x}], and the score of the Parzen density \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}) determine each other exactly: the score is the displacement from \tilde{x} to that estimate, divided by \sigma^{2}. If we estimate one, we can compute the other.
Two points are worth clarifying. First, the correction that moves \tilde{x} back toward the data is not the score itself but the score multiplied by \sigma^{2}. Second, the best estimate of the training sample behind \tilde{x} is \mathbb{E}[x\mid\tilde{x}], the posterior mean, not the particular x that generated it (Figure 26).








Figure 26: Tweedie’s formula as a weighted average of the training samples. A noisy observation \tilde{x} (diamond) is connected to every training sample; each line’s weight is the posterior probability that this sample produced \tilde{x}. The bold arrow is their weighted average: it points to the posterior mean \mathbb{E}[x \mid \tilde{x}], not to any single sample, and equals the displacement \sigma^2 \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_\sigma(\tilde{x}). The training samples are the source, on average. The optimal denoiser and the score determine each other.






4.10.1 SURE: why denoising score matching is denoising
Tweedie’s formula Eq. 47 gives the best estimate of x from \tilde x through the score of p_\sigma. A result of Stein’s [42] gives the converse view: the error of any estimate of x computed from \tilde x can itself be estimated from \tilde x alone, and that estimate is the implicit score matching objective in another form [19].
A denoiser is a map \hat x: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d that returns an estimate \hat x(\tilde x) of the x behind \tilde x = x + \sigma\epsilon, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). Its risk, the mean squared error for a given x,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big]

needs x, which a noisy observation does not reveal. Stein’s unbiased risk estimate (SURE) replaces it by a quantity computed from \tilde x alone,

\boxed{\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) = \lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^2\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \hat x(\tilde x) - d\,\sigma^2}
\tag{48}
For a differentiable denoiser with \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big] < \infty and a Jacobian \nabla_{\tilde x} \hat x(\tilde x) of finite expected norm, the expectation of SURE over the noise is the risk itself,

\boxed{\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) \,\big|\, x\big] = R(\hat x; x)}
\tag{49}
The first term measures how far the denoiser’s output lies from the noisy input, and alone it is a biased estimate of the risk, since \tilde x itself carries the noise. The divergence term corrects the bias through how strongly the denoiser responds to small changes of its input.
The proof expands the error around \tilde x and converts the cross term into the divergence term with Stein’s identity, an integration by parts against the Gaussian density.






NoteProof: SURE is unbiased





Adding and subtracting \tilde x inside the norm,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert (\hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x) + (\tilde x - x) \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big]

Expanding the square,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big] + 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(\tilde x - x)^\top(\hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x) \,\big|\, x\big] + \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \tilde x - x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big]

Substituting \tilde x - x = \sigma\epsilon in the last two terms,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big] + 2\sigma\,\mathbb{E}\big[\epsilon^\top(\hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x) \,\big|\, x\big] + \sigma^2\, \mathbb{E}\lVert \epsilon \rVert^2

Substituting \mathbb{E}\lVert \epsilon \rVert^2 = d, the sum of the d unit variances,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big] + 2\sigma\,\mathbb{E}\big[\epsilon^\top(\hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x) \,\big|\, x\big] + d\,\sigma^2

Stein’s identity [42] states that, for \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and a differentiable vector field a: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d whose Jacobian has finite expected norm,

\mathbb{E}\big[\epsilon^\top a(\epsilon)\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_\epsilon \cdot a(\epsilon)\big]

In each coordinate, with the other coordinates fixed and using their independence, it is \mathbb{E}[\epsilon_j a_j(\epsilon)] = \mathbb{E}[\partial a_j(\epsilon)/\partial \epsilon_j], which integration by parts in \epsilon_j gives, because the standard normal density \varphi satisfies \varphi'(u) = -u\,\varphi(u) and the boundary term a_j\varphi vanishes at \pm\infty under that condition. Applying it with x fixed and a(\epsilon) = \hat x(x + \sigma\epsilon) - (x + \sigma\epsilon),

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big] + 2\sigma\,\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_\epsilon \cdot \big(\hat x(x + \sigma\epsilon) - (x + \sigma\epsilon)\big) \,\big|\, x\big] + d\,\sigma^2

By the chain rule, \nabla_\epsilon = \sigma\nabla_{\tilde x},

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big] + 2\sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \big(\hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x\big) \,\big|\, x\big] + d\,\sigma^2

Substituting \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \big(\hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x\big) = \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \hat x(\tilde x) - d, since \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \tilde x = d,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 \,\big|\, x\big] + 2\sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \hat x(\tilde x) - d \,\big|\, x\big] + d\,\sigma^2

By linearity of the conditional expectation,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^2\big(\nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \hat x(\tilde x) - d\big) + d\,\sigma^2 \,\big|\, x\big]

Distributing 2\sigma^2,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^2\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \hat x(\tilde x) - 2d\,\sigma^2 + d\,\sigma^2 \,\big|\, x\big]

Collecting the constants, -2d\sigma^2 + d\sigma^2 = -d\sigma^2,

R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \hat x(\tilde x) - \tilde x \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^2\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \hat x(\tilde x) - d\,\sigma^2 \,\big|\, x\big]

Recognizing the integrand as \mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x),

\boxed{R(\hat x; x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) \,\big|\, x\big]}

which is Eq. 49. \square



Tweedie’s formula Eq. 47 suggests writing the denoiser through a score field, \hat x(\tilde x) = \tilde x + \sigma^2 s_\theta(\tilde x). Substituting it into Eq. 48,

\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) = \lVert \sigma^2 s_\theta(\tilde x) \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^2\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \big(\tilde x + \sigma^2 s_\theta(\tilde x)\big) - d\,\sigma^2

Factoring \sigma^2 out of the norm,

\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) = \sigma^4 \lVert s_\theta(\tilde x) \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^2\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \big(\tilde x + \sigma^2 s_\theta(\tilde x)\big) - d\,\sigma^2

Expanding the divergence, with \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot \tilde x = d,

\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) = \sigma^4 \lVert s_\theta(\tilde x) \rVert^2 + 2d\,\sigma^2 + 2\sigma^4\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot s_\theta(\tilde x) - d\,\sigma^2

Combining the constants,

\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) = \sigma^4 \lVert s_\theta(\tilde x) \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^4\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot s_\theta(\tilde x) + d\,\sigma^2

Writing the divergence as the trace of the Jacobian, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot s_\theta = \operatorname{tr}(\nabla_{\tilde x} s_\theta),

\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) = \sigma^4 \lVert s_\theta(\tilde x) \rVert^2 + 2\sigma^4 \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_{\tilde x} s_\theta(\tilde x)\big) + d\,\sigma^2

Factoring 2\sigma^4 out of the terms in s_\theta,

\boxed{\mathrm{SURE}(\hat x; \tilde x) = 2\sigma^4\Big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert s_\theta(\tilde x) \rVert^2 + \operatorname{tr}\big(\nabla_{\tilde x} s_\theta(\tilde x)\big)\Big] + d\,\sigma^2}
\tag{50}
Averaged over \tilde x \sim p_\sigma, the bracket of Eq. 50 is the integrand of \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_\sigma}} (Eq. 43). Minimizing the expected SURE therefore minimizes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ISM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta), whose minimizer is the score of p_\sigma because it is equivalent to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}, and the denoiser it gives is the posterior mean of Eq. 47. By Vincent’s theorem Eq. 45, denoising score matching has the same minimizer, so a score-based model trained by it is a denoiser, and SURE is the reason.


4.10.2 Generalized score matching
Explicit and implicit score matching are cases of one construction [43], which also learns the denoiser of Eq. 47. Each case fits a field to a ratio \mathcal{A}p/p, where \mathcal{A} is a linear operator that maps a differentiable function f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} to a vector field \mathcal{A}f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d. The gradient gives the score, \nabla_x p/p = \nabla_x \log p. For densities p and q, the generalized Fisher divergence is

D_{\mathcal{A}}(p, q) := \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} - \frac{\mathcal{A}q(x)}{q(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big]

and with \mathcal{A} = \nabla_x it is the Fisher divergence D_F(p, q) of explicit score matching. The adjoint \mathcal{A}^\dagger of \mathcal{A} maps a vector field g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d to a function \mathcal{A}^\dagger g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} with

\int (\mathcal{A}f)^\top g\, dx = \int f\, \mathcal{A}^\dagger g\, dx

whenever the boundary terms vanish. It plays the role that integration by parts plays in §3.3.1.2. Fitting a field h_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d to \mathcal{A}p/p under p minimizes the left-hand side below. Expanding the square inside the expectation,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2 - h_\theta(x)^\top \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\Big\lVert \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big]

By linearity of the expectation,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big] - \mathbb{E}_p\Big[h_\theta(x)^\top \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)}\Big] + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big]

Naming the last term C, which does not depend on \theta,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big] - \mathbb{E}_p\Big[h_\theta(x)^\top \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)}\Big] + C

Writing the cross term as an integral against p,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big] - \int p(x)\, h_\theta(x)^\top \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)}\, dx + C

Cancelling p,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big] - \int \big(\mathcal{A}p(x)\big)^\top h_\theta(x)\, dx + C

Transferring \mathcal{A} to h_\theta through its adjoint,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big] - \int p(x)\, \mathcal{A}^\dagger h_\theta(x)\, dx + C

Writing the integral as an expectation under p,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big] - \mathbb{E}_p\big[\mathcal{A}^\dagger h_\theta(x)\big] + C

By linearity of the expectation,

\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\Big\lVert h_\theta(x) - \frac{\mathcal{A}p(x)}{p(x)} \Big\rVert^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2 - \mathcal{A}^\dagger h_\theta(x)\big] + C

The part that depends on \theta is the generalized score matching (GSM) objective,

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GSM}_p}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(x)\rVert^2 - \mathcal{A}^\dagger h_\theta(x)\Big]}
\tag{51}
which needs only samples of p and has the minimizer of the left-hand side. \square
For \mathcal{A} = \nabla_x the adjoint is minus the divergence, \mathcal{A}^\dagger g = -\nabla_x \cdot g, so with h_\theta = s_\theta the objective is the implicit score matching objective Eq. 36. For the operator

(\mathcal{A}f)(\tilde x) = \tilde x f(\tilde x) + \sigma^2 \nabla_{\tilde x} f(\tilde x)

applied to the Parzen density, the ratio is \tilde x + \sigma^2 \nabla_{\tilde x} \log p_\sigma(\tilde x), the posterior mean of Eq. 47, so the field h_\theta learns the denoiser. Integration by parts gives its adjoint, \mathcal{A}^\dagger g = \tilde x^\top g - \sigma^2\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot g, so the objective is

\mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma(\tilde x)}\Big[\frac{1}{2}\lVert h_\theta(\tilde x)\rVert^2 - \tilde x^\top h_\theta(\tilde x) + \sigma^2\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \cdot h_\theta(\tilde x)\Big]

Operators that stack derivatives expose higher derivatives of the log-density [44], and operators on discrete spaces carry score matching to discrete data [45], [46], which this series does not develop.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.11 Pitfalls resolved

4.11.1 Gaussian perturbation resolves density-related pitfalls
The solution to the first three density-related pitfalls of §3.3.3 is Gaussian perturbation. Adding noise to the data:

thickens the manifold into a full-dimensional distribution, so the score is defined everywhere;
fills the low-density regions, so score estimation has data to learn from where Langevin trajectories travel;
connects the modes, so mixing reflects their weights.

Thus, the DSM framework helps us resolve these three pitfalls.


4.11.2 DSM improves computational efficiency from O(d) to O(1)



Table 5: The three score-matching objectives compared. All three estimate the score of the same smoothed density; they differ in what the regression target is and what it costs to evaluate.

DSM is an objective that is a plain regression (Table 5). No partition function, no trace, no derivatives of s_\theta in its input, and a target available in closed form. The cost per training example drops from order d backward passes to one, which is the difference between infeasible and routine at image scale. Sliced score matching [47] avoids the exact trace by another route. It estimates \operatorname{tr}(\nabla_x s_\theta) by Hutchinson’s random projections [48], v^\top (\nabla_x s_\theta)\, v for a random v \in \mathbb{R}^d with \mathbb{E}[v v^\top] = I, at the cost of one Jacobian-vector product per projection and the variance of the estimate, while DSM removes the trace altogether. P3:§A.4 develops sliced score matching.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.12 New pitfalls
Three new pitfalls replace them:

The objective is no longer maximum likelihood. Fisher divergence and KL rank models differently, so the fitted model is a different estimator, still consistent in the well-specified case [34], but not the maximum-likelihood estimator, and in general it is not asymptotically efficient.
The estimand is p_\sigma, not p_0. Every version of score matching in this section matches the score of a smoothed data density, with a bias proportional to the smoothing that vanishes only as \sigma \to 0. Yet high noise is what provides useful directional information for Langevin dynamics, so fidelity and signal require opposite choices of \sigma, as the opening of §5 discusses in more detail.
The score is a local quantity. If p_0 has two modes separated by a region of near-zero density, matching scores constrains the shape within each mode but says almost nothing about their relative mass, because there is no path between them along which the gradient carries information. Mixing proportions are therefore poorly estimated. Unlike the slow-mixing pitfall of §3.3.3, which afflicts the sampler even with the exact score in hand, this one afflicts the learned score itself. It is one of the reasons for using several noise levels (§5), since a large \sigma merges the modes and restores a usable gradient between them.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
4.13 Conclusion
Tweedie’s formula says the optimal s_\theta(\tilde{x}) equals \mathbb{E}[-\epsilon/\sigma \mid \tilde{x}]. It points from the noisy \tilde{x} toward the plausibility-weighted average of every training sample. The score is an optimal denoiser, rescaled. This is the bridge between “score” (the stochastic-calculus object) and “denoising network” (the object deep learning trains): each determines the other. A network trained only to remove noise has, without being told, learned the gradient of the log of the smoothed data density p_\sigma.
The operation that makes the theorem work (an intractable marginal target replaced by a tractable conditional one, with the equivalence holding in expectation) recurs throughout generative modeling. Recognizing that structure is worth more than memorizing this one proof.
Denoising score matching turned score estimation from a circular problem (the unknown density is needed to obtain its own score) into supervised learning. Perturbing the data with a known noise process makes the conditional score available in closed form, and the model learns it from samples. It removed the need to know the true density’s score, and the diffusion models for image and video generation that followed build on it.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
5.1 Choosing the noise levels
Song and Ermon derived both rules from two simplified models of the data [50]. The largest level comes from the data as its n training samples, and the ratio between levels from the data as a single point.

5.1.1 The largest level
Langevin MCMC (§3.3.2) explores a density only through its score. For the samples to be diverse, a chain started near one training sample must be affected by the others through the score. Smoothing the training samples at the largest level gives the Parzen density Eq. 39 with \sigma = \sigma_1. We write w_k(\tilde x) = p_{\sigma_1}(x^{(k)} \mid \tilde x) for the posterior weight of sample k, the probability under the posterior of §4.10 that x^{(k)} produced \tilde x. Differentiating the logarithm of the mixture, the score is the weighted average of the scores of the components,

\nabla_{\tilde x} \log p_{\sigma_1}(\tilde x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} w_k(\tilde x)\, \nabla_{\tilde x} \log p_{\sigma_1}(\tilde x \mid x^{(k)})

which agrees with Tweedie’s formula Eq. 47, since \mathbb{E}[x \mid \tilde x] = \sum_k w_k(\tilde x)\, x^{(k)}, the weights sum to 1, and each component has the score (x^{(k)} - \tilde x) / \sigma_1^2 by Eq. 38.
A component with a negligible weight does not affect the chain. For two samples j \ne k, Song and Ermon bound the average weight of x^{(k)} at points sampled around x^{(j)} (their Proposition 1) [50],

\boxed{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\sigma_1}(\tilde x \mid x^{(j)})}\big[w_k(\tilde x)\big] \le \frac{1}{2} \exp\Big(-\frac{\lVert x^{(j)} - x^{(k)} \rVert^2}{8 \sigma_1^2}\Big)}
\tag{52}






NoteProof: the weight of a distant sample





We write p_l = p_{\sigma_1}(\cdot \mid x^{(l)}) for each component, so that w_k = p_k / \sum_l p_l by Bayes’ rule with the equal weights 1/n of \hat p. By the definition of the expectation,

\mathbb{E}_{p_j}[w_k] = \int \frac{p_j(\tilde x)\, p_k(\tilde x)}{\sum_l p_l(\tilde x)}\, d\tilde x

Keeping only the terms l = j and l = k of the denominator, which makes it smaller,

\mathbb{E}_{p_j}[w_k] \le \int \frac{p_j(\tilde x)\, p_k(\tilde x)}{p_j(\tilde x) + p_k(\tilde x)}\, d\tilde x

Bounding p_j + p_k \ge 2 \sqrt{p_j\, p_k}, the inequality between the arithmetic and the geometric mean,

\mathbb{E}_{p_j}[w_k] \le \frac{1}{2} \int \sqrt{p_j(\tilde x)\, p_k(\tilde x)}\, d\tilde x

Substituting the Gaussian densities of Eq. 38,

\mathbb{E}_{p_j}[w_k] \le \frac{1}{2} \int (2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-d/2} \exp\Big(-\frac{\lVert \tilde x - x^{(j)} \rVert^2 + \lVert \tilde x - x^{(k)} \rVert^2}{4 \sigma_1^2}\Big)\, d\tilde x

Completing the square, \lVert \tilde x - a \rVert^2 + \lVert \tilde x - b \rVert^2 = 2 \lVert \tilde x - (a + b)/2 \rVert^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert a - b \rVert^2, with a = x^{(j)} and b = x^{(k)},

\mathbb{E}_{p_j}[w_k] \le \frac{1}{2} \int (2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-d/2} \exp\Big(-\frac{2 \lVert \tilde x - (x^{(j)} + x^{(k)})/2 \rVert^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert x^{(j)} - x^{(k)} \rVert^2}{4 \sigma_1^2}\Big)\, d\tilde x

Factoring the constant exponential out of the integral,

\mathbb{E}_{p_j}[w_k] \le \frac{1}{2} \exp\Big(-\frac{\lVert x^{(j)} - x^{(k)} \rVert^2}{8 \sigma_1^2}\Big) \int (2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-d/2} \exp\Big(-\frac{\lVert \tilde x - (x^{(j)} + x^{(k)})/2 \rVert^2}{2 \sigma_1^2}\Big)\, d\tilde x

The integral is that of a Gaussian density, which is 1,

\boxed{\mathbb{E}_{p_j}[w_k] \le \frac{1}{2} \exp\Big(-\frac{\lVert x^{(j)} - x^{(k)} \rVert^2}{8 \sigma_1^2}\Big)}

which is Eq. 52. \square



The bound decays exponentially once \sigma_1 is small against \lVert x^{(j)} - x^{(k)} \rVert. A chain started around x^{(j)} then behaves as if x^{(k)} were absent, and the samples lose diversity. Song and Ermon therefore set \sigma_1 equal to the largest distance between two training samples. On CIFAR-10, with pixel values scaled to [0, 1], the median distance between two training images is about 18, so the \sigma_1 = 1 of their first model makes the bound about 10^{-18} for two images at that distance.
They checked the rule with exact scores, on a mixture of 10,000 Gaussians centered at CIFAR-10 test images, running Langevin MCMC at a decreasing sequence of levels from uniform noise. With \sigma_1 = 50, the largest distance on CIFAR-10, the average distance between two samples was 18.65, close to the 17.78 of the data. With \sigma_1 = 1 it was 10.12.


5.1.2 The ratio between levels
Samples at level \sigma_{i-1} start the chain at level \sigma_i, so they must lie where p_{\sigma_i} has a high density, as Song and Ermon argued in their first paper [6]. Their follow-up made the requirement quantitative for data that is a single point at the origin, where p_{\sigma_i} = \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_i^2 I) [50]. The direction of a sample is then uniform at each level, so only its radius r = \lVert \tilde x \rVert matters.
At a level \sigma, the squared radius r^2 is the sum of the d squared coordinates, which are independent, each with mean \sigma^2 and variance 2\sigma^4. By the central limit theorem, which makes a normalized sum of many independent terms approximately normal, r^2 is approximately \mathcal{N}(d \sigma^2, 2 d \sigma^4) for large d. Expanding the square root to first order around d \sigma^2,

r \approx \sqrt{d}\, \sigma + \frac{r^2 - d \sigma^2}{2 \sqrt{d}\, \sigma}

whose variance is 2d\sigma^4/(4d\sigma^2) = \sigma^2/2, so approximately

r \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{d}\, \sigma,\ \sigma^2 / 2\big)

and their Proposition 2 states the limit, r - \sqrt{d}\, \sigma \to \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2/2) in distribution as d \to \infty.
A normal variable lies within three standard deviations of its mean with probability about 0.997 (the three-sigma rule), so with that probability the radius at level \sigma_{i-1} lies in

\mathcal{I}_{i-1} = \big[\sqrt{d}\, \sigma_{i-1} - 3 \sigma_{i-1} / \sqrt{2},\ \sqrt{d}\, \sigma_{i-1} + 3 \sigma_{i-1} / \sqrt{2}\big]

The requirement is therefore that p_{\sigma_i} puts substantial mass on \mathcal{I}_{i-1}. We write \gamma_i = \sigma_{i-1} / \sigma_i > 1 and \Phi for the standard normal distribution function. Standardizing the endpoints of \mathcal{I}_{i-1} by the mean \sqrt{d}\, \sigma_i and the standard deviation \sigma_i / \sqrt{2} of the normal approximation of the radius at level \sigma_i, the probability P_{\sigma_i} that a sample at level \sigma_i has its radius in \mathcal{I}_{i-1} is, in that approximation,

\boxed{P_{\sigma_i}\big(r \in \mathcal{I}_{i-1}\big) = \Phi\big(\sqrt{2d}\, (\gamma_i - 1) + 3 \gamma_i\big) - \Phi\big(\sqrt{2d}\, (\gamma_i - 1) - 3 \gamma_i\big)}
\tag{53}
Song and Ermon set this probability to the same constant \kappa at each level. The right side depends on i only through \gamma_i, and, for d \ge 5 and 0 < \kappa < \Phi(3) - \Phi(-3) \approx 0.997, it equals \kappa at exactly one \gamma_i > 1, as the proof below shows. All ratios are therefore equal, and the levels form a geometric sequence. They recommend \kappa \approx 0.5, since a larger \kappa needs more levels, each a run of Langevin MCMC at sampling time.






NoteProof: one ratio for each overlap





We assume d \ge 5, write k = \sqrt{2d} > 3, and write P(\gamma) for the right side of Eq. 53 with a = k (\gamma - 1) and b = 3 \gamma. Differentiating in \gamma, with \varphi = \Phi' the standard normal density,

P'(\gamma) = (k + 3)\, \varphi(a + b) - (k - 3)\, \varphi(a - b)

Factoring out (k - 3)\, \varphi(a - b) > 0, with \varphi(a + b) / \varphi(a - b) = e^{-2ab},

P'(\gamma) = (k - 3)\, \varphi(a - b) \Big(\frac{k + 3}{k - 3}\, e^{-2ab} - 1\Big)

On [1, \infty), ab = 3 k \gamma (\gamma - 1) increases strictly from 0 to \infty, so the bracket is positive at \gamma = 1, changes sign once, at some \gamma^\ast, and is negative after it. P therefore rises on [1, \gamma^\ast] from P(1) = \Phi(3) - \Phi(-3) and falls on [\gamma^\ast, \infty) toward 0, since both arguments of \Phi grow without bound (a - b = (k - 3) \gamma - k). On [1, \gamma^\ast] it stays at least P(1) > \kappa. On [\gamma^\ast, \infty) it is continuous and strictly decreasing from above \kappa toward 0, so P(\gamma) = \kappa has exactly one solution \gamma > 1. \square



For CIFAR-10 images, d = 3072, and \kappa = 0.5 gives \gamma \approx 1.04. The L = 10 levels from 1 to 0.01 of Song and Ermon’s first model have \gamma \approx 1.67, at which Eq. 53 is 0 to numerical precision. Their follow-up model for CIFAR-10 uses \sigma_1 = 50 and L = 232 levels [50].

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
5.2 Training: noise-conditional score networks
To train, instead of using L separate networks per noise level, a single NCSN s_\theta(x, \sigma) is trained to match the score at each level at once by minimizing the weighted sum of per-level denoising errors.

5.2.1 DSM loss for the NCSN
Denoising score matching is the natural loss to use as the goal is to estimate scores of perturbed distributions, so the overall training objective is a weighted sum of per-level score-matching losses. With the marginal score as the target, it is the weighted ESM objective,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta; \lambda) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^L \lambda(\sigma_i)\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\sigma_i}(\tilde{x})}\big[\|s_\theta(\tilde{x}, \sigma_i) - \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_{\sigma_i}(\tilde{x})\|^2\big]

In this Part the data distribution smoothed at level \sigma_i is

p_{\sigma_i}(\tilde{x}) := \int p_0(x)\, p_{\sigma_i}(\tilde{x} \mid x)\, dx

which is the Parzen density Eq. 39 with the empirical \hat{p} replaced by p_0. The DSM theorem Eq. 45 and its proof carry over to that replacement. The proof used three facts, that the factor p_0(x) of the joint is free of \tilde{x}, that the smoothed density is the integral of the joint over x, and that the gradient in \tilde{x} may be taken under that integral. With \hat{p} the integral was a finite sum. With p_0 the interchange holds because, for each x and \tilde{x},

\lVert \nabla_{\tilde{x}}\, p_{\sigma_i}(\tilde{x} \mid x) \rVert \le (2\pi\sigma_i^2)^{-d/2}\, e^{-1/2}/\sigma_i

a constant, which is integrable against p_0. The factor \tfrac{1}{2} of Eq. 44 is absorbed into the weights.
Replacing each marginal score by the conditional score and each marginal average by the joint average over x \sim p_0 and its perturbation \tilde{x} = x + \sigma_i \epsilon, which by the DSM theorem changes the objective only by a constant,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta; \lambda) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^L \lambda(\sigma_i)\, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_0,\, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\big[\|s_\theta(\tilde{x}, \sigma_i) - \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_{\sigma_i}(\tilde{x} \mid x)\|^2\big] + \text{const}

Substituting the Gaussian target

\nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log p_{\sigma_i}(\tilde{x} \mid x) = -\epsilon/\sigma_i

into the previous line,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta; \lambda) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^L \lambda(\sigma_i)\, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_0,\, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\left[\left\|s_\theta(x + \sigma_i \epsilon, \sigma_i) + \frac{\epsilon}{\sigma_i}\right\|^2\right] + \text{const}

There can be many possible choices of the weight \lambda(\sigma_i), however we choose \lambda(\sigma_i) = \sigma_i^2 as per Song and Ermon’s recommendation [6] as this value balances the losses across levels. The level-i target -\epsilon/\sigma_i carries a factor 1/\sigma_i, so the level’s squared error carries 1/\sigma_i^2 times a residual that does not scale with \sigma_i; multiplying by \sigma_i^2 cancels that factor and puts every level on the same footing, so none dominates.
Choosing \lambda(\sigma_i) = \sigma_i^2,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta; \lambda) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^L \sigma_i^2\, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_0,\, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\left[\left\|s_\theta(x + \sigma_i \epsilon, \sigma_i) + \frac{\epsilon}{\sigma_i}\right\|^2\right] + \text{const}

Dropping the \theta-free constant, which leaves the weighted DSM objective,

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta; \lambda) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^L \sigma_i^2\, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_0,\, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\left[\left\|s_\theta(x + \sigma_i \epsilon, \sigma_i) + \frac{\epsilon}{\sigma_i}\right\|^2\right]}
\tag{54}
Moving \sigma_i inside the norm,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta; \lambda) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^L \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_0,\, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\big[\|\sigma_i\, s_\theta(x + \sigma_i \epsilon, \sigma_i) + \epsilon\|^2\big]

Defining

\epsilon_\theta(\cdot, \sigma_i) := -\sigma_i\, s_\theta(\cdot, \sigma_i)

and substituting it into the previous line,

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}_{p_\sigma}}(\theta; \lambda) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^L \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_0,\, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\big[\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x + \sigma_i \epsilon, \sigma_i)\|^2\big]}
\tag{55}
This is the noise-prediction form. \square
The true score has the same 1/\sigma_i size. For data at a single point, the score at level \sigma is -\tilde x / \sigma^2, whose norm r / \sigma^2 is about \sqrt{d} / \sigma by the radius distribution of §5.1.2. Song and Ermon’s follow-up builds that scaling into the network, s_\theta(\tilde x, \sigma) = F_\theta(\tilde x) / \sigma with an unconditional network F_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d [50], so that \epsilon_\theta(\cdot, \sigma_i) = -F_\theta(\cdot) needs no noise input.


5.2.2 Training procedure
Training samples a mini-batch of data points, noise-scale indices, and Gaussian noise,

\begin{aligned}
\{x^{(1)}, \cdots, x^{(m)}\} &\sim p_0 \\[4pt]
\{i_1, \cdots, i_m\} &\sim \mathcal{U}\{1, 2, \cdots, L\} \\[4pt]
\{\epsilon_1, \cdots, \epsilon_m\} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
\end{aligned}

and minimizes the empirical mean

\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \big\|\epsilon_j - \epsilon_\theta\big(x^{(j)} + \sigma_{i_j}\, \epsilon_j,\ \sigma_{i_j}\big)\big\|^2

by stochastic gradient descent, which is as efficient as training a single DSM model at one noise level.

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
5.3 Sampling: annealed Langevin dynamics
Annealed Langevin dynamics runs Langevin MCMC against a sequence of noise-smoothed targets p_{\sigma_1} , \dots, p_{\sigma_L} with decreasing noise \sigma_1 > \cdots > \sigma_L, using the score at each level, and carries the samples from one level to the next.
Smoothing fills the low-density gaps so the score is informative everywhere; annealing gradually concentrates back to the data distribution (Figure 28). This is reverse diffusion at discrete noise levels: each level’s score-driven Langevin step is a denoising step.








Figure 28: Annealed Langevin dynamics descends through the noise levels. Each row is the noise-smoothed density p_{\sigma_i} for a decreasing sequence \sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > \sigma_3 > \sigma_4: broad and featureless at the top, concentrating toward the data density at the bottom. Four chains are initialized from a broad Gaussian and run a few Langevin steps at each level, each level warm-started from the one above; by the last level the chains lie on the two modes.





Algorithm 5 uses two constants. \varepsilon_0 is the base Langevin step size, used at the finest level \sigma_L and scaled at level i by \sigma_i^2/\sigma_L^2, so the step stays proportional to the level’s variance. K is the number of Langevin steps run at each level.
Algorithm 5 — Annealed Langevin dynamics [6]:
1: x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_1^2 I)
2: for i = 1, \ldots, L do
    3: \varepsilon_i = \varepsilon_0 \cdot \sigma_i^2 / \sigma_L^2
    4: for k = 1, \ldots, K do
        5: z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
        6: x = x + \varepsilon_i\, s_\theta(x, \sigma_i) + \sqrt{2\varepsilon_i}\, z
    7: end for
8: end for
9: return x
The sampler starts with the maximum value of \sigma_i and descends through the L levels one level at a time. At each level, it runs the Langevin MCMC of §3.3.2 with the learned score for that level s_\theta(x, \sigma_i) in place of \nabla_x \log p_{\sigma_i} as drift, starting from the sample the previous level returned. As we start with the maximum value of \sigma_i and go down with the schedule, it slowly concentrates the target from broad noise to the data distribution.
Each Langevin step evaluates the network once, so one sample costs L \cdot K network evaluations. Song and Ermon’s 2019 image experiments use L = 10 noise levels, a geometric sequence from \sigma_1 = 1 to \sigma_{10} = 0.01, with K = 100 steps at each level and \varepsilon_0 = 2 \times 10^{-5}, which comes to 1000 network evaluations for each sample [6].

title: The Variational Bound (ELBO) and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion
text:
6.1 What comes next
Post #3 brings the two sides together. The variational chain of Part 2 and the score-based construction of Parts 3 to 5 are two discretizations of a single continuous-time object, and once that object is written as an SDE the whole apparatus of stochastic calculus applies to it. The quantities the two routes learn (DDPM’s noise prediction and the score-based model’s score) are equivalent parameterizations of one quantity, the score of the data distribution smoothed at each noise level.

[48] M. F. Hutchinson, “A stochastic estimator of the trace of the influence matrix for laplacian smoothing splines,” Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation, vol. 19, no. 2, pp. 433–450, 1990, doi: 10.1080/03610919008812866.


[49] Y. Song, J. Sohl-Dickstein, D. P. Kingma, A. Kumar, S. Ermon, and B. Poole, “Score-based generative modeling through stochastic differential equations,” in International conference on learning representations (ICLR), 2021. Available: https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456


[50] Y. Song and S. Ermon, “Improved techniques for training score-based generative models,” in Advances in neural information processing systems, 2020.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
This series — Continuous-Time Generative Models
Diffusion models generate data by reversing a gradual transformation from data to noise. They learn the score of the intermediate distributions and use it to construct either a reverse-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) or a deterministic probability-flow ordinary differential equation (ODE). The score determines the drift of the reverse-time SDE and, together with the forward dynamics, the velocity field of the probability-flow ODE. The SDE combines this drift with stochastic noise, whereas the ODE generates samples using only its deterministic velocity field.
This raises a natural question: if generation with the probability-flow ODE requires only a velocity field, can we learn that field directly, by regression, without learning the score first?
Direct velocity learning is only part of the challenge. Diffusion models can require hundreds or thousands of network evaluations to generate a sample, their trajectories can curve and change speed, and the forward SDE fixes the path of distributions between data and noise. Generation also typically starts from Gaussian noise. We therefore want not just a way to learn velocity directly, but a simple and efficient way to learn a field whose trajectories are easy to solve.
We begin with normalizing flows, which transform a simple distribution into a data distribution through a sequence of invertible maps and provide exact likelihoods [1], [2]. Each map requires a tractable Jacobian determinant, restricting the choice of transformations and often requiring deep stacks to achieve sufficient expressiveness. Normalizing flows establish the idea of transporting probability distributions, but their discrete transformations can make the model cumbersome.
Flow models replace those transformations with an ODE [3]. Drawing their mathematics from Euler’s description of fluid motion [4], they represent generation through a time-dependent velocity field that transports noise toward data. Solving the ODE numerically generates samples, while the instantaneous change-of-variables formula gives their likelihoods.
This replaces a stack of maps with continuous dynamics, but maximum-likelihood training still requires solving the ODE at each training step. Methods such as FFJORD [5] and RNODE [6] reduce this computational burden without eliminating it. Moreover, likelihood training does not prescribe the path between noise and data, leaving the model to discover suitable dynamics while optimizing its objective.
Flow matching takes the next step: instead of learning the velocity indirectly through likelihood optimization, it specifies a path of intermediate distributions and learns the velocity field by regression [7], [8], [9]. Training no longer requires solving the ODE. This also offers a different way to view the probability-flow ODE from post #3: rather than deriving its velocity from a learned score, we can train a velocity field directly.
The continuity equation, which expresses conservation of probability, describes how this field transports distributions along the chosen path. The post re-derives post #3’s probability-flow ODE from this equation. Unlike diffusion, flow matching allows us to choose the path rather than inherit it from a prescribed forward SDE.
But specifying the path of distributions does not tell us how individual samples should move along it. The continuity equation constrains the velocity field to transport the distributions correctly, but does not uniquely determine it. The marginal velocity field we want to learn, the particular one that flow matching regresses onto, is intractable, because it depends on the intractable density of the path, leaving us without a direct regression target.
Lipman et al. resolve this by constructing the desired path from simpler conditional paths, one for each data point, whose velocity fields are known analytically. Each conditional path describes how noise moves toward a particular data point. The continuity equation shows that averaging these conditional velocity fields, weighted by the posterior probability of each data point given the current sample, produces a velocity field that transports the marginal distributions along the desired path.
This gives us a tractable regression target, but one question remains: does learning the conditional velocity fields learn the desired marginal velocity field? Lipman et al. prove that the conditional and marginal regression objectives have the same gradient and differ only by a constant. Minimizing the conditional objective therefore learns the desired marginal dynamics without ever requiring the unknown marginal velocity field itself.
To make these conditional paths easy to construct, Lipman et al. choose paths that are Gaussian at each time given the data point. This choice also connects flow matching back to diffusion: the perturbation kernels of the Variance-Preserving (VP) and Variance-Exploding (VE) SDEs, with time reversed, are examples of such Gaussian conditional paths. Diffusion is thus recovered, approximately, as a special case of a broader framework in which the path can be chosen freely.
The simplest Gaussian conditional path moves each noise sample along a straight line to the data point, at constant speed. Its velocity is the difference between the data point and the noise sample, making the regression target easy to compute. This completes the central construction of flow matching: we can learn a velocity field directly, without learning a score or solving an ODE during training, using regression targets that are available in closed form.
However, simple conditional paths do not guarantee simple marginal trajectories. Even when every conditional trajectory is straight, the learned marginal trajectories can still curve. Noise and data points are also paired independently, and the source distribution remains Gaussian. Flow matching therefore solves the problem of learning velocity directly, but not yet the problem of making the resulting flow maximally efficient to sample.
The next post builds on this foundation to address these remaining limitations by exploring straighter marginal trajectories, better endpoint pairings, and more flexible source distributions.
The presentation of flows, flow models and flow matching in Parts 3 to 6 follows Holderrieth and Erives’s MIT lecture notes [10], and Lipman et al.’s guide covers the same ground with code [11].

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
Roadmap

Part 1: Sets out the limits of the diffusion models of post #3 that led to flow matching, traces flow models to fluid mechanics, and places the landmark papers in a lineage diagram.
Part 2: Develops normalizing flows, from the change of variables to planar flows, coupling layers and residual flows, and the determinant that restricts them.
Part 3: Introduces flows and the ODEs behind them, with the flow maps between two times, and defines flow models, which Chen et al. call continuous normalizing flows. It samples from them with the Euler method, computes their exact likelihood and trains them by maximum likelihood, through FFJORD and RNODE, and ends with the two pitfalls of that training.
Part 4: Builds paths of distributions from noise to data and the velocity fields that follow them, and proves through the continuity equation that one of these fields carries noise to data. It ends by relating the four forms of the change of variables, from one map to the Fokker-Planck equation.
Part 5: Starts from the probability-flow ODE, the first flow model trained without solving its ODE, defines the flow-matching objective and conditional flow matching, the device that makes it tractable, and bounds the distance from the generated distribution to the data distribution by the flow-matching objective.
Part 6: Develops the paths that Lipman et al. train on, which are Gaussian at each time, extends them to affine conditional flows, obtains the diffusion paths and the path whose mean and standard deviation change linearly as two instances, and ends with three pitfalls that these paths keep.
Part 7: Summarizes how flow matching learns the velocity field directly and which pitfalls remain, and previews post #5.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
1.1 The limits of diffusion models
Diffusion models in the SDE framework of Song et al. generate high-quality samples, but four limitations motivated flow matching:

Slow sampling: A sample needs hundreds to thousands of network evaluations.
Curved and uneven trajectories: The trajectories a sampler follows bend and change speed, which enlarges the error of each solver step.
A fixed probability path: The forward SDE fixes the path of distributions that generation follows, so it cannot be chosen.
A restricted source distribution: Generation starts from a Gaussian, so the model cannot carry one data distribution to another.

Lipman et al. [7] and Liu et al. [8] identify these limitations in the introductions to their papers.
Flow matching keeps the regression training of diffusion models, which never solves an ODE, and addresses the four limitations:

Straighter trajectories and faster sampling (Part 6 and post #5): Straight segments between noise and data, and better pairings of the two, reduce the curvature of the trajectories, so generation needs fewer steps.
Flexible probability paths (Parts 4–6): The path between the source and target distributions becomes a design choice rather than being fixed by the forward SDE.
Flexible source distributions (post #5): The source can be any distribution, not only a Gaussian.


1.1.1 Slow sampling
A diffusion model generates a sample by solving the reverse-time SDE or the probability-flow ODE step by step, and each step evaluates the network once. Many steps are needed. Song et al.’s samplers use 1,000 to 2,000 evaluations per sample on CIFAR-10, a dataset of 32 \times 32 colour images [12]. The probability-flow ODE needs fewer, because an adaptive solver takes larger steps where the solution changes slowly. On 256 \times 256 face images it used 14 evaluations at a higher error tolerance and 548 at a lower one (Song et al.’s Figure 3).
Liu et al. identify the computational cost of inference as a key drawback of continuous-time models compared with generators that transform noise into data in a single evaluation [8]. Specialized samplers such as denoising diffusion implicit models (DDIM) [13] and DPM-Solver [14] reduce the number of evaluations [7].


1.1.2 Curved and uneven trajectories
How many steps a solver needs depends on the shape of the trajectories it follows. Each step of the Euler method [15] follows the velocity at the start of the step, so the step is exact only when that velocity stays fixed, that is, when the trajectory is a straight line traversed at constant speed. The more a trajectory bends or changes speed, the larger the error of each step, and the more steps a sampler needs to keep the error small.
Diffusion paths fall short of this. On the path of the VP SDE, the default for diffusion models, a noisy sample is a weighted sum of a data point and a noise sample, with weights whose squares sum to one, so with the data point and the noise sample held fixed its trajectory is an arc. On the path of the VE SDE the corresponding trajectory is a straight segment, but its speed changes over time.
Lipman et al. contrast these paths with the straight, constant-speed trajectories of an optimal-transport path [7], named after optimal transport, the least-cost way to rearrange one distribution into another [16], [17]. §6.4 draws the VP and optimal-transport trajectories side by side, and P5:§4.4 bounds the error of one Euler step by the trajectory’s acceleration.
A sampler, however, follows a velocity field that averages, at each point, the velocities of the trajectories through it, so its own trajectories bend even on the optimal-transport path (§6.5.1). They bend less there than on the VP path [8].


1.1.3 A fixed probability path
A diffusion model chooses its path of distributions by choosing a perturbation kernel from a short list, such as those of the VP, VE and sub-VP SDEs, and then learns the score along that path. Lipman et al. call this a confined space of probability paths, narrower than the range a flow can follow, and link it to very long training times and to the need for the specialized samplers above [7].
The path also reaches noise only in the limit. At the terminal time T the VP marginal still depends on the data, because the weight of the data in the VP perturbation kernel is small but not zero, so generation starts from \mathcal{N}(0, I), which is close to the terminal marginal but not equal to it [7].
The path is not the only choice made by hand. The weighting of the training loss over time, the cutoff near the data and the sampler are chosen too, and Karras et al. separated these choices and tuned each on its own [18]. Citing that study, Liu et al. still describe the design space of diffusion models as involved and poorly understood [8].


1.1.4 A restricted source distribution
The forward SDE carries each data distribution close to one fixed Gaussian, so a diffusion model generates only from noise. Carrying one data distribution to another, as image-to-image translation requires, needs separate constructions. Liu et al. note that generative modeling and domain transfer were treated as separate problems, and pose both as one problem of transporting one distribution to another [8].

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
1.2 The origin of flow models
Flow models derive both their name and their mathematics from fluid mechanics. Euler described a moving fluid by its velocity at each point and each time [4]. Each particle of the fluid follows that velocity, so its trajectory is determined by where it starts, and Euler wrote the position of each particle as a function of its starting point and of time [19]. Because the fluid’s mass is neither created nor destroyed, its density and its velocity obey a single partial differential equation, which Euler also derived, the continuity equation [4].
Probability behaves the same way. A cloud of samples is a fluid whose mass is probability, so a velocity field that moves each sample also moves the whole distribution, and the continuity equation describes how its density changes. A generative model of this form is a velocity field that carries a simple distribution, such as a Gaussian, into the data distribution. Following a noise sample from start to end then turns it into a data sample. The probability-flow ODE of post #3 is already a model of this kind, with a velocity field built from the score.
In machine learning, flow models arrived along two routes: normalizing flows for density estimation, which Chen et al. made continuous, and the probability-flow ODE of diffusion. The landmarks below follow both.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
1.3 Landmark papers
The papers this post and post #5 develop descend from two independent lines of work, normalizing flows and diffusion models, rather than from a single chain. The two lines meet in three methods of 2023, and three branches grow from those methods. Figure 1 below draws these dependencies, with each line running from a work to one that builds on it.








Figure 1: Lineage of the papers this post and post #5 develop. The left column is the normalizing-flow lineage and the right column the diffusion lineage, each in order of publication, and each line runs downward from a work to one that builds on it. Both lineages feed the three methods of 2023, which a dashed line joins because they appeared independently in the same year. Three branches build on those methods: the unifying framework of stochastic interpolants, minibatch pairing, and Schrödinger bridge matching, which also builds on De Bortoli et al. Colour marks the thread, and the grey phrase under each entry states its contribution.





In the left column, Tabak and Turner [2], building on Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden [1], composed invertible maps into a normalizing flow, whose density stays exact because the change of variables tracks it through each map. Rezende and Mohamed used such flows for variational inference [20]. Each map must have a Jacobian determinant that is inexpensive to compute, since the change of variables evaluates one for each map, and this restricts the maps that can be used.
Chen et al. removed this restriction by letting a neural network define the velocity field of an ODE, so that a trace replaces the determinant [3]. Training such a flow model by maximum likelihood, however, solves the ODE at each step.
In the right column, Song et al. gave the SDE of each diffusion model a deterministic counterpart, an ODE whose velocity field is built from the score and whose solution has the marginals of the SDE’s solution, and named it the probability-flow ODE [12]. They credit the idea to Maoutsa et al., who simulated such ODEs with interacting particles and estimated the score by score matching [21]. Because denoising score matching (DSM) learns the score by regression, the velocity field of the probability-flow ODE is trained without solving the ODE, but only along the path that the forward SDE fixes.
De Bortoli et al. then used repeated diffusion training to solve the Schrödinger bridge problem [22], [23], the entropic form of optimal transport between two distributions [24].
The three methods of 2023 draw on both columns. The flows contribute the flow model, an ODE whose velocity field is a network, and diffusion contributes training by regression, which never solves the ODE. What the methods add is the freedom to choose the path.
Lipman et al. regress onto the velocity field of a probability path built from Gaussian conditional paths [7], Liu et al. onto the velocity along straight segments between paired points [8], and Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden onto the velocity field of an interpolant between the two distributions [9]. Liu et al. call their method rectified flow, and Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden call the interpolant a stochastic interpolant. The three were posted independently within a month of one another in 2022 and published in 2023, as the dashed line marks.
Three branches grow from the 2023 methods. Albergo, Boffi and Vanden-Eijnden extended stochastic interpolants with a Gaussian latent term into a framework that learns a velocity field and a score together, and so unifies flows with diffusion [25]. Pooladian et al. [26] and Tong et al. [27] kept flow matching but paired noise with data by solving an optimal-transport problem within each minibatch, which straightens the learned flow. Shi et al. returned to the Schrödinger bridge of De Bortoli et al. and solved it by bridge matching, which recovers rectified flow in the limit of zero noise [28].
The post also relies on classical results that it states without developing them in the body, each due to the authors cited with it.

The change of variables, due to Euler [29], Lagrange [30] and Jacobi [31].
The existence and uniqueness of ODE solutions under a Lipschitz condition, due to Lipschitz [32], with the proof by successive approximations due to Picard [33] and Lindelöf [34].
The differentiable dependence of the solution on its initial condition, due to Grönwall [35].
The formula for the derivative of a determinant, due to Jacobi [36].
The stochastic trace estimator, due to Girard [37] and Hutchinson [38].
The fixed-point theorem for contractions, due to Banach [39].
The mimicking theorem, due to Gyöngy [40].
The divergence theorem, stated by Lagrange [41], proved in special cases by Gauss [42] and in general by Ostrogradsky [43].
The orders of accuracy of Heun’s method and the Runge-Kutta method, due to Heun [44] and Kutta [45].

The appendix proves two of these results, the change of variables in one dimension (§A.1) and the existence and uniqueness theorem (§A.2), and the post states the others, at most with a sketch, where it uses them.
Benamou and Brenier’s dynamic form of optimal transport [46] and the optimality of the conditional flow of the optimal-transport path [47] are stated where the post names them, and post #5 develops both.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
2.2 Normalizing flows
Let f_1, \ldots, f_K: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d be invertible and differentiable with differentiable inverses, h_0 \sim p^{(0)} a sample of a simple base density p^{(0)}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), such as that of \mathcal{N}(0, I), and h_k = f_k(h_{k-1}) for k = 1, \ldots, K, with density p^{(k)}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), so that

h_K = f_K \circ \cdots \circ f_1(h_0)

Since h_{k-1} \sim p^{(k-1)}, the change of variables Eq. 1 with f = f_k and p = p^{(k-1)} gives the density of h_k at y = h_k,

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}\big(f_k^{-1}(h_k)\big)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k^{-1}}{\partial h}(h_k) \Big\rvert

Substituting f_k^{-1}(h_k) = h_{k-1},

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1})\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k^{-1}}{\partial h}(h_k) \Big\rvert

By the inverse function theorem, the Jacobian of f_k^{-1} at h_k is the inverse of the Jacobian of f_k at h_{k-1},

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1})\, \Big\lvert \det \Big(\frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1})\Big)^{-1} \Big\rvert

Since the determinant of an inverse matrix is the reciprocal of its determinant,

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1})\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert^{-1}

Taking logarithms,

\log p^{(k)}(h_k) = \log p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1}) - \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert

Summing over k = 1, \ldots, K,

\sum_{k=1}^{K} \log p^{(k)}(h_k) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1}) - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert

Telescoping, the intermediate log-densities cancel [20],

\boxed{\log p^{(K)}(h_K) = \log p^{(0)}(h_0) - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert}
\tag{2}
\square
Evaluating Eq. 2 requires the determinant of a d \times d Jacobian for each layer, which costs O(d^3) operations for a general map, about 3 \times 10^{10} for one layer on a 32 \times 32 colour image (d = 3072).

2.2.1 Planar flows
Rezende and Mohamed built the planar layer so that its Jacobian determinant is inexpensive to compute [20]. It is the map

f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad h \mapsto h + u \tanh(w^\top h + b)

with parameters u, w \in \mathbb{R}^d and b \in \mathbb{R} learned in training. The vector w and the offset b define the hyperplane w^\top h + b = 0, and the layer displaces each point h along the direction u, by the amount \tanh(w^\top h + b), which depends on the side of the hyperplane on which h lies and on its distance from it, so the layer expands or contracts the density in a band around that hyperplane. A normalizing flow built from planar layers is a planar flow.
Differentiating f with respect to h by the chain rule,

\frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = I + u\, \tanh'(w^\top h + b)\, w^\top

Writing \psi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, h \mapsto \tanh'(w^\top h + b)\, w, the Jacobian is a rank-one update of the identity,

\frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = I + u\, \psi(h)^\top

Taking the determinant,

\det \frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = \det\big(I + u\, \psi(h)^\top\big)

The matrix determinant lemma states that \det(I + a\, b^\top) = 1 + a^\top b for a, b \in \mathbb{R}^d. It holds because a\, b^\top has rank at most one, so 0 is its eigenvalue with multiplicity at least d - 1 and its remaining eigenvalue is its trace b^\top a; the eigenvalues of I + a\, b^\top are therefore 1, d - 1 times, and 1 + b^\top a, and the determinant is their product. Applying the lemma with a = u and b = \psi(h),

\det \frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = 1 + u^\top \psi(h)

which costs O(d) operations instead of O(d^3).
The rank-one structure that makes the determinant inexpensive also limits the layer. It acts like a network with a single hidden unit, so each layer changes the density along one direction only. It is invertible only when w^\top u \ge -1 [20], and it has no inverse in closed form.
The lack of a closed-form inverse decides what a planar flow can be used for. Eq. 2 gives \log p^{(K)} at a point h_K through the points h_0, \ldots, h_{K-1} that lead to it. For a sample the flow generates, those points are computed on the way forward, from h_0 \sim p^{(0)} through each layer, so Eq. 2 needs no inverse. For a given x \in \mathbb{R}^d, such as a training image, only h_K = x is known. Recovering h_{K-1} = f_K^{-1}(x), and so on back to h_0, needs the inverse of each layer, which for a planar layer means solving a scalar equation for w^\top h numerically [20].
Planar flows therefore suit variational inference, which fits a flow to an intractable target distribution, such as a Bayesian posterior, using the flow’s own samples, their densities and the unnormalized target density. They do not suit training on data, which needs the density at each training image and so a numerical solve for each layer at each training step [5], [20].
A few planar layers already turn a Gaussian into a density with several modes. Because Eq. 2 runs forward, plotting the density p^{(k)} after k layers needs no inverse either. A fine grid of base points h_0 is pushed through the first k layers, and Eq. 2 gives \log p^{(k)} at each image h_k. Figure 2 below shows the result for four planar layers in two dimensions, each with w^\top u > -1, a condition that makes the layer invertible with a differentiable inverse [20].








Figure 2: Exact densities of a planar flow in two dimensions: the base density p^{(0)} of \mathcal{N}(0, I) and the densities p^{(1)}, p^{(2)} and p^{(4)} of h_1, h_2 and h_4 after one, two and four planar layers, computed with Eq. 2 at the images of a grid of base points. Two layers with w^\top u = 3.9 split the Gaussian into two and then four modes, and two volume-preserving layers shear them. Shading is proportional to the density, scaled to each panel’s maximum.





The determinant 1 + u^\top \psi(h) = 1 + (w^\top u)\, \tanh'(w^\top h + b) explains each panel. The first two layers have w^\top u = 3.9, so the determinant exceeds one near the line w^\top h + b = 0, where \tanh' is largest, and reaches 4.9 on the line itself. The density is divided by the determinant, so it drops along that line. A trough opens along the vertical axis and splits the Gaussian into two modes, and a second trough along the horizontal axis splits them into four. The last two layers have w^\top u = 0, so their determinant is one. They preserve volume and only shear the four modes along lines parallel to the two diagonals.


2.2.2 Coupling layers
A coupling layer splits its input into two halves, keeps one and updates the other by an invertible map whose parameters depend on the kept half. Coupling layers have an inverse in closed form, so a flow built from them can be trained on data by maximum likelihood.
Dinh et al. introduced them on arXiv in 2014, before planar flows, in Non-linear Independent Components Estimation (NICE) [48]. NICE splits h into two halves h_a, h_b \in \mathbb{R}^{d/2}, keeps h_a and replaces h_b by h_b + m(h_a), where m: \mathbb{R}^{d/2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d/2} is an arbitrary network. Because h_a passes through unchanged, subtracting m(h_a) undoes the update, so the inverse costs as much as the map itself. Its Jacobian is triangular with ones on the diagonal, so its determinant is one.
The real-valued non-volume-preserving (RealNVP) layer makes the update affine. It replaces h_b by h_b \odot \exp\big(s(h_a)\big) + t(h_a) with networks s, t: \mathbb{R}^{d/2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d/2} and \odot the elementwise product [49]. Its Jacobian is triangular, so its log-determinant is the sum of the entries of s(h_a). Glow inserts a learned invertible 1 \times 1 convolution, one linear map applied to the channels of each pixel, between coupling layers to mix the two halves. Writing its matrix as a permutation times triangular matrices (an LU factorization) makes the determinant, up to sign, the product of their diagonal entries [50].
These layers trained flows by maximum likelihood on images. On CIFAR-10, RealNVP [49] reaches 3.49 and Glow [50] 3.35 bits per dimension, the negative log-likelihood -\log_2 p(x)/d of a test image averaged over the test set, where lower is better. Since a density depends on the scale of x, these figures use the pixel values, integers from 0 to 255, made continuous by adding uniform noise on [0, 1).


2.2.3 Residual flows
A residual layer f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, h \mapsto h + g(h), adds the output of a differentiable network g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d to its input, as in the residual networks of He et al. [51]. Behrmann et al. [52] showed that a general network can serve as g in a flow when g is a contraction, a map with

\lVert g(h) - g(h') \rVert \le L\, \lVert h - h' \rVert

for each pair of points and a constant L < 1.
They build g from linear maps and from nonlinearities that increase no distance, and keep L below one by keeping the operator norm \lVert W \rVert of each weight matrix W, the largest factor by which W stretches the length of a vector, below one. They rescale W to c\, W / \hat s whenever \hat s > c, where \hat s is an estimate of \lVert W \rVert and c < 1 is a chosen coefficient. This is a variant of the spectral normalization of Miyato et al. [53].
The layer is then invertible.
