For each y \in \mathbb{R}^d the map h \mapsto y - g(h) is a contraction with the same constant L, so by Banach’s fixed-point theorem it has exactly one fixed point, and the iteration h \leftarrow y - g(h) converges to it from each starting point [39]. The fixed point satisfies h + g(h) = y, so it is f^{-1}(y), and the iteration computes the inverse.
The log-determinant has a power series instead of a closed form. The Jacobian of the layer is I + J_g, with J_g = \frac{\partial g}{\partial h}(h) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} the Jacobian of g. Its operator norm \lVert J_g \rVert is at most L, since for each a \in \mathbb{R}^d the vector J_g a is the limit of \big(g(h + \varepsilon a) - g(h)\big)/\varepsilon as \varepsilon \to 0, whose length the contraction bounds by L\, \lVert a \rVert. An eigenvector is stretched by the modulus of its eigenvalue, so the eigenvalues \lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_d of J_g, counted with multiplicity, satisfy \lvert \lambda_j \rvert \le L < 1.
The eigenvalues 1 + \lambda_j of I + J_g therefore have positive real parts. The real ones are positive, and the others come in conjugate pairs whose products \lvert 1 + \lambda_j \rvert^2 are positive, so the determinant, the product of the eigenvalues, is positive. The principal logarithms \log(1 + \lambda_j), those with imaginary part in (-\pi, \pi), of a conjugate pair are conjugate, so their imaginary parts cancel in the sum. Taking the logarithm of the product,

\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \log(1 + \lambda_j)

Expanding each logarithm in its power series, which converges since \lvert \lambda_j \rvert < 1,

\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\, \lambda_j^k

Exchanging the two sums, which converge absolutely,

\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{d} \lambda_j^k

Since the eigenvalues of J_g^k are the \lambda_j^k, whose sum is its trace,

\boxed{\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\, \operatorname{tr}\big(J_g^k\big)}
\tag{3}
\square
Behrmann et al. truncate the series after a fixed number of terms and estimate each trace stochastically, from products of the Jacobian with random vectors, each of which costs about as much as evaluating g, so no d \times d determinant is formed. The truncation biases the estimate. The residual flows of Chen, Behrmann, Duvenaud and Jacobsen remove the bias by truncating at a random number of terms and reweighting the terms that remain [54]. A general network as g thus comes with two requirements, the contraction constraint on each layer and an inverse computed by iteration rather than by a formula.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
2.3 Pitfalls
Normalizing flows built from a finite sequence of maps give exact likelihoods, or, with residual layers, estimates of them, but the determinant in Eq. 2 restricts them in two ways.

2.3.1 Restricted architectures
Each map must have a Jacobian whose determinant is inexpensive to compute, such as a rank-one update of the identity or a triangular matrix, so a general network cannot serve as a layer [5]. Chen et al. name this restriction as their reason to make flows continuous [3]. Residual layers, which came later, admit a general network only as a contraction, and their log-determinant is then a series that must be estimated (§2.2.3).


2.3.2 Deep stacks
To keep its Jacobian triangular, each coupling layer applies only an elementwise affine update to half the coordinates, conditioned on the other half. Two alternating layers already transform each coordinate [48], but a flow needs many such layers to be expressive. Glow uses 3 levels of 32 steps on CIFAR-10, each step a coupling layer with its 1 \times 1 convolution and a normalization, and 5 levels of 64 steps on 128 \times 128 images [50], and memory limits such deep stacks at high resolution [49], [50].

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
3.1 ODEs and flows
An ODE describes how a point moves through space over time, and three objects make this precise. All three come from Euler’s mechanics of fluids, which describes a fluid by its velocity field over space [4] and by the trajectories of its particles as functions of their initial positions and time, the flow below [19]. Lie later studied the maps that a velocity field fixed in time generates as a group of transformations [55].
Trajectory (X_t): A function that assigns a position in space \mathbb{R}^d to each time,

X: [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad t \mapsto X_t

Velocity field (v_t(x)): A function that assigns a velocity, a vector in \mathbb{R}^d, to each point of space at each time,

v: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad (x, t) \mapsto v_t(x)

An ODE requires a trajectory X to start at an initial condition x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d and to have, at each time t, the velocity v_t(X_t) of the point it occupies. A trajectory that meets both requirements is a solution of the ODE,

\boxed{X_0 = x_0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_t(X_t)}
\tag{4}
Flow (\phi_t(x)): The trajectories that solve the ODE Eq. 4, as a function of the initial condition and the time,

\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad (x, t) \mapsto \phi_t(x)

whose value \phi_t(x_0) is the position at time t of the trajectory X with the initial condition X_0 = x_0. Substituting X_t = \phi_t(x_0) into Eq. 4, the flow \phi_t(x_0) solves

\boxed{\phi_0(x_0) = x_0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0) = v_t\big(\phi_t(x_0)\big)}
\tag{5}
for each initial condition x_0. By the Picard-Lindelöf theorem [33], [34], [56], the flow \phi_t(x) exists and is unique on [0, 1] when v_t(x) is continuous in t and Lipschitz [32] in x uniformly in t, that is, when \lVert v_t(x) - v_t(y) \rVert \le K\, \lVert x - y \rVert \forall\, x, y \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ t \in [0, 1] for some constant K. §A.2 proves the theorem by Picard’s successive approximations.

3.1.1 Lamb-Oseen vortex: an example of a flow
Fluid dynamics gives these objects a direct physical meaning. In a moving fluid the velocity field v_t(x) is the fluid’s velocity at each point x, a trajectory X is the path of one fluid particle, and the flow \phi_t(x) carries each particle from its position x at t = 0 to its position at time t.
Here we draw the flow \phi_t(x) of a Lamb-Oseen vortex [57], [58], [59], the standard model of a viscous vortex such as a whirlpool. The fluid circles the origin counterclockwise, and at distance r from the origin its angular speed is

\omega: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty), \qquad r \mapsto \frac{\kappa}{r^2}\big(1 - e^{-r^2/r_c^2}\big)

where \kappa > 0 sets the vortex’s strength and r_c is the radius of its core, which we hold fixed. In Cartesian coordinates its velocity field is, the same at each time t,

v_t(x) = \omega(\lVert x \rVert)\, R\, x \quad (x \neq 0), \qquad v_t(0) = 0

with the counterclockwise rotation by a right angle

R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}

In polar coordinates (r, \vartheta), the trajectory (r_t, \vartheta_t) of a fluid particle of the Lamb-Oseen vortex solves the ODE,

(r_0, \vartheta_0) = (r, \vartheta), \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, (r_t, \vartheta_t) = \big(0,\ \omega(r_t)\big)

Since \frac{d}{dt}\, r_t = 0, the radius stays r_t = r and the angle grows at the constant rate \omega(r), so the solution of this ODE is the flow, in polar coordinates,

\phi_t(r, \vartheta) = \big(r,\ \vartheta + \omega(r)\, t\big)

which rotates a particle at a distance r from the origin by the angle \omega(r)\, t in time t while keeping the distance from the origin fixed.
Figure 3 below shows the flow as a deformed square grid, a device of D’Arcy Thompson [60]. The grid is made of fluid particles. It starts as a square at t = 0, and the flow deforms it as time passes. Each panel shows where the grid is at time t, which is \phi_t(x) for each point x of the initial grid. The arrows are the fluid velocity v_t(x) at the points x of a fixed lattice, the same in each panel.








Figure 3: The flow \phi_t(x) at t = 0 (left), t = 0.5 (middle) and t = 1 (right) for the velocity field v_t(x) of a Lamb-Oseen vortex. The grid shows where fluid particles that start on a square grid are at time t, and the arrows are the fluid velocity v_t(x). The grid winds into a spiral.





Particles near the core turn faster than those farther out, so the straight grid lines wind into a spiral that is tightest at the core.
In Figure 4 below, we follow fluid particles, drawn as dots, through the same vortex for t \in [0, 1]. Each dot carries an arrow along the fluid velocity v_t(x) at its position x, which is tangent to the circle the particle travels on and proportional in length to its speed.







Figure 4: Fluid particles, drawn as dots, carried by the Lamb-Oseen vortex of Figure 3 for t \in [0, 1], after which the animation restarts. Each arrow is the fluid velocity v_t(x) at its dot x, tangent to the dot’s circle about the origin and proportional in length to the speed. Dots that start inside the core (dashed circle) have their own colour.




Each dot moves along its arrow, and the arrow stays tangent to the dot’s circle about the origin as the dot circles it. Near the center the angular speed is almost constant, \omega(r) \approx \kappa / r_c^2, so the dots there turn together like points of a rigid disk and keep their arrangement. Farther out the angular speed falls off with distance, so the inner dots pull ahead of the outer ones and the initial lattice winds into a spiral. The speed \omega(r)\, r peaks at r \approx 1.12\, r_c, just outside the core, where the arrows are longest, and decays like \kappa / r beyond it.


3.1.2 Flow maps between two times
The flow \phi_t(x) starts each trajectory at t = 0, but the Picard-Lindelöf theorem gives a trajectory through each point at each time. Under its conditions, for each s \in [0, 1] and x \in \mathbb{R}^d, exactly one solution of \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_t(X_t) has X_s = x, and it exists on all of [0, 1], solved forward and backward from s (§A.2). Its value at a time t defines the flow map from s to t,

\phi_{s \to t}: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad x \mapsto X_t

the position at time t of the trajectory that occupies x at time s, for each s, t \in [0, 1]. The flow is the case s = 0, \phi_t = \phi_{0 \to t}.
Following a trajectory from s to r and then from r to t ends where following it from s to t ends. This is the semigroup property of the flow maps,

\boxed{\phi_{r \to t} \circ \phi_{s \to r} = \phi_{s \to t}, \qquad \phi_{s \to s} = \mathrm{id} \qquad \forall\, s, r, t \in [0, 1]}
\tag{6}






NoteProof: the semigroup property





For s, r, t \in [0, 1] and x \in \mathbb{R}^d, let X be the solution with X_s = x. At time r it occupies X_r = \phi_{s \to r}(x), so X is also a solution whose value at time r is \phi_{s \to r}(x). By uniqueness it is the solution that defines \phi_{r \to t} at that point, so \phi_{r \to t}\big(\phi_{s \to r}(x)\big) = X_t. By the definition of the flow map, X_t = \phi_{s \to t}(x). The second identity holds because \phi_{s \to s}(x) = X_s = x. \square



Setting t = s in Eq. 6 gives \phi_{r \to s} \circ \phi_{s \to r} = \mathrm{id}, and exchanging s and r gives \phi_{s \to r} \circ \phi_{r \to s} = \mathrm{id}, so each flow map is invertible, with the inverse \phi_{r \to s}, and the flow \phi_t has the inverse \phi_{t \to 0}. For a velocity field fixed in time, \phi_{s \to t} depends only on t - s, and Eq. 6 becomes the group property of the transformations that Lie studied [55]. For a velocity field that changes with time it follows from uniqueness alone [56]. Post #10 trains a network to approximate \phi_{s \to t} directly, so that one evaluation of the network replaces a numerical solve.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
3.2 Generation using flow models
This section builds a generative model from the ODE of §3.1 by learning its velocity field [3]. The field is learned so that a point sampled at t = 0 from a simple initial distribution, independent of the data distribution, follows the field to a point at t = 1 that is a random sample from the data distribution.
Chen et al. combined two earlier ideas. Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden had estimated densities with a map built as a flow that carries the samples toward a Gaussian [1]. E proposed treating deep networks as dynamical systems [61], and Lu et al. [62], Haber and Ruthotto [63], and Ruthotto and Haber [64] viewed residual networks as Euler steps of an ODE.

3.2.1 Definitions
The generative model built here has no forward process to reverse, so its time axis runs in the generative direction, from noise at t = 0 to data at t = 1, whereas the rest of the series has t = 0 as data. The model uses these objects, besides the trajectory X, velocity field v_t(x) and flow \phi_t(x) of §3.1.

Initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}}: A simple distribution on \mathbb{R}^d, such as \mathcal{N}(0, I), from which the initial condition is sampled, with density p_{\mathrm{init}}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty).
Data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}}: The distribution on \mathbb{R}^d that generated samples should follow, with density p_{\mathrm{data}}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty).
Probability path p_t: A probability distribution on \mathbb{R}^d for each time t \in [0, 1], with a density for each t \in [0, 1); the distribution at t = 1 may be concentrated at one point and then has no density. At a fixed x \in \mathbb{R}^d, the path gives how the density at x changes over time, 
p: [0, 1) \times \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), \qquad (t, x) \mapsto p_t(x)

Parameters \theta: The weights of a neural network.
Network velocity field v_\theta(x, t): The velocity field the network represents, 
v_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad (x, t) \mapsto v_\theta(x, t)

Flow \phi^\theta_t(x): The flow of v_\theta(x, t), \phi^\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto \phi^\theta_t(x), with \phi^\theta_t(x_0) the position at time t of the trajectory of v_\theta(x, t) with the initial condition X_0 = x_0.



3.2.2 Flow model
Generated samples must be random, but the solution of an ODE is deterministic for a given initial condition. The randomness therefore enters through the initial condition, sampled from p_{\mathrm{init}}. A flow model is the ODE Eq. 4 with this random initial condition X_0 and the network velocity field v_\theta(x, t),

\boxed{X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_\theta(X_t, t)}
\tag{7}
The model is trained to make its solution at t = 1 follow the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}},

X_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \phi^\theta_1(X_0) \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}

so that solving the ODE from the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} produces a sample of p_{\mathrm{data}}. The distribution p^\theta_t of X_t, a probability path p^\theta: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), (t, x) \mapsto p^\theta_t(x), starts at p^\theta_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}}, so the learned field v_\theta(x, t) transports the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} along a path of intermediate marginals p^\theta_t, ending at p_{\mathrm{data}}.
Since X_t = \phi^\theta_t(X_0), the distribution p^\theta_t is the pushforward (§2.1) of p_{\mathrm{init}} under the flow, the distribution of \phi^\theta_t(x) for x \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, written p^\theta_t = (\phi^\theta_t)_\# p_{\mathrm{init}}. For a velocity field that is continuously differentiable in x and Lipschitz as in the Picard-Lindelöf theorem above, the flow is invertible, with the inverse \phi^\theta_{t \to 0}, where \phi^\theta_{s \to t} denotes the flow maps of v_\theta (§3.1.2). The flow and its inverse are also differentiable in x, because the solution of an ODE with a continuously differentiable velocity field depends differentiably on its initial condition [35], [56]. So Eq. 1 gives the density of the pushforward,

p^\theta_t(x) = p_{\mathrm{init}}\big((\phi^\theta_t)^{-1}(x)\big)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial (\phi^\theta_t)^{-1}}{\partial x}(x) \Big\rvert

Chen et al. call this model a continuous normalizing flow [3], and Lipman et al. state flow matching in these terms [7].
The network computes the velocity field v_\theta(x, t) and never the flow \phi^\theta_t(x) that names the model, so producing a sample requires solving the ODE numerically (§3.3).

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
3.3 Sampling with the Euler method
A flow model generates a sample by solving Eq. 7 from the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} and returning X_1. The ODE is solved numerically, and the simplest scheme is the Euler method [15], which replaces the derivative in Eq. 7 by a forward difference over a step \Delta t. On the grid t_i = i\, \Delta t with \Delta t = 1/n, and with x_i the approximation of X_{t_i}, sampling runs as follows.
Algorithm 7 — Sampling from a flow model with the Euler method [15]:
1: x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}
2: for i = 0, \ldots, n - 1 do
    3: x_{i+1} = x_i + v_\theta(x_i, t_i)\, \Delta t
4: end for
5: return x_n
Each step moves the sample along the network velocity field v_\theta(x, t) for a time \Delta t, and the returned x_n approximates X_1 = \phi^\theta_1(x_0), a sample of the model’s distribution p^\theta_1.
The Euler method is a first-order method. Its error over one step, the local error, is of order \Delta t^2 when the solution is twice continuously differentiable, and the n = 1/\Delta t steps accumulate an error of order \Delta t at t = 1, the global error, when v_\theta(x, t) is also Lipschitz in x. §A.3 proves both orders and surveys methods of higher order, which evaluate the velocity field more than once per step or reuse earlier evaluations.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
section: 3.4 Exact likelihood via the instantaneous change of variables
text:
3.4 Exact likelihood via the instantaneous change of variables
A flow model also gives the exact likelihood of each point, which the stochastic samplers of the reverse-time SDE cannot. The likelihood comes from the instantaneous change of variables, the continuous-time form of the change of variables Eq. 1. Along each trajectory of a velocity field v_t(x), the log-density of the pushforward p_t = (\phi_t)_\# p_0 changes at the rate -\nabla_x \cdot v_t. This rate follows from Euler’s equation for the density of a moving fluid [4], and Chen et al. named the result and used it to compute likelihoods [3]. The derivation below applies Eq. 1 to the flow \phi_t and differentiates the result in time.
We assume that v_t(x) is continuously differentiable in x and Lipschitz, as in §3.2.2, and that p_0 > 0. Applying Eq. 1 with f = \phi_t, p = p_0 and y = \phi_t(x), so that f^{-1}(y) = x,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = p_0(x)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial \phi_t^{-1}}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big) \Big\rvert

By the inverse function theorem, the Jacobian of \phi_t^{-1} at \phi_t(x) is the inverse of the Jacobian J_t(x) = \frac{\partial \phi_t}{\partial x}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} of \phi_t at x,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = p_0(x)\, \big\lvert \det J_t(x)^{-1} \big\rvert

Since the determinant of an inverse matrix is the reciprocal of its determinant,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = p_0(x)\, \big\lvert \det J_t(x) \big\rvert^{-1}

The determinant \det J_t(x) equals \det I = 1 at t = 0, depends continuously on t and never vanishes, because J_t(x) has an inverse, the Jacobian of \phi_t^{-1} at \phi_t(x), so it stays positive. Dropping the absolute value,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{p_0(x)}{\det J_t(x)}

Taking logarithms,

\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \log p_0(x) - \log \det J_t(x)

Differentiating in t, where p_0(x) does not depend on t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\frac{d}{dt}\, \log \det J_t(x)

By Jacobi’s formula for the derivative of a determinant [36], \frac{d}{dt} \log \det J = \operatorname{tr}\big(J^{-1}\, \frac{d}{dt} J\big),

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(J_t(x)^{-1}\, \frac{d}{dt} J_t(x)\Big)

Differentiating the flow ODE Eq. 5 with respect to x, by the chain rule, shows that the Jacobian evolves as \frac{d}{dt} J_t(x) = \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\, J_t(x). Substituting it,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(J_t(x)^{-1}\, \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\, J_t(x)\Big)

By the cyclic property of the trace, \operatorname{tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{tr}(BCA),

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(\frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\, J_t(x)\, J_t(x)^{-1}\Big)

Since J_t(x)\, J_t(x)^{-1} = I,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(\frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\Big)

Since the trace of the Jacobian of v_t is its divergence, \operatorname{tr}\big(\frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \frac{\partial v_t^{j}}{\partial x^{j}} = \nabla_x \cdot v_t, with x^j and v_t^j the j-th coordinates of x and v_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -(\nabla_x \cdot v_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Integrating both sides from 0 to t, with s as the integration variable,

\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) - \log p_0\big(\phi_0(x)\big) = -\int_0^t (\nabla_x \cdot v_s)\big(\phi_s(x)\big)\, ds

Since \phi_0(x) = x by Eq. 5,

\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) - \log p_0(x) = -\int_0^t (\nabla_x \cdot v_s)\big(\phi_s(x)\big)\, ds

Adding \log p_0(x) to both sides,

\boxed{\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \log p_0(x) - \int_0^t (\nabla_x \cdot v_s)\big(\phi_s(x)\big)\, ds}
\tag{8}
\square

3.4.1 Exact likelihood of a flow model
For the flow model, p_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}} and the velocity field is v_\theta, so Eq. 8 at t = 1 gives the exact log-likelihood of each point x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d [3]. Applying it with x = x_0, where x_0 = (\phi^\theta_1)^{-1}(x_1) is the point that \phi^\theta_1 maps to x_1,

\log p^\theta_1(x_1) = \log p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0) - \int_0^1 (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)\big(\phi^\theta_s(x_0),\, s\big)\, ds

Solving the flow ODE of v_\theta backward, from x_1 at t = 1 to t = 0, gives x_0, and the same solve accumulates the integral of the divergence along the trajectory.
Compared with Eq. 2, the continuous form differs in two respects [3].

A trace instead of a determinant: The sum of log-determinants becomes the integral of a divergence, the trace of the Jacobian \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}. The trace needs only the d diagonal entries of that Jacobian, while a determinant costs O(d^3), so the velocity field needs no triangular Jacobian of the kind coupling layers build. The exact trace still costs d backward passes of reverse-mode automatic differentiation, one for each diagonal entry (P2:§3.3.3.4), a cost that §3.6 reduces.
No invertible building blocks: The flow needs no invertible maps as building blocks, since any velocity field that meets the Picard-Lindelöf conditions gives an invertible flow (§3.2.2).

The first difference appears in the discrete formula itself when its layers are small residual layers. One step of Algorithm 7, x \mapsto x + \Delta t\, v_\theta(x, t_i), is a residual layer (§2.2.3) with g = \Delta t\, v_\theta(\cdot, t_i), a contraction with the constant K\, \Delta t once K\, \Delta t < 1, where K is the Lipschitz constant of v_\theta, so that \lVert J_g \rVert \le K\, \Delta t as in §2.2.3. In Eq. 3 the Jacobian is

J_g = \Delta t\, \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(x, t_i)

so its k-th term is of order \Delta t^k. Separating the first term, \operatorname{tr}(J_g) = \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x, t_i), from the others,

\log \det\Big(I + \Delta t\, \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(x, t_i)\Big) = \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x, t_i) + \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\, \operatorname{tr}\big(J_g^k\big)

Bounding the remaining terms by the geometric series d\, K^2 \Delta t^2 / (1 - K\, \Delta t), since \operatorname{tr}(J_g^k) is the sum of the d values \lambda_j^k of §2.2.3, each of modulus at most \lVert J_g \rVert^k \le (K\, \Delta t)^k,

\log \det\Big(I + \Delta t\, \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(x, t_i)\Big) = \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x, t_i) + O(\Delta t^2)

This bound is the same at each x and t_i, so the constant in O(\Delta t^2) is the same for each layer. The sum of the log-determinants of n = 1/\Delta t such layers in Eq. 2 is then the Riemann sum \sum_i \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x_i, t_i) of the divergence at the layers’ inputs, up to n \cdot O(\Delta t^2) = O(\Delta t). The exact log-likelihood above has, in place of this sum, the integral of the divergence along the trajectory \phi^\theta_s(x_0), where the sum evaluates the divergence at the Euler iterates x_i.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
section: 3.5 Maximum-likelihood training and the adjoint method
text:
3.5 Maximum-likelihood training and the adjoint method
Since Eq. 8 gives the exact log-likelihood \log p^\theta_1(x_1) of each point, Chen et al. train a flow model by maximum likelihood [3]. The parameters \theta maximize the average log-likelihood of the data,

\max_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\big[\log p^\theta_1(x_1)\big]

Each training step therefore evaluates \log p^\theta_1(x_1) for each x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} in a minibatch, by the backward solve of §3.4. Writing L_t = -\int_t^1 \nabla_x \cdot v_\theta(X_s, s)\, ds \in \mathbb{R} for the integral accumulated from t = 1 back to t, the trajectory and the integral solve one joint ODE [3], [5],

\frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_\theta(X_t, t), \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, L_t = \nabla_x \cdot v_\theta(X_t, t), \qquad X_1 = x_1,\ L_1 = 0

Solving it from t = 1 back to t = 0 gives x_0 = X_0 and L_0, so \log p^\theta_1(x_1) = \log p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0) + L_0 by Eq. 8 at t = 1 for the flow model.
Backpropagating through the solver would store each of its internal steps, so the memory of a training step would grow with their number. The adjoint method computes the gradient with constant memory instead, by solving a second ODE from the end of the first solve back to its start. It comes from the optimal control of Pontryagin et al. [65], and Chen et al. brought it to neural ODEs, ODEs whose right-hand side is a neural network [3].
The method applies to any ODE

\frac{d}{dt}\, Z_t = f(Z_t, t, \theta)

with a state Z_t \in \mathbb{R}^m, parameters \theta \in \mathbb{R}^P and a right-hand side f: \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^P \to \mathbb{R}^m, (z, t, \theta) \mapsto f(z, t, \theta), solved from t_0 to t_1. The joint ODE above is one, with Z_t = (X_t, L_t), m = d + 1, t_0 = 1 and t_1 = 0. For a loss \mathcal{L} that depends on the final state Z_{t_1}, the adjoint is the row vector

a(t) = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial Z_t} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times m}

It is the sensitivity of the loss to the state at time t. Since \mathcal{L} depends on Z_t only through Z_{t+\varepsilon}, for a short step \varepsilon toward t_1, by the chain rule,

a(t) = a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial Z_{t+\varepsilon}}{\partial Z_t}

Expanding the solution to first order in \varepsilon,

Z_{t+\varepsilon} = Z_t + \varepsilon f(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)

Differentiating it in Z_t gives the Jacobian of the step,

\frac{\partial Z_{t+\varepsilon}}{\partial Z_t} = I + \varepsilon\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)

Substituting it,

a(t) = a(t + \varepsilon)\, \Big[I + \varepsilon\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)\Big]

Expanding the product,

a(t) = a(t + \varepsilon) + \varepsilon\, a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)

Moving a(t + \varepsilon) to the left-hand side,

a(t) - a(t + \varepsilon) = \varepsilon\, a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)

Dividing by -\varepsilon,

\frac{a(t + \varepsilon) - a(t)}{\varepsilon} = -\,a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon)

Letting \varepsilon \to 0,

\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\, a(t) = -\,a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta)}
\tag{9}
\square
The gradient with respect to \theta follows from the same argument, with \theta as a second state that does not change in time, \frac{d}{dt}\, \theta_t = 0 [3]. Its adjoint is the row vector

a_\theta(t) = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_t} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times P}

It is the sensitivity of the loss to the value of \theta used from time t on. The augmented state (Z_t, \theta_t) has the right-hand side (f, 0), whose Jacobian is

\begin{pmatrix} \partial f / \partial z & \partial f / \partial \theta \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

So the \theta-component of Eq. 9 for the augmented state is

\frac{d}{dt}\, a_\theta(t) = -\,a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}(Z_t, t, \theta)

Integrating from t_1 to t_0,

a_\theta(t_0) - a_\theta(t_1) = -\int_{t_1}^{t_0} a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}(Z_t, t, \theta)\, dt

The adjoint a_\theta starts at a_\theta(t_1) = 0, because no time is left after t_1 for \theta to act. It ends at a_\theta(t_0) = d\mathcal{L}/d\theta, because the value of \theta used from t_0 on is \theta itself. Substituting both values,

\boxed{\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\theta} = -\int_{t_1}^{t_0} a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}(Z_t, t, \theta)\, dt}

\square

3.5.1 The adjoint solve and its cost
The state Z_t, recomputed from its final value, and the adjoints a(t) and a_\theta(t) solve one joint ODE from t_1 back to t_0. It starts from Z_{t_1}, a(t_1) = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial Z_{t_1} and a_\theta(t_1) = 0 (Chen et al.’s Algorithm 1) [3]. The right-hand sides of the adjoint ODEs are vector-Jacobian products, a row vector times a Jacobian. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation computes each at about the cost of one evaluation of f.
This solve recomputes the state instead of storing the steps of the first solve, so the memory does not grow with the number of steps. The time does grow, since it is proportional to the number of function evaluations (NFE), the evaluations of f that a solve needs. Chen et al. use adaptive solvers, which choose their step sizes to meet an error tolerance, and in their experiments this number grew as training proceeded (their Figure 3d, for a classifier of MNIST, a dataset of 28 \times 28 images of handwritten digits).

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
3.6 Free-form flows: FFJORD
Grathwohl et al.’s Free-form Jacobian of Reversible Dynamics (FFJORD) replaces the exact divergence in Eq. 8 with a stochastic estimate [5]. Chen et al. had kept the cost of the exact divergence low by restricting the velocity field. They built it from sums of simple terms, each with a trace in closed form, and the trace of the sum is the sum of these traces [3].
The divergence is the trace of the d \times d Jacobian \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}, and computing it exactly costs the d backward passes of §3.4. The trace is also an expectation over a random probe \eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). For a constant matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, writing the scalar \eta^\top A\, \eta as its own trace and using the cyclic property of the trace,

\mathbb{E}\big[\eta^\top A\, \eta\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{tr}(A\, \eta \eta^\top)\big]

Exchanging the trace and the expectation, both linear, with A constant,

\mathbb{E}\big[\eta^\top A\, \eta\big] = \operatorname{tr}\big(A\, \mathbb{E}[\eta \eta^\top]\big)

Since \mathbb{E}[\eta \eta^\top] = I,

\mathbb{E}\big[\eta^\top A\, \eta\big] = \operatorname{tr}(A)

Applying it with A = \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}(x), whose trace is \nabla_x \cdot v_t(x),

\nabla_x \cdot v_t(x) = \mathbb{E}_{\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\Big[\eta^\top\, \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}(x)\, \eta\Big]

The Hutchinson trace estimator [37], [38] replaces this expectation with its value at one sample of \eta. Each such value costs one backward pass, which computes the vector-Jacobian product \eta^\top \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}, and then a dot product with \eta. Grathwohl et al. brought the estimator to flow models [5], Behrmann et al. used it for the traces in Eq. 3, and it is the same single-probe technique that makes Song et al.’s sliced score matching inexpensive [66].
Holding one probe \eta fixed for each solve keeps the ODE deterministic, as an adaptive solver requires. The estimate of \log p^\theta_1(x_1) stays unbiased, since the expectation over \eta can be taken outside the time integral [5]. The cost of the divergence falls from d backward passes to one, which Grathwohl et al. state as O(d^2) against O(d) time, so the velocity field v_\theta can be any network.
FFJORD reached 0.99 bits per dimension on MNIST, ahead of Glow’s 1.05 with less than 2% of Glow’s parameters, and 3.40 on CIFAR-10, against Glow’s 3.35 [5]. Its image models took about five days to train on six graphics processing units (GPUs).
Grathwohl et al. name two limitations. The NFE “tends to grow as the models trains and can become prohibitively large”, and general-purpose solvers restrict the flow to non-stiff dynamics. A stiff ODE has components that change on time scales differing by orders of magnitude, and an explicit solver stays stable on it only with steps on the shortest of those scales.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
3.7 Regularized flows: RNODE
Finlay et al. attributed the growing NFE to the learned velocity field itself [6]. The velocity field that maximizes the likelihood is not unique, because maximum likelihood constrains only the distribution at t = 1. Training can converge to a field whose trajectories turn sharply and change speed, which an adaptive solver follows only in small steps. Training FFJORD on CIFAR-10, they found the NFE strongly correlated with the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian of v_\theta, the square root of the sum of its squared entries.
Their method, the regularized neural ODE (RNODE), adds two penalties to FFJORD’s negative log-likelihood [6]. The first is the kinetic energy, the integral of the squared speed \lVert v_\theta \rVert^2 along a trajectory. The second is the integral of the squared Frobenius norm of the Jacobian \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x} along it. With X_t the trajectory of v_\theta that ends at X_1 = x_1, and weights \lambda_K, \lambda_J > 0, the objective is

\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\Big[-\log p^\theta_1(x_1) + \lambda_K \int_0^1 \big\lVert v_\theta(X_s, s) \big\rVert^2\, ds + \lambda_J \int_0^1 \Big\lVert \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(X_s, s) \Big\rVert_F^2\, ds\Big]

The kinetic term favours trajectories that run in straight lines at constant speed. Among the velocity fields that carry one distribution to another, those of least kinetic energy have such trajectories, by the dynamic formulation of optimal transport that Benamou and Brenier introduced and post #5 develops [46]. The kinetic term straightens only the trajectories that the training data follow, however, which is one reason Finlay et al. add the Jacobian term.
The Jacobian term needs no extra backward pass. Its integrand is an expectation over the same probe \eta as the divergence estimate, since

\lVert A \rVert_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A A^\top) = \mathbb{E}_{\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\lVert \eta^\top A \rVert^2

The vector-Jacobian product \eta^\top \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x} it needs is the one that estimate already computes.
With \lambda_K = \lambda_J = 0.01, RNODE trained about 2.8 times faster than FFJORD on MNIST and on CIFAR-10, at comparable bits per dimension [6]. On CIFAR-10 it reached 3.38, against 3.36 for Finlay et al.’s own FFJORD run and 3.40 as Grathwohl et al. reported. It also trained on ImageNet, a dataset of about 1.3 million natural images, downsampled to 64 \times 64 pixels, reaching 3.83, where their FFJORD run failed to train.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
3.8 Pitfalls
Maximum-likelihood training of flow models works, but it has two pitfalls, and flow matching, the subject of Parts 4 to 6, removes both.

3.8.1 Training solves the ODE
Each training step of §3.5 solves the ODE backward, from t = 1 to t = 0, for each x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} in the minibatch, and then solves the adjoint ODE from t = 0 back to t = 1. Both solves use an adaptive solver, whose NFE grows as training proceeds (§3.6). A training step therefore costs at least two solves of the ODE for each point of the minibatch, where generating a sample costs one. This cost is why FFJORD’s image models took days to train, and a stiff flow, which forces small steps, would raise it further.


3.8.2 The path is not specified
Maximum likelihood leaves the probability path from p_{\mathrm{init}} to p^\theta_1 to the optimizer, since the likelihood depends only on the distribution p^\theta_1 at t = 1 (§3.7). Many probability paths connect the same two distributions. Along each of them the velocity field is not unique either, since a field that moves mass without changing the intermediate distributions can be added, which Part 4 makes precise. The optimizer’s choice among them can be irregular.
Liu et al. call the maximum-likelihood problem for neural ODEs under-specified for this reason, as it leaves the paths “for the algorithm to figure out implicitly” [8]. RNODE’s penalties favour straighter paths but still leave the choice to the optimizer, whereas flow matching fixes the path before training.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
4.1 Conditional and marginal probability paths
A conditional probability path [7] is, for each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d, a probability density at each time t \in [0, 1),

p_t(\cdot \mid x_1): \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), \qquad x \mapsto p_t(x \mid x_1), \qquad t \in [0, 1)

that starts at the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} and ends, at t = 1, concentrated at x_1,

\boxed{p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = p_{\mathrm{init}}, \qquad p_1(\cdot \mid x_1) = \delta(\cdot - x_1)}
\tag{10}
The Dirac delta \delta(\cdot - a) [67] at a point a \in \mathbb{R}^d is the distribution that puts all its probability on a, so that each sample of it is a. It is written as a density that is zero away from a and integrates to 1, although it has no density in the ordinary sense, and it acts on a continuous function f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} by the sifting property \int \delta(x - y)\, f(y)\, dy = f(x).
The marginal probability path p_t is the distribution of a point sampled from the conditional path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) with x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}},

\boxed{x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, \quad x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x \sim p_t}
\tag{11}
so its density is the mixture

\boxed{p_t(x) = \int p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1}
\tag{12}
The integral over the data makes this density intractable, but Eq. 11 samples from p_t without it.
The marginal path p_t runs from the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} to the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}},

\boxed{p_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}}, \qquad p_1 = p_{\mathrm{data}}}
\tag{13}






NoteProof: the endpoints of the marginal path





Setting t = 0 in Eq. 12,

p_0(x) = \int p_0(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Substituting the boundary condition p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = p_{\mathrm{init}} of Eq. 10,

p_0(x) = \int p_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Taking p_{\mathrm{init}}(x), which does not depend on x_1, out of the integral,

p_0(x) = p_{\mathrm{init}}(x) \int p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Since p_{\mathrm{data}} integrates to 1,

p_0(x) = p_{\mathrm{init}}(x)

Setting t = 1 in Eq. 12,

p_1(x) = \int p_1(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Substituting the boundary condition p_1(\cdot \mid x_1) = \delta(\cdot - x_1) of Eq. 10,

p_1(x) = \int \delta(x - x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

By the sifting property of the Dirac delta,

p_1(x) = p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)

Together with the value at t = 0, this is Eq. 13. \square




4.1.1 Gaussian conditional path to a spiral
A two-dimensional example after Holderrieth and Erives [10] shows the two paths, with a Gaussian p_{\mathrm{init}} and a p_{\mathrm{data}} shaped into a spiral by a Lamb-Oseen vortex.
Initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}}: The standard Gaussian \mathcal{N}(0, I) on \mathbb{R}^2.
Data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}}: A spiral built from a disk using a Lamb-Oseen vortex, as Figure 5 and Figure 6 show below. The disk has radius \rho = 1.2 and center c = (1.5, 0) (left panel of Figure 5). Each of its points is carried by the flow \phi_1 of the Lamb-Oseen vortex of §3.1.1, with \kappa = 40.5 and r_c = 1.2, which turns a point at distance r from the origin by the angle \omega(r).








Figure 5: The support of p_{\mathrm{data}} as a disk turned into a spiral. Left: The disk of radius \rho = 1.2 centered at c = (1.5, 0); the dashed lines mark c and the disk’s edges 1.5 \pm \rho, and the curved arrow shows the counterclockwise rotation by \omega(r). Right: Its image under the rotation (r, \vartheta) \mapsto (r, \vartheta + \omega(r)) in polar coordinates, with \kappa = 40.5 and r_c = 1.2, on which p_{\mathrm{data}} is uniform; the dashed circle is the vortex core of radius r_c.





The angle \omega(r) is largest near the origin and falls off with distance, so the side of the disk nearest the origin winds into the inner turns of the spiral and the far side forms its outer end (right panel).
Figure 6 below animates the construction, turning each point of the disk by the fraction s of its angle \omega(r) as s runs from 0 to 1.







Figure 6: The construction of p_{\mathrm{data}}: each point of the disk of Figure 5 (left) is turned about the origin by the angle s\, \omega(r), for s from 0 to 1, ending at the spiral (right), after which the animation restarts. The dashed circle is the vortex core of radius r_c.




The resulting p_{\mathrm{data}} is uniform on the spiral. With D the disk of radius \rho centered at c, and p_{\mathrm{data}}(r, \vartheta) its density at the point with polar coordinates (r, \vartheta),

p_{\mathrm{data}}(r, \vartheta) = \begin{cases} 1 / (\pi \rho^2), & (r,\ \vartheta - \omega(r)) \in D \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

The spiral is the set of points that turning back by \omega(r), (r, \vartheta) \mapsto (r, \vartheta - \omega(r)), sends into D. That turn preserves the area element r\, dr\, d\vartheta, so the spiral has the area \pi \rho^2 of D and p_{\mathrm{data}} integrates to 1.
Conditional path: The example uses a conditional probability path of Lipman et al. that is Gaussian at each time [7],

p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}\big(t\, x_1,\ (1 - t)^2 I\big)

At t = 0 it is \mathcal{N}(0, I) = p_{\mathrm{init}}. At t = 1 its variance is zero, and a Gaussian with zero variance is the Dirac delta \delta(\cdot - x_1), so both boundary conditions of Eq. 10 hold. A sample of it is t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, \epsilon with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). The path contracts the Gaussian onto x_1, as its mean t\, x_1 runs along the segment from the origin to x_1 and its standard deviation 1 - t falls from one to zero. The left animation of Figure 7 below shows this path for one fixed x_1, marked by the star, and the right animation the marginal path p_t.







Figure 7: The conditional probability path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}(t\, x_1, (1 - t)^2 I) for one fixed x_1 on the spiral, marked by the star (left), and the marginal path p_t for a data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}} uniform on a spiral (right), for t \in [0, 1], after which the animations restart. The faint outline marks the support of p_{\mathrm{data}}, and each frame shows the density scaled to its own maximum. After Holderrieth and Erives [10], whose example uses a checkerboard for p_{\mathrm{data}}.




Marginal path: By Eq. 11, sampling x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} and then t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, \epsilon gives a sample of the marginal path p_t, so p_t is the distribution of t\, x_1, the spiral contracted toward the origin by the factor t, convolved with \mathcal{N}(0, (1 - t)^2 I). The right animation shows it. At t = 0 it starts at the same Gaussian as the conditional path does, but at t = 1, instead of at a single point x_1, it ends at p_{\mathrm{data}}, the spiral.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
4.2 Conditional and marginal velocity fields
A probability path prescribes the distribution that the solution X_t of an ODE should have at each time. This section defines the velocity fields of such ODEs, first for the conditional probability path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) of each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d (§4.2.1) and then, by averaging these fields over x_1, for the marginal probability path p_t (§4.2.2). §4.5 proves that the solution of the averaged field’s ODE has p_t as its distribution at each time. Lipman et al. [7] and Holderrieth and Erives [10] call the two fields defined below the conditional and marginal vector fields.

4.2.1 Conditional velocity field
For each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d, a conditional velocity field u(\cdot \mid x_1): \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto u_t(x \mid x_1), is a velocity field whose ODE solution, with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} and with X_1 = \lim_{t \to 1} X_t, has the conditional probability path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) of §4.1 as its distribution at each time t,

\boxed{X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = u_t(X_t \mid x_1) \ \ (t < 1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_t \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) \quad \forall t \in [0, 1]}
\tag{14}
By Eq. 14 and the endpoint \delta(\cdot - x_1) of Eq. 10, the ODE solution of the conditional velocity field u_t(\cdot \mid x_1) ends at X_1 = x_1. In isolation, the conditional velocity field is of little use, as it carries a distribution to a single point, but taking a weighted average of these conditional fields over x_1 gives a marginal velocity field that carries p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}}.


4.2.2 Marginal velocity field
Averaging the conditional velocity fields over x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, weighted by how likely each x_1 is to have produced the point x, gives the marginal velocity field u: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto u_t(x),

\boxed{u_t(x) = \int u_t(x \mid x_1)\, \frac{p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}{p_t(x)}\, dx_1 \qquad p_t(x) > 0}
\tag{15}
By Bayes’ rule [68], the weight in Eq. 15 is the posterior p_t(\cdot \mid x): \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), x_1 \mapsto p_t(x_1 \mid x),

\frac{p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}{p_t(x)} = p_t(x_1 \mid x)

Substituting it into Eq. 15,

u_t(x) = \int u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x_1 \mid x)\, dx_1

The integral is the expectation over the posterior,

\boxed{u_t(x) = \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\big[\, u_t(x \mid x_1) \,\big]}
\tag{16}
\square

4.2.2.1 The marginal velocity as a posterior average
For the spiral example of §4.1.1, the conditional path \mathcal{N}\big(t\, x_1, (1 - t)^2 I\big) is the distribution of X_t = t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, X_0 with X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}. This X_t satisfies

\frac{d}{dt} X_t = x_1 - X_0 = \frac{x_1 - X_t}{1 - t}

so

u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{x_1 - x}{1 - t}

is a conditional velocity field of the path, since the ODE has a unique solution (§3.1).
By Eq. 16, the marginal velocity field at a point x is the average of these fields under the posterior

p_t(x_1 \mid x) \propto \mathcal{N}\big(x;\ t\, x_1, (1 - t)^2 I\big)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)

As a function of x_1, the Gaussian factor is proportional to

\mathcal{N}\big(x_1;\ x / t,\ ((1 - t)/t)^2 I\big)

so the posterior is p_{\mathrm{data}} reweighted by a Gaussian centered at x / t with standard deviation (1 - t)/t. The average at one point x and two times is drawn as arrows, as Figure 8 shows below.








Figure 8: The marginal velocity field u_t as a posterior average for the spiral example, at the point x = (1, -0.8) (black dot) at t = 0.25 (left) and t = 0.8 (right). The thin arrows, each shaded by its posterior weight p_t(x_1 \mid x), are the conditional velocities u_t(x \mid x_1) toward 200 of 4000 points x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, over the support of p_{\mathrm{data}} in grey. The thick arrow is the posterior average of the conditional velocities toward all 4000 points, an estimate of the marginal velocity u_t(x). All arrows are scaled by 1 - t, so each thin arrow ends at its x_1 and the thick arrow at the posterior mean of x_1. After Lipman et al.’s guide (their Figure 3) [11] and Lai et al. (their Figure 5.7) [69].





At t = 0.25 the standard deviation is 3, wider than the spiral, so the posterior spreads over the whole spiral and the conditional velocities point in all directions. They largely cancel in the average, and the thick arrow ends at the posterior mean (0.72, -0.27), between the arms, where p_{\mathrm{data}} has no mass.
At t = 0.8 the standard deviation is 0.25, so the posterior concentrates on the part of the arm just outside x near x / t = (1.25, -1), and the average follows the few arrows that carry its weight. As (1 - t)/t falls from infinity to zero, u_t at each point averages over the whole spiral early and over the nearby data late.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
4.3 The continuity equation
The continuity equation, first written by Euler for the density of a fluid [4], is a partial differential equation that relates a probability path p_t to a velocity field v_t(x),

\boxed{\partial_t p_t(x) + \nabla_x \cdot \big( p_t(x)\, v_t(x) \big) = 0}
\tag{17}
The product p_t(x)\, v_t(x) is the probability flux, the probability mass that crosses a unit area per unit time. In a time \Delta t, the probability that crosses a unit area perpendicular to v_t(x) is the mass of the particles within the length \lVert v_t(x) \rVert\, \Delta t behind it, p_t(x)\, \lVert v_t(x) \rVert\, \Delta t, so per unit time the flux is p_t(x)\, \lVert v_t(x) \rVert, along v_t(x). Figure 9 below shows this flux (left) and its net outflow from a small box (right).








Figure 9: The probability flux and its divergence. Left: The particles that cross a unit area (shaded) in a time \Delta t are those in the cylinder of length \lVert v_t(x) \rVert\, \Delta t behind it. Right: The net outflow from a small box of width h, per unit volume.





Here \nabla_x \cdot is the divergence, defined in §3.4. The divergence of the flux is its net outflow per unit volume, as the right panel shows. For a box of width h, the flux out through its faces minus the flux in, divided by its volume, tends to \nabla_x \cdot \big(p_t(x)\, v_t(x)\big) as h \to 0. So Eq. 17 states that the density at a point changes only by the net outflow of the flux, which is conservation of probability. §A.4 derives Eq. 17 twice more, from one step of the flow and from the flux through the boundary of a region.
The continuity equation is the deterministic special case of the d-dimensional Fokker-Planck equation, P1:Eq. 45, which for an SDE dx = f(x, t)\,dt + g(t)\,dW, with drift f, diffusion coefficient g and W a Brownian motion, is

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

where \Delta_x = \nabla_x \cdot \nabla_x is the Laplacian. Setting g \equiv 0 and f(x, t) = v_t(x) turns the SDE into the ODE of v_t(x) and the Fokker-Planck equation into Eq. 17.
Along each trajectory, the continuity equation gives the rate of change of the log-density of §3.4 without Jacobi’s formula. Let v_t(x) be continuously differentiable in x and Lipschitz, as in §3.4, let p_t be positive, continuously differentiable in (t, x) and satisfy Eq. 17, and let \phi_t be the flow of v_t (Eq. 5). By the chain rule,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{(\partial_t p_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big) + \frac{d}{dt}\phi_t(x) \cdot (\nabla_x p_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big)}{p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big)}

Substituting \frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x) = v_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) from Eq. 5,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{\partial_t p_t + v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Substituting \partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x \cdot (p_t\, v_t) from Eq. 17,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{-\nabla_x \cdot (p_t\, v_t) + v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Expanding the divergence of the product, \nabla_x \cdot (p_t\, v_t) = v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t + p_t\, \nabla_x \cdot v_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{-v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t - p_t\, \nabla_x \cdot v_t + v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Cancelling the two terms with \nabla_x p_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{-p_t\, \nabla_x \cdot v_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Cancelling the factor p_t, which is positive,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -(\nabla_x \cdot v_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

which is the rate that §3.4 derived from the Jacobian of the flow, and integrating it gives Eq. 8.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
section: 4.4 Distribution of an ODE’s solution ⟺ continuity equation
text:
4.4 Distribution of an ODE’s solution ⟺ continuity equation
This section states and proves the equivalence between the continuity equation Eq. 17 and the distribution of the solution of an ODE, on a time interval (0, T] with T > 0. Its proofs adapt those of the Fokker-Planck equivalence in P3:§2.1 to an equation with no diffusion term.
That equivalence, with zero diffusion, already covers an ODE whose velocity field is infinitely differentiable with bounded derivatives and whose initial condition is at t = 0. The theorem below needs only a continuously differentiable Lipschitz velocity field and allows the initial condition at a time t_0 \in (0, T], with the ODE solved in both directions. Part 5 needs this generality, since generation there solves the probability-flow ODE backward from t_0 = T.
In the theorem, the velocity field and the probability path are defined for t \in (0, T] instead of [0, 1], the interval of §3.1 and §3.2.1.
Definitions:

A velocity field v_t(x) satisfies the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions when it is Lipschitz in x uniformly in t with a constant K, as defined in §3.1 with (0, T] in place of [0, 1], and \lVert v_t(x) \rVert \le K\, (1 + \lVert x \rVert) for each x \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in (0, T].
A function of x decays at infinity when it and its first two derivatives tend to zero as \lVert x \rVert \to \infty fast enough to leave no boundary terms when it is integrated by parts against a bounded function with bounded derivatives. This must hold also after the function is multiplied by one that grows at most linearly in x, such as a velocity field that satisfies the linear-growth condition.
A probability path p_t is dominated when, on each interval [a, b] with 0 < a \le b \le T, the functions (1 + \lVert x \rVert)\, p_t(x) and \lvert \partial_t p_t(x) \rvert, for t \in [a, b], are bounded by one integrable function of x.

Assumptions:

The velocity field v_t(x) is continuously differentiable and satisfies the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions. So exactly one trajectory passes through each point at each time.
The ODE \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_t(X_t) has the initial condition X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} at a time t_0 \in (0, T] and is solved forward and backward in time from there. Its solution is X_t.
The probability path p_t is continuously differentiable in t and twice continuously differentiable in x, decays at infinity for each t and is dominated.

Theorem:
Under these assumptions,

\boxed{\begin{aligned}
&X_t \sim p_t \ \forall t \in (0, T] \\[4pt]
\Longleftrightarrow\quad &\partial_t p_t(x) + \nabla_x \cdot \big( p_t(x)\, v_t(x) \big) = 0 \ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ t \in (0, T]
\end{aligned}}
\tag{18}
The left side of Eq. 18 states that p_t is the distribution of X_t at each time, and the right side is the continuity equation Eq. 17. So the continuity equation is a necessary and sufficient condition for p_t to be the distribution of X_t.

Necessity (\Rightarrow): If the solution X_t of the ODE of v_t(x) has X_t \sim p_t for each t, then p_t and v_t(x) satisfy Eq. 17.
Sufficiency (\Leftarrow): If p_t and v_t(x) satisfy Eq. 17, then the solution X_t of the ODE of v_t(x) with the initial condition X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} has X_t \sim p_t for each t.


4.4.1 Proof of necessity (⇒)
The ODE is the SDE with drift v_t and diffusion coefficient g = 0. The derivation of the Fokker-Planck equation in P1:§8.3 applies Itô’s lemma to a test function, a function \psi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} that is infinitely differentiable and zero outside a bounded set, and integrates by parts. It holds for g = 0, where Itô’s lemma reduces to the chain rule, with the time integrals taken from t_0 instead of 0, which the chain rule allows in either direction of time.
The derivation’s hypotheses hold here, since assumption 3 makes p_t continuously differentiable in t and twice in x, and assumptions 1 and 3 make v_t continuous and v_t\, p_t continuously differentiable in x. So p_t, the distribution of X_t by the left side of Eq. 18, satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation with the drift v_t and with g = 0,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 \cdot \Delta_x p_t

Dropping the zero diffusion term,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big)

Moving the divergence to the left-hand side,

\boxed{\partial_t p_t + \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big) = 0}

which is Eq. 17. \square


4.4.2 Proof of sufficiency (⇐)
The proof is the argument of P3:§2.1.2, which proves the sufficiency part of the Fokker-Planck equivalence, with g = 0 and the initial condition at t_0. It is outlined here and given in full below. The solution of the ODE is deterministic, which changes the first two steps.

The function U(x, t) = \psi(Y_s), the value of a test function \psi at time s along the trajectory Y through x at time t, carries the test function along the trajectories.
U is constant along each trajectory, so by the chain rule it satisfies the transport equation \partial_t U + v_t\cdot\nabla_x U = 0, the backward Kolmogorov equation with g = 0.
When p_t satisfies the continuity equation, \int U\, p_t\, dx is constant in time, as in post #3.
Comparing its values at t = t_0, where X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0}, and at t = s gives \int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}[\psi(X_s)] for each test function, so p_s is the density of X_s.







NoteProof: sufficiency of the continuity equation





Let p_t satisfy the continuity equation, and fix s \in (0, T] and a test function \psi.
Step 1 — a function that carries the test function along the trajectories:
Let \mathcal{T} be the closed interval between s and t_0. For x \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in \mathcal{T}, let Y: \mathcal{T} \to \mathbb{R}^d, r \mapsto Y_r, be the trajectory with Y_t = x. With g = 0, the function of post #3’s proof becomes U: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{T} \to \mathbb{R},

U(x, t) = \psi(Y_s)

the value of \psi at time s along the trajectory through x at time t. At t = s, Y_s = x, so U(x, s) = \psi(x).
Step 3 needs U to be bounded with a bounded gradient. It is bounded because \psi is. Under assumption 1, the trajectory depends continuously differentiably on x and t [35], [56], so U is continuously differentiable, and its gradient is bounded once nearby trajectories separate at a bounded rate.
For two trajectories Y and Y', the rate of change of \chi: \mathcal{T} \to [0, \infty), r \mapsto \lVert Y_r - Y'_r \rVert^2, is

\chi'(r) = 2\,(Y_r - Y'_r) \cdot \big(v_r(Y_r) - v_r(Y'_r)\big)

which is at most 2K\chi(r) in absolute value, where K is the Lipschitz constant of v_t. Grönwall’s inequality [35] states that

\lvert \chi' \rvert \le 2K\chi \;\Longrightarrow\; \chi(s) \le \chi(t)\, e^{2K\lvert s - t \rvert}

Applied to \chi, it shows that the trajectories Y, Y' through two points x, y at time t are at most \lVert x - y \rVert\, e^{K\lvert t - s \rvert} apart at time s.
So, with C the Lipschitz constant of the test function \psi, \lvert U(x, t) - U(y, t) \rvert = \lvert \psi(Y_s) - \psi(Y'_s) \rvert \le C\, \lVert x - y \rVert\, e^{K\lvert t - s \rvert}. The gradient of U is therefore bounded by C\, e^{K\lvert t - s \rvert}.
Step 2 — U satisfies the transport equation:
Let x \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in \mathcal{T} be fixed, with Y the trajectory of Step 1. For each r \in \mathcal{T}, the trajectory through Y_r at time r is Y itself, because exactly one trajectory passes through each point at each time (assumption 1). By the definition of U,

U(Y_r, r) = \psi(Y_s)

Differentiating both sides in r, the left by the chain rule with dY_r/dr = v_r(Y_r) and the right, which does not depend on r, to zero,

\partial_t U(Y_r, r) + v_r(Y_r)\cdot\nabla_x U(Y_r, r) = 0

Setting r = t, where Y_t = x,

\partial_t U(x, t) + v_t(x)\cdot\nabla_x U(x, t) = 0

This holds for each x and each t \in \mathcal{T}. Together with U(x, s) = \psi(x) from Step 1, U satisfies the transport equation, the backward Kolmogorov equation of post #3’s proof with g = 0,

\partial_t U + v_t\cdot\nabla_x U = 0, \qquad U(x, s) = \psi(x)

Step 3 — the integral of U against p_t is constant on \mathcal{T}:
Differentiating \int U\, p_t\, dx in t under the integral, for t in the interior of \mathcal{T}, which the domination of assumption 3 permits because U is bounded and \partial_t U = -v_t\cdot\nabla_x U grows at most linearly in x (Steps 1 and 2, assumption 1),

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \partial_t U\, p_t\, dx + \int U\, \partial_t p_t\, dx

Substituting the continuity equation for \partial_t p_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \partial_t U\, p_t\, dx - \int U\, \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big)\, dx

Integrating the second term by parts, with no boundary term because p_t decays at infinity (assumption 3), v_t grows at most linearly (assumption 1) and U is bounded with a bounded gradient (Step 1),

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \partial_t U\, p_t\, dx + \int v_t\cdot\nabla_x U\; p_t\, dx

Combining the two integrals,

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \big(\partial_t U + v_t\cdot\nabla_x U\big)\, p_t\, dx

Substituting the transport equation of Step 2,

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = 0

This holds for each t in the interior of \mathcal{T}, and \int U\, p_t\, dx is continuous on \mathcal{T} by the same domination, so it is constant on \mathcal{T}.
Step 4 — \int \psi\, p_s\, dx equals \mathbb{E}[\psi(X_s)]:
Using U(x, s) = \psi(x) from Step 1,

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \int U(x, s)\, p_s(x)\, dx

By Step 3, the integral takes the same value at t = t_0,

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \int U(x, t_0)\, p_{t_0}(x)\, dx

Since X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} (assumption 2),

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}\big[U(X_{t_0}, t_0)\big]

Substituting U(X_{t_0}, t_0) = \psi(X_s), since X_s lies on the trajectory through X_{t_0} at time t_0,

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}\big[\psi(X_s)\big]

A density that gives each test function its expected value under X_s is the density of X_s, so X_s \sim p_s. As s \in (0, T] was arbitrary, X_t \sim p_t for each t \in (0, T]. \square

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
4.5 Marginal velocity field ⟹ marginal path
This section applies Eq. 18 to the conditional and the marginal velocity fields.
Assumptions:

On each interval [0, T] with T < 1, each conditional pair \big(p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), u_t(\cdot \mid x_1)\big) and the marginal pair (p_t, u_t) meet assumptions 1 and 3 of §4.4, with the domination of assumption 3 holding on each interval [a, b] with 0 \le a \le b \le T. §4.4 places the initial condition at a time t_0 \in (0, T], and its proofs use only the interval between t_0 and the time considered, so Eq. 18 holds here with the initial condition at t_0 = 0.
For t \in [0, 1), the functions \partial_t p_t(x \mid x_1) and the first x-derivatives of u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1) are bounded, locally uniformly in (x, t), by a p_{\mathrm{data}}-integrable function of x_1.
The conditional path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) converges in distribution to \delta(\cdot - x_1) as t \to 1.
The solution of the ODE of u_t with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} exists on [0, 1].

Assumption 1 lets Eq. 18 apply to the conditional and the marginal pairs, and assumption 2 lets derivatives pass under the integral over x_1. Both stop short of t = 1, where the conditional path is the Dirac delta \delta(\cdot - x_1), which has no derivatives in the ordinary sense, and a conditional velocity field can grow without bound. For the Gaussian path of §4.1.1, the conditional velocity field u_t(x \mid x_1) = (x_1 - x)/(1 - t) of §4.2.2.1 is unbounded near t = 1 at each x \neq x_1. Assumptions 3 and 4 handle t = 1.
Theorem:
Under these assumptions, the ODE solution of the marginal velocity field u_t, with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, has the marginal probability path p_t as its distribution at each time t \in [0, 1],

\boxed{X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = u_t(X_t) \ \ (t < 1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_t \sim p_t \quad \forall t \in [0, 1]}
\tag{19}
In particular X_1 \sim p_1 = p_{\mathrm{data}} by Eq. 13, so u_t carries the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} to the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}}.
The theorem is the flow counterpart of Gyöngy’s mimicking theorem for Itô processes [40], in which a diffusion whose drift and diffusion matrix are the conditional expectations, given the current state, of another Itô process’s drift and diffusion matrix has the same distribution at each time. Brigo stated the mixture form for diffusions [70] and Peluchetti in general [71], and Lipman et al. note that their Theorem 1, the statement above for flows, also follows from Peluchetti’s result [7].
Proof:
For t \in [0, 1), Eq. 14 states that the solution of the ODE of u_t(\cdot \mid x_1) has X_t \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1). So by the necessity part of Eq. 18, which applies by assumption 1, each conditional pair satisfies Eq. 17,

\partial_t p_t(x \mid x_1) = -\nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]

Integrating both sides against p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1),

\int \partial_t p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1 = -\int \nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Taking \partial_t outside the integral on the left, which assumption 2 allows,

\partial_t \int p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1 = -\int \nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Substituting the marginal path Eq. 12,

\partial_t p_t(x) = -\int \nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Taking \nabla_x\cdot outside the integral, which assumption 2 also allows,

\partial_t p_t(x) = -\nabla_x \!\cdot\! \Big[\int u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1\Big]

By Eq. 15, the bracketed integral is u_t(x)\, p_t(x),

\partial_t p_t(x) = -\nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x)\, p_t(x)\big]

So the marginal pair (p_t, u_t) satisfies Eq. 17 on (0, 1), and the marginal path starts at p_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}} by Eq. 13. By the sufficiency part of Eq. 18 on (0, T] for each T < 1, with the initial condition at t_0 = 0, which applies by assumption 1, the solution of the ODE of u_t with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} has X_t \sim p_t for each t \in [0, 1).
As t \to 1, X_t \to X_1 along each trajectory, because the solution exists on [0, 1] (assumption 4). Each conditional path converges in distribution to \delta(\cdot - x_1) (assumption 3), so by dominated convergence over x_1 their mixture p_t converges in distribution to \int \delta(\cdot - x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1 = p_1. A limit in distribution is unique, so X_1 \sim p_1 as well, which is Eq. 19. \square

4.5.1 Generated paths and the non-uniqueness of the velocity field
A velocity field v_t(x) generates a probability path p_t when the two satisfy Eq. 17, so the proof above shows that the marginal velocity field u_t generates the marginal path p_t on (0, 1).
The continuity equation does not determine the velocity field that generates a probability path. A field w: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto w_t(x), is divergence-free when \nabla_x \cdot w_t = 0 for each t. For a divergence-free w, adding w_t / p_t to u_t adds w_t to the flux p_t\, u_t without changing its divergence, so u_t + w_t / p_t also generates p_t. Eq. 15 is one choice among these, the one the flow-matching loss of §5.2 regresses onto.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
section: 4.6 Four forms of the change of variables
text:
4.6 Four forms of the change of variables
The change of variables of §2.1 has now appeared in three forms, and the Fokker-Planck equation adds a fourth. Each describes how a density changes when its samples are transported, and each extends the one before it, a sequence that Lai et al. call the change-of-variable hierarchy [69].

One invertible map: Eq. 1 gives the density of the pushforward f_\# p from p and the Jacobian determinant of f^{-1}.
A composition of maps: The log-density of a normalizing flow subtracts the log-determinants of its layers one after another, Eq. 2.
A flow: For layers of the form x \mapsto x + \Delta t\, v_t(x), which are steps of the Euler method, the sum of the log-determinants is a Riemann sum of the divergence up to O(\Delta t) (§3.4.1). The exact flow replaces it by the integral of the divergence along each trajectory, Eq. 8. At a fixed point, the same conservation law is the continuity equation Eq. 17, and Eq. 18 shows that it determines the distribution of the ODE’s solution.
A flow with noise: An SDE adds a diffusion term to the ODE, and the continuity equation becomes the Fokker-Planck equation, P1:Eq. 45, which reduces to Eq. 17 when g \equiv 0 (§4.3). P3:§2.1 proves its equivalence with the distribution of the SDE’s solution, the counterpart of Eq. 18.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
section: 5.1 The probability-flow ODE: training without solving the ODE
text:
5.1 The probability-flow ODE: training without solving the ODE
Song et al. gave the first flow model trained without solving its ODE [12]. Its velocity field is built from a diffusion model’s score, which DSM learns by regression (P3:§4), so training never solves the ODE.
The solution of the probability-flow ODE of post #3 has the diffusion marginals, which post #3 proves through the Fokker-Planck equation and §5.1.1 below proves a second way, through the continuity equation of §4.4.
Here f(x,t) and g(t) are the drift and diffusion coefficients of the forward SDE dx = f\,dt + g\,dW (P3:Eq. 1). The field below is stated in the diffusion’s own time, where t = 0 is data and t increases toward noise up to the terminal time T, the reverse of this post’s convention. In this section p_t likewise denotes the diffusion marginals, which start at p_0 = p_{\mathrm{data}}. From §5.2 on, t is again the time of this post’s convention and p_t the marginal path of Part 4.
The probability-flow ODE is dx_t/dt = \tilde f(x_t, t), with the velocity field \tilde f: \mathbb{R}^d \times (0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^d,

\boxed{\tilde f(x, t) = f(x, t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x)}
\tag{20}
As written it transports data to noise.
The path, however, is fixed by the forward SDE, and three pitfalls follow, the first two pointed out by Lipman et al. [7] and Liu et al. [8]. The marginals reach the noise distribution only as the diffusion time goes to infinity, so the initial distribution of generation is an approximation (§6.2). The VP trajectories are curved and move slowly at first (§6.4). And the velocity is available only through the score, whose regression target, the conditional score, diverges where the noise vanishes (P3:§4.2.3). Flow matching keeps the regression and frees the path.

5.1.1 Deriving the probability-flow ODE using the continuity equation
The derivation, for data supported in a bounded set, has three steps. Step 1 shows that the diffusion marginals p_t satisfy a continuity equation, with the velocity field \tilde f of Eq. 20. Step 2 checks that v_t = \tilde f(\cdot, t) and p_t meet the assumptions of the equivalence of §4.4. Step 3 combines the two. By the sufficiency part of that equivalence, p_t is the distribution of the solution of the ODE with the velocity field \tilde f, the probability-flow ODE. P3:§A.4 treats the general SDE.
Step 1 — p_t satisfies a continuity equation:
Starting from the Fokker-Planck equation of the forward SDE, which p_t satisfies by the necessity part of P3:Eq. 20,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

Substituting the log-derivative identity \Delta_x p_t = \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big) of P3:Eq. 21, which follows from \nabla_x \log p_t = \nabla_x p_t / p_t,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big)

Writing \tfrac{1}{2} g^2, which depends on t only, inside the divergence,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\Big)

Combining into one divergence,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\Big(f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t\Big)\, p_t\Big]

Substituting the velocity field \tilde f = f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t of Eq. 20,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(\tilde f\, p_t\big)
\tag{21}
So the diffusion marginals p_t, which satisfy the Fokker-Planck equation, also satisfy the continuity equation with the velocity field \tilde f.
Step 2 — the assumptions of the equivalence hold:
The equivalence of §4.4 has three assumptions, and each holds for v_t = \tilde f(\cdot, t) and p_t on each interval [t_{\min}, T] with t_{\min} > 0, in place of (0, T].
Assumption 1 — Lipschitz velocity field: The drift f is affine in x for each SDE of post #3, so it is Lipschitz. For data supported in a solid sphere of radius R centered at the origin, P3:Eq. 23 bounds each derivative of \log p_t of order two or more uniformly in time,

\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\, t \in [t_{\min}, T]} \lVert \nabla_x^k \log p_t(x) \rVert < \infty \quad \text{for each } k \ge 2

where \nabla_x^k is the k-th derivative in x. With order two it bounds the Hessian of \log p_t, so the score \nabla_x \log p_t is Lipschitz in x. Both terms of \tilde f are continuously differentiable and Lipschitz, so \tilde f is too, and hence of at most linear growth.
Assumption 2 — initial condition: The ODE dx_t/dt = \tilde f(x_t, t) has the initial condition x_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} at a time t_0 \in [t_{\min}, T], and x_t denotes its solution. Solving forward from a t_0 near 0 maps data to noise, and solving backward from t_0 = T generates samples.
Assumption 3 — regularity and decay at infinity: The marginal p_t is a Gaussian convolution of data with bounded support, so it is smooth in t and x, decays at infinity and is dominated, because its Gaussian tails, and those of \partial_t p_t, are uniform in t on each [a, b] \subset (0, T].
Step 3 — the sufficiency part applies:
By Step 1, p_t satisfies the continuity equation Eq. 21 with v_t = \tilde f(\cdot, t), and by Step 2 the assumptions of Eq. 18 hold. Its sufficiency part therefore makes p_t the distribution of x_t for each t \in [t_{\min}, T], where x_t is the solution of the ODE dx_t/dt = \tilde f(x_t, t) with the initial condition x_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} at a time t_0 \in [t_{\min}, T]. As t_{\min} > 0 is arbitrary, this holds for each t_0 \in (0, T] and each t \in (0, T]. Writing \tilde f out, the ODE is

\boxed{\frac{dx_t}{dt} = f(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)}

which is the probability-flow ODE with the velocity field Eq. 20. \square

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
5.2 Flow-matching loss
The network is trained to equal the marginal velocity field u_t, since its trajectories then follow the marginal path p_t by Eq. 19.

5.2.1 The objective we wish we could optimize
The natural objective regresses the network onto the marginal velocity field u_t of Eq. 15,

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1]}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t} \big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x) \|^2 \,\big]}
\tag{22}
This objective is simulation-free, which means that training with it never solves the ODE, unlike maximum-likelihood training of a flow model [3]. The obstacle is that the density p_t is intractable, and with it u_t, which divides by it.


5.2.2 Conditional flow matching
The conditional flow matching objective regresses the network onto the conditional velocity field u_t(\cdot \mid x_1), which the choice of conditional path makes known in closed form, at points sampled by Eq. 11,

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1]}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x \mid x_1)} \big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \|^2 \,\big]}
\tag{23}
The central theorem of flow matching is Lipman et al.’s Theorem 2 [7].
Assumptions:

The marginal path is positive, p_t(x) > 0 for each x \in \mathbb{R}^d and each t \in [0, 1), so that the posterior p_t(x_1 \mid x) of §4.2.2 is defined.
Under t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1], x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} and x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), the second moments \mathbb{E}\lVert v_\theta(x, t) \rVert^2, for each \theta, and \mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(x \mid x_1) \rVert^2 are finite, which makes both objectives and each term of their expanded squares finite.

Theorem:
Under these assumptions, the conditional flow matching objective Eq. 23 and the objective Eq. 22 differ by a constant that does not depend on \theta, so they have the same gradient,

\boxed{\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)}
\tag{24}
Minimizing the tractable conditional flow matching objective Eq. 23 therefore trains v_\theta(x, t) to match the intractable marginal velocity field u_t.
This equivalence is the flow-matching analogue of Vincent’s equivalence between explicit and denoising score matching [72], which P2:§4.8 proves.
Proof:
The identity Eq. 16, derived in §4.2.2, gives the gradient equality.
By the definition Eq. 23,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \|^2 \,\big]

Expanding the square, into three expectations that are finite by assumption 2, the cross term because \lvert a \cdot b \rvert \le \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert a \rVert^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert b \rVert^2,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\|u_t(x \mid x_1)\|^2\big]

The last term carries no \theta; naming it C_1,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big] + C_1

Averaging over x_1 then x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) reproduces the marginal p_t; for the first term, whose integrand has no x_1,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big] + C_1
