Writing the joint density of (x_1, x) in the cross term as p_t(x)\, p_t(x_1 \mid x), by Bayes’ rule (§4.2.2) with the posterior defined by assumption 1,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\Big] + C_1

Taking v_\theta(x, t), which does not depend on x_1, out of the inner expectation,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\Big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\Big] + C_1

Substituting the identity Eq. 16,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x)\big] + C_1

The constant

C_2 = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|u_t(x)\|^2\big]

is free of \theta and finite, since Eq. 16 gives

\lVert u_t(x) \rVert^2 \le \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\lVert u_t(x \mid x_1) \rVert^2

Their difference is the conditional variance \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\lVert u_t(x \mid x_1) - u_t(x) \rVert^2 \ge 0. Averaging over x \sim p_t and t then gives C_2 \le C_1, which is finite by assumption 2. Adding and subtracting C_2,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x)\big] + C_2 + (C_1 - C_2)

Completing the square,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x) \|^2 \,\big] + (C_1 - C_2)

By the definition Eq. 22,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) + (C_1 - C_2)

The two objectives therefore differ only by the \theta-independent constant C_1 - C_2, so they have the same minimizers, and if the family \{v_\theta\} contains u_t, the minimizer satisfies v_\theta(x, t) = u_t(x) for p_t-almost every x, at almost every t. Taking the gradient in \theta, which annihilates the constant,

\boxed{\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)}

which is Eq. 24. \square

5.2.2.1 General conditioning
Neither the proof of Eq. 19 in §4.5 nor the proof above uses that the conditioning variable is x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. The conditioning variable can be any latent variable z \sim q, with q a distribution on \mathbb{R}^k, conditional paths p_t(x \mid z) and conditional velocity fields u_t(x \mid z). Both proofs then carry over when the conditional paths have densities. Integrals against q replace those against p_{\mathrm{data}}, the marginal velocity field u_t is defined by Eq. 15 with z and q in place of x_1 and p_{\mathrm{data}}, and the tower property of conditional expectation, that the expectation of a conditional expectation is the unconditional expectation, applies as before.
The boundary conditions do not carry over, since p_0(\cdot \mid z) need no longer equal the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}}. What must be checked instead is that the mixtures satisfy \int p_0(x \mid z)\, q(z)\, dz = p_{\mathrm{init}} and \int p_1(x \mid z)\, q(z)\, dz = p_{\mathrm{data}}. Post #5 uses this with z = (x_0, x_1) sampled from a coupling, a joint distribution \gamma(x_0, x_1) whose marginals are p_{\mathrm{init}} and p_{\mathrm{data}}, so q is the coupling \gamma, with k = 2d. The conditional paths there are Dirac deltas, which have no densities, and post #5 extends the gradient equality to them.


5.2.2.2 Training and sampling
By Eq. 24, flow-matching training minimizes the conditional flow matching objective Eq. 23. It needs samples x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1] and x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), and the conditional velocity field u_t(\cdot \mid x_1) in closed form, and it never solves the ODE.
Algorithm 8 — Flow-matching training [7]:
1: repeat
    2: x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1], x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1)
    3: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \lVert v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \rVert^2
    4: take a gradient step on \mathcal{L}(\theta)
5: until converged
In practice line 2 samples a minibatch and line 3 averages the loss over it.
If the network equals the marginal velocity field u_t, its trajectories follow the marginal path p_t by Eq. 19, so solving Eq. 7 with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} ends at X_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. A trained network only approximates u_t, and §5.2.2.3 bounds how far the distribution p^\theta_1 of its X_1 then lies from p_{\mathrm{data}}. Training by Algorithm 8 followed by sampling with Algorithm 7 is the flow-matching pipeline. §6 makes the procedure concrete for Gaussian conditional paths.


5.2.2.3 The flow-matching loss bounds the distance to the data distribution
Training stops at a loss above its minimum, so the distribution p^\theta_1 of the generated X_1 can differ from p_{\mathrm{data}}. Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden’s Proposition 3 [9] bounds the difference by the flow-matching objective. It measures the difference by the 2-Wasserstein distance [17], [73] of P1:§4.1.2,

W_2^2(p, q) = \inf_{\gamma}\ \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim \gamma} \lVert X - Y \rVert^2

where the infimum runs over the couplings \gamma of p and q (§5.2.2.1).
Assumptions:

The assumptions of §4.5 hold, so the solution X_t of the ODE of u_t with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} has X_t \sim p_t for each t \in [0, 1], by Eq. 19.
The network velocity field v_\theta(x, t) is continuously differentiable in (t, x) and Lipschitz in x uniformly in t \in [0, 1], with a constant K_\theta.

Theorem:
Under these assumptions,

\boxed{W_2^2\big(p_{\mathrm{data}}, p^\theta_1\big) \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta}\, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)}
\tag{25}
Under the assumptions of §5.2.2 as well, substituting \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) - (C_1 - C_2) from the proof of Eq. 24, the bound is in terms of the objective that Algorithm 8 minimizes,

W_2^2\big(p_{\mathrm{data}}, p^\theta_1\big) \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta}\, \big(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) - C_1 + C_2\big)

The proof follows two trajectories from one initial point, the exact one of u_t and the generated one of v_\theta, in three steps:

The squared distance \chi between them satisfies \chi' \le (1 + 2K_\theta)\, \chi + \delta, where \delta is the squared error of v_\theta along the exact trajectory.
An integrating factor bounds \chi at t = 1 by e^{1 + 2K_\theta} times the integral of \delta.
Averaging over the initial point turns the integral of \delta into \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta). The pair of endpoints is a coupling of p_{\mathrm{data}} and p^\theta_1, so its mean squared distance is at least W_2^2.







NoteProof: the flow-matching loss bounds the 2-Wasserstein distance





Fixing x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d, let X_t and X^\theta_t be the solutions of the ODE of u_t and of Eq. 7 with X_0 = X^\theta_0 = x_0. The first exists on [0, 1] for p_{\mathrm{init}}-almost every x_0 by assumption 4 of §4.5. The second exists on [0, 1] by the Picard-Lindelöf theorem and assumption 2, and X^\theta_1 \sim p^\theta_1 when x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}. Their squared distance is \chi: [0, 1] \to [0, \infty), t \mapsto \lVert X_t - X^\theta_t \rVert^2, and for t \in [0, 1) its rate of change is

\chi'(t) = 2\,(X_t - X^\theta_t) \cdot \big(u_t(X_t) - v_\theta(X^\theta_t, t)\big)

Adding and subtracting v_\theta(X_t, t) inside the second factor,

\chi'(t) = 2\,(X_t - X^\theta_t) \cdot \big(u_t(X_t) - v_\theta(X_t, t)\big) + 2\,(X_t - X^\theta_t) \cdot \big(v_\theta(X_t, t) - v_\theta(X^\theta_t, t)\big)

Bounding the first term by 2\, a \cdot b \le \lVert a \rVert^2 + \lVert b \rVert^2,

\chi'(t) \le \chi(t) + \big\lVert u_t(X_t) - v_\theta(X_t, t) \big\rVert^2 + 2\,(X_t - X^\theta_t) \cdot \big(v_\theta(X_t, t) - v_\theta(X^\theta_t, t)\big)

Bounding the last term by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

\chi'(t) \le \chi(t) + \big\lVert u_t(X_t) - v_\theta(X_t, t) \big\rVert^2 + 2\, \lVert X_t - X^\theta_t \rVert\, \big\lVert v_\theta(X_t, t) - v_\theta(X^\theta_t, t) \big\rVert

Applying the Lipschitz bound \lVert v_\theta(X_t, t) - v_\theta(X^\theta_t, t) \rVert \le K_\theta\, \lVert X_t - X^\theta_t \rVert of assumption 2,

\chi'(t) \le \chi(t) + \big\lVert u_t(X_t) - v_\theta(X_t, t) \big\rVert^2 + 2K_\theta\, \chi(t)

Writing \delta: [0, 1) \to [0, \infty), \delta(t) = \lVert v_\theta(X_t, t) - u_t(X_t) \rVert^2, for the squared error of the network along the exact trajectory,

\chi'(t) \le \chi(t) + \delta(t) + 2K_\theta\, \chi(t)

Collecting the terms in \chi,

\chi'(t) \le (1 + 2K_\theta)\, \chi(t) + \delta(t)

Multiplying by e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t} > 0,

e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \chi'(t) \le (1 + 2K_\theta)\, e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \chi(t) + e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \delta(t)

Subtracting (1 + 2K_\theta)\, e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \chi(t) from both sides,

e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \chi'(t) - (1 + 2K_\theta)\, e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \chi(t) \le e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \delta(t)

Recognizing the left side as the derivative of a product,

\frac{d}{dt}\Big(e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \chi(t)\Big) \le e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \delta(t)

Integrating from 0 to \tau < 1, with \chi(0) = 0 because both trajectories start at x_0,

e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) \tau}\, \chi(\tau) \le \int_0^\tau e^{-(1 + 2K_\theta) t}\, \delta(t)\, dt

Multiplying by e^{(1 + 2K_\theta) \tau},

\chi(\tau) \le \int_0^\tau e^{(1 + 2K_\theta)(\tau - t)}\, \delta(t)\, dt

Bounding e^{(1 + 2K_\theta)(\tau - t)} by e^{1 + 2K_\theta}, since 0 \le \tau - t \le 1,

\chi(\tau) \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta} \int_0^\tau \delta(t)\, dt

Extending the integral to [0, 1), since \delta \ge 0,

\chi(\tau) \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta} \int_0^1 \delta(t)\, dt

Letting \tau \to 1, where X_\tau \to X_1 along the trajectory (assumption 4 of §4.5) and X^\theta_\tau \to X^\theta_1 by continuity,

\lVert X_1 - X^\theta_1 \rVert^2 \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta} \int_0^1 \delta(t)\, dt

Averaging over x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}},

\mathbb{E}\lVert X_1 - X^\theta_1 \rVert^2 \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta}\, \mathbb{E} \int_0^1 \delta(t)\, dt

Exchanging the expectation and the time integral, which Tonelli’s theorem allows for the nonnegative \delta,

\mathbb{E}\lVert X_1 - X^\theta_1 \rVert^2 \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta} \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}\, \delta(t)\, dt

Substituting \mathbb{E}\, \delta(t) = \mathbb{E}_{p_t} \lVert v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x) \rVert^2, since X_t \sim p_t by assumption 1,

\mathbb{E}\lVert X_1 - X^\theta_1 \rVert^2 \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta} \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}_{p_t} \lVert v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x) \rVert^2\, dt

By the definition Eq. 22, whose average over t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1] is the integral over [0, 1],

\mathbb{E}\lVert X_1 - X^\theta_1 \rVert^2 \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta}\, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)

The distribution of the pair (X_1, X^\theta_1) is a coupling of p_{\mathrm{data}} and p^\theta_1, since X_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} by assumption 1. Bounding the left side below by the infimum over couplings,

\boxed{W_2^2\big(p_{\mathrm{data}}, p^\theta_1\big) \le e^{1 + 2K_\theta}\, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)}

which is Eq. 25. \square



The factor e^{1 + 2K_\theta} grows exponentially with the Lipschitz constant of the network velocity field v_\theta(x, t). Where nearby trajectories separate quickly, a small regression error can carry the endpoint far, so the bound is informative for regular velocity fields and loose for fields with sharp variations. It concerns sampling by the ODE. For a sampler that solves an SDE, P6:§3.2 bounds the KL divergence from the data distribution to the generated distribution by the g^2-weighted error of the score plus the mismatch between the prior and p_T instead.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
section: 6.1 Gaussian paths and their conditional velocity fields
text:
6.1 Gaussian paths and their conditional velocity fields
Lipman et al. train on conditional paths that are Gaussian at each time, which meet the two needs of the conditional flow matching objective Eq. 23. They can be sampled, and their conditional velocity fields are known in closed form. A Gaussian conditional path has, for each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d, the form

\boxed{p_t(x \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}\big(x;\ m_t(x_1),\ \sigma_t(x_1)^2\, I\big)}
\tag{26}
with a mean m: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, (t, x_1) \mapsto m_t(x_1), and a standard deviation \sigma: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), (t, x_1) \mapsto \sigma_t(x_1), both differentiable in t. With p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I), the boundary conditions Eq. 10 fix their values at the two ends,

m_0(x_1) = 0, \quad \sigma_0(x_1) = 1, \qquad m_1(x_1) = x_1, \quad \sigma_1(x_1) = 0

Between the two ends we require \sigma_t(x_1) > 0 for t \in [0, 1), so that p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) has a density before t = 1. Lipman et al. end the path at a small \sigma_1(x_1) = \sigma_{\min} > 0, a narrow Gaussian around x_1, in place of the Dirac delta of Eq. 10. This post uses \sigma_{\min} = 0, which keeps the Dirac delta. Below, m_t and \sigma_t stand for m_t(x_1) and \sigma_t(x_1) at a fixed x_1.
Each Gaussian conditional path is the pushforward of p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I) under an affine map. That map is the conditional flow \phi(\cdot \mid x_1): \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto \phi_t(x \mid x_1),

\boxed{\phi_t(x \mid x_1) = \sigma_t\, x + m_t}
\tag{27}
It carries x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} to \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) \sim \mathcal{N}(m_t, \sigma_t^2\, I) = p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), because an affine function \sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t of a standard Gaussian is Gaussian with mean m_t and covariance \sigma_t^2\, I.
Many velocity fields generate the same path, as §4.5.1 shows. Lipman et al. choose the one whose flow is this affine map, the simplest of them [7]. The others add components that leave the distribution unchanged, such as rotations about m_t, which preserve the isotropic Gaussian \mathcal{N}(m_t, \sigma_t^2\, I), and these components only add computation.
Differentiating the conditional flow in t at a fixed x_0, with \dot\sigma_t = d\sigma_t/dt and \dot m_t = dm_t/dt,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t

Writing x for the point \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) and substituting x_0 = (x - m_t)/\sigma_t, which inverts Eq. 27 for t \in [0, 1), where \sigma_t > 0,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\, (x - m_t) + \dot m_t

By Eq. 5, the velocity field whose flow is \phi_t(\cdot \mid x_1) takes this value at x, so it is

\boxed{u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\, (x - m_t) + \dot m_t \qquad t \in [0, 1)}
\tag{28}
Its flow is the conditional flow Eq. 27, which carries p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), so it is a conditional velocity field in the sense of Eq. 14 on [0, 1). This is Lipman et al.’s Theorem 3. \square
The conditional flow also simplifies training. Changing variables in Eq. 23 from x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) to x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, with x = \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t,

\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)} \big[\, &\| v_\theta(\sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t,\ t) \\[4pt]
&- u_t(\sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t \mid x_1) \|^2 \,\big]
\end{aligned}

Since the conditional velocity field at \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) is the velocity of the conditional flow, u_t\big(\phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) \mid x_1\big) = \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t by differentiating Eq. 27 in t,

\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)} \big[\, &\| v_\theta(\sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t,\ t) \\[4pt]
&- (\dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t) \|^2 \,\big]
\end{aligned}}
\tag{29}
\square
The target \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t has no factor 1/\sigma_t, so it stays bounded up to t = 1 whenever \dot\sigma_t and \dot m_t do. Evaluating u_t(x \mid x_1) from Eq. 28 at a sampled x instead divides x - m_t by \sigma_t, which tends to 0 as t \to 1. When \dot\sigma_t itself diverges at t = 1, the target diverges too.
In diffusion time, the sampling step of DDIM follows a Gaussian conditional path with the network’s estimates of the data and of the noise in place of x_1 and x_0, as P8:§2.5 shows.

6.1.1 Affine conditional flows
The derivation of Eq. 28 used two properties of the conditional flow Eq. 27, that it is affine in x and invertible for t \in [0, 1). It used neither that the coefficient of x is a multiple of I nor that p_{\mathrm{init}} is Gaussian, and Lai et al. state the result without either restriction [69].
An affine conditional flow has, for each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d, the form

\phi_t(x \mid x_1) = A_t\, x + m_t

with a matrix A: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, (t, x_1) \mapsto A_t(x_1), differentiable in t and invertible for t \in [0, 1), and an offset m: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, (t, x_1) \mapsto m_t(x_1), differentiable in t, which is the mean of p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) when x_0 has mean zero, as in Eq. 26. The boundary values A_0 = I, m_0 = 0, A_1 = 0 and m_1 = x_1 make it the identity at t = 0 and send each point to x_1 at t = 1. The conditional flow Eq. 27 is the case A_t = \sigma_t\, I.
Differentiating in t at a fixed x_0, with \dot A_t = dA_t/dt,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \dot A_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t

Writing x for the point \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) and substituting x_0 = A_t^{-1}(x - m_t), which inverts the flow for t \in [0, 1),

\frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \dot A_t\, A_t^{-1}\, (x - m_t) + \dot m_t

By Eq. 5, the velocity field whose flow is \phi_t(\cdot \mid x_1) takes this value at x, so it is

\boxed{u_t(x \mid x_1) = \dot A_t\, A_t^{-1}\, (x - m_t) + \dot m_t \qquad t \in [0, 1)}
\tag{30}
With A_t = \sigma_t\, I, the inverse is A_t^{-1} = I/\sigma_t, and Eq. 30 is Eq. 28.
An initial distribution that is not Gaussian: The derivation did not use the distribution of x_0, so Eq. 30 is the conditional velocity field for each initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}}. The change of variables that gave Eq. 29 gives the target \dot A_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t at the point A_t\, x_0 + m_t. The conditional path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), the distribution of A_t\, x_0 + m_t, is Gaussian for t \in [0, 1) only when p_{\mathrm{init}} is, because an affine map with an invertible matrix carries Gaussian distributions to Gaussian distributions, and so does its inverse. Liu et al.’s straight paths from any initial distribution, x_t = (1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1, are the case A_t = (1 - t)\, I and m_t = t\, x_1 [8], which post #5 develops.
Gaussian endpoints without conditioning: When p_{\mathrm{init}} and p_{\mathrm{data}} are both Gaussian, a probability path between them can itself be Gaussian, with no conditioning. We write it as p_t = \mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \nu_t^2\, I), with a mean \mu: [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d and a standard deviation \nu: [0, 1] \to (0, \infty), both differentiable, so that p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \nu_0^2\, I) and p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \nu_1^2\, I).
The affine flow

\phi_t(x) = \mu_t + \frac{\nu_t}{\nu_0}\, (x - \mu_0)

carries p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_t, since it standardizes x_0 and then scales and shifts it. Its matrix is A_t = (\nu_t / \nu_0)\, I and its offset is c_t = \mu_t - (\nu_t / \nu_0)\, \mu_0. The derivation of Eq. 30 used neither the boundary values A_1 = 0 and m_1 = x_1 nor the conditioning, so with c_t in place of m_t it gives the velocity field v_t(x) whose flow is \phi_t,

v_t(x) = \dot A_t\, A_t^{-1}\, (x - c_t) + \dot c_t

Substituting \dot A_t\, A_t^{-1} = (\dot\nu_t / \nu_0)(\nu_0 / \nu_t)\, I = (\dot\nu_t / \nu_t)\, I,

v_t(x) = \frac{\dot\nu_t}{\nu_t}\, (x - c_t) + \dot c_t

Substituting c_t and its derivative \dot c_t = \dot\mu_t - (\dot\nu_t / \nu_0)\, \mu_0,

v_t(x) = \frac{\dot\nu_t}{\nu_t}\, \Big(x - \mu_t + \frac{\nu_t}{\nu_0}\, \mu_0\Big) + \dot\mu_t - \frac{\dot\nu_t}{\nu_0}\, \mu_0

Expanding the first term,

v_t(x) = \frac{\dot\nu_t}{\nu_t}\, (x - \mu_t) + \frac{\dot\nu_t}{\nu_0}\, \mu_0 + \dot\mu_t - \frac{\dot\nu_t}{\nu_0}\, \mu_0

Cancelling the two terms in \mu_0,

v_t(x) = \frac{\dot\nu_t}{\nu_t}\, (x - \mu_t) + \dot\mu_t

It has the form of Eq. 28, and it generates p_t itself, so a flow model between two isotropic Gaussian distributions, with covariances proportional to I, needs no regression. Lipman et al. state their Theorem 3 for conditional paths that start at \mathcal{N}(0, I) [7], and Lai et al. state it for Gaussian endpoints of any mean and variance [69].

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
6.2 Diffusion conditional paths
The perturbation kernels of the diffusion SDEs of posts #1 and #3, with time reversed, have the Gaussian form Eq. 26. The time is reversed because diffusion has the data at t = 0, where flow matching has the noise. Lipman et al. set the terminal time T of the diffusion to 1, and the point the kernel conditions on, x_0 in posts #1 and #3, is written x_1 here.
The VP SDE has, in the diffusion’s time t, the perturbation kernel \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_1,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(t))\, I\big) (P1:Eq. 41), with the noise schedule \beta: [0, 1] \to (0, \infty) and the cumulative product

\bar\alpha: [0, 1] \to (0, 1], \qquad t \mapsto \exp\Big(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\Big)

Reversing time in the kernel, with 1 - t in place of t, gives the VP path

m_t(x_1) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1 - t)}\, x_1, \qquad \sigma_t(x_1) = \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t)}

Its conditional velocity field follows from Eq. 28. Writing \beta and \bar\alpha for \beta(1 - t) and \bar\alpha(1 - t), and substituting the VP mean into Eq. 28,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\, \big(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1\big) + \dot m_t

Substituting \dot\sigma_t / \sigma_t = -\beta \bar\alpha / \big(2 (1 - \bar\alpha)\big), the time derivative of \log \sigma_t = \tfrac{1}{2} \log\big(1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t)\big), where \frac{d}{dt} \bar\alpha(1 - t) = \beta \bar\alpha,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{\beta \bar\alpha}{2 (1 - \bar\alpha)}\, \big(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1\big) + \dot m_t

Substituting \dot m_t = \tfrac{1}{2} \beta \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1, the time derivative of \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1 - t)}\, x_1,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{\beta \bar\alpha}{2 (1 - \bar\alpha)}\, \big(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} \beta \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1

Combining over the common denominator 2 (1 - \bar\alpha),

\boxed{u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{\beta\, \big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1 - \bar\alpha\, x\big)}{2 (1 - \bar\alpha)}}

\square
The VE SDE (P3:§1.3) has the perturbation kernel \mathcal{N}\big(x_1,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(t)^2\, I\big), with a noise level \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}: [0, 1] \to [0, \infty) that increases from \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(0) = 0 to \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1) \gg 1. The kernel’s variance \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(t)^2 is that of the VE kernel of post #3. Post #3’s noise level starts at a small positive value at t = 0, and \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(t)^2 is the increase of its square since then. Reversing time in the kernel gives the VE path

m_t(x_1) = x_1 \qquad \sigma_t(x_1) = \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t)

Substituting its derivatives \dot m_t = 0 and \dot\sigma_t = -\sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}'(1 - t), with \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}' the derivative of \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}, into Eq. 28,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}'(1 - t)}{\sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t)}\, (x - x_1)

Neither path meets the boundary condition p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = p_{\mathrm{init}} of Eq. 10 exactly. The VP path starts at

\mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(1)}\, x_1,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(1))\, I\big)

which is close to \mathcal{N}(0, I) only because \bar\alpha(1) is small. The VE path starts at

\mathcal{N}\big(x_1,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1)^2\, I\big)

which is close to \mathcal{N}\big(0,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1)^2\, I\big) only because \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1) is large, so for the VE path p_{\mathrm{init}} is this wider Gaussian rather than \mathcal{N}(0, I). The start of each path still depends on x_1, because a diffusion forgets its initial condition only as its time goes to infinity. The paths inherit this from the SDEs they come from [7].
On these paths the conditional velocity field is the velocity field \tilde f of the probability-flow ODE (Eq. 20) when the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}} is the Dirac delta at x_1, written in flow time, which runs opposite to the diffusion’s time.
For the VP path, the VP SDE (P3:Eq. 9)

dx_t = -\tfrac{1}{2} \beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t

has the drift f(x, t) = -\tfrac{1}{2} \beta(t)\, x and the diffusion coefficient g(t) = \sqrt{\beta(t)}. Substituting these and the kernel’s score -(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1)/(1 - \bar\alpha) into Eq. 20, and negating the result for the reversed time, gives

\frac{\beta\, \big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1 - \bar\alpha\, x\big)}{2 (1 - \bar\alpha)}

which is the field above. Post #5 shows the same for the marginal velocity field of the VP path. Lipman et al. find flow matching on these paths more stable in training than score matching on the same paths [7].
On both paths \sigma_t^2 vanishes linearly as t \to 1. For the VP path,

\sigma_t^2 = 1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t) \approx \beta(0)\, (1 - t)

For the VE path,

\sigma_t^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t)^2 \approx c\, (1 - t)

where c is the derivative at t = 0 of the square of post #3’s noise level. That noise level is a positive constant times an increasing exponential in t, so c > 0.
Hence \sigma_t behaves like \sqrt{1 - t} near t = 1 and \dot\sigma_t like 1/\sqrt{1 - t}, so the second moment \mathbb{E}\lVert \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t \rVert^2 of the target of Eq. 29 grows like 1/(1 - t), and its integral over [0, 1] is infinite. Lipman et al. sample t only up to 1 - 10^{-5} (their Appendix E), so that assumption 2 of §5.2.2 holds with t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1 - 10^{-5}] in place of \mathcal{U}[0, 1].

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
6.3 Optimal-transport conditional path
Lipman et al.’s second instance, the optimal-transport path, lets the mean and the standard deviation change linearly in time [7],

m_t(x_1) = t\, x_1, \qquad \sigma_t(x_1) = 1 - t

which is the path of §4.1.1. §6.3.1 explains its name. Lipman et al. write \sigma_t = 1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min})\, t, which ends at \sigma_{\min}. The conditional flow Eq. 27 of the optimal-transport path is

\phi_t(x \mid x_1) = (1 - t)\, x + t\, x_1

Each x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} therefore moves along the segment from x_0 to x_1 at the constant velocity x_1 - x_0. Substituting the path’s derivatives, through \dot\sigma_t / \sigma_t = -1/(1 - t) and \dot m_t = x_1, into Eq. 28,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{x - t\, x_1}{1 - t} + x_1

Combining over the common denominator 1 - t,

\boxed{u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{x_1 - x}{1 - t}}
\tag{31}
which is the field that §4.2.2.1 derived from the trajectories directly. \square

6.3.1 Objective and name of the optimal-transport path
The target \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t of Eq. 29 is x_1 - x_0, so the objective is

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)} \big[\, \| v_\theta\big((1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1,\ t\big) - (x_1 - x_0) \|^2 \,\big]}
\tag{32}
Lipman et al. [7] call it the optimal-transport path because, for \sigma_{\min} > 0, its conditional flow at t = 1 is the optimal-transport map [47] from p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}(0, I) to p_1(\cdot \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}(x_1, \sigma_{\min}^2 I). For t < 1 the flow moves each point along a straight line to its image, at constant speed. Post #5 defines optimal transport and shows why such motion is optimal.
At each point x the conditional velocity field Eq. 31 keeps the direction x_1 - x for each t, whereas that of the VP path, \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1 - \bar\alpha\, x, turns as \bar\alpha changes. The conditional flow being optimal does not make the trajectories of the marginal velocity field u_t straight, so its flow is not the motion of optimal transport from p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}}, as Lipman et al. note and P5:§3.3 shows.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
6.4 Diffusion and optimal-transport paths compared
Under a Gaussian conditional path, each x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} moves along the trajectory \sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t of the conditional flow. Figure 10 below draws these trajectories for the VP path and the optimal-transport path, for one x_1 and the same twelve x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, with markers at t = 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4.








Figure 10: Conditional trajectories \sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t of the VP path (left) and the optimal-transport path (right), for one x_1 (star) and the same twelve x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} (dots), with markers at t = 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4. The shape of each trajectory shows whether the path is straight, and the spacing of the markers shows whether its speed is constant. The VP noise schedule \beta is linear in time, from 0.1 to 20, as in Lipman et al.’s experiments.





The optimal-transport trajectories are segments traversed at constant speed, so the markers divide each into quarters. The VP trajectories are curved. Their coefficients \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1 - t)} and \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t)} have squares that sum to one, so the pair of coefficients lies on the unit circle. Each trajectory is therefore the image of a circular arc under the linear map (a, b) \mapsto a\, x_1 + b\, x_0, an arc of an ellipse, which is curved unless x_0 and x_1 are parallel.
The first two VP markers lie near the start of each trajectory, because the coefficients change slowly while t < 1/2, so each point covers most of its trajectory after t = 1/2. Liu et al. call this a non-uniform speed, since the VP trajectories are slow at first and speed up later [8]. Lipman et al. see the same in generated images, where on the diffusion paths noise dominates until the last time steps [7]. The VE trajectories, x_1 + \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t)\, \epsilon with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), are segments toward x_1, but their speed \lvert \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}'(1 - t) \rvert\, \lVert \epsilon \rVert varies as well [8].
Lipman et al. trained one network with each objective and path on CIFAR-10 and on ImageNet at 32 \times 32 and 64 \times 64 pixels, and the optimal-transport path alone at 128 \times 128 [7]. The objectives are flow matching, score matching and the simple objective of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [74], a regression onto the noise. Lipman et al. report three measures.
The negative log-likelihood (NLL) in bits per dimension (§2.2) is computed with Eq. 8. The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [75] is the Fréchet distance between Gaussians fitted to the features that a pretrained Inception network extracts from generated and from real images. The NFE (§3.5) is that of an adaptive Runge-Kutta solver [45], [76], Dormand and Prince’s [77], at tolerance 10^{-5}. Unlike Algorithm 7, which takes n equal steps, such a solver shrinks the step where the trajectory bends. Lower is better for all three, and Table 1 gives two of the datasets.



Table 1: Lipman et al.’s results (their Table 1) for one U-Net architecture trained with each objective and path [7]. A U-Net is a convolutional network that lowers and then restores the image resolution, with skip connections between layers of equal resolution [78], here in Dhariwal and Nichol’s version [79]. The best value in each column is bold.

The optimal-transport path is best on each measure and needs about half the NFE of DDPM, 142 against 274 on CIFAR-10. Flow matching on the VP path already improves on score matching on the same path, so part of the gain comes from the objective and part from the path. Lipman et al. also report that the optimal-transport path lowers the FID faster during training. With fixed-step solvers on ImageNet at 32 \times 32 pixels, it reaches the same error as the diffusion models, measured against a 1000-step solution, with about 60% of their function evaluations [7].

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
6.5 Pitfalls
Flow matching with the optimal-transport path trains by regression and samples in fewer steps than a diffusion model, but it has three pitfalls. All three come from the way Lipman et al.’s conditional paths pair p_{\mathrm{init}} with p_{\mathrm{data}}, from a Gaussian and independently. Rectified flow, the subject of post #5, addresses each.

6.5.1 Curved trajectories
The conditional trajectories of the optimal-transport path are straight, but the trajectories of the marginal velocity field u_t are, in general, not. By Eq. 16, u_t(x) averages the conditional velocity fields u_t(x \mid x_1) under the posterior p_t(x_1 \mid x). Where segments toward different x_1 cross, it averages different directions. The trajectories of u_t cannot cross, because the ODE has a unique solution through each point (§3.1), so they bend instead.
For the optimal-transport path the average is u_t(x) = \big(\mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}[x_1] - x\big)/(1 - t).
For Gaussian data the curved trajectories have a closed form. The marginal velocity field is then a case of Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden’s formula for Gaussian mixtures (their Proposition C.1) [9], and Lai et al. use it to show that the trajectories are not straight [69].
Let p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2) on the line, with \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} > 0. For independent x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} and x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, the point x_t = t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, x_0 has mean zero, the variance

V(t) = t^2 \sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 + (1 - t)^2

and the covariance t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 with x_1. So x_1 - (t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 / V(t))\, x_t is uncorrelated with x_t, and independent of it, since the two are jointly Gaussian. Its mean is zero. Given x_1, the point x_t has the conditional path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) (§6.1), so p_t(x_1 \mid x) is the distribution of x_1 given x_t = x. Writing x_1 as the difference above plus (t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 / V(t))\, x_t and conditioning on x_t = x, the posterior mean is

\mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}[x_1] = \frac{t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2\, x}{V(t)}

Substituting it into the average,

u_t(x) = \frac{t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 / V(t) - 1}{1 - t}\, x

Writing the numerator over V(t),

u_t(x) = \frac{t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - V(t)}{(1 - t)\, V(t)}\, x

Cancelling 1 - t, a factor of the numerator, since t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - V(t) = t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 (1 - t) - (1 - t)^2 = (1 - t)\big(t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - (1 - t)\big),

u_t(x) = \frac{t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - (1 - t)}{V(t)}\, x

Since the numerator is half of V'(t) = 2t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - 2(1 - t),

u_t(x) = \frac{V'(t)}{2V(t)}\, x

The trajectory from x_0 satisfies \frac{d}{dt} X_t = \frac{V'(t)}{2V(t)}\, X_t with X_0 = x_0. So does \sqrt{V(t)}\, x_0, since V(0) = 1 and its derivative is \frac{V'(t)}{2\sqrt{V(t)}}\, x_0. Since V is positive and continuously differentiable on [0, 1], the field u_t(x) is continuous in t and Lipschitz in x uniformly in t, so by the uniqueness of the solution (§3.1) the trajectory is

X_t = \sqrt{t^2\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 + (1 - t)^2}\; x_0

It ends at X_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} x_0, and the segment between its ends is (1 - t + t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}})\, x_0. Since

(1 - t + t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}})^2 = V(t) + 2t(1 - t)\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}

which exceeds V(t) for t \in (0, 1), each trajectory with x_0 \ne 0 runs strictly closer to zero than that segment, so it is curved for each \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} > 0. For \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} = 1, where p_{\mathrm{init}} = p_{\mathrm{data}}, the segment is the constant x_0, but the trajectory passes through x_0 / \sqrt{2} at t = 1/2. The flow contracts toward zero and expands again, because each x_0 is paired with points x_1 of both signs, whose velocities partly cancel in the average.
With p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and p_{\mathrm{data}} an equal mixture of two narrow Gaussians at \pm 2, the posterior mean of x_1 has a closed form as well, by the same formula of Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden. So the segments and the trajectories of u_t can both be drawn in one dimension, as Figure 11 shows below.








Figure 11: Straight conditional trajectories and curved marginal trajectories in one dimension, for p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and p_{\mathrm{data}} an equal mixture of \mathcal{N}(-2, 0.25^2) and \mathcal{N}(2, 0.25^2). Left: Segments (1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1 for 24 pairs, with x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} and x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} sampled independently, which cross where they run to different modes. Right: Trajectories of the marginal velocity field u_t from 24 quantiles of p_{\mathrm{init}}, the points below which it has the probabilities 0.02 to 0.98 in equal steps, solved with small Runge-Kutta steps, which do not cross and bend toward the modes.





Segments from starting points near zero run to both modes and cross. The trajectories of u_t from the same region first move little, while the posterior p_t(x_1 \mid x) still puts comparable weight on both modes. They turn toward one mode once the posterior concentrates on it. An adaptive solver takes small steps where a trajectory turns, which is one reason why even the optimal-transport path needs 142 function evaluations on CIFAR-10 (Table 1).


6.5.2 A fixed coupling of noise and data
The bending is a property of the target u_t, not of the network, so a larger network or longer training does not remove it. The target is fixed by the coupling of p_{\mathrm{init}} with p_{\mathrm{data}} that the conditional path builds in. For each x_1 the conditional path starts from the whole of p_{\mathrm{init}}, so x_0 is sampled independently of x_1, and the pairs (x_0, x_1) have the joint density p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1). The objective of Eq. 29 samples its pairs in this way, and nothing in it changes the coupling.
A trained flow does pair each x_0 with one endpoint \phi^\theta_1(x_0), because its trajectories do not cross, so the pairs (x_0, \phi^\theta_1(x_0)) form a deterministic coupling. Flow matching has no step that trains on this coupling. Its trajectories are also not, in general, the straight lines of the motion of optimal transport from p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}} (§6.3.1).


6.5.3 A Gaussian source
A Gaussian conditional path starts at m_0 = 0 and \sigma_0 = 1, so each conditional path starts at \mathcal{N}(0, I), and so does the marginal path, its average over x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. The initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} must therefore be this Gaussian. Each diffusion path of §6.2 starts at a Gaussian that depends on x_1, close to \mathcal{N}(0, I) for the VP path and to a wider Gaussian for the VE path.
Flow matching with these paths generates from Gaussian noise, but it cannot carry one data distribution to another, as translating images of one domain into another requires. The general conditioning of §5.2.2.1 allows other initial distributions, but Lipman et al.’s Gaussian paths, which condition on x_1 alone, do not use it. An affine conditional flow (§6.1.1) also conditions on x_1 alone and allows any initial distribution, at the cost of conditional paths that are no longer Gaussian, and post #5 develops it.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
7.1 What comes next
Post #5 addresses the three pitfalls above. It conditions on pairs of points from any two distributions, through rectified flow and stochastic interpolants, and develops optimal transport and Schrödinger bridges to choose the pairing. It then places diffusion inside flow matching as one path. Flow matching on the VP path learns the velocity field of post #3’s probability-flow ODE. Solving that ODE gives a diffusion model’s exact likelihood, and its solution transports Gaussian data optimally but not data in general. Score matching and flow matching become two parameterizations of one path.

title: Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid
text:
Appendix

A.1 The change of variables in one dimension
§2.1 states the change of variables Eq. 1 in d dimensions without a proof. In one dimension the proof needs only the distribution function, and it shows why the derivative of the inverse map enters with an absolute value.
Set-up:
Let X be a random variable with a continuous density p: \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty) and the distribution function F: \mathbb{R} \to [0, 1], F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} p(r)\, dr, so that F' = p. Let f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} be invertible and differentiable, with a differentiable inverse, and let Y = f(X). A differentiable function is continuous, and a continuous invertible function on \mathbb{R} is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.
Increasing f:
The event f(X) \le y is the event X \le f^{-1}(y), so the distribution function of Y is

P(Y \le y) = F\big(f^{-1}(y)\big)

Differentiating in y by the chain rule, with F' = p,

p_Y(y) = p\big(f^{-1}(y)\big)\, (f^{-1})'(y)

Decreasing f:
The event f(X) \le y is now the event X \ge f^{-1}(y). Its probability is 1 - F\big(f^{-1}(y)\big), since X has a density and so takes the value f^{-1}(y) with probability zero,

P(Y \le y) = 1 - F\big(f^{-1}(y)\big)

Differentiating in y by the chain rule,

p_Y(y) = -p\big(f^{-1}(y)\big)\, (f^{-1})'(y)

Both cases:
The derivative (f^{-1})' is nonnegative when f increases and nonpositive when it decreases, so in both cases

\boxed{p_Y(y) = p\big(f^{-1}(y)\big)\, \big\lvert (f^{-1})'(y) \big\rvert}

which is Eq. 1 with d = 1, where the determinant of the 1 \times 1 Jacobian is the derivative itself. \square
By the inverse function theorem, \lvert (f^{-1})'(y) \rvert = 1 / \lvert f'(x) \rvert at x = f^{-1}(y). An interval near x that f stretches by the factor \lvert f'(x) \rvert keeps its probability, so the density falls by that factor. In d dimensions the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant replaces \lvert (f^{-1})' \rvert and measures volume instead of length. That case rests on the change of variables in multiple integrals, which Jacobi proved in general [31].


A.2 Existence and uniqueness of ODE solutions
§3.1 states the Picard-Lindelöf theorem [33], [34] for solutions that start at t = 0, and §3.1.2 needs solutions through each point at each time. This section proves the theorem in that form, by Picard’s successive approximations, first on a short time interval around the initial time and then on all of [0, 1]. The argument is the standard one of Coddington and Levinson [56].
A continuous function X solves \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_t(X_t) with X_s = x exactly when it satisfies the integral equation

X_t = x + \int_s^t v_r(X_r)\, dr

by the fundamental theorem of calculus, once the integrand is continuous. The proof builds a solution of the integral equation as the limit of the Picard iterates

X^{(0)}_t = x, \qquad X^{(n+1)}_t = x + \int_s^t v_r\big(X^{(n)}_r\big)\, dr

each of which inserts the previous one into the right-hand side.
Assumptions:

The initial time is s \in [0, 1] and the initial point is x \in \mathbb{R}^d. For constants a, b > 0, I_a = [s - a, s + a] \cap [0, 1] is a time interval around s, and B_b = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^d: \lVert y - x \rVert \le b\} is the solid sphere of radius b centered at x, its boundary included.
The velocity field v_t(y) is continuous in t, Lipschitz in y with a constant K > 0, and bounded by a constant M > 0, for each t \in I_a and y \in B_b.

Theorem:
Under these assumptions, with \delta = \min(a, b/M) and I_\delta = [s - \delta, s + \delta] \cap [0, 1], exactly one solution with X_s = x exists on I_\delta.
Step 1 — the iterates stay in the solid sphere:
If X^{(n)} is continuous on I_\delta with values in B_b, the integrand r \mapsto v_r\big(X^{(n)}_r\big) is continuous, since

\big\lVert v_r\big(X^{(n)}_r\big) - v_{r'}\big(X^{(n)}_{r'}\big) \big\rVert \le K\, \big\lVert X^{(n)}_r - X^{(n)}_{r'} \big\rVert + \big\lVert v_r\big(X^{(n)}_{r'}\big) - v_{r'}\big(X^{(n)}_{r'}\big) \big\rVert

and both terms tend to zero as r \to r'. It is also bounded by M, so \lVert X^{(n+1)}_t - x \rVert \le M\, \lvert t - s \rvert \le M \delta \le b for each t \in I_\delta. Starting from X^{(0)} = x, induction makes each iterate continuous on I_\delta with values in B_b. The bound for n = 0, \lVert X^{(1)}_t - X^{(0)}_t \rVert \le M\, \lvert t - s \rvert, is the first case of Step 2.
Step 2 — successive iterates approach each other:
For each n \ge 0 and t \in I_\delta, the bound

\big\lVert X^{(n+1)}_t - X^{(n)}_t \big\rVert \le \frac{M K^n\, \lvert t - s \rvert^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}

holds by induction on n, with the case n = 0 from Step 1. Assuming it for n - 1 and subtracting the definitions of X^{(n+1)} and X^{(n)},

\big\lVert X^{(n+1)}_t - X^{(n)}_t \big\rVert = \Big\lVert \int_s^t \Big(v_r\big(X^{(n)}_r\big) - v_r\big(X^{(n-1)}_r\big)\Big)\, dr \Big\rVert

Bounding the norm of the integral by the integral of the norm,

\big\lVert X^{(n+1)}_t - X^{(n)}_t \big\rVert \le \Big\lvert \int_s^t \big\lVert v_r\big(X^{(n)}_r\big) - v_r\big(X^{(n-1)}_r\big) \big\rVert\, dr \Big\rvert

By the Lipschitz condition,

\big\lVert X^{(n+1)}_t - X^{(n)}_t \big\rVert \le K\, \Big\lvert \int_s^t \big\lVert X^{(n)}_r - X^{(n-1)}_r \big\rVert\, dr \Big\rvert

By the bound for n - 1,

\big\lVert X^{(n+1)}_t - X^{(n)}_t \big\rVert \le K\, \Big\lvert \int_s^t \frac{M K^{n-1}\, \lvert r - s \rvert^{n}}{n!}\, dr \Big\rvert

Integrating,

\big\lVert X^{(n+1)}_t - X^{(n)}_t \big\rVert \le \frac{M K^n\, \lvert t - s \rvert^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}

Step 3 — the iterates converge to a solution:
The bounds of Step 2 have a finite sum,

\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{M K^n \delta^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} = \frac{M}{K}\, \big(e^{K\delta} - 1\big)

so by the Weierstrass test, the series

X^{(0)} + \sum_{n \ge 0} \big(X^{(n+1)} - X^{(n)}\big)

converges uniformly on I_\delta, and its partial sums X^{(n)} converge uniformly to a continuous function X with values in B_b, which is closed. The integrand r \mapsto v_r(X_r) is continuous, by the inequality of Step 1 with X in place of X^{(n)}. By the Lipschitz condition,

\lVert v_r(X^{(n)}_r) - v_r(X_r) \rVert \le K\, \lVert X^{(n)}_r - X_r \rVert

which tends to zero uniformly in r, so letting n \to \infty in the definition of X^{(n+1)} gives the integral equation for X. So X solves the ODE with X_s = x on I_\delta.
Step 4 — the solution is unique:
Let Y be a solution on I_\delta with Y_s = x. It stays in B_b. Suppose instead that \lVert Y_{t_1} - x \rVert > b at some t_1 \in I_\delta with t_1 > s, and let \tau = \inf\{t \in [s, t_1]: \lVert Y_t - x \rVert > b\}. By continuity, \lVert Y_\tau - x \rVert = b, \tau < t_1 and Y_t \in B_b for t \in [s, \tau]. On [s, \tau] the velocity of Y is bounded by M, so b = \lVert Y_\tau - x \rVert \le M\, (\tau - s), which gives \tau - s \ge b/M \ge \delta, a contradiction with \tau < t_1 \le s + \delta. The same argument in reversed time covers t_1 < s. Subtracting the integral equations of X and Y and applying the Lipschitz condition, the continuous function w_t = \lVert X_t - Y_t \rVert satisfies

w_t \le K\, \Big\lvert \int_s^t w_r\, dr \Big\rvert

For t \ge s, the function W_t = \int_s^t w_r\, dr then has W'_t = w_t \le K W_t, so \frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{-K(t - s)}\, W_t\big) \le 0. Since W_s = 0, this gives e^{-K(t - s)}\, W_t \le 0, and since W_t \ge 0, W_t = 0, so w_t = W'_t = 0. This is Grönwall’s argument [35], and the same argument in reversed time covers t \le s. So Y = X on I_\delta. \square
On all of [0, 1]:
When v_t(y) is continuous in t and Lipschitz in y with one constant K > 0 for each t \in [0, 1] and y \in \mathbb{R}^d, as in §3.1, no solid sphere is needed. The constant M_x = \max_{t \in [0, 1]} \lVert v_t(x) \rVert is finite, because v_t(x) is continuous in t.
The iterates are then defined for each t \in [0, 1] without a constraint on their values, the case n = 0 of Step 2 holds with M_x in place of M, since \lVert X^{(1)}_t - x \rVert \le \lvert \int_s^t \lVert v_r(x) \rVert\, dr \rvert \le M_x\, \lvert t - s \rvert, and its induction uses only the Lipschitz condition. So Steps 2 and 3 hold on all of [0, 1], with M_x in place of M, \delta = 1 and no solid sphere, and Step 4 holds from its integral inequality on, which uses only the Lipschitz condition.
So for each s \in [0, 1] and x \in \mathbb{R}^d, exactly one solution with X_s = x exists on all of [0, 1], solved forward and backward from s, which is the form of the theorem that §3.1 and §3.1.2 use. \square
Without the uniform Lipschitz condition: The local theorem still applies when v_t(y) is Lipschitz only on each bounded set, but then a solution need not reach t = 1. For d = 1 and the velocity field v_t(y) = y^2, which is Lipschitz on each bounded set but not on \mathbb{R}, the solution with X_0 = 1 is X_t = 1/(1 - t), since \frac{d}{dt}\, (1 - t)^{-1} = (1 - t)^{-2}. It grows without bound as t \to 1, a finite-time blow-up. By Step 4, each solution with X_0 = 1 equals 1/(1 - t) where it exists, so none exists on [0, 1].


A.3 Numerical solvers of ODEs
§3.3 samples a flow model with the Euler method. This section proves the method’s orders and surveys the methods that improve on it, and post #8 develops the solvers designed for diffusion models. Each method approximates the solution of \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_t(X_t) on the grid t_i = i\, \Delta t with \Delta t = 1/n by values x_i, starting from x_0 = X_0. Over one step the solution satisfies

X_{t_{i+1}} = X_{t_i} + \int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}} v_r(X_r)\, dr

and each method approximates this integral from values of the velocity field [69].
Categories:

Time stepping and time parallel: A time-stepping method computes x_{i+1} from earlier values, one step after another, as the Euler method does. A time-parallel method updates its approximation at several times at once. Picard’s iteration of §A.2 is one, since each iterate updates the whole trajectory from the previous one.
One step and multistep: A one-step method computes x_{i+1} from x_i alone. A multistep method also reuses earlier values, as the two-step Adams-Bashforth method [80] does for i \ge 1, with one new evaluation per step and x_1 from a one-step method, 
x_{i+1} = x_i + \Delta t\, \Big(\tfrac{3}{2}\, v_{t_i}(x_i) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, v_{t_{i-1}}(x_{i-1})\Big)

Explicit and implicit: An explicit method computes x_{i+1} from known values. An implicit method also evaluates the velocity field at x_{i+1} and solves an equation for it, as the step x_{i+1} = x_i + \Delta t\, v_{t_{i+1}}(x_{i+1}) does, the implicit counterpart of the Euler step. Implicit methods such as this one remain stable with larger steps on stiff equations, whose solutions have components that decay at very different rates, at the cost of that solve.

The orders of the Euler method:
Assume that v_t(x) is continuously differentiable in (t, x) and Lipschitz in x with a constant K. Then the solution is twice continuously differentiable, with \ddot X_t = \partial_t v_t(X_t) + \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}(X_t)\, v_t(X_t) by the chain rule. This is continuous on [0, 1], so \lVert \ddot X_t \rVert \le C for some constant C.
Local error:
The error of one Euler step started on the solution is \tau_i = X_{t_{i+1}} - X_{t_i} - \Delta t\, v_{t_i}(X_{t_i}). By Taylor’s theorem with the integral remainder, with \dot X_{t_i} = v_{t_i}(X_{t_i}),

\tau_i = \int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}} (t_{i+1} - r)\, \ddot X_r\, dr

Bounding the norm of the integral, with \lVert \ddot X_r \rVert \le C,

\lVert \tau_i \rVert \le C \int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}} (t_{i+1} - r)\, dr

Integrating,

\lVert \tau_i \rVert \le \tfrac{1}{2}\, C\, \Delta t^2

Global error:
The error e_i = x_i - X_{t_i} starts at e_0 = 0. Subtracting X_{t_{i+1}} = X_{t_i} + \Delta t\, v_{t_i}(X_{t_i}) + \tau_i from x_{i+1} = x_i + \Delta t\, v_{t_i}(x_i),

e_{i+1} = e_i + \Delta t\, \big(v_{t_i}(x_i) - v_{t_i}(X_{t_i})\big) - \tau_i

Taking norms, by the triangle inequality,

\lVert e_{i+1} \rVert \le \lVert e_i \rVert + \Delta t\, \big\lVert v_{t_i}(x_i) - v_{t_i}(X_{t_i}) \big\rVert + \lVert \tau_i \rVert

Bounding the middle term by the Lipschitz condition, \lVert v_{t_i}(x_i) - v_{t_i}(X_{t_i}) \rVert \le K\, \lVert e_i \rVert,

\lVert e_{i+1} \rVert \le (1 + K \Delta t)\, \lVert e_i \rVert + \lVert \tau_i \rVert

Bounding the last term by the local bound,

\lVert e_{i+1} \rVert \le (1 + K \Delta t)\, \lVert e_i \rVert + \tfrac{1}{2}\, C\, \Delta t^2

Applying this bound n times from e_0 = 0,

\lVert e_n \rVert \le \tfrac{1}{2}\, C\, \Delta t^2 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (1 + K \Delta t)^j

Summing the geometric series,

\lVert e_n \rVert \le \frac{C\, \Delta t}{2K}\, \big((1 + K \Delta t)^n - 1\big)

Bounding 1 + K \Delta t \le e^{K \Delta t}, with n\, \Delta t = 1,

\lVert e_n \rVert \le \frac{C\, \big(e^{K} - 1\big)}{2K}\, \Delta t

so the global error at t = 1 is of order \Delta t. \square
Methods of higher order: Heun’s method [44] averages the velocity at the start of the step and at an Euler prediction \tilde x_{i+1} of its end,

\tilde x_{i+1} = x_i + \Delta t\, v_{t_i}(x_i), \qquad x_{i+1} = x_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \Delta t\, \big(v_{t_i}(x_i) + v_{t_{i+1}}(\tilde x_{i+1})\big)

Its local error is of order \Delta t^3 and its global error of order \Delta t^2, for two evaluations of the velocity field per step. Karras et al. sample diffusion models with it [18]. The classical Runge-Kutta method of fourth order [45], [76] averages four slopes,

\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= v_{t_i}(x_i), & k_2 &= v_{t_i + \Delta t/2}\big(x_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \Delta t\, k_1\big), \\[4pt]
k_3 &= v_{t_i + \Delta t/2}\big(x_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \Delta t\, k_2\big), & k_4 &= v_{t_{i+1}}\big(x_i + \Delta t\, k_3\big)
\end{aligned}

and then steps by their weighted average,

x_{i+1} = x_i + \tfrac{1}{6}\, \Delta t\, \big(k_1 + 2 k_2 + 2 k_3 + k_4\big)

Its local error is of order \Delta t^5 and its global error of order \Delta t^4, for four evaluations per step. These orders hold for velocity fields that are smooth enough, and the post states them without proof, as Heun [44] and Kutta [45] derived them. An adaptive method, such as the Runge-Kutta pair of Dormand and Prince [77] that §6.4 uses, compares two estimates of different orders at each step and chooses the next step size from their difference.
Picard’s iteration as a solver: With the integral of each iterate replaced by a sum over the grid, one sweep of Picard’s iteration evaluates the velocity field at each grid time on the previous trajectory. These evaluations do not depend on one another, so they can run in parallel. For the iteration with exact integrals, Step 3 of §A.2 bounds the error after \ell sweeps over [0, 1] by the tail \sum_{j \ge \ell} M_x K^j / (j+1)! of a convergent series. Its terms grow until j is about K and shrink only beyond, so a field with a large Lipschitz constant K needs many sweeps.


A.4 Two further derivations of the continuity equation
§4.3 derives Eq. 17 from the flux through a small box, and §4.4 proves its equivalence with the distribution of the ODE’s solution by test functions. This section derives it twice more, following Lai et al. [69]. The first derivation follows one short step of the flow with the change of variables, which connects it to §3.4. The second writes conservation of probability for a region of any shape and closes it with the divergence theorem.
From one step of the flow:
Assume that v_t(x) is twice continuously differentiable with bounded derivatives, that the solution of the ODE has X_t \sim p_t for each t, and that p_t(x) is positive and continuously differentiable in (t, x). By the definition of the flow map (§3.1.2), X_{t + \Delta t} = \phi_{t \to t + \Delta t}(X_t), so p_{t + \Delta t} is the pushforward of p_t under \phi_{t \to t + \Delta t}, which is invertible by Eq. 6. The first steps of §3.4, from the change of variables to its logarithm, applied with \phi_{t \to t + \Delta t} in place of \phi_t, p_t in place of p_0 and the Jacobian J(x) of \phi_{t \to t + \Delta t} in place of J_t(x), give

\log p_{t + \Delta t}\big(\phi_{t \to t + \Delta t}(x)\big) - \log p_t(x) = -\log \det J(x)

Over a short step, by Taylor’s theorem in \Delta t,

\phi_{t \to t + \Delta t}(x) = x + \Delta t\, v_t(x) + O(\Delta t^2), \qquad J(x) = I + \Delta t\, \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}(x) + O(\Delta t^2)

since the derivative of \phi_{t \to t + \Delta t}(x) in \Delta t is the velocity at its current point, and its Jacobian changes at the rate \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\, J (§3.4), both with bounded derivatives. Expanding the log-determinant as in §3.4.1, \log \det J(x) = \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x) + O(\Delta t^2),

\log p_{t + \Delta t}\big(\phi_{t \to t + \Delta t}(x)\big) - \log p_t(x) = -\Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x) + O(\Delta t^2)

Expanding the left side to first order in \Delta t, with the displacement \Delta t\, v_t(x) + O(\Delta t^2) of the point and a remainder o(\Delta t) that vanishes faster than \Delta t,

\Delta t\, \partial_t \log p_t(x) + \Delta t\, v_t(x) \cdot \nabla_x \log p_t(x) + o(\Delta t) = -\Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x) + O(\Delta t^2)

Dividing by \Delta t, with o(1) for a quantity that tends to zero with \Delta t,

\partial_t \log p_t(x) + v_t(x) \cdot \nabla_x \log p_t(x) + o(1) = -(\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x) + O(\Delta t)

Letting \Delta t \to 0,

\partial_t \log p_t(x) + v_t(x) \cdot \nabla_x \log p_t(x) = -(\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x)

Multiplying both sides by p_t(x),

p_t(x)\, \partial_t \log p_t(x) + p_t(x)\, v_t(x) \cdot \nabla_x \log p_t(x) = -p_t(x)\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x)

Writing p_t\, \partial_t \log p_t = \partial_t p_t and p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t = \nabla_x p_t,

\partial_t p_t(x) + v_t(x) \cdot \nabla_x p_t(x) = -p_t(x)\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x)

Adding p_t(x)\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x) to both sides,

\partial_t p_t(x) + v_t(x) \cdot \nabla_x p_t(x) + p_t(x)\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_t)(x) = 0

By the product rule \nabla_x \cdot (p_t\, v_t) = v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t + p_t\, \nabla_x \cdot v_t,

\partial_t p_t(x) + \nabla_x \cdot \big(p_t(x)\, v_t(x)\big) = 0

which is Eq. 17. \square
From a region of any shape:
Let V \subset \mathbb{R}^d be a bounded region with a smooth boundary \partial V, with the outward unit normal n(x) at each x \in \partial V and the surface element dS. Assume that the solution of the ODE has X_t \sim p_t for each t, with p_t(x) continuously differentiable in (t, x) and v_t(x) continuously differentiable in x. The probability in V at time t is P(X_t \in V) = \int_V p_t(x)\, dx.
As in §4.3, the particles that cross a surface element dS in a time \Delta t fill a cylinder with base dS and slant length \lVert v_t \rVert\, \Delta t along v_t. Its height along the normal is \lVert v_t \rVert\, \Delta t \cos\theta = v_t \cdot n\, \Delta t, with \theta the angle between v_t and n, so its volume is v_t \cdot n\, \Delta t\, dS. The probability that crosses dS outward per unit time is therefore p_t\, v_t \cdot n\, dS, negative where the flow enters V. Probability is conserved, so the probability in V changes only by what crosses \partial V,

\frac{d}{dt} \int_V p_t(x)\, dx = -\int_{\partial V} p_t(x)\, v_t(x) \cdot n(x)\, dS

By the divergence theorem [41], [42], [43], \int_{\partial V} F \cdot n\, dS = \int_V \nabla_x \cdot F\, dx for a continuously differentiable field F, here F = p_t\, v_t,

\frac{d}{dt} \int_V p_t(x)\, dx = -\int_V \nabla_x \cdot \big(p_t(x)\, v_t(x)\big)\, dx

Differentiating under the integral on the left, which the continuity of \partial_t p_t on the bounded region allows,

\int_V \partial_t p_t(x)\, dx = -\int_V \nabla_x \cdot \big(p_t(x)\, v_t(x)\big)\, dx

Collecting both integrals on the left,

\int_V \Big(\partial_t p_t(x) + \nabla_x \cdot \big(p_t(x)\, v_t(x)\big)\Big)\, dx = 0

This holds for each region V, and the integrand is continuous. If it were positive at a point, it would be positive on a small solid sphere centered there, and its integral over that sphere would be positive, and the same holds for a negative value. So the integrand is zero at each point, which is Eq. 17. \square

title: FLUX LoRA Influencer-Likeness Research
text:
Question: Which Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) training hyperparameters and inference-time settings give a FLUX.1-dev adapter the best trade-off between identity fidelity and prompt adherence for one subject, and how should that trade-off be measured so the answer transfers? Identity fidelity means the image looks like the subject. Prompt adherence means the image follows the requested scene, style, outfit or product.
Design: The study has three stages on a single subject, a well-known public figure with 30 openly licensed photographs. One evaluation serves all stages. It uses 25 prompts in five buckets of five prompts each, one demand per bucket: identity_only asks for the subject and nothing else, product_conditioning adds a product beside her, style_shift changes the rendering style, outfit_shift specifies clothing, and context_shift places her in a scene with priors of its own. Every checkpoint is scored on two metrics. The first is a commercial face_sim score against held-out reference photographs. The second is an image-prompt cosine for prompt adherence. They are reported separately throughout. The one place they combine is the face_sim × cosine_sim checkpoint-selection rule. Identity is read on two test sets, one sharing events with the training data and one not. A Pilot validated the toolchain and set the checkpoints to evaluate. A Partial Sweep of six configurations at a fixed 2000 steps under a cosine schedule found that configurations converge at widely different step counts. A fixed budget therefore confounds every comparison, so the sweep was stopped and redesigned. The Full Sweep trains each cell to a per-LR cap at constant LR and selects the best checkpoint afterwards from the scored trajectory. It screens learning rate (LR) {5e-5, 1e-4, 2e-4} × rank {4, 8, 16, 32} in full. Dataset size, timestep sampling, LoRA dropout and inference-time adapter scale are tested at one cell.
Findings: Trained to convergence, learning rate × rank stops differentiating: the twelve screen cells sit within 6.9 face_sim points and 0.005 cosine_sim of each other, and no cell wins by a clear margin. Across those cells the identity-versus-prompt-adherence trade-off is real but weak (correlation −0.33), far steeper along training than across converged configurations. Training steps matter more than learning rate. The configuration the Partial Sweep had written off (lr 5e-5, rank 8, transfer face_sim 16) reaches 82 when trained to its own convergence. Twenty images is the working point; thirty may trade face_sim for prompt adherence rather than improve both. Learning rate separates viable from non-viable configurations at a fixed budget, rank separates second within a learning rate, and a face fits in rank 8. Among timestep samplers shift is the clear loser; between sigmoid and linear no winner can be declared, and the switch’s effect changes between ranks. LoRA dropout and scaling the adapter down move along the trade-off rather than to a better one. Nothing supports moving off the near-universal inference-scale default of 1.0, though scaling up buys face_sim at the lowest-cost slope measured. The base model carries no usable prior on this subject (no-adapter identity_only 26 against 97-99 trained). The adapter therefore teaches an identity rather than sharpening one. Same-event references make an easier test, not a memorization trap: they flatter every checkpoint, most mid-learning, and flip the best-checkpoint pick in half the cells. Every headline number is therefore read on the event-clean set.
What this does not establish: Fine rankings within the screen. A mechanism for the identity-versus-transfer gap, which neither regularizer relieved. Every cell ran once, and every reported best-checkpoint score is selected on the metric it reports, so it is an upper bound. The numbers come from one subject, one dataset and one face-recognition model. What transfers is the procedure: held-out multi-reference scoring on two test sets, and per-LR training caps with retrospective checkpoint selection. The values do not.

title: FLUX LoRA Influencer-Likeness Research
text:
2.1 Subject and reference data
All experiments use a single subject, a well-known public figure with an ample supply of openly licensed photographs. The reference data is 30 photos from Wikimedia Commons, restricted to Creative Commons-licensed and public-domain releases. Each photo is face-cropped to 1024×1024 with RetinaFace [1] and deduplicated by perceptual hash. Training uses subsets of this pool of 10, 20 or 30 images. The subsets are recorded as fixed manifests, so every run at a given n trains on the same images. The n=30 subset is the whole pool.
Captions are generated by Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct [2] in the form "ohwx, A woman with ...". They deliberately carry no ethnicity descriptor. The model’s own demographic defaults then fill the gap [3]. This interaction surfaces in the context_shift bucket and is kept as a research observation rather than corrected. The trigger token is ohwx. It is a single rare token of the Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) text encoder, CLIP-L, with a weak prior, so nothing already attached to it competes with the learned identity [4].

title: FLUX LoRA Influencer-Likeness Research
text:
2.2 Hardware
Training and evaluation run on a single L40S (g6e.2xlarge, 48 GB VRAM) at a measured 3.2 s/step. The Pilot Experiment is the exception. It predates the L40S tier and ran on an A10G, 4-bit quantized, at about 8.4 s/step. Its figures are compared only across its own checkpoints, never against a sweep cell.
Eval inference is 4-bit quantized (4-bit NormalFloat, NF4 [5]) for every scored image in both sweeps. This is hardcoded in the eval script and is a property of the inference pipeline, not of the hardware tier. Training is unquantized (quantize: false, verified in the generated configs). Every score therefore describes quantized generations of an unquantized adapter. The quantization is constant across all comparisons, so rankings are unaffected. Absolute values are not what a bf16 pipeline would produce.

title: FLUX LoRA Influencer-Likeness Research
text:
2.3 Eval prompt set
The eval prompt set is 25 prompts in 5 buckets: identity_only, product_conditioning, style_shift, outfit_shift and context_shift. Every prompt pairs the identifier with the class noun “a woman”, which tethers the class prior to the subject [4]. Every prompt also adds explicit face-forward language (“facing the camera”) to keep generated faces inspectable. Without these anchors FLUX-dev tends to produce back-of-head or far-shot compositions on which face_sim is hard to interpret. The context_shift prompts place the subject in scenes that carry priors of their own, such as Alpine hiking or Tokyo at night. Text-to-image models attach demographic attributes from context alone and resist counter-cues in the prompt [3], [6]. The adapter must therefore override that prior to keep the face.

title: FLUX LoRA Influencer-Likeness Research
text:
2.4 Scoring

face_sim: Amazon Web Services (AWS) Rekognition CompareFaces similarity score, 0-100 [7]. It is called with the similarity threshold lowered to 0 so every comparison returns a score. Scores are taken against two test sets (below).
cosine_sim: OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 [8], [9] image-prompt cosine similarity, the prompt-adherence axis. It is largely set by the base model and perturbed by the adapter in proportion to how much identity it has learned. It is stored as clip_cosine per image and mean_cosine per bucket. Raw CLIP cosine_sim values occupy a narrow band of roughly 0 to 0.4 in practice, which is why CLIPScore rescales them by 2.5 [10]. Matched image-prompt pairs here sit near 0.21-0.25, so differences of a few thousandths are meaningful.

The two metrics are reported separately throughout, per bucket. Per-bucket values are arithmetic means over the bucket’s 5 prompts, unweighted and without outlier filtering. They are the axes of the trade-off this project characterizes. The pair is the one the identity-personalization literature uses: a face-embedding similarity on detected face crops for identity and CLIP text-image similarity for prompt adherence [4], [11], with the held-out-reference discipline of [12]. The difference here is that the face embedding comes from a commercial recognition service rather than FaceNet or ArcFace.
Best checkpoints are selected by maximising face_sim × cosine_sim on the transfer buckets, the four buckets other than identity_only. In practice face_sim dominates the product, because its checkpoint-to-checkpoint spread is far larger than cosine_sim’s. cosine_sim breaks ties on face_sim plateaus.

2.4.1 The two test sets
A face_sim score conflates two quantities. One is whether the generated face is the subject’s. The other is whether the generated image happens to share lighting, styling and framing with the reference photograph. One number cannot separate them. Identity is therefore scored against two test sets that differ in one property: whether the reference shares an event with the training data.



Table 1: The two test sets.

Both sets were built by the same pipeline. Rekognition CompareFaces was run against three training anchors, all three had to match, the face box had to be at least 200 px, and the crop is 1024x1024 at 2.2x the box. Test set 1 was cut from raw images rejected during dataset preparation, mostly multi-person shots. The subject was identified against known-good training images and cropped out. Test set 2 was fetched fresh under Creative Commons licences, because the processed pool is exactly 30 images and fully consumed at n=30. Reusing a training image for evaluation inflates estimates [12]. Neither set therefore enters any training subset.
Admission to either set used the same CompareFaces model that scores the generations. Absolute scores therefore lean high relative to an unfiltered test set. The filter applies to both sets equally, so between-set gaps and between-checkpoint comparisons are less affected than absolute levels.
Per generated image, Rekognition CompareFaces is called once per reference and the mean across references is the score. This is the multiple-source-image comparison the API reference itself recommends against false negatives [7]. Per-reference scores are stored per image, so the aggregation rule can change without re-calling the API. Every run retains its generated images, so scoring a second set costs Rekognition calls only.
Which is canonical: Test set 2, the harder set, is the headline number throughout. A score against it is the more conservative claim. Test set 1 is reported alongside it wherever the gap between the two is informative.

title: FLUX LoRA Influencer-Likeness Research
text:
4.1 Question
The Pilot asks two questions. After how many training steps does identity binding complete? How many checkpoints does each adapter need evaluated?
The planned sweep has 14 configurations. Evaluating two checkpoints per configuration instead of four would halve its eval cost, provided two are informationally sufficient.

Each of the 4 saved checkpoints was run through the standard eval (Eval prompt set, Scoring) at LoRA scale 1.0 with no additional conditioning.

4.4 Analysis

4.4.1 Identity binding largely completes by step 1000






Figure 2: The same trajectories as gains per interval: nearly all of the binding lands in the first interval in every bucket.



Identity binding lands between step 500 and step 1000. In the three buckets the adapter governs most directly (identity_only, product_conditioning, style_shift) the gain in that interval is 41–61 points. Only 4.7–6.2 more points arrive by step 2000 (Figure 1). Step 500 is not a viable checkpoint. It detects a face (face_detected_rate = 1.0 throughout), but not the subject’s.


4.4.2 Prompt adherence moves little at this configuration






Figure 3: The same intervals for cosine_sim. The first interval is the largest and mixed in sign; after binding no bucket changes by more than 0.0016.



After binding (1000–2000) cosine_sim changes by at most 0.0016 per bucket, with mixed signs. The largest face_sim gain, context_shift’s +7.5, comes with cosine_sim rising at +0.00017 cosine/face, not a trade-off at all. The flatness belongs to the configuration, not to the metric. Little additional identity is learned after step 1000, so prompt adherence barely changes.


4.4.3 context_shift remains the weakest bucket at every checkpoint
context_shift is the lowest bucket at every checkpoint (Figure 1). An example prompt is “ohwx, a woman, smiling at the camera while hiking in the Swiss Alps”. The scene prior is what the bucket was designed to probe (Eval prompt set). context_shift also shows the largest 1000→2000 gain, +7.5. For prior-loaded prompts the adapter keeps recovering identity late in training.


4.4.4 Step 1500 is redundant
Step 1500 adds little. It sits between 1000 and 2000 on nearly every metric and much closer to 2000. On test set 2 the 1500→2000 face_sim gain is −0.1 to +2.4, against +3.4 to +6.3 for 1000→1500. Evaluating it would add a third checkpoint’s worth of eval cost for little beyond what 1000 and 2000 already give.
